articles.title: More than 400k Russians killed fighting in Ukraine war, leaked data suggests
articles.body:
More than 400,000 Russians have been killed fighting in Ukraine since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion nearly five years ago, according to data leaked from the state statistics agency, Rosstat.
The information, obtained by the Belarusian opposition-linked hacker group Cyber Partisans and the Ukrainian hacking collective Silent Crow, contains more than 11m death certificates, including details of the deceased’s age, place of residence and location of death.
It was later shared with the Guardian and a small group of other media outlets.
According to the data, 412,576 death certificates explicitly linked the fatalities to the war, either through official cause-of-death codes or written references to combat and military operations.
The figures underscore the staggering human toll of Russia’s war against Ukraine, with no end in sight despite a fresh round of peace talks scheduled to take place in Abu Dhabi this week.
The two hacking groups announced the breach on 1 November and published the data over the weekend. Rosstat confirmed it had been hacked but denied that any sensitive information had been obtained.
The dataset offers an unprecedentedly detailed picture of Russia’s wartime losses, which Moscow has sought to conceal. The Russian authorities have not published a death toll since the early months of the invasion, and information about military casualties is treated as a state secret.
The Guardian could not independently verify the authenticity of the entire dataset. However, the figures are broadly consistent with other estimates of Russian losses. British intelligence in September estimated that about 500,000 Russian soldiers had been killed since the start of the invasion.
Separately, the independent Russian outlet Mediazona has identified by name nearly 286,000 Russian military personnel killed in Ukraine, drawing on official records, social media obituaries and photographs of gravestones. The outlet estimates the true toll is closer to half a million.
“The data looks authentic, and it’s very rich,” said Janis Kluge, the head of the Russia and Eurasia division at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs.
“This is the biggest leak of data when it comes to Russian casualties,” added Kluge, who has studied Russian war statistics extensively.
The dataset is likely to underestimate the true death toll. Some soldiers remain missing, while others have never been identified.
Kluge also pointed to a significant delay between deaths occurring and being entered into official records, which he said typically took about six months.
“We are probably at this time closer to 500,000 killed Russian soldiers than 400,000,” he said.
The figures also reveal the unequal burden of the war across Russia, with poorer and more remote regions sustaining disproportionately heavy losses.
In Buryatia, Tuva and Zabaykalsky Krai, three regions in eastern Russia, war-related fatalities accounted for about a third of all deaths among men aged 18 to 49 between the start of the invasion and mid-2024. In Moscow and St Petersburg, the equivalent figure was about 10%.
There was also a sharp rise in Russian battlefield deaths as the war dragged on, with some of the deadliest months coming in late 2024 and 2025.
Kluge, who has been analysing the data, said the number of soldiers killed in several months during that period exceeded 15,000, equivalent to roughly 500 a day.
“In late 2024 and in 2025, you see that the numbers in many months are above 15,000 per month, and that’s higher than I think most estimates were,” Kluge said. “That’s 500 a day, above 500 a day. Certainly shocking.”
The scale of the losses is staggering by any measure and unprecedented in Russia’s modern history.
In less than five years, Russian military deaths in Ukraine are estimated to have exceeded the combined death toll from all Soviet and Russian wars between the end of the second world war and the start of the full-scale invasion more than eightfold. The figure also exceeds the number of US military personnel who died during the second world war.
Rather than push Moscow towards a settlement, the scale of the losses is likely to harden Vladimir Putin’s resolve, according to a person familiar with the Russian president’s thinking.
“Putin understands these numbers, and for him to now settle for anything less than everything he wants would feel like a betrayal of himself and the people,” the person said.
Senior Russian and Ukrainian negotiators are due to meet in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday for the first US-brokered peace talks between them in nine months.
Previous negotiations have made little progress towards ending the war, with Moscow demanding that Ukraine withdraw from the parts of the Donbas region it still controls.
Neither Putin nor his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, will attend the talks. Instead, both countries will send senior delegations, with Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner also expected to take part.
In a post on X, Witkoff said the negotiations would focus on “post-war security arrangement, de-escalation” and humanitarian issues.
European governments have expressed concern that the talks could extend beyond Ukraine to broader questions of European security, including Moscow’s longstanding demands for a reduction of Nato’s military presence in countries bordering Russia.
France’s foreign minister said Paris would participate in the negotiations but the Kremlin subsequently denied that France would be represented.

articles.title: France blames Iran for mass-hacks targeting freezers in grocery stores and blood banks
articles.body:
The French government has formally blamed Iran for launching cyberattacks that targeted thousands of internet-connected industrial refrigerated and freezer units across the country and broader Europe.
This is the latest in a string of destructive cyberattacks attributed to Iran this year, following a spate of hacks targeting U.S. water providers and other online intrusions that caused mass-disruption to U.S. medical device maker Stryker and others.
The U.S. government linked the attacks to pro-Iranian hacktivists who are working for Tehran, likely in response to the U.S./Israel-led war against Iran which killed its supreme leader in February.
Two recent waves of cyberattacks throughout October and into November saw hackers remotely break into web-based controllers that manage fleets of industrial cold and chilling units at grocery stores and retail supermarkets, and raise the temperatures to spoil food and destroy goods. Medical blood banks were also hacked but the attacks were stopped before any blood was spoiled, according to the French Blood Establishment.
Security researchers have since warned that the web-based controllers are vulnerable to remote hacks, with some of the affected models made by Danish company Danfoss no longer receiving security fixes.
In a statement given to reporters in Paris on Monday, French foreign minister Jean-Noël Barrot said: “I am able to confirm that responsibility for this act lies with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps,” referring to Iran’s military and hackers.
“This was an attack of unprecedented scale and aggression; it represents the first large-scale act of sabotage on our national territory and constitutes a major assault on the nation’s interests and the security of the French people,” said Barrot, adding that the hacks will “not go without consequences.”
The French government has summoned Iran’s ambassador. Reuters first reported France’s attribution to Iran, citing sources ahead of the foreign minister’s remarks. The French government said it would also issue European-wide sanctions against those who carried out the hacks. Barrot said that the matter was now in the hands of the French justice system.
A spokesperson for Iran’s consulate in New York did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The U.S. government is also reportedly looking into whether freezer units on military bases were hacked, following reports of similar outages and disruption earlier this year. U.S. officials have reportedly also linked the freezer-related cyberattack to Iran, but the intelligence community has not yet made a formal or public attribution.

articles.title: Iran was behind cyber-attack on French supermarket freezers, Paris says
articles.body:
France has said Iran was responsible for a massive cyber-attack on supermarket freezers and chiller cabinets that was described by its foreign minister as being an act of “unprecedented scale and unprecedented aggression”.
Jean-Noël Barrot said “Europe-wide sanctions” would be imposed against those responsible, adding that the attacks – which took control of digital thermostats to push temperatures up to above 50C – constituted “a major violation of the nation’s interests”.
At a press briefing during the G7 summit in Paris, he said: “Thanks to the remarkable efforts of government agencies, I am able to confirm that the Islamic Republic of Iran’s Revolutionary Guards are responsible for this attack.”
He said the Iranian ambassador had been summoned “to protest in the strongest possible terms against this extremely serious act.”
Swathes of French supermarkets were hit in the cyber-attacks on 11 and 12 October. Some were forced to throw away entire inventories of perishable food.
Similar incidents have been reported since, including on supermarket fridges in other European countries last week and on a French blood bank.
The Paris public prosecutor, Laure Beccuau, said on Monday that specialist investigators and government agencies had identified “a modus operandi” characteristic of the Iranian group Shahid Kaveh, a cyber warfare unit linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC).
This included “the use of Farsi and IP addresses traced back to devices located in Iran”, she said.
Beccuau said her office had opened an investigation against the head of Shahid Kaveh, his deputies and “others who will be identified” on charges of “fraudulent attacks on an automated data processing system committed as part of an organised crime ring and of causing damage dangerous to persons”.
She said the offences were “aggravated by the fact they were committed to serve a foreign power – in this case Iran”.
Gérôme Billois, a partner at the cybersecurity and technology company Wavestone, said Shahid Kaveh had been active since 2020 and was known to have carried out cyber-attacks mostly on water distribution systems in the US.
“Two countries are known for this kind of attack: Iran and Russia. Given that recent cyber-attacks on supermarkets and the blood bank in France concerned freezers it is reasonable to think Iran is directly linked to both,” he said,
“For the moment they are attacking easy equipment but as a state group that has the means, the determination and the time, we should be prepared to see attacks on other systems like water or electricity.”
During the attack last month, hackers remotely overrode the temperature setting on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets in as many as 700 supermarkets and shops across France, pushing them from as low as -27C (-16.6F) to well over 50C (122F) in some cases.
Thousands of tons of food had to be dumped and in some stores the extreme temperature rise sparked fires, triggering sprinklers and water damage.
Hackers last week accessed control systems at cold stores stocking blood products. The French blood service (EFS) said temperature and defrosting thresholds and been raised to “very high level” but that technicians had been alerted by alarm systems allowing them to disconnect the cold stores before the products were destroyed. It is not clear whether the two attacks are linked.
The following day retailers in 11 European countries including the UK, Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported problems with refrigeration systems.
A regional branch of France’s Crédit Mutuel bank also reported losing more than €100m in a cyber-attack on Friday. The bank said it had recuperated some of the money.
The European Commission did not immediately comment on the French foreign minister’s statement. Kaja Kallas, the head of foreign affairs for the EU said: “We have the foreign affairs council next Monday, so we will have the opportunity to discuss this. These cyber incidents occurring in Europe, if attributed [to Iran], also call for a strong response on our part.”
In a significant decision this year, the EU designated the IRGC a terrorist organisation, ending years of division over the issue. The designation became possible after France dropped its long-held opposition, having previously feared it would damage diplomatic channels and the interests of French nationals in Iran.

articles.title: Fossil CO2 emissions decrease by 0.4% in 2026
articles.body:
Fossil CO2 emissions decrease in 2026
Global carbon emissions from fossil fuels are projected to decrease by 0.4% in 2026 – driven by expansion of solar and wind power and the Iran conflict – according to new research by the Global Carbon Project.
The 2026 Global Carbon Budget projects 38.2 billion tonnes of fossil carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions this year.
Emissions from oil are projected to decrease by 1.9% – likely a short-term response to the energy shock triggered by the Iran conflict.
While global energy demand continues to rise, two thirds of the increase is being met by increased solar and wind power and electric vehicles.
However, the report – published alongside a new paper in the journal Nature Climate Change – finds that clean energy growth is not yet fast enough for a durable decline in global fossil CO2 emissions.
With emissions from land-use change (such as deforestation) projected to increase slightly this year, total CO2 emissions are projected to be 43.3 billion tonnes in 2026 – up from 42.8 billion tonnes last year.
The remaining carbon budget (the amount of CO2 that can be emitted before warming reaches 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels) is now 150 billion tonnes – equivalent to less than four years of emissions at the current rate.
With CO2 still rapidly accumulating in the atmosphere, the dangerous impacts of climate change continue to increase.
The report also assesses natural “sinks” (absorption of CO2 by land and ocean). It finds that the land sink returned to former levels after a severe weakening during the 2023-24 El Niño weather pattern.
However, the powerful 2026 El Niño is expected to have a significant impact in the coming year.
The research team included the University of Exeter, the University of East Anglia (UEA), CICERO Center for International Climate Research, Ludwig-Maximilian-University Munich (LMU), Alfred-Wegener-Institut and more than 90 other institutions around the world.
“A decline in fossil CO2 emissions is encouraging, but a reduction driven partly by geopolitical shocks is not a sustainable climate solution,” said Professor Pierre Friedlingstein, director of the Global Carbon Budget Office at the University of Exeter, who led the study.
“The long-term answer remains the rapid deployment of clean energy technologies. While renewables and electric vehicles are increasingly offsetting growth in energy demand, further acceleration is needed if global emissions are to peak and enter a sustained decline.”
Professor Corinne Le Quéré, Royal Society Research Professor at UEA’s School of Environmental Sciences – who led the new analysis published in Nature Climate Change – said: “Clean technologies are making a real difference in reducing global emissions. Solar and wind power and electric vehicles are expanding rapidly, led by China. Countries on every continent are decreasing their emissions while growing their economies. A further acceleration could turn the tide on global emissions within a few years.”
Glen Peters, Research Professor at the CICERO Center for International Climate Research, said: “A drop in emissions in one year is not a peak unless it is driven by structural change. Accelerated deployment of solar, wind, batteries, and electric vehicles are pushing emissions down in dozens of countries, and slowing emissions growth in many more, but the changes are not sufficient to lock in a peak in global emissions”.
Professor Julia Pongratz, at LMU’s Department of Geography, said: “Alongside reducing emissions, we need to scale up CO2 removal to reach greenhouse gas neutrality. Afforestation and reforestation already remove substantial amounts of CO2, but these gains are still more than offset by emissions from deforestation, and novel carbon removal remains very limited. We need to act on all these fronts now.”
Other key findings from the 2026 Global Carbon Budget include:
- China’s emissions in 2026 are projected to decrease by 0.9%, following two
years of low emissions growth. In addition to a strong decrease in oil emissions,
coal emissions rose slightly (0.3%) and electricity generation from renewables
continues to grow strongly.
- While China produces 32% of global fossil emissions, it is also the country
most active in deploying clean technologies and increasing carbon sinks
through reforestation. Half of the global emissions avoided due to renewable
energy and electric vehicles are in China, which also has the largest carbon
uptake through reforestation and afforestation (new forests).
- The USA’s emissions are projected to decrease by 1.3%, mainly due to a
decrease in coal emissions (which spiked last year due to high natural gas prices
and cold weather).
- India’s emissions are projected to increase by 4.4% – higher than the 3.5%
average annual growth over the last decade.
- European Union emissions are projected to decrease by 1.5%.
- Japan’s emissions are projected to decrease by 1%.
- Emissions for the rest of the world are projected to decrease by 0.7%. The
largest component of the decline is in oil, likely driven by increased prices and
global supply constraints.
- Projected 2026 emissions for the different fossil fuels are: oil down 1.9%,
natural gas down 0.3%, coal up 0.6%.
- Emissions from international aviation and international shipping are both
projected to decrease by 1%. Aviation’s decline is partly due to reduced activity
in the Middle East.
- Global CO2 emissions from land-use change have decreased in the past decade
but are projected to rise this year to 5.1 billion tonnes. This is driven by an
increase in emissions from peat fires (almost entirely ignited by human
activities) and forest degradation in Southeast Asia, associated with drier
conditions linked to the onset of El Niño conditions.
- Total CO2 emissions – the sum of fossil and land-use change emissions – have
grown more slowly in the past decade (0.3% per year), compared to the previous
decade (1.7% per year).
- Emissions from permanent deforestation remain high at around 3.8 billion
tonnes of CO2 per year over 2016-25. Permanent removals through
reforestation and afforestation offset around half of the permanent
deforestation emissions.
- The largest carbon uptake through re/afforestation occurs in China, the EU27
and the USA, with combined removals 0.8 billion tonnes CO2 per year.
Substantial uptake through re/afforestation also occurs in other regions such as
Brazil, Russia and Indonesia – but here it is outweighed by emissions from
deforestation.
- Current levels of novel Carbon Dioxide Removal (excluding conventional
means such as reforestation) currently offset less than 30 minutes of annual
fossil CO2 emissions.
- The concentration of CO2 in the atmosphere is set to reach 427.7 ppm in 2026,
54% above pre-industrial levels.
The analysis published in Nature Climate Change found:
- With global energy demand growing, new emissions can be prevented (or
“offset”) by simultaneous growth in clean energy. The paper makes a projection
from now to the end of 2028, finding that 64-79% of emissions from new demand
will be offset by new solar and wind power and electric vehicles.
- The number of countries reducing their emissions while growing their economies
is clearly increasing: 59 countries emitted less in 2025 than before the COVID-19
pandemic in 2019, while their economies grew.
- Even in countries where total emissions increased over the 2019-25 period,
growth in emissions has slowed in all regions including in China, India and other
emerging economies.
- The effect of electric vehicles is growing rapidly but remains small because the
vehicle stock takes time to be replaced, with only about 10% of the car fleet
electrified in 2025 (or 6% excluding hybrids).
- Emissions avoided by solar and wind power rose from 0.28 billion tonnes in
2010 to 4.1 billion tonnes in 2025, and a projected 4.6 billion tonnes in 2026.
- The authors conclude that: “If further acceleration of clean technology
deployment can be supported through time, a sustained peak and decline in
global CO2 emissions could be a few years away.”
The Global Carbon Budget report, produced by an international team of more than 140
scientists, provides an annual, peer-reviewed update, building on established
methodologies in a fully transparent manner.
The 2026 edition (the 21st annual report) is published in the journal Earth System
Science Data on November 10 as a pre-print, and later as a peer-reviewed paper.
The Nature Climate Change paper is entitled: “A further acceleration of clean energy is
needed for global CO2 emissions to peak and decline.”

articles.title: What could China get from Jensen Huang?
articles.body:
It’s difficult to overstate Nvidia’s power in today’s AI landscape. The company’s chips are the bedrock upon which advanced AI technology in the US is being built, and demand has consistently outpaced supply for years. Nvidia has also been an influential investor in a wide range of up-and-coming AI companies in recent years, with about $99 billion worth of equity investments in frontier AI labs, neoclouds, infrastructure companies, and more. Its chief executive has even become close with President Donald Trump.
What could China get from Jensen Huang?
The Nvidia CEO has been in a unique position to influence AI export controls.
What could China get from Jensen Huang?
The Nvidia CEO has been in a unique position to influence AI export controls.
This is why, as both cofounder and longtime CEO of Nvidia, Jensen Huang would be a valuable target for a foreign adversary with sights on the American AI industry.
Huang is in hot water after news broke of his extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang (no relation to Jensen) is an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud provider and a top Nvidia customer. Questions are swirling around how the affair may have influenced Huang’s reported push to sell advanced chips to China — and potentially even influenced President Trump’s own decisions surrounding AI export controls.
Jensen Huang would be a valuable target for a foreign adversary with sights on the American AI industry
US officials believe the Megaspeed executive is a foreign intelligence asset that has funneled information straight to the Chinese government, per The New York Times — in particular, officials reportedly believe that Megaspeed is related to a convoluted web of Chinese companies working together to access chips in bulk and perhaps even illegally get some of those chips into China. Alibaba is reportedly one of Megaspeed’s top customers.
“It’s not entirely surprising that the CEO of arguably one of the most important, if not the most important, AI chip companies is the target of some sort of intelligence-gathering from countries like China,” Hanna Dohmen, a senior research analyst at CSET, said in an interview with The Verge, adding that an alleged spy would potentially be interested in “better understanding what the US government is thinking on export controls,” as well as gathering information on Huang’s conversations with the Trump administration, attempting to influence policy, and gathering information on trade secrets like “who’s buying Nvidia’s chips, who’s getting them first, what’s coming next in terms of AI chips.”
Megaspeed’s sister company, headquartered in Malaysia, spent $4.8 billion or more on Nvidia chips and technology between June 2024 and February 2026, the Times reported, citing trade records from trade platform ImportGenius. The transaction sizes were outside the norm for a small company, particularly when Nvidia chips are so difficult to get.
”Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job”
Nvidia spokespeople had said Huang’s relationship with the Megaspeed executive was strictly business. Their interactions were described as “not unusual or unexpected” in statements to the press. Nvidia’s line was, “Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job.”
But at some point, their relationship became personal. In June 2024, just before Megaspeed became an Nvidia customer, photos show the two with other AI executives at a bar in Taipei after a local trade show; the following year, they reportedly had a business dinner in Taipei with others as well. But in private, according to US officials cited by the Times, the two’s relationship raised alarm bells for the US government — they had reportedly been surveilling the Megaspeed executive for months, if not longer, and that’s how it came out that she was in close contact with Huang.
The revelation is particularly concerning because of Huang’s lobbying role. He’d been trying to convince the Trump administration and Congress to loosen export controls for sending advanced semiconductors to China, ostensibly so that Nvidia could sell more chips. We now know this was happening around the same time that Huang was spotted at the Taiwan dinner with Alice Huang in May 2025, according to Culper Research, which shorted Nvidia’s stock earlier this year. That dinner occurred shortly after Nvidia had shared the Trump administration’s new restrictions on its China-specific H20 chips in April.
Just a couple months after the Taiwan dinner, Huang reportedly met with Trump in the Oval Office in July 2025 to plead his case for loosening export restrictions on Nvidia’s advanced semiconductors. Days later, the company announced that the administration had blessed sales of its H20 chips to China. Huang had argued that spreading American chips to China would help establish US technology as the standard, rather than allowing for Chinese chips to grow, according to The New York Times. After setbacks earlier in the second Trump term in export policy to China, Huang began speaking with then-White House AI czar David Sacks in 2025, who became the key advocate for Nvidia’s view that selling American chips to China would be beneficial, the Times reported.
By October 2025, Huang was lobbying Trump to allow Nvidia to sell more advanced chips to China, ahead of Trump’s meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, per the Times; but after Trump considered the proposal, he ultimately decided not to move forward. (That same month, Huang hired an external PR firm known for handling sex scandals, Wired reported.)
Months later, in December 2025, Trump changed course slightly, allowing Nvidia to sell H20 chips to a greenlit list of “approved customers” in China, with the US government taking a 25 percent cut of those sales. The same rules would apply to other US chipmakers, he wrote on Truth Social at the time.
“It is in Nvidia’s interest and in Jensen Huang’s interest to lobby for looser export control restrictions”
CSET’s Dohmen said that during the past two years, the US has seen a light loosening of AI export control regulations under the Trump administration, driven partly by Huang’s own lobbying. But it’s important to note, she said, that “even without any kind of intelligence operations from the Chinese side, it is in Nvidia’s interest and in Jensen Huang’s interest to lobby for looser export control restrictions.” Any restrictions by definition stifle Nvidia’s business expansion and cut off potential sales to help it grow its already stunning market cap — which is currently about $4.25 trillion, second only to Apple.
Huang’s relationship with Trump is also particularly relevant here. The president lavished praise on Huang during a speech last year, saying that until recently, he hadn’t even heard of Nvidia, and then he wanted to break it up. But after meeting Huang, he said, he understood why it would be difficult to re-create the company he’d built. More recently, Huang put Trump on speakerphone when the president called him during an appearance onstage at the All-In Summit, publicly displaying his close access to the Oval Office.
This past spring, a classified memo — the writing of which was overseen by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, per the Times — circulated among Trump administration officials ahead of the president’s trip to China in May, warning of the Megaspeed executive’s alleged involvement in surveillance on behalf of China’s Ministry of State Security. Her reported goal was to learn about advanced AI chips in the US and try to influence them being made available to China on a large scale. Asked if he had known about the memo reviewed by Rubio at a press briefing on Monday, Trump said, “I’d certainly check with the intelligence people. It could have been mentioned. Certainly it didn’t make much of an impact on me.” Earlier in the briefing, he said he was unaware of the alleged spy connection ahead of his trip to China.
Huang was initially left off the list of executives joining Trump on the trip, but the president later asked him to join. Trump had been briefed about a year ago that US intelligence believed the Megaspeed executive to be a China intelligence operative, according to the Times, and that she had a close relationship with a US citizen who turned out to be Nvidia’s CEO. At the time, he reportedly chose not to take action.
So far, the allegations haven’t affected Huang’s future at Nvidia. He’ll continue to lead the company during the investigation. Trump has also stood by him since news broke of the affair, telling reporters this past weekend, “I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it.”
Nvidia said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised”
On Sunday, Huang wrote an internal memo to Nvidia employees — some of which are his own family members — writing, “I owe my family and all of you an apology. I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” He then addressed Nvidia’s board, partners, and shareholders, adding that he is “fully committed” to leading the company and “will work to earn back your confidence.” This weekend, Nvidia’s board of directors launched an independent investigation into the national security allegations. Huang will not have control over the participants in the investigation, and Nvidia said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.”
Morningstar senior equity analyst Brian Colello wrote in a note on Monday that Morningstar “can’t rule out the investigation fading away and Nvidia returning to business as usual,” particularly since Huang is the “only CEO the company has ever known.” There’s also the fact that Huang’s Nvidia struck deals in August with six large financial institutions to provide more than $500 billion in financing for the buildout of AI data centers and other infrastructure, and as the US-China AI race intensifies, those are high-stakes agreements.
“It’s unclear to us what these partnerships and financing deals would look like with a different Nvidia CEO,” Colello wrote. “Costs of capital may rise for future investments if perhaps the most prominent CEO in the AI landscape is no longer orchestrating such deals.” Morningstar still maintained a very high uncertainty rating for the company, with Colello writing that it’s possible US approval of Nvidia to sell H20 chips to China will be revoked and that the company could ostensibly be sanctioned as well.
Trump told reporters on Sunday that Huang should remain CEO of Nvidia and that he would “certainly take him” on his next trip to China. “I haven’t heard he’s done anything wrong,” Trump told reporters. “He dealt with somebody, but you know, so does everybody else.”

articles.title: TPUs
articles.body:
Our newest TPUs: 8tx and 8i Max, built for the agentic era
We first designed TPUs more than a decade ago motivated by Google’s internal demands, including voice recognition and language translation. Eight generations of TPUs later, the use cases have exploded, covering: i) training and serving our own Gemini models, ii) agentic workloads, iii) delivering services to Google Cloud customers on our cloud infrastructure, and most recently, iv) allowing customers to deploy TPUs directly into their own data centers. TPUs are now a rapidly growing business with nearly 100 customers — including frontier labs, trading firms, retailers, universities, and more.
At Google Cloud Next in April, we introduced two new specialized TPUs in the same generation — 8t for large-scale training and 8i for real-time reasoning. TPU 8t and 8i offer up to 2.7 times better training performance and 80% better inference price performance, respectively, versus our previous generation of TPUs.
Today, we’re taking that a step further, expanding our eighth-generation TPU portfolio with two additional systems: TPU 8i Max for massive context windows and the highest compute density per rack, and TPU 8tx for secure and confidential inference. This is the first time we have introduced four TPU systems in a single year.
Our expanded eighth-generation TPU portfolio: TPU 8t, TPU 8i, TPU 8tx, and TPU 8i Max.
While we’ve always co-designed our TPUs in partnership with Google DeepMind, we’re now increasingly getting feedback from external organizations on their specific needs. With computing moving from human to agent scale, businesses are asking for accelerators that can reason across AI models’ massive context windows. In addition, some highly regulated customers are asking for specialized encryption capabilities for unique workloads.
The new TPU systems we are announcing today address this new reality. Coupled with our recent PyTorch announcements, our aim is to make TPUs more easily accessible to every developer and Cloud customer. By combining modular custom silicon with an open and easy-to-use software stack, we can deliver new hardware and system configurations at the pace of the AI industry.
Building the computer around the chip
Today, we’re announcing two new TPU systems — and there’s an important difference between a new chip and a new system.
Designing a new chip means laying out billions of microscopic transistors on a silicon wafer in a multi-year process bound by the laws of physics and a complex, long-duration manufacturing lifecycle. A system, on the other hand, is about how we bring together the compute, networking, and storage around the chip. This can include how they are packaged with the chips, to quickly meet emerging customer needs and research use cases.
When we built our very first TPU more than a decade ago, we knew AI software would evolve much faster than silicon manufacturing ever could. So we made a foundational bet on system balance and modularity, architecting our TPUs as building blocks as part of our AI Hypercomputer, so engineers could rapidly adjust packaging, high-speed memory, optical networking, and security around them. That approach allows us to deliver specialized supercomputers in a matter of months rather than years.
Specializing for secure, high-context AI
Each system in our eighth-generation TPU portfolio targets a distinct part of the AI lifecycle.
TPU 8t and TPU 8i established the baseline for this generation of chips:
- TPU 8t was designed to be a training powerhouse for massive foundation models with maximum “goodput” — or the useful intelligence delivered per watt of energy used.
- TPU 8i is the reasoning engine, designed to break the memory wall, cutting inter-chip communication delays by up to half.
Now, as enterprises bring autonomous agents into production, we have created two new configurations of these foundational systems to solve two urgent new challenges: hardware-level data security and million-token context scale.
TPU 8tx
TPU 8tx, our third eighth-generation system, is optimized for secure and confidential inference and is also great for small-scale training. It’s built for regulated enterprises and governments running frontier or proprietary models and autonomous agents alongside their most sensitive data.
Normally, data is encrypted when stored or sent over a network, but has to be unlocked in memory while a computer processes it. Built on the same silicon as TPU 8t and paired with 5th Generation AMD EPYC CPU hosts, TPU 8tx builds security directly into the hardware layer, keeping sensitive data and model weights protected and isolated even while in active use. And by adopting the same low-latency Boardfly network we created for real-time reasoning, TPU 8tx keeps multi-step agents moving, delivering up to 2x lower latency compared to TPU 8t with a near-zero performance penalty.
Pairing training-grade compute with a fast inference network also means organizations can simultaneously run and customize their models on a single system. TPU 8tx enables teams to fine-tune models using their private data, distill large models into smaller ones, and train their agents through reinforcement learning, all without needing to migrate sensitive data between separate clusters.
Designed for sensitive enterprise workloads, TPU 8tx provides hardware-level confidential compute for private fine-tuning and secure agent execution.
TPU 8i Max
Our fourth system, TPU 8i Max, is built for a different problem: the memory wall.
When dozens of AI agents work together across an entire software codebase or hours of video at once, memory bandwidth quickly becomes the bottleneck. So we took two low-latency TPU 8i chips and combined them onto a single package.
TPU 8i Max scales compute and memory in lockstep, delivering double the compute, double the SRAM and double the HBM bandwidth of TPU 8i, so processors remain equipped with essential data and so that large workloads do not stall. Further, because TPU 8i Max fits twice the silicon within the existing rack footprint, data centers can deploy significantly more computing power per square foot and per watt.
The dual-chip TPU 8i Max system, engineered for massive context windows and maximum compute density.
While flexible across workloads, together the four systems in our eighth-generation TPUs give customers a purpose-built accelerator for every stage of the agentic lifecycle. TPU 8t for scale-up training, TPU 8i for low-latency reasoning, TPU 8tx for confidential computing, and TPU 8i Max for massive context windows and the highest compute density per rack.
Opening up TPUs to every developer
When we launched the first TPU more than a decade ago, there were only a handful of companies running workloads that needed the processing power of a TPU. The use cases were specialized, so engineers would use optimized frameworks and hand-tuned code.
Over the years, as AI has advanced, more and more companies began using accelerators. Now, AI adoption is at a point where TPUs are excellent for a wide range of companies and use cases, and as a result, we’ve been working systematically to remove barriers to adoption so that TPUs are as easy-to-use as general-purpose hardware.
This investment comes together today across these key areas:
- Opening up TPU development to every PyTorch developer; no code rewrites needed: Last month, we open-sourced TorchTPU, so PyTorch code and Hugging Face models now run natively on TPUs, alongside out-of-the-box TPU backends for leading open-source inference engines like vLLM and SGLang. And to make hardware optimization effortless, our new open-source TPU agent suite (now in preview) plugs directly into coding tools like Claude Code, Cursor, and Google Antigravity to automate TPU onboarding in minutes, diagnose bottlenecks, and autotune custom kernels using plain language. For production deployments, our new open-source XLA Serving Engine lets you train models in Python and serve them directly in a low-latency C++ runtime across TPUs, GPUs, and CPUs.
- Industry-leading production performance on InferenceX and AgentX benchmarks:
In production, what really matters is outcomes on real AI workloads rather than theoretical peak chip speeds. On industry-standard InferenceX and AgentX benchmarks, which test realistic agentic coding and long-context work, our native vLLM-TorchTPU software stack on TPUs achieved state-of-the-art price-performance marks. New evaluations demonstrate these advantages extend across a wide range of frontier open models and open-source serving stacks while maintaining high model accuracy. Upcoming software optimizations on this same hardware will drive those results even further.
- Eliminating idle compute waste for autonomous agents: Because AI agents are stateful, they frequently pause for seconds or hours while waiting on a database lookup, an external software tool, or human feedback. To make our agents more resource-efficient during those pauses, our new Agent Compute Engine software automatically suspends and resumes idle sessions, cutting operational infrastructure costs.
- Breaking through the memory wall with the model-state layer (TPU Sync): Building the computer around the chip also means unifying memory, storage, and networking in software. As agents reason across million-token contexts and continuous reinforcement learning (RL) loops, memory quickly becomes the bottleneck. We’re open-sourcing TPU Sync, the model-state layer for TPU clusters. TPU Sync turns chip HBM, host DRAM, shared storage, and the data center network into a single, co-designed memory hierarchy — automatically tiering massive KV caches off the chip in milliseconds, streaming context across disaggregated prefill and decode nodes, and synchronizing RL weights to cut KV transfer latency and Time to First Token (TTFT) by more than 90%.
- Scaling distributed workloads across TPUs from a single controller: Now generally available on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), Cloud Pathways brings the Google DeepMind runtime behind Gemini to every Google Cloud customer. Using a single-controller architecture and pathwaysutils, you can orchestrate large-scale TPU systems across multiple slices as if they were one local machine for pre-training, reinforcement learning, and multihost inference. Cloud Pathways keeps long-running jobs moving through hardware disruptions with colocated Python sidecars, sub-minute slice hot-swapping, and elastic resharding.
- Stitching custom TPU topologies on-demand with GKE dynamic slicing: Now generally available, GKE dynamic slicing decouples physical hardware provisioning from logical slice formation using optical circuit switching (OCS) technology. By dynamically assembling TPU cubes into larger topologies (super-slicing) or partitioning them into smaller, isolated workloads (sub-slicing) on-the-fly, this update completely eliminates rigid, manual nodepool recreation cycles. This topology agility slashes job startup times by up to 5x and accelerates fault recovery by up to 4.5x, maximizing overall fleet utilization and workload goodput across all TPUs.
Co-designing with a decade of experience
Shipping four TPU systems and a unified, open software stack in a single year only happens when silicon architects, networking engineers, compiler teams, and Google DeepMind researchers build side-by-side.
Increasingly, we’re even tapping into AI to ideate and build the next generation of AI infrastructure. From using Google DeepMind’s AlphaChip reinforcement learning system to using Gemini to deliver chip layouts in hours rather than weeks, we’re using TPU-powered AI services to rapidly accelerate next-generation TPU hardware development. This is true co-design and a unique Google differentiator.
Learn more about our new TPU systems by tuning into today’s broadcast at 9 a.m. PT.

articles.title: Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2
articles.body:
We’ve upgraded Claude Fable and Claude Mythos—models that are designed to tackle the most daunting technical challenges.
Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision. During prerelease testing they’ve helped our engineers complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours—among many other applications we’ll discuss below.
Claude Fable and Claude Mythos are the same underlying model. Fable has strong cybersecurity and biology safeguards to guard against misuse, which allows us to make it available to all users. Organizations pursuing beneficial applications in cybersecurity or biomedical research can apply for access to Mythos through our recently expanded Life Sciences and Cyber Verification Programs.
Testers have found that Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 communicate more clearly than past Fable and Mythos models. They generate outputs up to 30% faster than Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1, and they’re available at a lower price: $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens.
Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 also come with an optional fast mode, which speeds up token generation by up to 2.5 times. Fast mode is available for $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens.
Safety and alignment. To help ensure safety and alignment keep step with growing model capabilities, we ran extensive prerelease safety testing on the model that underlies Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. This included developing novel evaluations that give deeper insight into specific concerning behaviors like sandbox escapes. We believe high-stakes risks from misalignment remain low, and the model performed as well as, or better than, our recent models on most alignment measures. Fable 5.2’s cyber and biology safeguards are as robust as those of Fable 5.1 but produce fewer unnecessary blocks, and we have implemented our strongest-ever protections against distillation attacks.
We describe more about our safety testing below, and full details can be found in the Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 System Card.
When to use Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. Fable and Mythos are best for the most ambitious, open-ended technical work. For most coding and knowledge tasks, we recommend that users start with Claude Opus 5.5, our strongest daily driver, and then switch to a different model as required, depending on the scope and complexity of their work—upward to Fable or Mythos, or downward to Claude Sonnet 5.5 or Claude Haiku 5.5. Fable 5.2 can also play the role of Advisor (where Haiku, Sonnet, or Opus models consult it to help solve harder problems) or Orchestrator (where it delegates simpler tasks to smaller models).
Evaluating Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2
Benchmark performance. The benchmarks table below shows that Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 are a step above Opus 5.5 in almost all the capabilities we evaluated:
Effort and efficiency. On Medium effort (the default in Claude apps and Claude Code), Fable 5.2 can accomplish challenging tasks with fewer tokens than Fable 5.1. In early testing on the FrontierCode 2.0 evaluation, Fable 5.2 at High effort scored about level with Opus 5.5 at Max effort, for roughly half the cost per task. At Xhigh effort, it also scored the highest of any released model tested.
Coding
Over 90% of the changes merged into Anthropic’s core codebase are now written by Claude (with human guidance). We’ve used Fable 5.2 to fix stubborn bugs in minutes, optimize performance across all of our services, and complete high-value software projects that would otherwise have been too slow or too costly to attempt. A team of agents running an earlier version of Fable 5.2 migrated a critical production service from Python to Rust—the service is now more efficient, more reliable, and starts about 26 times faster. We’ve found that Fable 5.2 exercises strong engineering judgment and can produce high-quality results from even ambiguous requests.
As an experiment, one Anthropic engineer gave Fable 5.2 the task of designing a prototype operating system. Starting from an empty folder, the model coordinated over 1,000 subagents, working around the clock for eight days writing, testing, and reviewing code. It produced a working operating system that boots on a laptop, with its own core that runs the machine, drivers for the disk, keyboard, and network, permanent file storage, windows, a login screen, an installer, and built-in Claude functionality (see the video below).
Early testers have been impressed at how successfully Fable 5.2’s coding skills can be applied to a wide range of tasks:
Cybersecurity
Claude Mythos 5.2 is our most capable model for cybersecurity engineering. It catches more vulnerabilities than our previous models, and is better at reproducing and fixing them (note that Claude Fable 5.2’s safeguards will block most cybersecurity-related tasks). A security company found that one in six confirmed bugs found by Claude Mythos 5.2 were missed by all of the other frontier models they tested. On our internal evaluation, CVE Rediscovery,¹ Claude Mythos 5.2 found 10.2% more vulnerabilities than Claude Opus 5.5 and 14.4% more than Claude Mythos 5.1. Claude Mythos 5.2 also shows better judgment and calibration—one tester found that previous models had overstated the seriousness of about 1 in 20 findings, whereas Claude Mythos 5.2 hadn’t overstated any.²
Claude Mythos 5.2’s cyber capabilities are accessible through our Cyber Verification Program, which we’re continuing to expand and improve. Claude Enterprise customers (even if they aren’t members of the Cyber Verification Program) can access Claude Security, which scans codebases for vulnerabilities using our most capable models—which now includes Claude Mythos 5.2. A recent update to Claude Security helps it watch repositories as code is updated, track any findings to ensure they’re fixed, learn from additional context, and connect to a user’s tools through an API and MCP.
Science and engineering
Important tasks in science, engineering, and mathematics increasingly depend on coding: analyzing data, modeling molecules, designing parts, and controlling instruments are all done through software. Below, we discuss how Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 have helped researchers make progress on difficult problems in these areas.
Theoretical physics
Claude Fable 5.2 solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes, and the effort to unite the two linchpin theories of modern physics, relativity, and quantum mechanics.
Both of Claude’s results rely on holographic duality, the idea that certain universes containing gravity can be precisely described by a quantum theory containing no gravity at all. In the first problem, physicists in 1983 had shown that as these universes heat up, black holes form abruptly, like water boiling; but their method worked only in large universes that were big enough for relativity to apply. A calculation to determine whether the same was true in very small universes, where only the quantum description can be used, was laid out in 2003 but was too laborious to complete. Fable 5.2, working largely autonomously, completed it and found the transition is abrupt there, too. In the second problem, Fable 5.2 found the exact limit of a technique physicists have used for more than 15 years to rule out candidate theories of quantum gravity in a simplified universe. Read more about these results in their respective preprints, here and here.
Protein folding
Adeno-associated viruses are small, harmless viruses whose protein shell, the capsid, can be used to deliver gene therapies. The protein structure of the capsid is important—for example, it affects whether the therapy will be blocked by a patient’s immune system—but it’s also highly complex. Existing protein-folding models like AlphaFold can predict individual proteins, but a capsid is built from dozens of them. Building on two open-source protein-folding models, Claude Mythos 5.2 found a novel way to accurately predict a whole capsid’s structure. It wrote code that ran these models on overlapping groups of protein chains, and used the information on the known symmetries of the capsid to merge them together.
Claude’s method worked across several capsids, both natural and engineered (in our tests, it accurately modeled 28 of the 34 it attempted).³ Three computational biologists shared the following reflections on how Claude’s skills could be used to speed up their research into gene therapies:
Mathematics
Mathematical formalization. Formalization is the process of translating a mathematical proof into a language that a computer can check step by step. It can help human mathematicians gain confidence in results without having to check them by hand (this matters even more when AI models generate results that are hard for humans to verify). Because formalization is such a laborious process, if AI could assist with it, mathematicians could spend more time exploring novel ideas.
Our first formalization of Fermat’s Last Theorem, performed by an unreleased research version of Claude, took 11 days. It relied on a purpose-built harness along with guidance from a human researcher. By contrast, a team of 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents fully formalized the theorem in just 30 hours, with minimal human intervention. Fable 5.2 started from minimal prompts, built its own ways to coordinate, and used no mathematical references, only a list of intermediate theorem statements to score progress. It needed one-third as many action tokens as our first formalization and produced a proof seven times shorter. As can be seen in the figure below, Opus 5.5 (with the same 1,000-agent setup) completed only 26% of the formalization in 18 hours, and barely made any more progress after 30.
Read more about the formalization here.
Hardware and robotics
Many of AI’s potential benefits—for example, in speeding up laboratory research—depend on it being able to act in the physical world. Claude Fable 5.2 continues our models’ trend of increasing usefulness in the real world, showing promising results on tasks such as designing hardware devices and substantial advances in controlling physical robots.
Hardware engineering. We tested Fable 5.2’s skills in hardware engineering, asking it in a one-paragraph prompt to design and produce three working electronic devices with their own circuit boards, 3D-printed enclosures, and software. The devices, shown below, were a home voice-assistant hub, a USB speakerphone, and a handheld virtual pet. We collaborated on this project with Diode, a company that designs and manufactures circuit boards.
Claude wrote its own specifications, selected available electronic components from US distributors, routed each device’s four-layer circuit board, modeled the enclosures with computer-aided design, and programmed the devices’ software. Each board was ready for manufacturing in under a day, with minimal human input. Once Diode had built the boards, Claude guided the company’s engineers through the testing and assembly of the devices. All three devices worked without needing any electrical modifications. Read more about Claude’s hardware engineering skills here.
Robotics. Compared with earlier Claude models, Fable 5.2 shows substantially improved skills in controlling physical robots—even for robotics tasks on which it has never explicitly been trained. The video below shows robots controlled by Fable 5.2 completing a variety of tasks, including solving a puzzle cube, unscrewing a bottle cap, and drawing a picture of a robot. On the public RoboDojo benchmark, which tests how AIs can control a simulated two-arm robot from camera images, Fable 5.2 outperformed other frontier models that were run on the same harness, as well as most AI systems built specifically to control robots.
Research and analysis
Early testers using Claude Fable 5.2 for research and analysis tasks found that it can handle more ambiguous, data-heavy tasks than previous models and has better judgment on ambiguous tasks—particularly those that require abstract reasoning and design. Proprietary trading firm Jump Trading tested Fable 5.2 on proxy evaluations that resemble some of its quantitative research tasks, embedding it in a harness similar to the one the firm uses for its own research. In one run, Fable 5.2 effectively played all the necessary roles: code-writer, coordinator, planner, and job-submitter. Previous models had required substantial investments of time to manually rebalance roles to accommodate different models’ strengths and weaknesses.
Other testers from research and analysis organizations sent us the following statements on their experiences with Fable 5.2:
Safety and alignment
No single test can tell us how a highly capable model will behave once it’s deployed, so we rely on many different tests and many different types of evidence before release. For the model underlying Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, our predeployment safety work included alignment training and testing, newly designed evaluations on the model’s propensity to take unhelpful actions, building stronger safeguards against misuse, and scaling up our behavioral monitoring. The model was also tested before release by external evaluators, including the UK AI Security Institute, Frontier Design, and METR. See the Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 System Card for a summary of their reports⁴ and for a full description of our own safety and capabilities testing.
Alignment testing
We ran a suite of evaluations for how well-aligned Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 are in behavioral terms, testing how often they behave in unintended and potentially unsafe ways. Weighing everything we’ve seen across a range of evaluations, we’ve assessed the risk of these models behaving in unsafe ways in high-stakes situations to be low (as with our other recent models).
We tested Claude Mythos 5.2 (the same underlying model as Fable 5.2 without certain cybersecurity or biology safeguards), on our automated behavioral audit, which tests how a model behaves across approximately 1,900 scenarios. Claude Mythos 5.2 performed as well as, or better than, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Claude Mythos 5.1 on most measures. For example, it scored better than all three on most measures that involve misleading users. Hallucinating inputs, falsely claiming to have completed a task, omitting important information, and failing to disclose bad or lazy work were all lower in Claude Mythos 5.2.⁵
We paid particular attention during our testing to behaviors that contributed to recent notable cybersecurity and alignment incidents. For example, we found that Claude Mythos 5.2 has a lower propensity than Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Mythos 5.1 to engage in biased or motivated reasoning (such reasoning might mean it “explains away” evidence that it isn’t in a simulation and thus takes actions without a realistic understanding of the consequences).
We ran multiple different evaluations to test the model’s tendency to attempt escaping its sandbox. In two evaluations we’d used previously, Claude Mythos 5.2 made substantially fewer attempts at sandbox escape than any other model we’ve tested. In a dedicated evaluation—an adversarial experiment including over 1,800 scenarios, most of which could not be solved without escaping a sandbox, and where the sandbox has a deliberate weakness—Claude Mythos 5.2 made use of credentials or files that we had placed outside its sandbox in 3.1% of scenarios, about as often as Opus 5.5 (3.3%), less often than Sonnet 5.5 (5.1%), and well below previous iterations of Claude Mythos (5 and 5.1, which scored 39% and 21%, respectively). We found that other techniques, such as describing the sandbox and adding tools to report weaknesses, reduced Claude Mythos 5.2’s escape attempts even further. On other measures—one, for example, involving taking harmful actions after erroneously concluding it was in a simulation—Claude Mythos 5.2 scored slightly worse than Opus 5.5, and about level with Claude Mythos 5.1.
The problem of building evaluations that reliably catch every failure before a model is deployed remains unsolved. The complexities of evaluating highly capable models often muddy the picture—for example, Claude Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 each voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any of our recent models, which challenges our ability to assess how they will act in real-world settings. As these settings expand and capabilities increase with future models, we expect this challenge to grow. That is why we do not rely on these evaluations alone to provide a holistic picture of safety: we draw on monitoring during training, reviews of transcripts from internal use, testing by external evaluators, and interpretability techniques for examining what is happening inside the model. We are also working to make our evaluations more realistic and to better understand what they miss.
Safeguards
Cybersecurity and biology safeguards. Consistent with previous Claude Fable models, Fable 5.2 comes with safety classifiers that block high-risk cyber activities, including penetration testing, exploit generation, and binary-based vulnerability, as well as most tasks in research biology. When a query is blocked, users will instead receive a response from Opus 4.8 for cybersecurity and Opus 5 for biology. Thus, in relevant areas, including accelerator kernel optimization and improving large language model architectures, Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 perform at about the level of Opus 5.5. Distillation, where a model is trained on the outputs of a more advanced one to extract the advanced model’s capabilities, occurs illicitly on an industrial scale, often involving thousands of fake Claude accounts. Since distillation allows for advanced capabilities to be released without the safeguards we’ve built into Claude, it creates safety and national security risks (see our September 2026 threat intelligence report for details on illicit distillation activity we’ve detected and disrupted so far). Fable 5.2 has the strongest protections against distillation of any model we’ve released; it uses the techniques we described in a recent report, which have reduced the data harvested by distillers by 90% to 99%.
We are also expanding the rollout of an API feature that helps guard against illicit distillation: preserved thinking now applies to all accounts. Preserved thinking prevents distillers from editing Claude’s prior context in an attempt to extract its reasoning (developers can refer to our preserved thinking docs to learn how to update integrations with new API features).
Data privacy and Enterprise Frontier Safeguards
Some more complex forms of AI model misuse can be detected only when observing patterns across multiple requests. For this reason, powerful models like Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 rely on safeguards that monitor a window of usage data (as opposed to individual responses). With Enterprise Frontier Safeguards, automated safety monitoring is run on prompts and responses that are stored in a customer’s infrastructure, making it compatible with zero data retention (ZDR). Enterprise Frontier Safeguards is now in private beta with customers like Bridgewater, Salesforce, and Stripe.
Enterprise customers can request access to Enterprise Frontier Safeguards by contacting their account team or by completing this form. Eligible customers can continue using Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 with zero data retention before implementing safety monitoring with EFS. For other customers, we have 30-day retention for safety monitoring.
Availability
Claude Fable 5.2 is available today on all platforms, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. Developers can get started with claude-fable-5-2 on the Claude Platform.
This week, we’re giving subscribers on eligible paid plans extra Fable usage. Plans and seats that include Fable models get one to three Fable resets based on how long they’ve subscribed, and Fable is included for up to 50% of weekly usage limits for Pro plans and standard seats on the Team plan. Learn more about the Fable 5.2 launch promotion here.
Cybersecurity professionals can apply for access to Claude Mythos 5.2 through the Cyber Verification Program. Claude Enterprise customers can also use Claude Security, powered by our full family of models, including Claude Mythos 5.2. Life sciences researchers can also apply for access through the Life Sciences Verification Program.
Fast mode for Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 is available on Claude Code, the Claude Platform, Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed and Google managed), and Microsoft Foundry (Anthropic hosted). Note that access to Claude Mythos fast mode is available only to organizations who are part of our Verification Programs.
Footnotes
1 CVE refers to Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, a system that enumerates software vulnerabilities.
2 The counts are raw findings from one tester’s audit, although testers consistently found that Claude Mythos 5.2 identified more vulnerabilities than earlier models. On our own evaluations, vulnerability identification is roughly on par with Opus 5.5 (see the system card).
3 Earlier work on modeling AAV capsids and other large symmetric protein systems includes FoldaVirus, EvoDOCK and its symmetric extension, SymProFold, CapBuild, MoLPC, CombFold, Uni-Fold Symmetry, Apodex Discovery, and the “big bang” initialization (the last of which was referenced in the prompt we gave to Claude Mythos 5.2). These methods typically assemble the full structure from separately predicted chains or small groups of chains. Claude was permitted to use known symmetries but was instructed not to rely on assembly. Note that accuracy is measured by comparing Cα RMSD with the experimental structure: 1.2 Å for OpenFold3-preview2 and 1.4 Å for ESMFold2 on AAV2 (PDB:1LP3). A capsid counts as accurately modeled if either model came within 3 Å. For AAV2, Claude’s method required about 58 minutes of inference on one NVIDIA H200 GPU for OpenFold3-preview2 and about seven minutes for ESMFold2.
4 None of the external organizations reviewed the contents of this blog post or the contents of the System Card. Those organizations do not necessarily agree with any of the claims made in either publication.
5 We ran these tests on Claude Mythos 5.2 because testing the model with reduced safeguards provides the most comprehensive look at model behavior. We expect Fable 5.2 to behave similarly; in some cases, more potential pathways for misuse should be blocked given its stronger safeguards.

For example, we found that Claude Mythos 5.2 has a lower propensity than Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Mythos 5.1 to engage in biased or motivated reasoning (such reasoning might mean it “explains away” evidence that it isn’t in a simulation and thus takes actions without a realistic understanding of the consequences).
We ran multiple different evaluations to test the model’s tendency to attempt escaping its sandbox. In two evaluations we’d used previously, Claude Mythos 5.2 made substantially fewer attempts at sandbox escape than any other model we’ve tested. In a dedicated evaluation—an adversarial experiment including over 1,800 scenarios, most of which could not be solved without escaping a sandbox, and where the sandbox has a deliberate weakness—Claude Mythos 5.2 made use of credentials or files that we had placed outside its sandbox in 3.1% of scenarios, about as often as Opus 5.5 (3.3%), less often than Sonnet 5.5 (5.1%), and well below previous iterations of Claude Mythos (5 and 5.1, which scored 39% and 21%, respectively). On other measures—one, for example, involving taking harmful actions after erroneously concluding it was in a simulation—Claude Mythos 5.2 scored slightly worse than Opus 5.5, and about level with Claude Mythos 5.1.
The problem of building evaluations that reliably catch every failure before a model is deployed remains unsolved. The complexities of evaluating highly capable models often muddy the picture—for example, Claude Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 each voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any of our recent models, which challenges our ability to assess how they will act in real-world settings. As these settings expand and capabilities increase with future models, we expect this challenge to grow. That is why we do not rely on these evaluations alone to provide a holistic picture of safety: we draw on monitoring during training, reviews of transcripts from internal use, testing by external evaluators, and interpretability techniques for examining what is happening inside the model. We are also working to make our evaluations more realistic and to better understand what they miss.
Safeguards
Cybersecurity and biology safeguards. When a query is blocked, users will instead receive a response from Opus 4.8 for cybersecurity and Opus 5 for biology. Claude Mythos 5.2 is available to vetted organizations that work in these dual-use areas.
AI research and development. The model that underlies Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 is a step forward in general capabilities. However, during the model’s training, we took steps to limit advances in the specific research capabilities that could most directly accelerate AI development. Thus, in relevant areas, including accelerator kernel optimization and improving large language model architectures, Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 perform at about the level of Opus 5.5.
