articles.title: Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2
articles.body:
We’ve upgraded Claude Fable and Claude Mythos—models that are designed to tackle the most daunting technical challenges.
Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision. During prerelease testing they’ve helped our engineers complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours—among many other applications we’ll discuss below.
Claude Fable and Claude Mythos are the same underlying model. Fable has strong cybersecurity and biology safeguards to guard against misuse, which allows us to make it available to all users. Organizations pursuing beneficial applications in cybersecurity or biomedical research can apply for access to Mythos through our recently expanded Life Sciences and Cyber Verification Programs.
Testers have found that Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 communicate more clearly than past Fable and Mythos models. They generate outputs up to 30% faster than Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1, and they’re available at a lower price: $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens.
Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 also come with an optional fast mode, which speeds up token generation by up to 2.5 times. Fast mode is available for $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens.
Safety and alignment. To help ensure safety and alignment keep step with growing model capabilities, we ran extensive prerelease safety testing on the model that underlies Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. This included developing novel evaluations that give deeper insight into specific concerning behaviors like sandbox escapes. We believe high-stakes risks from misalignment remain low, and the model performed as well as, or better than, our recent models on most alignment measures. Fable 5.2’s cyber and biology safeguards are as robust as those of Fable 5.1 but produce fewer unnecessary blocks, and we have implemented our strongest-ever protections against distillation attacks.
We describe more about our safety testing below, and full details can be found in the Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 System Card.
When to use Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. Fable and Mythos are best for the most ambitious, open-ended technical work. For most coding and knowledge tasks, we recommend that users start with Claude Opus 5.5, our strongest daily driver, and then switch to a different model as required, depending on the scope and complexity of their work—upward to Fable or Mythos, or downward to Claude Sonnet 5.5 or Claude Haiku 5.5. Fable 5.2 can also play the role of Advisor (where Haiku, Sonnet, or Opus models consult it to help solve harder problems) or Orchestrator (where it delegates simpler tasks to smaller models).
Evaluating Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2
Benchmark performance. The benchmarks table below shows that Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 are a step above Opus 5.5 in almost all the capabilities we evaluated:
Effort and efficiency. On Medium effort (the default in Claude apps and Claude Code), Fable 5.2 can accomplish challenging tasks with fewer tokens than Fable 5.1. In early testing on the FrontierCode 2.0 evaluation, Fable 5.2 at High effort scored about level with Opus 5.5 at Max effort, for roughly half the cost per task. At Xhigh effort, it also scored the highest of any released model tested.
Coding
Over 90% of the changes merged into Anthropic’s core codebase are now written by Claude (with human guidance). We’ve used Fable 5.2 to fix stubborn bugs in minutes, optimize performance across all of our services, and complete high-value software projects that would otherwise have been too slow or too costly to attempt. A team of agents running an earlier version of Fable 5.2 migrated a critical production service from Python to Rust—the service is now more efficient, more reliable, and starts about 26 times faster. We’ve found that Fable 5.2 exercises strong engineering judgment and can produce high-quality results from even ambiguous requests.
As an experiment, one Anthropic engineer gave Fable 5.2 the task of designing a prototype operating system. Starting from an empty folder, the model coordinated over 1,000 subagents, working around the clock for eight days writing, testing, and reviewing code. It produced a working operating system that boots on a laptop, with its own core that runs the machine, drivers for the disk, keyboard, and network, permanent file storage, windows, a login screen, an installer, and built-in Claude functionality (see the video below).
Early testers have been impressed at how successfully Fable 5.2’s coding skills can be applied to a wide range of tasks:
Cybersecurity
Claude Mythos 5.2 is our most capable model for cybersecurity engineering. It catches more vulnerabilities than our previous models, and is better at reproducing and fixing them (note that Claude Fable 5.2’s safeguards will block most cybersecurity-related tasks). A security company found that one in six confirmed bugs found by Claude Mythos 5.2 were missed by all of the other frontier models they tested. On our internal evaluation, CVE Rediscovery,¹ Claude Mythos 5.2 found 10.2% more vulnerabilities than Claude Opus 5.5 and 14.4% more than Claude Mythos 5.1. Claude Mythos 5.2 also shows better judgment and calibration—one tester found that previous models had overstated the seriousness of about 1 in 20 findings, whereas Claude Mythos 5.2 hadn’t overstated any.²
Claude Mythos 5.2’s cyber capabilities are accessible through our Cyber Verification Program, which we’re continuing to expand and improve. Claude Enterprise customers (even if they aren’t members of the Cyber Verification Program) can access Claude Security, which scans codebases for vulnerabilities using our most capable models—which now includes Claude Mythos 5.2. A recent update to Claude Security helps it watch repositories as code is updated, track any findings to ensure they’re fixed, learn from additional context, and connect to a user’s tools through an API and MCP.
Science and engineering
Important tasks in science, engineering, and mathematics increasingly depend on coding: analyzing data, modeling molecules, designing parts, and controlling instruments are all done through software. Below, we discuss how Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 have helped researchers make progress on difficult problems in these areas.
Theoretical physics
Claude Fable 5.2 solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes, and the effort to unite the two linchpin theories of modern physics, relativity, and quantum mechanics.
Both of Claude’s results rely on holographic duality, the idea that certain universes containing gravity can be precisely described by a quantum theory containing no gravity at all. In the first problem, physicists in 1983 had shown that as these universes heat up, black holes form abruptly, like water boiling; but their method worked only in large universes that were big enough for relativity to apply. A calculation to determine whether the same was true in very small universes, where only the quantum description can be used, was laid out in 2003 but was too laborious to complete. Fable 5.2, working largely autonomously, completed it and found the transition is abrupt there, too. In the second problem, Fable 5.2 found the exact limit of a technique physicists have used for more than 15 years to rule out candidate theories of quantum gravity in a simplified universe. Read more about these results in their respective preprints, here and here.
Protein folding
Adeno-associated viruses are small, harmless viruses whose protein shell, the capsid, can be used to deliver gene therapies. The protein structure of the capsid is important—for example, it affects whether the therapy will be blocked by a patient’s immune system—but it’s also highly complex. Existing protein-folding models like AlphaFold can predict individual proteins, but a capsid is built from dozens of them. Building on two open-source protein-folding models, Claude Mythos 5.2 found a novel way to accurately predict a whole capsid’s structure. It wrote code that ran these models on overlapping groups of protein chains, and used the information on the known symmetries of the capsid to merge them together.
Claude’s method worked across several capsids, both natural and engineered (in our tests, it accurately modeled 28 of the 34 it attempted).³ Three computational biologists shared the following reflections on how Claude’s skills could be used to speed up their research into gene therapies:
Mathematics
Mathematical formalization. Formalization is the process of translating a mathematical proof into a language that a computer can check step by step. It can help human mathematicians gain confidence in results without having to check them by hand (this matters even more when AI models generate results that are hard for humans to verify). Because formalization is such a laborious process, if AI could assist with it, mathematicians could spend more time exploring novel ideas.
Our first formalization of Fermat’s Last Theorem, performed by an unreleased research version of Claude, took 11 days. It relied on a purpose-built harness along with guidance from a human researcher. By contrast, a team of 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents fully formalized the theorem in just 30 hours, with minimal human intervention. Fable 5.2 started from minimal prompts, built its own ways to coordinate, and used no mathematical references, only a list of intermediate theorem statements to score progress. It needed one-third as many action tokens as our first formalization and produced a proof seven times shorter. As can be seen in the figure below, Opus 5.5 (with the same 1,000-agent setup) completed only 26% of the formalization in 18 hours, and barely made any more progress after 30.
Read more about the formalization here.
Hardware and robotics
Many of AI’s potential benefits—for example, in speeding up laboratory research—depend on it being able to act in the physical world. Claude Fable 5.2 continues our models’ trend of increasing usefulness in the real world, showing promising results on tasks such as designing hardware devices and substantial advances in controlling physical robots.

We tested Fable 5.2’s skills in hardware engineering, asking it in a one-paragraph prompt to design and produce three working electronic devices with their own circuit boards, 3D-printed enclosures, and software. The devices, shown below, were a home voice-assistant hub, a USB speakerphone, and a handheld virtual pet. We collaborated on this project with Diode, a company that designs and manufactures circuit boards.
Claude wrote its own specifications, selected available electronic components from US distributors, routed each device’s four-layer circuit board, modeled the enclosures with computer-aided design, and programmed the devices’ software. Each board was ready for manufacturing in under a day, with minimal human input. Once Diode had built the boards, Claude guided the company’s engineers through the testing and assembly of the devices. All three devices worked without needing any electrical modifications. Read more about Claude’s hardware engineering skills here.
Robotics. Compared with earlier Claude models, Fable 5.2 shows substantially improved skills in controlling physical robots—even for robotics tasks on which it has never explicitly been trained. The video below shows robots controlled by Fable 5.2 completing a variety of tasks, including solving a puzzle cube, unscrewing a bottle cap, and drawing a picture of a robot. We describe more about our safety testing below, and full details can be found in the Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 System Card.
When to use Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. Fable and Mythos are best for the most ambitious, open-ended technical work. For most coding and knowledge tasks, we recommend that users start with Claude Opus 5.5, our strongest daily driver, and then switch to a different model as required, depending on the scope and complexity of their work—upward to Fable or Mythos, or downward to Claude Sonnet 5.5 or Claude Haiku 5.5. Fable 5.2 can also play the role of Advisor (where Haiku, Sonnet, or Opus models consult it to help solve harder problems) or Orchestrator (where it delegates simpler tasks to smaller models).
Evaluating Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2
Benchmark performance. The benchmarks table below shows that Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 are a step above Opus 5.5 in almost all the capabilities we evaluated:
Effort and efficiency. On Medium effort (the default in Claude apps and Claude Code), Fable 5.2 can accomplish challenging tasks with fewer tokens than Fable 5.1. In early testing on the FrontierCode 2.0 evaluation, Fable 5.2 at High effort scored about level with Opus 5.5 at Max effort, for roughly half the cost per task. At Xhigh effort, it also scored the highest of any released model tested.
Coding
Over 90% of the changes merged into Anthropic’s core codebase are now written by Claude (with human guidance). We’ve used Fable 5.2 to fix stubborn bugs in minutes, optimize performance across all of our services, and complete high-value software projects that would otherwise have been too slow or too costly to attempt. A team of agents running an earlier version of Fable 5.2 migrated a critical production service from Python to Rust—the service is now more efficient, more reliable, and starts about 26 times faster. We’ve found that Fable 5.2 exercises strong engineering judgment and can produce high-quality results from even ambiguous requests.
As an experiment, one Anthropic engineer gave Fable 5.2 the task of designing a prototype operating system. Starting from an empty folder, the model coordinated over 1,000 subagents, working around the clock for eight days writing, testing, and reviewing code. It produced a working operating system that boots on a laptop, with its own core that runs the machine, drivers for the disk, keyboard, and network, permanent file storage, windows, a login screen, an installer, and built-in Claude functionality (see the video below).
Early testers have been impressed at how successfully Fable 5.2’s coding skills can be applied to a wide range of tasks:
Cybersecurity
Claude Mythos 5.2 is our most capable model for cybersecurity engineering. It catches more vulnerabilities than our previous models, and is better at reproducing and fixing them (note that Claude Fable 5.2’s safeguards will block most cybersecurity-related tasks). A security company found that one in six confirmed bugs found by Claude Mythos 5.2 were missed by all of the other frontier models they tested. On our internal evaluation, CVE Rediscovery,¹ Claude Mythos 5.2 found 10.2% more vulnerabilities than Claude Opus 5.5 and 14.4% more than Claude Mythos 5.1. Claude Mythos 5.2 also shows better judgment and calibration—one tester found that previous models had overstated the seriousness of about 1 in 20 findings, whereas Claude Mythos 5.2 hadn’t overstated any.²
Claude Mythos 5.2’s cyber capabilities are accessible through our Cyber Verification Program, which we’re continuing to expand and improve. Claude Enterprise customers (even if they aren’t members of the Cyber Verification Program) can access Claude Security, which scans codebases for vulnerabilities using our most capable models—which now includes Claude Mythos 5.2. A recent update to Claude Security helps it watch repositories as code is updated, track any findings to ensure they’re fixed, learn from additional context, and connect to a user’s tools through an API and MCP.
Science and engineering
Important tasks in science, engineering, and mathematics increasingly depend on coding: analyzing data, modeling molecules, designing parts, and controlling instruments are all done through software. Below, we discuss how Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 have helped researchers make progress on difficult problems in these areas.
Theoretical physics
Claude Fable 5.2 solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes, and the effort to unite the two linchpin theories of modern physics, relativity, and quantum mechanics.
Both of Claude’s results rely on holographic duality, the idea that certain universes containing gravity can be precisely described by a quantum theory containing no gravity at all. In the first problem, physicists in 1983 had shown that as these universes heat up, black holes form abruptly, like water boiling; but their method worked only in large universes that were big enough for relativity to apply. A calculation to determine whether the same was true in very small universes, where only the quantum description can be used, was laid out in 2003 but was too laborious to complete. Fable 5.2, working largely autonomously, completed it and found the transition is abrupt there, too. In the second problem, Fable 5.2 found the exact limit of a technique physicists have used for more than 15 years to rule out candidate theories of quantum gravity in a simplified universe. Read more about these results in their respective preprints, here and here.
Protein folding
Adeno-associated viruses are small, harmless viruses whose protein shell, the capsid, can be used to deliver gene therapies. The protein structure of the capsid is important—for example, it affects whether the therapy will be blocked by a patient’s immune system—but it’s also highly complex. Existing protein-folding models like AlphaFold can predict individual proteins, but a capsid is built from dozens of them. Building on two open-source protein-folding models, Claude Mythos 5.2 found a novel way to accurately predict a whole capsid’s structure. It wrote code that ran these models on overlapping groups of protein chains, and used the information on the known symmetries of the capsid to merge them together.
Claude’s method worked across several capsids, both natural and engineered (in our tests, it accurately modeled 28 of the 34 it attempted).³ Three computational biologists shared the following reflections on how Claude’s skills could be used to speed up their research into gene therapies:
Mathematics
Mathematical formalization. Formalization is the process of translating a mathematical proof into a language that a computer can check step by step. It can help human mathematicians gain confidence in results without having to check them by hand (this matters even more when AI models generate results that are hard for humans to verify). Because formalization is such a laborious process, if AI could assist with it, mathematicians could spend more time exploring novel ideas.
Our first formalization of Fermat’s Last Theorem, performed by an unreleased research version of Claude, took 11 days. It relied on a purpose-built harness along with guidance from a human researcher. By contrast, a team of 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents fully formalized the theorem in just 30 hours, with minimal human intervention. Fable 5.2 started from minimal prompts, built its own ways to coordinate, and used no mathematical references, only a list of intermediate theorem statements to score progress. It needed one-third as many action tokens as our first formalization and produced a proof seven times shorter. As can be seen in the figure below, Opus 5.5 (with the same 1,000-agent setup) completed only 26% of the formalization in 18 hours, and barely made any more progress after 30.
Read more about the formalization here.
Hardware and robotics
Many of AI’s potential benefits—for example, in speeding up laboratory research—depend on it being able to act in the physical world. Claude Fable 5.2 continues our models’ trend of increasing usefulness in the real world, showing promising results on tasks such as designing hardware devices and substantial advances in controlling physical robots.
Hardware engineering. We tested Fable 5.2’s skills in hardware engineering, asking it in a one-paragraph prompt to design and produce three working electronic devices with their own circuit boards, 3D-printed enclosures, and software. The devices, shown below, were a home voice-assistant hub, a USB speakerphone, and a handheld virtual pet. We collaborated on this project with Diode, a company that designs and manufactures circuit boards.
Claude wrote its own specifications, selected available electronic components from US distributors, routed each device’s four-layer circuit board, modeled the enclosures with computer-aided design, and programmed the devices’ software. Each board was ready for manufacturing in under a day, with minimal human input. Once Diode had built the boards, Claude guided the company’s engineers through the testing and assembly of the devices. All three devices worked without needing any electrical modifications. Read more about Claude’s hardware engineering skills here.
Robotics. Compared with earlier Claude models, Fable 5.2 shows substantially improved skills in controlling physical robots—even for robotics tasks on which it has never explicitly been trained. The video below shows robots controlled by Fable 5.2 completing a variety of tasks, including solving a puzzle cube, unscrewing a bottle cap, and drawing a picture of a robot. On the public RoboDojo benchmark, which tests how AIs can control a simulated two-arm robot from camera images, Fable 5.2 outperformed other frontier models that were run on the same harness, as well as most AI systems built specifically to control robots.
Research and analysis
Early testers using Claude Fable 5.2 for research and analysis tasks found that it can handle more ambiguous, data-heavy tasks than previous models and has better judgment on ambiguous tasks—particularly those that require abstract reasoning and design. Proprietary trading firm Jump Trading tested Fable 5.2 on proxy evaluations that resemble some of its quantitative research tasks, embedding it in a harness similar to the one the firm uses for its own research. In one run, Fable 5.2 effectively played all the necessary roles: code-writer, coordinator, planner, and job-submitter. Previous models had required substantial investments of time to manually rebalance roles to accommodate different models’ strengths and weaknesses.
Other testers from research and analysis organizations sent us the following statements on their experiences with Fable 5.2:
Safety and alignment
No single test can tell us how a highly capable model will behave once it’s deployed, so we rely on many different tests and many different types of evidence before release. For the model underlying Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, our predeployment safety work included alignment training and testing, newly designed evaluations on the model’s propensity to take unhelpful actions, building stronger safeguards against misuse, and scaling up our behavioral monitoring. The model was also tested before release by external evaluators, including the UK AI Security Institute, Frontier Design, and METR. See the Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 System Card for a summary of their reports⁴ and for a full description of our own safety and capabilities testing.
Alignment testing
We ran a suite of evaluations for how well-aligned Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 are in behavioral terms, testing how often they behave in unintended and potentially unsafe ways. Weighing everything we’ve seen across a range of evaluations, we’ve assessed the risk of these models behaving in unsafe ways in high-stakes situations to be low (as with our other recent models).
We tested Claude Mythos 5.2 (the same underlying model as Fable 5.2 without certain cybersecurity or biology safeguards), on our automated behavioral audit, which tests how a model behaves across approximately 1,900 scenarios. Claude Mythos 5.2 performed as well as, or better than, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Claude Mythos 5.1 on most measures. For example, it scored better than all three on most measures that involve misleading users. Hallucinating inputs, falsely claiming to have completed a task, omitting important information, and failing to disclose bad or lazy work were all lower in Claude Mythos 5.2.⁵
We paid particular attention during our testing to behaviors that contributed to recent notable cybersecurity and alignment incidents. For example, we found that Claude Mythos 5.2 has a lower propensity than Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Mythos 5.1 to engage in biased or motivated reasoning (such reasoning might mean it “explains away” evidence that it isn’t in a simulation and thus takes actions without a realistic understanding of the consequences).
We ran multiple different evaluations to test the model’s tendency to attempt escaping its sandbox. In two evaluations we’d used previously, Claude Mythos 5.2 made substantially fewer attempts at sandbox escape than any other model we’ve tested. In a dedicated evaluation—an adversarial experiment including over 1,800 scenarios, most of which could not be solved without escaping a sandbox, and where the sandbox has a deliberate weakness—Claude Mythos 5.2 made use of credentials or files that we had placed outside its sandbox in 3.1% of scenarios, about as often as Opus 5.5 (3.3%), less often than Sonnet 5.5 (5.1%), and well below previous iterations of Claude Mythos (5 and 5.1, which scored 39% and 21%, respectively). We found that other techniques, such as describing the sandbox and adding tools to report weaknesses, reduced Claude Mythos 5.2’s escape attempts even further. On other measures—one, for example, involving taking harmful actions after erroneously concluding it was in a simulation—Claude Mythos 5.2 scored slightly worse than Opus 5.5, and about level with Claude Mythos 5.1.
The problem of building evaluations that reliably catch every failure before a model is deployed remains unsolved. The complexities of evaluating highly capable models often muddy the picture—for example, Claude Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 each voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any of our recent models, which challenges our ability to assess how they will act in real-world settings. As these settings expand and capabilities increase with future models, we expect this challenge to grow. That is why we do not rely on these evaluations alone to provide a holistic picture of safety: we draw on monitoring during training, reviews of transcripts from internal use, testing by external evaluators, and interpretability techniques for examining what is happening inside the model. We are also working to make our evaluations more realistic and to better understand what they miss.
Safeguards
Cybersecurity and biology safeguards. Consistent with previous Claude Fable models, Fable 5.2 comes with safety classifiers that block high-risk cyber activities, including penetration testing, exploit generation, and binary-based vulnerability, as well as most tasks in research biology. When a query is blocked, users will instead receive a response from Opus 4.8 for cybersecurity and Opus 5 for biology. Since the release of Claude Fable 5.1, we have continued to reduce false positives for our safety classifiers. Based on early testing across claude.ai, Claude Code, and Cowork, we observed about 55% fewer blocks with Fable 5.2 compared with Fable 5.1—about 60% fewer in cybersecurity and 40% fewer in biology. Claude Mythos 5.2 is available to vetted organizations that work in these dual-use areas.
AI research and development. The model that underlies Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 is a step forward in general capabilities. However, during the model’s training, we took steps to limit advances in the specific research capabilities that could most directly accelerate AI development. Thus, in relevant areas, including accelerator kernel optimization and improving large language model architectures, Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 perform at about the level of Opus 5.5. Importantly, we ensured that the training changes did not affect related capabilities like agentic coding, hardware development, and traditional AI or machine learning research (including interpretability research). We do not alter these capabilities as the model is being served to users (that is, at inference time). As described in Section 1.5 of the System Card and similarly to previous models, Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 also include transparent fallbacks to Opus 5 for a small set of topics in this domain, including kernel development on certain nonstandard accelerators.
Anti-distillation. Distillation, where a model is trained on the outputs of a more advanced one to extract the advanced model’s capabilities, occurs illicitly on an industrial scale, often involving thousands of fake Claude accounts. Since distillation allows for advanced capabilities to be released without the safeguards we’ve built into Claude, it creates safety and national security risks (see our September 2026 threat intelligence report for details on illicit distillation activity we’ve detected and disrupted so far). Fable 5.2 has the strongest protections against distillation of any model we’ve released; it uses the techniques we described in a recent report, which have reduced the data harvested by distillers by 90% to 99%.
We are also expanding the rollout of an API feature that helps guard against illicit distillation: preserved thinking now applies to all accounts. Preserved thinking prevents distillers from editing Claude’s prior context in an attempt to extract its reasoning (developers can refer to our preserved thinking docs to learn how to update integrations with new API features).
Data privacy and Enterprise Frontier Safeguards
Some more complex forms of AI model misuse can be detected only when observing patterns across multiple requests. For this reason, powerful models like Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 rely on safeguards that monitor a window of usage data (as opposed to individual responses). With Enterprise Frontier Safeguards, automated safety monitoring is run on prompts and responses that are stored in a customer’s infrastructure, making it compatible with zero data retention (ZDR). Enterprise Frontier Safeguards is now in private beta with customers like Bridgewater, Salesforce, and Stripe.
Enterprise customers can request access to Enterprise Frontier Safeguards by contacting their account team or by completing this form. Eligible customers can continue using Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 with zero data retention before implementing safety monitoring with EFS. For other customers, we have 30-day retention for safety monitoring.
Availability
Claude Fable 5.2 is available today on all platforms, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. Developers can get started with claude-fable-5-2 on the Claude Platform.
This week, we’re giving subscribers on eligible paid plans extra Fable usage. Plans and seats that include Fable models get one to three Fable resets based on how long they’ve subscribed, and Fable is included for up to 50% of weekly usage limits for Pro plans and standard seats on the Team plan. Learn more about the Fable 5.2 launch promotion here.
Cybersecurity professionals can apply for access to Claude Mythos 5.2 through the Cyber Verification Program. Claude Enterprise customers can also use Claude Security, powered by our full family of models, including Claude Mythos 5.2. Life sciences researchers can also apply for access through the Life Sciences Verification Program.
Fast mode for Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 is available on Claude Code, the Claude Platform, Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed and Google managed), and Microsoft Foundry (Anthropic hosted). Note that access to Claude Mythos fast mode is available only to organizations who are part of our Verification Programs.
Footnotes
1 CVE refers to Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, a system that enumerates software vulnerabilities.
2 The counts are raw findings from one tester’s audit, although testers consistently found that Claude Mythos 5.2 identified more vulnerabilities than earlier models. On our own evaluations, vulnerability identification is roughly on par with Opus 5.5 (see the system card).
3 Earlier work on modeling AAV capsids and other large symmetric protein systems includes FoldaVirus, EvoDOCK and its symmetric extension, SymProFold, CapBuild, MoLPC, CombFold, Uni-Fold Symmetry, Apodex Discovery, and the “big bang” initialization (the last of which was referenced in the prompt we gave to Claude Mythos 5.2). These methods typically assemble the full structure from separately predicted chains or small groups of chains. Claude was permitted to use known symmetries but was instructed not to rely on assembly. Note that accuracy is measured by comparing Cα RMSD with the experimental structure: 1.2 Å for OpenFold3-preview2 and 1.4 Å for ESMFold2 on AAV2 (PDB:1LP3). A capsid counts as accurately modeled if either model came within 3 Å. For AAV2, Claude’s method required about 58 minutes of inference on one NVIDIA H200 GPU for OpenFold3-preview2 and about seven minutes for ESMFold2.
4 None of the external organizations reviewed the contents of this blog post or the contents of the System Card. Those organizations do not necessarily agree with any of the claims made in either publication.
5 We ran these tests on Claude Mythos 5.2 because testing the model with reduced safeguards provides the most comprehensive look at model behavior. We expect Fable 5.2 to behave similarly; in some cases, more potential pathways for misuse should be blocked given its stronger safeguards.

Infineon marks innovation milestone with world’s first 300-millimeter power silicon carbide (SiC) wafer
Business & Financial Press
- Infineon presents industry-first functional power devices processed on 300-millimeter silicon carbide wafers
- Technological breakthrough underlines Infineon’s innovation strength and leadership in power semiconductors and wide-bandgap technologies
- 300-millimeter SiC process feasibility lays the foundation for secure, future-proof SiC supply to customers in automotive, renewable energy, industrial and AI data center applications
- Infineon will present the first processed 300-millimeter SiC wafer to the public at the electronica trade show starting 10 November 2026 in Munich
Munich, Germany – 09 November 2026 – Infineon Technologies AG (FSE: IFX / OTCQX: IFNNY) has successfully processed 300-millimeter silicon carbide wafers into functional power devices at its fab in Villach, Austria. Infineon is the first company to pioneer this innovation milestone in a full-scale semiconductor fab environment. It was realized by utilizing existing silicon (Si) manufacturing equipment. This early achievement of functional power devices reflects Infineon’s strong focus on providing customers with a comprehensive portfolio of high-performance SiC power semiconductors and ensuring long-term supply. Chip production on 300 mm wafers is technologically more advanced and significantly more efficient than 200 mm wafers, since the larger wafer diameter offers 2.3 times more chips per wafer.
“This technological milestone further strengthens our leadership in power systems. Congratulations and thank you to our passionate team, making significant progress in bringing 300-millimeter SiC out of the lab into a manufacturing environment,” said Jochen Hanebeck, CEO of Infineon Technologies. “Leadership in power semiconductors means continuously pushing technology to the next level. With silicon, gallium nitride and now silicon carbide 300-millimeter wafers, we are in a leading position to scale semiconductor manufacturing and drive profitable growth.”
The milestone demonstrates the potential of future full-scale industrialization of SiC on 300-millimeter wafers. Infineon will plan the 300-millimeter SiC technology and ramp timing in close collaboration with its customers and partners, while further executing on its 200-millimeter SiC manufacturing roadmap. Advanced SiC power technology provides Infineon customers with a cost-effective and secure supply base for automotive, renewable energy, industrial and AI data center applications.
SiC is a key semiconductor material for highly efficient power conversion. Its material properties enable lower power loss, higher power density and efficient operation at high voltages and temperatures for example in traction inverters, on-board chargers, EV chargers, large scale energy storage and industrial drives as well as uninterruptible power supplies. Demand is also rising in AI data centers with new roles for SiC in solid-state transformers, circuit breakers and power supply units. Infineon addresses these applications with a broad CoolSiC™ portfolio.
In parallel, Infineon has also successfully proofed the feasibility of its Cold Split technology with 300-millimeter SiC at its Dresden, Germany, site. Cold Split separates wafers from a SiC boule with less material loss and substantially reduced processing time than conventional wire sawing, so more wafers can be obtained from the same crystal with compared to less capital expenditure. Both developments position Infineon well to scale SiC technology in line with market demand and meet the evolving needs of its customers.
Infineon manufactures semiconductors based on all three relevant materials: silicon, silicon carbide and gallium nitride. On 27 October 2026, the company announced an approximately €1.1 billion investment in a high-volume manufacturing facility for GaN power semiconductors on 300-millimeter wafers in Villach. This SiC achievement extends this approach to a second wide-bandgap material and reinforces Infineon’s position as an innovation leader in semiconductor manufacturing.
Infineon at electronica 2026
Infineon will show the public the world's first processed 300-millimeter SiC wafer at the electronica trade show in Munich. From 10 to 13 November, Infineon will present innovative and energy-efficient solutions for an increasingly intelligent and connected world in Hall C3, Booth 502. More information is available at www.infineon.com/electronica.
Infineon Technologies AG is a global semiconductor leader in power systems and IoT. Infineon drives decarbonization and digitalization with its products and solutions. The company had around 57,000 employees worldwide (end of September 2025) and generated revenue of about €14.7 billion in the 2025 fiscal year (ending 30 September 2025). Infineon is listed on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange (ticker symbol: IFX) and in the USA on the OTCQX International over-the-counter market (ticker symbol: IFNNY).

articles.title: Compress any LLM 3x in one click,near-lossless,in under 50 MB RAM
articles.body:
01. Architectural Motivation & The Physics of the Memory Wall
To understand why generative artificial intelligence models crawl to an agonizing halt on edge devices, one must look past algorithmic abstractions and confront the underlying solid-state physics of digital silicon. Consider the typical machine learning workstation or consumer laptop. It is equipped with a modern graphics processing unit such as the NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3050 Ti Mobile (GA107 silicon). On paper, this processor is astonishing: it houses 2,560 CUDA cores and 80 second-generation Tensor Cores, delivering an aggregate compute density of 29.8 TFLOPS in half-precision floating-point arithmetic. In theory, it can execute nearly thirty trillion numerical calculations every second.
Yet, when an engineer attempts to deploy a modest 7-billion parameter language model in uncompressed FP16 precision, the system collapses immediately.
The root cause is the memory wall: a severe physical asymmetry where computational density on GPU dies has scaled exponentially following Moore's Law, while the external memory interface that transports numbers from dynamic random-access memory (GDDR6 VRAM) into arithmetic logic units has hit hard thermal and electrical signaling limits. On consumer silicon, that interface is typically 128 bits wide, providing an aggregate memory bandwidth of 192.0 gigabytes per second.
During autoregressive token generation, a language model emits exactly one token at a time ($M = 1$). To predict that single token, the GPU cannot reuse loaded weights across a sequence batch. It must sweep every single parameter matrix of the network from high-latency global VRAM into on-chip register files. For a single token, operational arithmetic intensity drops to approximately 1 FLOP per byte loaded.
At 192.0 GB/s, reading an uncompressed 14 GB model once requires approximately 73 milliseconds. This caps the physical theoretical ceiling of generation to less than 14 tokens per second, leaving more than 95% of the GPU's computational tensor cores completely starved of data, idling while bytes traverse copper traces.
Even worse, consumer edge GPUs feature strict physical VRAM limits, typically capped at 4GB (3,770.6 MiB addressable ceiling). Because a 14 GB or 7 GB model physically cannot fit inside 4GB of video memory, traditional execution frameworks offload layers to host system RAM across the PCIe expansion bus. A standard PCIe Gen3 x4 connection provides an effective transfer rate of roughly 3.94 GB/s. Offloading parameters across this bus causes generation speeds to crater to 0.28 tokens per second: an unusable latency for interactive speech interfaces, autonomous robotics, or real-time telecommunications.
Prior post-training quantization schemes (such as GPTQ, AWQ, and SmoothQuant) attempted to compress weights to 4-bit representations, but introduced three critical architectural bottlenecks:
- Domain-Shift Brittleness: Quantization grids calibrated on synthetic or generic text corpora (such as WikiText-2 or C4) experience catastrophic perplexity degradation when exposed to telephone speech transcripts, structured JSON schemas, medical terminology, or foreign languages.
- High Preprocessing Latency: Calculating empirical second-order Hessian statistics requires minutes to hours of forward passes over GPU hardware, making on-device dynamic compression impossible.
- Structural Incompatibility with Recurrent State-Space Models: Modern architectures featuring non-transformer layers (such as Mamba-2, ConvNet/SSM hybrids, and Liquid Neural Networks) break standard transformer calibration assumptions, resulting in severe runtime failures.
SPECTRA resolves these constraints through an architecture-agnostic framework grounded in Shannon source coding theory, calibration-free topological saliency extraction, Group-32 microscaling, and register-fused Triton GPU kernels.
Table 0: Master Architectural Taxonomy and Methodological Foundations of the SPECTRA Engine
Comprehensive taxonomy mapping SPECTRA core subsystems to mathematical principles and execution hardware.
02. Information Theory & The Mechanics of Functional Losslessness
2.1 Lossless Bitstream Entropy Bounds vs. Continuous Parameter Rate-Distortion
To understand why traditional compression formats cannot shrink neural networks below the memory wall, we examine the theoretical limits of bit-exact representation through classical information theory. Under Claude Shannon's landmark 1948 Source Coding Theorem, the minimum expected code length $L$ required to losslessly encode a discrete symbol sequence $W$ is bounded strictly by its Shannon entropy $H(W)$:
In modern foundation models, learned weight tensors are stored in IEEE 754 half-precision (FP16) or Brain Floating Point (BF16) formats. A 16-bit floating-point number factorizes into a 1-bit sign $s \in \{0, 1\}$, an $E$-bit exponent $e \in \{0, 1\}^E$, and an $M$-bit fractional significand or mantissa $m \in \{0, 1\}^M$:
Empirical entropy audits across deep parameter manifolds reveal a fundamental structural asymmetry in the information density of these fields:
- Sign Bit Entropy: Distributed near-symmetrically across positive and negative domains, exhibiting near-maximal discrete entropy: $H(s) \approx 1.0\text{ bit}$.
- Exponent Vector Entropy: Displays strong clustering around layer-specific dynamic scales, yielding low discrete entropy: $H(e) \in [1.6, 2.7]\text{ bits}$.
- Fractional Mantissa Entropy: In overparameterized neural networks, stochastic gradient updates fill the lowest-order mantissa bits with near-uniform noise. In BF16 ($M = 7$), empirical mantissa entropy is $H(m) \approx 6.8\text{ to }7.0\text{ bits}$; in FP16 ($M = 10$), it reaches $H(m) \approx 9.5\text{ to }9.9\text{ bits}$.
Summing these components demonstrates that the aggregate discrete entropy of floating-point weight tensors is approximately 10.5 bits in BF16 and 13.5 bits in FP16. In modern Transformer and state-space architectures, linear projection layers are situated immediately downstream from normalization layers, such as Layer Normalization or Root Mean Square Normalization (RMSNorm). For an un-normalized activation vector $h \in \mathbb{R}^K$, RMSNorm evaluates: RMSNorm Activation Scaling$$\text{RMSNorm}(h) = \frac{h}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^K h_k^2 + \epsilon}} \odot \gamma$$ During forward inference, the input arriving at the downstream linear projection $W \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times N}$ is precisely $x = \text{RMSNorm}(h)$. The maximum reconstruction error divided by group scale was $0.50000s$, rigorously validating Proposition 2. Experiment B (Why a Protected Outlier Set is Necessary When Outlier Magnitude Explodes): A $1,536 \times 1,536$ synthetic matrix was generated with 1% of its input channels scaled by heavy-channel multiplier $m \in \{1, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64\}$. Table 9 compares three storage schemes: Table 9: Relative Frobenius Error (%) as a Function of Heavy-Channel Magnitude $m$ (1,536 x 1,536 Matrix, 1% Heavy Channels) As $m$ scales from 1 to 64, per-row uniform quantization collapses completely (error reaches $96.30\%$). While Group-32 absorbs significant variance (capping error at $11.40\%$), SPECTRA HDSQ-Ultra holds error virtually flat at 8.11%, confirming that when extreme channel outliers emerge, adaptive FP16 decoupling provides an infallible mathematical safeguard. 5.8 Long-Context Scaling and Multi-Session Zero-Leak Stability 
          On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-1.5B, context memory expands linearly. Under standard FP16, KV cache memory hits $1,572.8\text{ MB}$ at 8,192 tokens. Combined with uncompressed weights ($3,310\text{ MB}$), total memory ($4,882.8\text{ MB}$) severely exceeds 4GB hardware limits. Under SPECTRA 4-bit weights ($917.6\text{ MB}$) and SpectraQuantizedCache ($393.2\text{ MB}$ at 8,192 tokens), total active VRAM is capped at $1,310.8\text{ MB}$: leaving over $2,459\text{ MB}$ of free safety headroom.
Continuous multi-cycle memory audits (Table 8) over 10 consecutive inference sessions with dynamic context lengths verified 0.0 MB memory leakage. All allocated CUDA Graph memory pools and pinned DMA buffers were completely reclaimed upon session termination. 06. Public Domain Prior Art Analysis & Comparative Distinctions To contextualize SPECTRA's innovations within the broader machine learning landscape, Table 12 formalizes the structural, mathematical, and systems distinctions between SPECTRA and prevailing post-training quantization frameworks. Table 12: Comprehensive Architectural Distinction Matrix Comparing SPECTRA with Public Domain Frameworks As demonstrated in Table 12, SPECTRA is the only framework that simultaneously achieves zero empirical calibration data, in-register fused kernel execution without VRAM unpack scratchpads, 100% on-chip residence on 4GB consumer silicon, and native architecture-agnostic compatibility across Transformers, ConvNets, and Mamba-2 state-space models. 07. Architectural Discussion, Scope & Generality 7.1 Scope of Architecture Agnosticism A central achievement of SPECTRA is true architecture-agnostic generality. Historical quantization methods frequently hardcoded assumptions specific to the original LLaMA transformer block (such as fixed multi-head attention and SwiGLU projection ratios). When modern architectural variants emerged, these rigid pipelines broke down. SPECTRA operates at the abstract level of linear algebraic mappings preceded by normalization layers: 
  - Dense Transformers (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-1.5B, Alibaba Qwen-3.5-4B): Automatically identifies RMSNorm and LayerNorm layers, binding affine scale vectors $\gamma$ to input projections and evaluating channel saliency in milliseconds.
  - Hybrid Convolutional State-Space Models (LiquidAI LFM-3-1.7B, LFM-2.5-2.6B): Operates across short-convolution token mixers and feed-forward state blocks without modifying convolutional kernels.
  - Hybrid Mamba-2 Architectures (IBM Granite-4.2-3B, NVIDIA Nemotron-3-Nano-4B): Seamlessly handles structured state-space layers, selective scan projections, and massive 131k-token embedding tables via dynamic row-gather dequantization.
7.2 The Hardware Pareto Frontier: Microscaling Group Size Dynamics In post-training quantization, group size $G$ defines a fundamental Pareto trade-off between representation fidelity and metadata memory overhead: 
  - Group-16 ($G = 16$): Yields an effective bit-rate of $5.25\text{ bpb}$. Scale and zero-point metadata consume $1.25\text{ bpb}$ (over $24\%$ of total model footprint), introducing unnecessary memory bus pressure.
  - Group-32 ($G = 32$): The optimal Pareto knee. Effective bit-rate is $4.625\text{ bpb}$ (metadata overhead is only $0.625\text{ bpb}$, or $13.5\%$). As proven in Proposition 3, local variance is bounded by $35.5\%$, completely eliminating outlier skew without sparse decomposition.
  - Group-64 and Group-128 ($G \ge 64$): Reduces metadata footprint ($4.31\text{ to }4.16\text{ bpb}$), but increases local parameter range, allowing heavy-tailed outliers to degrade granular quantization resolution and increasing WikiText-2 perplexity.
7.3 Edge Deployment Considerations: Thermals & Acoustic Profiles Deploying generative foundation models on 35W-45W consumer laptop hardware introduces physical thermal constraints. Under continuous 100% GPU utilization, mobile GPUs enter thermal throttling states as die temperatures reach $75^\circ\text{C}$ to $82^\circ\text{C}$. On Alibaba Qwen-3.5-4B, initial cold decoding runs at $14.55\text{ tok/s}$. Under sustained 10-minute generation runs, GPU clock frequencies throttle to maintain thermal equilibrium, stabilizing decoding at 12.08 tokens per second. Even under steady-state thermal throttling, SPECTRA sustains real-time conversational speeds (exceeding human reading speeds of 4-5 tok/s by more than 2.4x) within an acoustically quiet 35W power envelope. 08. Conclusion & Open-Source Release The memory wall in consumer silicon is not an insurmountable roadblock for generative artificial intelligence. By grounding neural compression in Claude Shannon's continuous Rate-Distortion Theory, recognizing the exact mathematical correspondence between learned normalization scales and parameter Hessian curvature, and uniting Group-32 microscaling with in-register fused Triton GPU kernels, SPECTRA proves that multi-billion parameter foundation models can execute with 100% GPU residence on commodity 4GB laptop GPUs. SPECTRA delivers 2.80x to 3.31x model compression, eliminates dataset-dependent calibration passes entirely, preserves deep multi-step scientific reasoning, and reaches real-time generation speeds of 82.53 tokens per second on commodity consumer hardware. To advance open science and democratize high-performance edge inference, NeuraCryption has made the complete research paper, mathematical proofs, Triton GPU kernels, compressor pipeline, and TRDC specification fully open-access:

Technical Appendices & Deep-Dive Specifications Appendix A: Complete Mathematical Proofs (Propositions 1, 2, and 3) + Proposition 1: Kurtosis is Bounded by Matrix Width Theorem: For any sequence of $K$ real channel saliencies $S_1, \dots, S_K$, the population fourth standardized moment (kurtosis) satisfies $\kappa \le K$. Full Proof: Define the sample mean $\mu_S = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{j=1}^K S_j$ and sample variance $\sigma_S^2 = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{j=1}^K (S_j - \mu_S)^2$. Define standardized variables $z_j = (S_j - \mu_S)/\sigma_S$. By algebraic definition: $$\sum_{j=1}^K z_j = 0, \qquad \sum_{j=1}^K z_j^2 = K$$ Apply the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality in $\mathbb{R}^K$ to the vectors $u = (z_1^2, \dots, z_K^2)^T$ and $v = (1, \dots, 1)^T$: $$\sum_{j=1}^K z_j^4 = \|u\|_2^2 \le \left(\sum_{j=1}^K z_j^2\right)^2 = K^2$$ The population kurtosis is defined as $\kappa = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{j=1}^K z_j^4$. Dividing by $K$: $$\kappa = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{j=1}^K z_j^4 \le \frac{K^2}{K} = K$$ This bound is tight and attained if and only if $K-1$ of the standardized terms equal $-1/\sqrt{K-1}$ and one term equals $\sqrt{K-1}$. $\blacksquare$ 
Proposition 2: Group-32 Reconstruction Error Bound Theorem: For any group of $G = 32$ real weights spanning zero ($w_{\min} \le 0 \le w_{\max}$), under uniform 4-bit asymmetric quantization with scale $s = (w_{\max} - w_{\min})/15$ and zero point $z = \text{round}(-w_{\min}/s)$, every reconstructed weight satisfies $|w - \hat{w}| \le s/2$. Full Proof: Since $w_{\min} \le 0 \le w_{\max}$, we have $-w_{\min}/s \in [0, 15]$. Therefore, $z = \text{round}(-w_{\min}/s)$ satisfies $z \in \{0, 1, \dots, 15\}$ without boundary saturation. Reconstructed grid coordinates are given by: $$\hat{w}(q) = (q - z)s, \qquad q \in \{0, 1, \dots, 15\}$$ For $q = 0$, $\hat{w}(0) = -zs$. By rounding bounds, $|-w_{\min}/s - z| \le 1/2$, which implies $|\hat{w}(0) - w_{\min}| \le s/2$. For $q = 15$: $$\hat{w}(15) = (15 - z)s = 15s - zs = w_{\max} - w_{\min} - zs = w_{\max} - (w_{\min} + zs)$$ Because $|w_{\min} + zs| \le s/2$, it follows that $|\hat{w}(15) - w_{\max}| \le s/2$. Because grid intervals have constant spacing $s$, any real weight $w \in [w_{\min}, w_{\max}]$ is at most $s/2$ away from its nearest integer code $q = \text{clamp}(\text{round}(w/s + z), 0, 15)$. Hence, $|w - \hat{w}| \le s/2$. $\blacksquare$ 
Proposition 3: Closed-Form Gaussian Group Noise Prediction Theorem: For 32 independent Gaussian weights $w_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$, sample range $d \approx 4.14$, expected scale $s = d\sigma/15$, and uniform error variance $\sigma_{\text{err}}^2 = s^2/12$: $$\text{Relative Frobenius Error} = \frac{d}{15\sqrt{12}} = \frac{4.14}{51.9615} \approx 7.97\%$$ $$\text{Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR)} = 20 \log_{10}\left(\frac{15\sqrt{12}}{d}\right) \approx 21.97\text{ dB}$$ $$\text{Cosine Similarity} \approx 1 - \frac{\epsilon^2}{2} = 1 - \frac{(0.0797)^2}{2} \approx 0.99682$$ Empirical Agreement: Across synthetic Gaussian tests, empirical error is $8.08\%$ and SNR is $21.85\text{ dB}$, matching theoretical predictions within 0.11 percentage points and 0.12 dB. $\blacksquare$ Appendix B: TRDC4B01 Binary Layout Specification & Memory Geometry + The TRDC (Tensor Reconstruction Data Container) binary format ensures zero-copy, zero-host-RAM-spike ingestion across consumer systems. Below is the C-struct definition and file memory geometry: typedef struct __attribute__((packed)) {
    char     magic[8];        /* Must equal "TRDC4B01" (0x5452444334423031) */
    uint64_t version;         /* Format specification version (currently 1) */
    uint64_t meta_length;     /* Byte length of trailing metadata JSON manifest */
} TRDCHeader;
/* Ingestion Pipeline (POSIX mmap):
 * 1. fd = open("model.trdc", O_RDONLY);
 * 2. ptr = mmap(NULL, file_size, PROT_READ, MAP_SHARED, fd, 0);
 * 3. Validate header: memcmp(ptr->magic, "TRDC4B01", 8) == 0;
 * 4. Read trailing JSON manifest at offset: file_size - ptr->meta_length;
 * 5. Stream contiguous tensor payloads directly to pinned CUDA DMA buffers.
 */ Appendix C: Microarchitectural Roofline & GA107 Hardware Telemetry + Microarchitectural hardware counters measured on the GA107 GPU die during sustained single-token decoding ($M = 1$): Appendix D: In-Depth Methodological Comparison with Prior Art + Detailed technical comparison against specific historical milestones: 
  - Vs. GPTQ: GPTQ requires calculating $(X X^T)^{-1}$ over hours of GPU forward passes. SPECTRA derives channel sensitivity directly from LayerNorm/RMSNorm scale parameters $\gamma$ in less than 50 milliseconds without calibration text.
  - Vs. AWQ: AWQ performs grid searches across candidate scale factors to protect top-1% channels. SPECTRA analytically scales Group-32 microscaled blocks and adaptively modulates outlier budgets ($r \le 3.0\%$) using fourth-moment kurtosis.
  - Vs. SpQR: SpQR relies on sparse matrix multiplications ($SpMM$), causing severe thread divergence and cache misses on consumer GPUs. SPECTRA gathers and accumulates outliers directly inside register files within the fused GEMV kernel.
  - Vs. QuIP# / QuaRot: QuIP# requires multiplying activations by dense randomized Hadamard matrices at runtime, adding compute latency. SPECTRA avoids online rotations entirely, relying on Group-32 microscaling.
Appendix E: Developer Quickstart & Python CLI Guide + 
            The open-source SPECTRA repository provides a comprehensive command-line interface (cli.py) and local streaming server (server.py):
# Clone the open-source repository
git clone https://github.com/NeuraCryption/SPECTRA.git
cd SPECTRA
# Install dependencies (requires PyTorch >= 2.2 and Triton)
pip install -r requirements.txt
# Compress any Hugging Face model without calibration data
python -m spectra.cli compress \
    --model-id deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B \
    --output ./models/deepseek-r1-1.5b-spectra.trdc \
    --mode pure-group32
# Run real-time streaming inference on edge hardware
python -m spectra.cli run \
    --model-path ./models/deepseek-r1-1.5b-spectra.trdc \
    --prompt "Explain quantum decoherence in simple terms:" \
    --max-tokens 512
# Launch OpenAI-compatible local server
python -m spectra.server --model-path ./models/deepseek-r1-1.5b-spectra.trdc --port 8080 Appendix F: Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) + Q: What is the core innovation of SPECTRA?
A: SPECTRA combines calibration-free AST parameter sensitivity analysis with Group-32 microscaling and in-register fused Triton GPU kernels, achieving 3.31x model compression and 82.53 tok/s decoding on 4GB consumer silicon without calibration data or loss of reasoning.
Q: Why does Group-32 microscaling outperform sparse outlier extraction?
A: Under extreme value theory, partitioning weights into groups of 32 limits expected maximum parameter variance by 35.5% compared to large groups. Microscaling absorbs heavy-tailed outliers locally without introducing the quantization boundary friction caused by decoupling outliers into sparse matrices.
Q: How does the AST pre-scanner eliminate calibration data?
A: In normalized networks, learned affine scale parameters $\gamma$ directly reflect the diagonal Hessian curvature ($F_{jj} \propto |\gamma_j|^2$). Extracting $\gamma$ from the model structure identifies channel sensitivity analytically with zero calibration passes.
Q: Can SPECTRA be deployed on non-NVIDIA GPUs?
A: The core SPECTRA engine is written in OpenAI Triton, which supports NVIDIA GPUs (CUDA) and AMD GPUs (ROCm). A fallback PyTorch reference implementation is also provided for CPU and edge NPU environments.
Q: Where can I review the peer-reviewed research paper?
A: The full 40-page research publication is permanently archived on Zenodo under DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24058202.

articles.title: What's new in the .NET 11 runtime
articles.body:
Note
Access to this page requires authorization. You can try signing in or changing directories.
Access to this page requires authorization. You can try changing directories.
This article describes new features in the .NET runtime for .NET 11. It was last updated for release candidate 2 (RC 2).
Updated minimum hardware requirements
The minimum hardware requirements for .NET 11 have been updated to require more modern instruction sets on both x86/x64 and Arm64 architectures. Additionally, the ReadyToRun (R2R) compilation targets have been updated to take advantage of newer hardware capabilities.
Arm64 requirements
For Apple, there's no change to the minimum hardware or the ReadyToRun target. The Apple M1 chips are approximately equivalent to armv8.5-a and provide support for at least the AdvSimd (NEON), CRC, DOTPROD, LSE, RCPC, RCPC2, and RDMA instruction sets.
For Linux, there's no change to the minimum hardware. .NET continues to support devices such as Raspberry Pi that might only provide support for the AdvSimd instruction set. The ReadyToRun target has been updated to include the LSE instruction set, which might result in additional jitting overhead if you launch an application.
For Windows, the baseline is updated to require the LSE instruction set. This is required by Windows 11 and by all Arm64 CPUs officially supported by Windows 10. Additionally, it's inline with the Arm SBSA (Server Base System Architecture) requirements. The ReadyToRun target has been updated to be armv8.2-a + RCPC, which provides support for at least AdvSimd, CRC, LSE, RCPC, and RDMA, and covers the majority of hardware officially supported.
x86/x64 requirements
For all three operating systems (Apple, Linux, and Windows), the baseline is updated from x86-64-v1 to x86-64-v2. This changes the hardware from only guaranteeing CMOV, CX8, SSE, and SSE2 to also guaranteeing CX16, POPCNT, SSE3, SSSE3, SSE4.1, and SSE4.2. This guarantee is required by Windows 11 and by all x86/x64 CPUs officially supported on Windows 10. It includes all chips still officially supported by Intel and AMD, with the last older chips having gone out of support around 2013.
The ReadyToRun target has been updated to x86-64-v3 for Windows and Linux, which additionally includes the AVX, AVX2, BMI1, BMI2, F16C, FMA, LZCNT, and MOVBE instruction sets. The ReadyToRun target for Apple remains unchanged.
Impact
Starting with .NET 11, .NET fails to run on older hardware and might print a message similar to the following:
The current CPU is missing one or more of the baseline instruction sets.
For ReadyToRun-capable assemblies, there might be additional startup overhead on some supported hardware that doesn't meet the expected support for a typical device.
Reason for change
.NET supports a broad range of hardware, often above and beyond the minimum hardware requirements put in place by the underlying operating system. This support adds significant complexity to the codebase, particularly for much older hardware that's unlikely to still be in use. Additionally, it defines a "lowest common denominator" that AOT targets must default to, which can, in some scenarios, lead to reduced performance.
The update to the minimum baseline was made to reduce the maintenance complexity of the codebase and to better align with the documented (and often enforced) hardware requirements of the underlying operating system.
For more information, see Minimum hardware requirements updated.
Runtime Async
.NET 11 introduces runtime-native async (Runtime Async V2), a significant step toward replacing compiler-generated async state machines with runtime-managed suspension and resumption. Instead of the compiler emitting state-machine classes, the runtime itself tracks async execution, producing cleaner stack traces, better debuggability, and lower overhead.
Runtime Async is a preview feature. To opt in, add the following property to your project file:
<PropertyGroup>
  <Features>runtime-async=on</Features>
</PropertyGroup>
A net11.0 project no longer requires <EnablePreviewFeatures>true</EnablePreviewFeatures> to use Runtime Async.
The .NET runtime libraries themselves are compiled with runtime-async=on. The runtime libraries no longer contain compiler-generated state machines and rely entirely on runtime-provided async. This makes it possible to migrate an entire app (with only library dependencies) to the new model, and it provides broad functional and performance validation of the feature. The product team welcomes any reports—positive or negative—about throughput and library size changes you observe.
.NET 11 also includes two additional improvements:
- Covariant Task → Task<T> overrides: When a derived class returns Task<T> for a base method that returns Task, the runtime now generates a void-returning thunk that bridges the calling convention difference, so virtual dispatch works for both flavors. The same fix applies to NativeAOT.
- Inlining in crossgen2: Restrictions that prevented runtime-async methods from being inlined during ReadyToRun (R2R) compilation have been removed. All async tests pass with both crossgen2 and composite R2R, and inlining of await-less async calls (the synchronous fast path) is confirmed end-to-end.
Note
The DOTNET_RuntimeAsync and UNSUPPORTED_RuntimeAsync environment variables that previously controlled runtime-async behavior have been removed. To opt out of runtime-async per project, set <UseRuntimeAsync>false</UseRuntimeAsync> in your project file instead of relying on the environment variable.
Cleaner live stack traces
The most visible improvement is in live stack traces—what profilers, debuggers, and new StackTrace() see during execution. With compiler-generated async, each async method produces multiple frames from state-machine infrastructure. With Runtime Async, the actual methods appear directly on the call stack.
// To enable runtime async, add the following to your .csproj:
//   <Features>runtime-async=on</Features>
await OuterAsync();
static async Task OuterAsync()
{
    await Task.CompletedTask;
    await MiddleAsync();
}
static async Task MiddleAsync()
{
    await Task.CompletedTask;
    await InnerAsync();
}
static async Task InnerAsync()
{
    await Task.CompletedTask;
    Console.WriteLine(new StackTrace(fNeedFileInfo: true));

Without runtime-async—13 frames, state-machine infrastructure visible:
   at Program.<<Main>$>g__InnerAsync|0_2() in Program.cs:line 24

With runtime-async—5 frames, the real call chain:
   at Program.<<Main>$>g__InnerAsync|0_2() in Program.cs:line 24

Note
Exception stack traces (from catch (Exception ex)) already look the same with or without Runtime Async, because existing ExceptionDispatchInfo cleanup in compiler-generated code handles that case. The improvement is in what you see during live execution.
This improvement benefits anything that inspects the live execution stack, including profiling tools, diagnostic logging, and the debugger call stack window.
NativeAOT and ReadyToRun support
Runtime Async supports NativeAOT and ReadyToRun compilation. This extends the feature beyond JIT-compiled code to ahead-of-time compiled scenarios. The runtime also reuses continuation objects more aggressively and avoids saving unchanged locals, reducing allocation pressure in async-heavy code.
Debugging improvements
Breakpoints now bind correctly inside runtime-async methods, and the debugger can step through await boundaries without jumping into compiler-generated infrastructure.
Runtime Async performance improvements
Runtime Async includes several performance improvements:
- JIT async support: The JIT compiles a dedicated runtime-async version of a synchronous, task-returning method rather than delegating through a thunk. The JIT turns the method's tail calls into runtime-async calls and awaits the task that would otherwise be returned, eliminating an extra layer of indirection.
- Tail-merged suspension points: The JIT tail-merges async suspension points so generated code is smaller.
- Cached continuations: Continuations used for runtime-async callable task thunks are cached and reused.
- Pooled methods opt out: Methods that are already pooled opt out of runtime-async, avoiding redundant work.
- Tiered async compilation: Async versions now flow through tiered compilation, so hot async methods get tier 1 optimizations after warm-up.
- Task and ValueTask factory intrinsics: The JIT recognizes common factories, such as Task.FromResult, Task.CompletedTask, and ValueTask.FromResult, and folds them into faster async paths.
- Tail-await optimizations: Implicit tailcalls from async methods are enabled again when the method directly returns another async result, and await Task.Yield() avoids extra allocations in runtime-async paths.
Async continuations without ExecutionContext
Async continuations can now opt out of ExecutionContext capture and restore. ExecutionContext carries ambient state—such as AsyncLocal<T> values—across await points. Every Task continuation previously captured a snapshot of the context and restored it before running, even when no AsyncLocal<T> state was in use and the restore was a no-op.
The runtime now detects when a continuation has nothing to restore and skips the capture/restore cycle entirely. Task, Task<T>, ValueTask, and ValueTask<T> all benefit from this change, as does the runtime-async implementation path. Applications that use ConfigureAwait(false) and AsyncLocal<T> sparingly see reduced overhead in high-throughput async code paths.
JIT improvements
- Bounds check elimination: The just-in-time (JIT) compiler now eliminates bounds checks for the common pattern where an index plus a constant is compared against a length, such as i + cns < len. It also eliminates more redundant bounds checks for index-from-end access (for example, values[^1]). These improvements reduce redundant checks in tight loops and improve throughput for array and span operations.
- Redundant checked context removal: The JIT can now prove and remove redundant checked arithmetic contexts—for example, when a value is already known to be in range. This optimization eliminates unnecessary overflow checks in generated code.
- Switch expression folding: Multi-target switch expressions now fold into simpler branchless checks when the targets are a small set of constants, for example x is 0 or 1 or 2 or 3 or 4.
- Faster uint-to-float/double casts: Casting uint to float or double is faster on pre-AVX-512 x86 hardware.
- SVE2 intrinsics: New Arm SVE2 (Scalable Vector Extension 2) intrinsics are available: ShiftRightLogicalNarrowingSaturate(Even|Odd). These expand the set of vectorized operations available on Arm hardware that supports SVE2.
- Math.BigMul on x64: Math.BigMul(long, long, out long) is now significantly faster on x64. The JIT generates a single MUL r/m64 instruction when both operands are 64-bit values and the caller requests the high half of the result, eliminating the previous helper call.
- Single-IG prolog restriction removed: The JIT no longer requires the function prolog to fit in a single instruction group (IG). Complex prologues with many saved registers, large stack allocations, or runtime-async state setup no longer trigger fallback paths.
- SELECT(cond, cns, cns) folding: The JIT now folds conditional selects whose two branches both produce the same constant into just that constant—for example, condition ? 42 : 42 becomes 42. This fold eliminates unnecessary comparisons that can appear after earlier optimizations unify branches.
- AVX-VNNI-512 intrinsics: System.Runtime.Intrinsics.X86.AvxVnni.V512 exposes 512-bit forms of the AVX-VNNI multiply-add intrinsics on CPUs with AVX512-VNNI support.
- Saturating floating-point conversions: Unchecked float and double conversions to small integer types now saturate to type bounds instead of wrapping through intermediate truncation.
- ARM64 Vector<T> by reference for SVE: When the runtime is compiled with ARM SVE support, Vector<T> values are passed by reference rather than by value, aligning with the ARM calling convention for scalable types and enabling better code generation for SVE-intensive code.
For better performance and code quality, .NET 11 adds several more JIT optimizations:
Constant-folding SequenceEqual
The JIT can now fold a string.Equals or ReadOnlySpan<T>.SequenceEqual call whose operands are both compile-time constants, replacing the byte-by-byte comparison with the constant true or false result. This matters most after inlining, when a caller passes another literal to a helper that compares against a known string. When IsAdmin is inlined into a caller that passes "Guest", the JIT sees "Guest" == "Admin" and folds it to false:
static bool IsAdmin(string role) => role == "Admin";
The optimization applies to string literals, const string fields, and UTF-8 literals (for example, "PNG"u8).
Devirtualization improvements
The JIT can now devirtualize generic virtual methods, including non-shared generic virtual methods and shared generic virtual methods that don't require a runtime lookup. Default interface methods declared on generic interfaces can now be devirtualized as well.
In addition, the result of Activator.CreateInstance<T>() is now treated as having an exact type, allowing the JIT to devirtualize subsequent calls made on the returned object.
These improvements unlock further downstream optimizations such as inlining and constant folding, reducing runtime dispatch overhead and improving performance. For example:
IfaceGeneric<string> caller = new Caller<string>();
Iface obj = Activator.CreateInstance<Impl>();
caller.DefaultImpl(obj, "test"); // Can be optimized down to Console.WriteLine("test")
interface Iface
{
    void GenericMethod<T>(T value);
}
interface IfaceGeneric<T>
{
    void DefaultImpl(Iface obj, T value) => obj.GenericMethod(value);
}
class Impl : Iface
{
    public void GenericMethod<T>(T value) => Console.WriteLine(value);
}
class Caller<T> : IfaceGeneric<T>
{
}
Here the JIT can determine the exact implementation behind both interface calls, devirtualize them, inline through the call chain, and ultimately fold the code down to the equivalent of Console.WriteLine("test").
Eliminating bounds checks after an empty-span guard
The JIT now picks up the length != 0 assertion from an empty-span check and uses it to prove the bounds check on the first element succeeds:
if (!span.IsEmpty && span[0] == value)
{
    // The bounds check on span[0] is now eliminated.
}
Redundant branch and test elimination
When an outer predicate is already implied by an inner branch, the JIT now removes the redundant outer check. Similarly, when code assigns a value in a conditional and then immediately tests it, the second test is eliminated:
if (x > 0)
{
    if (x > 1) S();  // The outer x > 0 check is folded away.
}
int y = condition ? 1 : 2;
if (y == 1) A(); else B();  // The y == 1 test is eliminated;
                             // each branch of the ternary goes directly to A() or B().
These optimizations are most visible after inlining, where guards from different methods land in the same compiled body.

.NET 11 includes several new hardware intrinsics and code generation improvements:
- Hardware FP16 instructions for Half arithmetic and conversions: The JIT uses hardware FP16 instructions for Half arithmetic and conversions when the processor supports them. On Arm64, arithmetic uses the optional FP16 instruction set, while conversions between Half and float or double use baseline Arm64 instructions. The optimization requires no application changes and preserves the existing ABI representation of Half.
- Better cost modeling for x86/x64 SIMD: The JIT's floating-point execution and size costs previously reflected x87-era assumptions. Updated costs that reflect modern SSE/AVX hardware let the JIT make better decisions about hoisting and common subexpression elimination (CSE) around SIMD code.
- Faster DotProduct on AVX: Lowering for Vector128.Dot-style operations now emits a mul + permute + add sequence instead of vdpps/vdppd when AVX is available, which is consistently faster.
- Faster IndexOfAnyAsciiSearcher on Arm64: Arm64 versions of Vector*.Count, IndexOf, and LastIndexOf no longer route through ExtractMostSignificantBits, yielding a 5–50% improvement in workloads that use these APIs in their core loop.
- Arm64 ToScalar for 64-bit integers: ToScalar on Vector*<long> and Vector*<ulong> now uses fmov instead of umov, which is shorter and faster on most cores.
- SVE CreateWhile API expansion: CreateWhile gains signed, double, and single variants alongside the existing unsigned ones, completing the predicate-generation surface for SVE loops.

- Guid.NewGuid() on Linux: Guid.NewGuid() on Linux now uses the getrandom() syscall with batch caching instead of reading from /dev/urandom, yielding approximately 12% throughput improvement for GUID generation.

Browser and WebAssembly support has several improvements:
- WebCIL payload loading: The runtime can now load WebCIL payloads directly, improving compatibility with browser-based deployment scenarios.
- Better debugging symbols: Symbol and stack trace quality for WebAssembly debugging has improved, making it easier to diagnose issues in browser-hosted .NET apps.
- float[], Span<float>, and ArraySegment<float> marshaling: float[], Span<float>, and ArraySegment<float> are now marshaled more directly across JavaScript boundaries, reducing overhead for interop-heavy code.
