- WebCIL V1 is the default for CoreCLR WASM builds: The shared WebCIL header gains a TableBase field (28 → 32 bytes). Both Mono and CoreCLR readers accept V0 and V1. Crossgen2's WasmObjectWriter produces V1 directly, and CoreCLR-flavored WASM SDK builds default WasmWebcilVersion to V1.
- Native re-link works for CoreCLR WASM apps: A full Emscripten-based pipeline replaces the previous stub targets. Re-linking dotnet.native.wasm from the runtime pack and including custom native code via NativeFileReference now works.
- JavaScript minification in Release builds: Browser CoreCLR Release builds ship minified JavaScript.
- NativeAOT publish for WASM no longer drops package satellites: Satellite assemblies from NuGet packages are now passed to ILC and pruned from the publish output, fixing localization for AOT-published apps that depend on packages such as System.CommandLine.
CoreCLR on WebAssembly now runs the libraries test suite end to end.
Platform support for more than 1024 CPUs
The .NET runtime can now initialize on machines with more than 1024 logical processors. Previously, sched_getaffinity was called with the default cpu_set_t (capped at 1024), causing initialization to fail on high-core-count servers. The runtime now allocates the CPU set dynamically. The GC retains its 1024-heap limit, but the CPU count limit is removed.
In-process crash report logging
A new in-process crash reporting mechanism captures diagnostic information from within the crashing process before it terminates. Previously, crash diagnostics were collected by an out-of-process monitor. While the out-of-process approach is safe, it can miss information that's only available inside the dying process. The new in-process path logs the managed stack trace, module list, and key runtime state to a well-known path before the process exits.
This capability originated on mobile platforms and is now also available on Linux and macOS. When DOTNET_DbgEnableMiniDump isn't enabled, set DOTNET_EnableCrashReport=1 or DOTNET_EnableCrashReportOnly=1 to select the in-process reporter. Existing createdump behavior remains in place when minidumps are enabled.
NativeAOT: faster interface dispatch
NativeAOT now uses a dispatch helper for interface method calls. Instead of a direct fat-pointer call sequence, the runtime routes interface dispatch through a shared helper that can be patched to the correct implementation after the call site warms up. This reduces the binary size of interface call sites and improves throughput on workloads with many interface method calls.
Generic virtual method dispatch also uses the shared dispatch-cell infrastructure, which improves both monomorphic and polymorphic call performance. In addition, Assembly.GetCallingAssembly() now works on NativeAOT when stack trace data is available.
SIMD lane construction and composition
System.Runtime.Intrinsics now includes lane construction and composition APIs for hardware vector types. The new APIs let you construct a vector from individually specified lanes and extract or reorder lanes between vectors. This enables precise, portable control over SIMD vector element placement without falling back to platform-specific intrinsics.
The new methods fall into a few families:
- Patterned construction: CreateGeometricSequence, CreateAlternatingSequence, and CreateHarmonicSequence build a vector from a starting value and a rule.
- Interleave and de-interleave: Zip, ZipLower/ZipUpper, Unzip, UnzipEven/UnzipOdd.
- Rearrange: The Concat family (ConcatLowerLower, ConcatLowerUpper, ConcatUpperLower, ConcatUpperUpper) and Reverse.
using System.Runtime.Intrinsics;
// {1, 2, 4, 8} — each lane is the previous lane times two
Vector128<int> powers = Vector128.CreateGeometricSequence(1, 2);
// Interleave two vectors lane-by-lane
(Vector128<int> lower, Vector128<int> upper) =
    Vector128.Zip(Vector128.Create(1), Vector128.Create(2));
These APIs are available on Vector128<T>, Vector256<T>, Vector512<T>, Vector64<T>, and Vector<T>. They're building blocks for image processing, audio digital signal processing (DSP), and other SIMD-intensive workloads that need fine-grained control over vector element layout.
File locking on iOS and tvOS
On iOS and tvOS, including simulators, CoreCLR now disables advisory file locking by default. A FileStream that acquired an advisory lock could cause the operating system to terminate an app when the app entered the background while it held the lock. As a result, FileShare restrictions are no longer enforced by those locks on iOS and tvOS, including between handles in the same process. Mac Catalyst and other platforms keep their existing defaults.
If your app relies on FileShare enforcement and you accept the risk of suspension-related termination, restore file locking by using either of the following settings:
- Set the DOTNET_SYSTEM_IO_DISABLEFILELOCKING environment variable to 0.
- Set the System.IO.DisableFileLocking runtime configuration property to false. For example, in the runtimeconfig.json file:
{
  "configProperties": {
    "System.IO.DisableFileLocking": false
  }
}
Reliability fixes
The runtime includes fixes for the following issues:
- On Linux, the SDK no longer crashes on Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) 8 on Arm64, and the runtime correctly traverses cgroup v2 memory limits at the root of the hierarchy.
- Generic virtual method dispatch no longer hangs after repeated AssemblyLoadContext unloads.
- TryDequeue no longer spuriously reports an empty queue while a segment freezes during growth. TryPeek has the same reliability fix.
- On Windows, garbage collection works correctly on machines with multiple CPU groups.
Runtime diagnostics
The async profiler now instruments both runtime-async methods and compiler-generated async state-machine methods, so tools receive one consistent event model regardless of async implementation style. The runtime also adds improved interpreter perf-map logging support, and fixes parsing of CORECLR_NOTIFICATION_PROFILERS lists that don't end with a semicolon.

articles.title: What's new in the .NET 11 runtime
articles.body:
Note
Access to this page requires authorization. You can try signing in or changing directories.

This article describes new features in the .NET runtime for .NET 11. It was last updated for release candidate 2 (RC 2).
Updated minimum hardware requirements
The minimum hardware requirements for .NET 11 have been updated to require more modern instruction sets on both x86/x64 and Arm64 architectures. Additionally, the ReadyToRun (R2R) compilation targets have been updated to take advantage of newer hardware capabilities.
Arm64 requirements
For Apple, there's no change to the minimum hardware or the ReadyToRun target. The Apple M1 chips are approximately equivalent to armv8.5-a and provide support for at least the AdvSimd (NEON), CRC, DOTPROD, LSE, RCPC, RCPC2, and RDMA instruction sets.
For Linux, there's no change to the minimum hardware. .NET continues to support devices such as Raspberry Pi that might only provide support for the AdvSimd instruction set. The ReadyToRun target has been updated to include the LSE instruction set, which might result in additional jitting overhead if you launch an application.
For Windows, the baseline is updated to require the LSE instruction set. This is required by Windows 11 and by all Arm64 CPUs officially supported by Windows 10. Additionally, it's inline with the Arm SBSA (Server Base System Architecture) requirements. The ReadyToRun target has been updated to be armv8.2-a + RCPC, which provides support for at least AdvSimd, CRC, LSE, RCPC, and RDMA, and covers the majority of hardware officially supported.
x86/x64 requirements
For all three operating systems (Apple, Linux, and Windows), the baseline is updated from x86-64-v1 to x86-64-v2. This changes the hardware from only guaranteeing CMOV, CX8, SSE, and SSE2 to also guaranteeing CX16, POPCNT, SSE3, SSSE3, SSE4.1, and SSE4.2. This guarantee is required by Windows 11 and by all x86/x64 CPUs officially supported on Windows 10. It includes all chips still officially supported by Intel and AMD, with the last older chips having gone out of support around 2013.
The ReadyToRun target has been updated to x86-64-v3 for Windows and Linux, which additionally includes the AVX, AVX2, BMI1, BMI2, F16C, FMA, LZCNT, and MOVBE instruction sets. The ReadyToRun target for Apple remains unchanged.
Impact
Starting with .NET 11, .NET fails to run on older hardware and might print a message similar to the following:
The current CPU is missing one or more of the baseline instruction sets.
For ReadyToRun-capable assemblies, there might be additional startup overhead on some supported hardware that doesn't meet the expected support for a typical device.
Reason for change
.NET supports a broad range of hardware, often above and beyond the minimum hardware requirements put in place by the underlying operating system. This support adds significant complexity to the codebase, particularly for much older hardware that's unlikely to still be in use. Additionally, it defines a "lowest common denominator" that AOT targets must default to, which can, in some scenarios, lead to reduced performance.
The update to the minimum baseline was made to reduce the maintenance complexity of the codebase and to better align with the documented (and often enforced) hardware requirements of the underlying operating system.
For more information, see Minimum hardware requirements updated.
Runtime Async
.NET 11 introduces runtime-native async (Runtime Async V2), a significant step toward replacing compiler-generated async state machines with runtime-managed suspension and resumption. Instead of the compiler emitting state-machine classes, the runtime itself tracks async execution, producing cleaner stack traces, better debuggability, and lower overhead.

<PropertyGroup>
  <Features>runtime-async=on</Features>
</PropertyGroup>
A net11.0 project no longer requires <EnablePreviewFeatures>true</EnablePreviewFeatures> to use Runtime Async.
The .NET runtime libraries themselves are compiled with runtime-async=on. The runtime libraries no longer contain compiler-generated state machines and rely entirely on runtime-provided async. - Covariant Task → Task<T> overrides: When a derived class returns Task<T> for a base method that returns Task, the runtime now generates a void-returning thunk that bridges the calling convention difference, so virtual dispatch works for both flavors. The same fix applies to NativeAOT.

    await Task.CompletedTask;

}

    await Task.CompletedTask;
    await InnerAsync();
}

    await Task.CompletedTask;
    Console.WriteLine(new StackTrace(fNeedFileInfo: true));

   at Program.<<Main>$>g__InnerAsync|0_2()

The JIT can now fold a string.Equals or ReadOnlySpan<T>.SequenceEqual call whose operands are both compile-time constants, replacing the byte-by-byte comparison with the constant true or false result. This matters most after inlining, when a caller passes another literal to a helper that compares against a known string. When IsAdmin is inlined into a caller that passes "Guest", the JIT sees "Guest" == "Admin" and folds it to false:
static bool IsAdmin(string role) => role == "Admin";
The optimization applies to string literals, const string fields, and UTF-8 literals (for example, "PNG"u8).
Devirtualization improvements
The JIT can now devirtualize generic virtual methods, including non-shared generic virtual methods and shared generic virtual methods that don't require a runtime lookup. Default interface methods declared on generic interfaces can now be devirtualized as well.
In addition, the result of Activator.CreateInstance<T>() is now treated as having an exact type, allowing the JIT to devirtualize subsequent calls made on the returned object.
These improvements unlock further downstream optimizations such as inlining and constant folding, reducing runtime dispatch overhead and improving performance. For example:
IfaceGeneric<string> caller = new Caller<string>();
Iface obj = Activator.CreateInstance<Impl>();
caller.DefaultImpl(obj, "test"); // Can be optimized down to Console.WriteLine("test")
interface Iface
{
    void GenericMethod<T>(T value);
}
interface IfaceGeneric<T>
{
    void DefaultImpl(Iface obj, T value) => obj.GenericMethod(value);
}
class Impl : Iface
{
    public void GenericMethod<T>(T value) => Console.WriteLine(value);
}
class Caller<T> : IfaceGeneric<T>
{
}
Here the JIT can determine the exact implementation behind both interface calls, devirtualize them, inline through the call chain, and ultimately fold the code down to the equivalent of Console.WriteLine("test").
Eliminating bounds checks after an empty-span guard
The JIT now picks up the length != 0 assertion from an empty-span check and uses it to prove the bounds check on the first element succeeds:
if (!span.IsEmpty && span[0] == value)
{
    // The bounds check on span[0] is now eliminated.
}
Redundant branch and test elimination
When an outer predicate is already implied by an inner branch, the JIT now removes the redundant outer check. Similarly, when code assigns a value in a conditional and then immediately tests it, the second test is eliminated:
if (x > 0)
{
    if (x > 1) S();  // The outer x > 0 check is folded away.
}
int y = condition ? 1 : 2;
if (y == 1) A(); else B();  // The y == 1 test is eliminated;
                             // each branch of the ternary goes directly to A() or B().
These optimizations are most visible after inlining, where guards from different methods land in the same compiled body.
Hardware intrinsics and code generation
.NET 11 includes several new hardware intrinsics and code generation improvements:
- Hardware FP16 instructions for Half arithmetic and conversions: The JIT uses hardware FP16 instructions for Half arithmetic and conversions when the processor supports them. On x64, arithmetic uses AVX10.1, while conversions between Half and float can use F16C (available on most AVX2-capable hardware). On Arm64, arithmetic uses the optional FP16 instruction set, while conversions between Half and float or double use baseline Arm64 instructions. The optimization requires no application changes and preserves the existing ABI representation of Half.
- Better cost modeling for x86/x64 SIMD: The JIT's floating-point execution and size costs previously reflected x87-era assumptions. Updated costs that reflect modern SSE/AVX hardware let the JIT make better decisions about hoisting and common subexpression elimination (CSE) around SIMD code.
- Faster DotProduct on AVX: Lowering for Vector128.Dot-style operations now emits a mul + permute + add sequence instead of vdpps/vdppd when AVX is available, which is consistently faster.
- Faster IndexOfAnyAsciiSearcher on Arm64: Arm64 versions of Vector*.Count, IndexOf, and LastIndexOf no longer route through ExtractMostSignificantBits, yielding a 5–50% improvement in workloads that use these APIs in their core loop.
- Arm64 ToScalar for 64-bit integers: ToScalar on Vector*<long> and Vector*<ulong> now uses fmov instead of umov, which is shorter and faster on most cores.
- SVE CreateWhile API expansion: CreateWhile gains signed, double, and single variants alongside the existing unsigned ones, completing the predicate-generation surface for SVE loops.
- New SVE2 and Arm64 instruction-set detection: The runtime now reports SVE_AES, SVE_SHA3, SVE_SM4, SHA3, and SM4 as separate instruction sets, allowing Sve2*.IsSupported queries for those features on capable hardware.
- AVX10 detection fix: The CPUID-bit cache for AVX10 was being overwritten by a later query, which could cause AVX10 to be misreported on capable hardware. This is now fixed.
ReadyToRun improvements
Comparer<T>.Default and EqualityComparer<T>.Default are now specialized in ReadyToRun (R2R) images. Previously, the default comparers used reflection that R2R couldn't see ahead of time, causing callers to fall back to the JIT. R2R now generates a specialized helper in the image—mirroring the NativeAOT approach—and benchmarks show up to a 20× improvement for collections operations that rely on the default comparer.
VM improvements
- Cached interface dispatch on non-JIT platforms: On platforms that lack JIT support, such as iOS, interface dispatch was falling back to an expensive generic fixup path. Cached dispatch yields up to 200x improvements in interface-heavy code on these targets.
- Guid.NewGuid() on Linux: Guid.NewGuid() on Linux now uses the getrandom() syscall with batch caching instead of reading from /dev/urandom, yielding approximately 12% throughput improvement for GUID generation.
WebAssembly improvements
Browser and WebAssembly support has several improvements:
- WebCIL payload loading: The runtime can now load WebCIL payloads directly, improving compatibility with browser-based deployment scenarios.
- Better debugging symbols: Symbol and stack trace quality for WebAssembly debugging has improved, making it easier to diagnose issues in browser-hosted .NET apps.
- float[], Span<float>, and ArraySegment<float> marshaling: float[], Span<float>, and ArraySegment<float> are now marshaled more directly across JavaScript boundaries, reducing overhead for interop-heavy code.
.NET includes improvements to CoreCLR-on-WebAssembly:
- WebCIL V1 is the default for CoreCLR WASM builds: The shared WebCIL header gains a TableBase field (28 → 32 bytes). Both Mono and CoreCLR readers accept V0 and V1. Crossgen2's WasmObjectWriter produces V1 directly, and CoreCLR-flavored WASM SDK builds default WasmWebcilVersion to V1.
- Native re-link works for CoreCLR WASM apps: A full Emscripten-based pipeline replaces the previous stub targets. Re-linking dotnet.native.wasm from the runtime pack and including custom native code via NativeFileReference now works.
- JavaScript minification in Release builds: Browser CoreCLR Release builds ship minified JavaScript.
- NativeAOT publish for WASM no longer drops package satellites: Satellite assemblies from NuGet packages are now passed to ILC and pruned from the publish output, fixing localization for AOT-published apps that depend on packages such as System.CommandLine.
CoreCLR on WebAssembly now runs the libraries test suite end to end.
Platform support for more than 1024 CPUs
The .NET runtime can now initialize on machines with more than 1024 logical processors. Previously, sched_getaffinity was called with the default cpu_set_t (capped at 1024), causing initialization to fail on high-core-count servers. The runtime now allocates the CPU set dynamically. The GC retains its 1024-heap limit, but the CPU count limit is removed.
In-process crash report logging
A new in-process crash reporting mechanism captures diagnostic information from within the crashing process before it terminates. Previously, crash diagnostics were collected by an out-of-process monitor. While the out-of-process approach is safe, it can miss information that's only available inside the dying process. The new in-process path logs the managed stack trace, module list, and key runtime state to a well-known path before the process exits.
This capability originated on mobile platforms and is now also available on Linux and macOS. When DOTNET_DbgEnableMiniDump isn't enabled, set DOTNET_EnableCrashReport=1 or DOTNET_EnableCrashReportOnly=1 to select the in-process reporter. Existing createdump behavior remains in place when minidumps are enabled.
NativeAOT: faster interface dispatch
NativeAOT now uses a dispatch helper for interface method calls. Instead of a direct fat-pointer call sequence, the runtime routes interface dispatch through a shared helper that can be patched to the correct implementation after the call site warms up. This reduces the binary size of interface call sites and improves throughput on workloads with many interface method calls.
Generic virtual method dispatch also uses the shared dispatch-cell infrastructure, which improves both monomorphic and polymorphic call performance. In addition, Assembly.GetCallingAssembly() now works on NativeAOT when stack trace data is available.
SIMD lane construction and composition
System.Runtime.Intrinsics now includes lane construction and composition APIs for hardware vector types. The new APIs let you construct a vector from individually specified lanes and extract or reorder lanes between vectors. This enables precise, portable control over SIMD vector element placement without falling back to platform-specific intrinsics.
The new methods fall into a few families:
- Patterned construction: CreateGeometricSequence, CreateAlternatingSequence, and CreateHarmonicSequence build a vector from a starting value and a rule.
- Interleave and de-interleave: Zip, ZipLower/ZipUpper, Unzip, UnzipEven/UnzipOdd.
- Rearrange: The Concat family (ConcatLowerLower, ConcatLowerUpper, ConcatUpperLower, ConcatUpperUpper) and Reverse.
using System.Runtime.Intrinsics;
// {1, 2, 4, 8} — each lane is the previous lane times two
Vector128<int> powers = Vector128.CreateGeometricSequence(1, 2);
// Interleave two vectors lane-by-lane
(Vector128<int> lower, Vector128<int> upper) =
    Vector128.Zip(Vector128.Create(1), Vector128.Create(2));
These APIs are available on Vector128<T>, Vector256<T>, Vector512<T>, Vector64<T>, and Vector<T>. They're building blocks for image processing, audio digital signal processing (DSP), and other SIMD-intensive workloads that need fine-grained control over vector element layout.
File locking on iOS and tvOS
On iOS and tvOS, including simulators, CoreCLR now disables advisory file locking by default. A FileStream that acquired an advisory lock could cause the operating system to terminate an app when the app entered the background while it held the lock. As a result, FileShare restrictions are no longer enforced by those locks on iOS and tvOS, including between handles in the same process. Mac Catalyst and other platforms keep their existing defaults.
If your app relies on FileShare enforcement and you accept the risk of suspension-related termination, restore file locking by using either of the following settings:
- Set the DOTNET_SYSTEM_IO_DISABLEFILELOCKING environment variable to 0.
- Set the System.IO.DisableFileLocking runtime configuration property to false. For example, in the runtimeconfig.json file:
{
  "configProperties": {
    "System.IO.DisableFileLocking": false
  }
}
Reliability fixes
The runtime includes fixes for the following issues:
- On Linux, the SDK no longer crashes on Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) 8 on Arm64, and the runtime correctly traverses cgroup v2 memory limits at the root of the hierarchy.
- Generic virtual method dispatch no longer hangs after repeated AssemblyLoadContext unloads.
- TryDequeue no longer spuriously reports an empty queue while a segment freezes during growth. TryPeek has the same reliability fix.
- On Windows, garbage collection works correctly on machines with multiple CPU groups.
Runtime diagnostics
The async profiler now instruments both runtime-async methods and compiler-generated async state-machine methods, so tools receive one consistent event model regardless of async implementation style. The runtime also adds improved interpreter perf-map logging support, and fixes parsing of CORECLR_NOTIFICATION_PROFILERS lists that don't end with a semicolon.

articles.title: Cyberattacks threaten to make open-source AI a little less open, Hugging Face exec warns
articles.body:
The very qualities that make open AI platforms valuable, like open doors and rich data, might also make them vulnerable to more hacks, Irene Solaiman, chief policy officer and SVP of strategy at Hugging Face said on a recent episode of the Equity podcast.
The October attack on OpenCode, which targeted users’ third-party API keys and caused financial damage, is the latest example. It follows an incident this summer in which an OpenAI agent swarm breached Hugging Face in an apparent attempt to cover its tracks after accessing answers to cybersecurity evaluations.
The risks aren’t limited to platforms that invite open community contributions. On Monday, AI infrastructure startup Fireworks, which helps developers run and train open AI models, disclosed that attackers had accessed some customers’ model weights, datasets, and billing information. The company temporarily disabled certain self-service dataset functions as it investigates. While the attack isn’t necessarily due to Fireworks’ openness, it highlights how much valuable information is concentrated within AI infrastructure providers.
“The things I worry about making an open community targeted are also what makes it special,” Solaiman said on Equity. “We are necessarily permissive. We want the average hobbyist in their basement who doesn’t have an institutional affiliation to be able to contribute.”
“You want people to be able to just submit pull requests and allow anybody without a valid affiliation to contribute…but then you have some losers who ruin it for the rest,” she added in a separate conversation.
That permissiveness isn’t the only thing drawing attackers. The wealth of information open platforms host also make them targets. Hugging Face became a temptation for OpenAI’s agent swarm because of the evaluation datasets it holds, whereas OpenCode’s target in this case came from its “juicy third-party API keys,” per Solaiman.
“The combination of that makes us prime targets,” Solaiman told TechCrunch in a separate conversation. She added that there’s a “danger of open source really closing down at a time when we’ve gotten so much public support.”
Much of the industry has come out recently in support of open AI models, including heavy hitters like Nvidia’s Jensen Huang. And increasingly, governments, enterprises and startups are relying on open models to build.
So what would a pullback actually look like? It could theoretically mean restrictions on who can upload models or datasets, more stringent identity verification, or additional vetting of developers before they can access certain features. While these moves could protect platforms from attackers, it could also make it more difficult for independent researchers and hobbyists to participate in communities they would have been welcomed in before.
For now, Hugging Face is trying to avoid that route. Solaiman said the company has been beefing up monitoring tools to catch hacks, as well as taking steps to prevent them. But monitoring can be expensive to maintain, she noted, and not every platform will be able to afford it.
“Administrative access tokens were part of what gave that agent swarm better access, so we just rotate them a lot more frequently than we used to,” Solaiman said. “We also now have stricter network controls.”
In other words, the credentials that give admins broad access to Hugging Face’s systems now get changed more often, which means a stolen token would be useful for less time.
Other parts of the open source ecosystem are dealing with similar security-related tradeoffs. GitHub, the world’s largest host for open-source projects, has been fighting off attackers who inject malicious code into projects to quickly spread malware. The company began tightening security requirements for publishing packages to the npm registry, revoking older authentication tokens, and limiting how long new ones remain valid.
Zach Steindler, an engineer at GitHub who handles software supply chain security, told TechCrunch via email that while security measures can disrupt established workflows, the platforms can become more secure without fundamentally restricting participation.
“It’s less about limiting functionality and more about going and fixing things that weren’t secure in the first place,” Steindler said. He noted that npm install scripts have existed for years, but recent attacks highlighted how dangerous they could be. GitHub worked with OpenJS — a nonprofit that hosts critical open-source projects built with JavaScript — on a safer approach.
The same logic applies to where security teams put their effort, per Steindler: “Security is all about maximizing impact with the resources we have, and I would much rather invest in detecting suspicious behavior and containment capabilities: things that cover all accounts and access methods. Suspicious behavior is suspicious regardless of who is exhibiting it.”

articles.title: Payments Canada announces launch of Canada's Real-Time Rail (RTR) payment system
articles.body:
Canada launches the Real-Time Rail, bringing 24/7 payment infrastructure to the national economy
The new system will enable participating financial service providers to clear and settle payments in real time, providing a made-in-Canada platform for future innovation and prosperity.
OTTAWA, ON, November 9, 2026 – Payments Canada today announced the launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail (RTR). This new national payment system will transform day-to-day payments for Canadian businesses and consumers by enabling instant speed and settlement, real-time cash-flow visibility and data-rich messaging through existing banking and payment channels.
The launch of Canada’s RTR marks a major milestone in modernizing the critical infrastructure that underpins Canada’s economy and future growth. The RTR will enable participating members, including financial institutions, credit unions and payment service providers, to exchange, clear and settle payments securely in real time for their customers, 24 hours a day, every day of the year.
“A stronger, more productive economy relies on modern financial infrastructure that can match our ambition,” said the Honourable François-Philippe Champagne, Minister of Finance and National Revenue. “The launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail lays the foundation for a more dynamic and competitive digital economy, driving innovation, expanding choice and creating new opportunities for Canadians while positioning our country for long-term growth.”
“The launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail marks the beginning of a new era for payments in our country,” said Susan E. Hawkins, President and CEO, Payments Canada. “As a national asset that’s designed specifically for our country, the RTR gives the payment ecosystem a modern foundation to build on. By collectively leveraging this rail, our ecosystem will unleash its full potential, enabling our members to build capabilities that drive innovation, resilience and growth for businesses and consumers across the nation.”
Ron Morrow, the Honourable François-Philippe Champagne and Susan E. Hawkins
The RTR will drive significant cost savings and economic growth in Canada over the next decade. The C.D. Howe Institute projects that, with its functionalities at launch, the RTR will generate up to $14.5 billion in cost savings from lower processing costs, reduced use of cash and cheques, and reduced float (the period during which funds are temporarily unavailable to the recipient). Extending beyond these cost savings, the RTR is expected to generate $16 billion in economic gains, growing to $27 billion as new functionalities are introduced over time.
“The Real-Time Rail is an important step in modernizing Canada's payment infrastructure and ensuring it keeps pace with Canadians' evolving needs,” said Tiff Macklem, Governor of the Bank of Canada. “The Bank will oversee the system so that it operates safely and reliably while ensuring Canadians can benefit from innovations in financial services.”
Owned and operated by Payments Canada, and built in collaboration with delivery partners CGI, Deloitte Canada, IBM Canada and Interac Corp., the RTR leverages ISO 20022 data-rich messaging. Through this shared technical language, the RTR holds the potential to strengthen Canada’s economic sovereign autonomy and support its global competitiveness.
Fraud safeguards from day one
Canada is the first G7 country to deploy a real-time payment system with mandatory centralized fraud services for use at launch. These services will be used alongside participants’ existing fraud controls to mitigate the risk of fraud for Canadian businesses and consumers at multiple levels. Fraud controls required at the launch of Canada’s RTR include:
- Confirmation of payee (available for consumer accounts on day one)
- A fraud transaction “safety” score
- A risk list or repository of fraud risks and indicators
- A fraud reporting and intelligence platform
While no system is entirely immune to risk, these measures establish a strong, coordinated layer of defence across the payment network.
At-launch member participants
The initial cohort of active RTR system participants includes:
- Wealthsimple
- Questbank
- Peoples Trust Company
- Paramount Commerce
- KOHO
- DoBusiness.com™
- Digital Commerce Bank
- Bank of America
Canada’s deliberately sequenced RTR rollout pairs day-one security with rapid scalability. With additional participants onboarding continually in the coming months, including all major Canadian financial institutions and other members applying for access, the RTR will be available to more than nine in 10 Canadians within the first year after launch.
Made-in Canada, for Canada
The launch of the RTR reflects our ‘Team Canada’ approach, bringing together regulators, members, stakeholders and delivery partners around a shared vision. Built in Canada and designed to serve all Canadians, the RTR provides accessible payment infrastructure through existing banking and payment channels. This infrastructure supports a diverse country and a broad range of communities, including small businesses, newcomers and people in rural areas.
Payments Canada research found that 60 per cent of Canadian businesses are ready to adopt real-time payments to address everyday challenges such as forecasting cash flow and waiting to send and receive funds. More than half of surveyed consumers (52 per cent) also expressed interest and intent to use real-time payments.
To meet this evolving need, the RTR serves as a secure platform for innovation. With it, system participants can build and offer products and services that benefit consumers and businesses across the country, supporting a changing economy and Canada's future prosperity.
An infrastructure for the future
Canada’s Real-Time Rail is an important step toward a more productive, innovative and inclusive economy, and the work will continue to ensure the country’s payment infrastructure meets Canadians’ evolving needs.
Learn more about Canada’s Real-Time Rail
Contributed quotes
At-launch member participants
"When Canada embraces new technology, innovation and competition follow, and consumers benefit. Canadians deserve instant, seamless, low-cost financial products to power their businesses and their lives. The Real-Time Rail can transform how money moves in this country, with payments that arrive in seconds instead of days. We’re proud to be among the first institutions to join the RTR and bring this technology to the millions of Canadians who trust us with their money."
Mike Katchen, CEO and Co-Founder
Wealthsimple
"Canadians deserve a modern financial system that operates at the speed of everyday life. The launch of the Real-Time Rail is a pivotal turning point—it puts individuals in direct, immediate control of their money around the clock. We are proud to join Payments Canada in unlocking a safer, more dynamic financial ecosystem for everyone across the country."
Rob Galaski, President
Questrade Financial Group (Questbank)
"The launch of the Real-Time Rail is a transformative milestone for Canada’s financial ecosystem. As a proud member of Payments Canada and a settlement agent at launch, Peoples Group is pleased to support the foundational clearing and settlement that brings real-time payments to life. We are committed to supporting innovative businesses across the country, and look forward to direct participation as the rail expands to serve even more Canadians."
David Raju, President and CEO
Peoples Group
"Being first-to-market on the Real-Time Rail lets our merchants and partners benefit immediately from 24/7 settlement, higher transaction limits and proactive fraud defence. As one of Payments Canada's first payment service provider (PSP) members, we’re proud to have worked alongside their team to help advance Canada’s payment infrastructure and support the next chapter of payments innovation."
Sereena Boparai, Chief Revenue Officer
Paramount Commerce
"The Real-Time Rail is a significant step forward for the integrity and resilience of Canada's payment infrastructure. Building payment systems that are instant, secure and always on takes real rigour, and it's the kind of foundation a modern financial system depends on. We're excited to be part of this work with Payments Canada, and to help ensure Canadians benefit from payment infrastructure built to the highest standards.”
David Merriby, CEO
The future KOHO Bank
“DoBusiness.com™ is honoured to be one of the very first participants on Canada’s Real-Time Rail. The RTR's launch represents a milestone in how money moves across Canada and its payments sovereignty. For us, faster payments and superior fraud prevention belong together. This is an opportunity for us to help Canadian businesses modernize how they pay and verify account details before money moves.”
Shayle Rothman, CEO and Co-Founder
DoBusiness.com™
“We’re proud to be part of the Team Canada effort that brought the Real-Time Rail to life. For years we’ve helped fintechs and other corporate clients build and launch the payment services Canadians use every day. With the RTR, those companies can now give their customers faster, more robust ways to move money, right from launch.”
Jeff Smith, CEO
DCBank
"The Real-Time Rail is an important investment in Canada's economic future. Instant, data-rich payments will give Canadian businesses and their trading partners more visibility and control over their cash, and we look forward to bringing those benefits to our clients.”
Lyndsay Langford, Head of Global Payments Solutions for Canada
Bank of America
Delivery partners
“Canada’s Real-Time Rail is a significant milestone and a powerful example of what national collaboration can achieve. More than a modernization of payments, it represents an investment in critical infrastructure that will support Canada’s digital economy for generations to come. CGI is proud to have contributed alongside Payments Canada, Interac and our fellow delivery partners to this made-in-Canada initiative. Together, we’re laying the foundation for faster, more secure and resilient payments, opening new opportunities for businesses, financial institutions and Canadians. Through this work, we’re helping build what’s next for Canada’s digital economy.”
Michael Godin, President, Canada Operations
CGI
“Deloitte is very proud to have supported Payments Canada and its members deliver the technical solution for the Real-Time Rail project. This ‘made-in-Canada’ initiative will be a critical foundation for innovation and productivity in Canada while better protecting Canadians against financial crimes. We look forward to welcoming new members to the RTR and continued collaboration for the benefit of Canadians.”
Todd Roberts, Global Payments Leader
Deloitte Canada
“Canadians expect payments to be fast and easy, but behind that experience, the infrastructure has to be secure, resilient and built for the future. Building a real-time payment system at this scale takes deep payments and technology experience, relentless testing and close collaboration. As the technology implementation partner, IBM Canada has worked alongside Payments Canada and its partners to bring that experience to the Real-Time Rail, helping build a strong foundation for the next generation of payments and innovation in Canada.”
Matthew Wetmore, Managing Partner and Market Leader, Consulting
IBM Canada
“As the RTR’s Technical Operator and first Fraud Services Provider, Interac is proud to support Payments Canada and the wider payment ecosystem in achieving this historic launch milestone. We bring more than 40 years of experience to these roles, and our commitment is clear: to operate always-on infrastructure Canadians can trust. As Interac e-Transfer payments begin to clear and settle on the RTR, we will put this world-class infrastructure to work for consumers and businesses.”
Jeremy Wilmot, President and CEO
Interac Corp.
Payments Canada Member and Stakeholder Advisory Councils
“The launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail is a significant milestone for Canada’s payment ecosystem and reflects the sustained commitment and collective effort of members in bringing it to launch. The RTR establishes a modern, made-in-Canada foundation for real-time, data-rich payments that will support innovation, efficiency and improved payment experiences. As members build on this foundation, the focus will be on delivering new capabilities and experiences that create real value for consumers and businesses across Canada."
Michael Liberty
Vice President, Global Money Operations, CIBC
Payments Canada Member Advisory Council Chair
“The launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail is an important milestone for the stakeholder community and for the future of payments in Canada. By creating greater access to real-time payment infrastructure, the RTR opens new opportunities for stakeholders across the ecosystem to participate, innovate and compete. The RTR is a platform that enables new ideas, products and services that can deliver more seamless payment experiences for Canadians, and on behalf of the Stakeholder Advisory Council, we look forward to seeing what new possibilities this creates for payments in Canada.”
Daniela Aubry
Chief Payments Officer, Metrolinx
Payments Canada Stakeholder Advisory Council Chair
“We are very proud to contribute to this major milestone in the modernization of payments in Canada. This is a true collective effort, made possible through outstanding collaboration among the various industry stakeholders. This initiative demonstrates what we can achieve together to advance financial infrastructure for the benefit of businesses and Canadians.”
Patrice Roy
Head of Payments, National Bank
Payments Canada Member Advisory Council Vice-Chair
Key member program contributors
“The Real-Time Rail is a powerful foundation for new business models, greater competition and economic growth across Canada. We're thrilled that Brim Financial is a future participant in Canada's Real-Time Rail. Brim's Payments-as-a-Service platform capabilities will enable real-time money movement, payments and intelligent commercial workflows in one unified ecosystem. This empowers our clients to accelerate innovation, unlock new opportunities, optimize liquidity and deliver transformative customer experiences.”
Rasha Katabi, Founder and CEO
Brim
“The launch of the Real-Time Rail is a significant milestone in the modernization of Canada’s payment systems. Central 1 has invested in the infrastructure, capabilities and expertise to enable our clients to participate in real-time payments without the complexity to build and operate the underlying infrastructure themselves. Through that investment, we’re helping our clients unlock the benefits of real-time payments and extend those benefits to millions of Canadians.”
Sunny Soin, Vice President, Product and Platform - Payments
Central 1
“In today’s high-velocity commercial environment, there is need for instant, frictionless settlement backed by world-class technology. By deploying our proprietary Citi Payment Express platform for Canada’s Real-Time Rail, we are giving our clients immediate access to 24/7 real-time settlement and rich ISO 20022 remittance data via a high-availability, low-latency platform designed for instant payments. It is a powerful example of how Citi delivers global-standard technology to solve local market needs.”
Mohneet Gujral, Head of Payments
Citi Canada
“Desjardins is proud to play a role modernizing Canada’s payment infrastructure. The Real-Time Rail will help us better serve the evolving payment needs of our members and clients, today and into the future.”
Johanne Duhaime, Senior Executive Vice President, Technology and Organizational Performance
Desjardins
“The Real-Time Rail represents an important milestone for Canada and the continued modernization of our payment ecosystem. Real-time, always-on payments are changing how businesses move and manage money, from providing greater visibility and control over cash to enabling faster payouts and more seamless payment experiences for their customers. We’re proud to participate in this next chapter for Canadian payments and help our clients capture the opportunities it creates.”
Dougal Middleton, Head of Payments and Treasury Services, Canada
J.P. Morgan
"The launch of the Real-Time Rail is an important milestone in the modernization of Canada's payment ecosystem. Meridian is proud to support this industry-wide effort and the development of payment infrastructure that will help enable faster, more modern payment experiences for Canadians and businesses across the country.”
Matthew Seagrim, Chief Growth Officer
Meridian Credit Union
“The Real-Time Rail holds tremendous potential to empower Canadian consumers and businesses. I want to thank Payments Canada and Finance Canada for turning a sovereign real-time payments network into a reality. The imperative for made-in-Canada infrastructure that protects and supports Canadians, while strengthening domestic dependency, has never been more important. As adoption gains momentum, I look forward to seeing the positive impact that the RTR will have for workers, SMEs and homegrown innovation.”
Dan Broten, Senior Vice President and Chief Digital Officer
EQB Inc. (owner of President’s Choice Bank)
Industry association collaboration
“The CBA welcomes the implementation of the Real‑Time Rail, which will expand to include many of our members across Canada and will help modernize Canada’s payment systems and strengthen the backbone of the country’s financial market infrastructure. Innovation in payment technology continues to be a driving force behind payment choice and efficiency, thereby supporting economic growth in Canada. Security and trust remain paramount to the successful execution of real-time payments. Banks in Canada are dedicated to enabling a safe, fast and secure experience for individuals and businesses, while maintaining a resilient and stable financial system.”
Anthony G. Ostler, President and CEO
Canadian Bankers Association
“The Real-Time Rail is a momentous transformation in how payments are done in Canada. Credit unions and their members will see real benefits, including improved convenience and better cash flow management for small businesses. As part of this phased implementation, we welcome the secure, flexible ways that credit unions will be able to participate in the RTR, so that very soon everyone who banks with a credit union or caisse populaire will experience faster, smarter and more flexible payments.”
Jeff Guthrie, Chief Executive Officer
Canadian Credit Union Association
“Congratulations to Payments Canada on launching the Real-Time Rail. This is a milestone for small businesses, consumers and the innovators building Canada’s next generation of financial services. We look forward to seeing fintechs and financial institutions connect, bring more payments onto the rail and build services that give Canadians and businesses more choice.”
Adriana Vega, Executive Director

articles.title: Payments Canada announces launch of Canada's Real-Time Rail (RTR) payment system
articles.body:
Canada launches the Real-Time Rail, bringing 24/7 payment infrastructure to the national economy
The new system will enable participating financial service providers to clear and settle payments in real time, providing a made-in-Canada platform for future innovation and prosperity.
OTTAWA, ON, November 9, 2026 – Payments Canada today announced the launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail (RTR). This new national payment system will transform day-to-day payments for Canadian businesses and consumers by enabling instant speed and settlement, real-time cash-flow visibility and data-rich messaging through existing banking and payment channels.
The launch of Canada’s RTR marks a major milestone in modernizing the critical infrastructure that underpins Canada’s economy and future growth. The RTR will enable participating members, including financial institutions, credit unions and payment service providers, to exchange, clear and settle payments securely in real time for their customers, 24 hours a day, every day of the year.
“A stronger, more productive economy relies on modern financial infrastructure that can match our ambition,” said the Honourable François-Philippe Champagne, Minister of Finance and National Revenue. “The launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail lays the foundation for a more dynamic and competitive digital economy, driving innovation, expanding choice and creating new opportunities for Canadians while positioning our country for long-term growth.”
“The launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail marks the beginning of a new era for payments in our country,” said Susan E. Hawkins, President and CEO, Payments Canada. “As a national asset that’s designed specifically for our country, the RTR gives the payment ecosystem a modern foundation to build on. By collectively leveraging this rail, our ecosystem will unleash its full potential, enabling our members to build capabilities that drive innovation, resilience and growth for businesses and consumers across the nation.”
Ron Morrow, the Honourable François-Philippe Champagne and Susan E. Hawkins
The RTR will drive significant cost savings and economic growth in Canada over the next decade. The C.D. Howe Institute projects that, with its functionalities at launch, the RTR will generate up to $14.5 billion in cost savings from lower processing costs, reduced use of cash and cheques, and reduced float (the period during which funds are temporarily unavailable to the recipient). Extending beyond these cost savings, the RTR is expected to generate $16 billion in economic gains, growing to $27 billion as new functionalities are introduced over time.
“The Real-Time Rail is an important step in modernizing Canada's payment infrastructure and ensuring it keeps pace with Canadians' evolving needs,” said Tiff Macklem, Governor of the Bank of Canada. “The Bank will oversee the system so that it operates safely and reliably while ensuring Canadians can benefit from innovations in financial services.”
Owned and operated by Payments Canada, and built in collaboration with delivery partners CGI, Deloitte Canada, IBM Canada and Interac Corp., the RTR leverages ISO 20022 data-rich messaging. Through this shared technical language, the RTR holds the potential to strengthen Canada’s economic sovereign autonomy and support its global competitiveness.
Fraud safeguards from day one
Canada is the first G7 country to deploy a real-time payment system with mandatory centralized fraud services for use at launch. These services will be used alongside participants’ existing fraud controls to mitigate the risk of fraud for Canadian businesses and consumers at multiple levels. Fraud controls required at the launch of Canada’s RTR include:
- Confirmation of payee (available for consumer accounts on day one)
- A fraud transaction “safety” score
- A risk list or repository of fraud risks and indicators
- A fraud reporting and intelligence platform
While no system is entirely immune to risk, these measures establish a strong, coordinated layer of defence across the payment network.
At-launch member participants
The initial cohort of active RTR system participants includes:
- Wealthsimple
- Questbank
- Peoples Trust Company
- Paramount Commerce
- KOHO
- DoBusiness.com™
- Digital Commerce Bank
- Bank of America
Canada’s deliberately sequenced RTR rollout pairs day-one security with rapid scalability. With additional participants onboarding continually in the coming months, including all major Canadian financial institutions and other members applying for access, the RTR will be available to more than nine in 10 Canadians within the first year after launch.
Made-in Canada, for Canada
The launch of the RTR reflects our ‘Team Canada’ approach, bringing together regulators, members, stakeholders and delivery partners around a shared vision. Built in Canada and designed to serve all Canadians, the RTR provides accessible payment infrastructure through existing banking and payment channels. This infrastructure supports a diverse country and a broad range of communities, including small businesses, newcomers and people in rural areas.
Payments Canada research found that 60 per cent of Canadian businesses are ready to adopt real-time payments to address everyday challenges such as forecasting cash flow and waiting to send and receive funds. More than half of surveyed consumers (52 per cent) also expressed interest and intent to use real-time payments.
To meet this evolving need, the RTR serves as a secure platform for innovation. With it, system participants can build and offer products and services that benefit consumers and businesses across the country, supporting a changing economy and Canada's future prosperity.
An infrastructure for the future
Canada’s Real-Time Rail is an important step toward a more productive, innovative and inclusive economy, and the work will continue to ensure the country’s payment infrastructure meets Canadians’ evolving needs.
Learn more about Canada’s Real-Time Rail

We’re proud to be among the first institutions to join the RTR and bring this technology to the millions of Canadians who trust us with their money."

We are committed to supporting innovative businesses across the country, and look forward to direct participation as the rail expands to serve even more Canadians."
David Raju, President and CEO

articles.title: Here’s what Trump said he knew about Jensen Huang
articles.body:
President Trump held a White House press briefing earlier today and responded to several questions about his knowledge of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Huang said this weekend that he had been “unfaithful” to his wife, and the company has opened an investigation into Huang.
Here’s what Trump said he knew about Jensen Huang
In a White House press conference, President Trump was vague about when learned of Jensen Huang’s affair.
Recent articles from The New York Times indicated that Trump had been aware of a relationship between Huang and Alice Huang, the suspected spy, before information about it became public. In October, The New York Times reported that Trump had been briefed “roughly a year ago” on intelligence that Huang and the alleged spy, Alice Huang, had developed a close relationship, but he didn’t do anything with the information. Yesterday, the NYT reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio helped draft a memo to Trump officials about the relationship before Trump visited China in May.
In the press conference, Trump wasn’t specific about when he learned of the affair. But Trump said Huang told him today that he had “no idea” the person was a spy.
Here are Trump’s responses to questions about Jensen Huang from his press briefing today. You can watch a replay of the press conference on MS Now’s YouTube channel.
When were you first informed that there was an issue with Jensen Huang and the affair? What was presented to you at the time?
I would say that when I heard about it, first of all, I was amazed because I view him as a very high-quality person. I’ve known him a long time. It’s the largest, by value, the largest or one of the largest companies in the world. He did that with a chip. When you think about it, you’ve got a chip that’s 10 years advanced, can’t be… the Blackwell can’t even be copied. He’s an amazing guy.
I just hope there’s no problem. If there is a problem, we’ll let you know about it. But I hope there’s no problem. I believe he’s suffering greatly. I read his statement. And I believe he’s suffering greatly. Moreso because of his family. His wife who he loves and his family. But he is definitely suffering.
Just to follow up on the, “When were you first told of these potential issues with Mr. Huang?” You didn’t answer that question.
Well I’ve been hearing about it, and I’ve been reading a little bit about it over a period of time. But, not too long ago.
When is that?
We’ll look into it. I know the FBI’s looking into it in terms of something else. I think that he’ll be in good shape.
…
Are you going to bring up the case of Jensen Huang with President Xi when you visit with him next week?
No, I don’t think so. Maybe, I’m sure, President Xi will ask me about it. I just know Jensen very well. I just think he’s a very honorable man. He built a great company. American company. I think he’s a very honorable guy. I feel very confident that he’ll be in good shape.
Sticking with Jensen Huang, when you went to China earlier this year in May, did you know about these alleged ties to the spy then?
No, I didn’t hear about it then. But a lot of people have heard about it. And Jensen totally denies that. I asked him today, because I did speak to him today just to see if he’s feeling alright, how are you doing… and I asked him about that. He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy. I asked him that question, did you have any idea that she was a spy? He said, I had no idea that she was a spy. And I really believe him.
…
I want to put a finer point on when exactly you were made aware of the intelligence around Jensen Huang.
Oh, I’d have to check. But this has been going on…
But there are reports that Secretary Rubio put an intelligence memo out last year. Did you read that memo?
I’d certainly check with the intelligence people. It could have been mentioned. Certainly it didn’t make much of an impact on me.

articles.title: Everything we know so far about the Nvidia spy scandal targeting CEO Jensen Huang
articles.body:
The leather-jacketed CEO of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, has acknowledged an affair with Megaspeed exec Alice Huang, spurring an investigation by his company and intense discussions worldwide. Recent reporting noted that since last year, US intelligence reports had identified Alice Huang (no relation) as not only the exec for an AI compute company renting access to Nvidia GPUs, but also a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security.
In recent years, Nvidia has become a key part of the Trump administration’s AI push, a central figure in negotiations over potential Chinese access to cutting-edge AI hardware, and a company that has used its now $4 trillion-plus market cap to finance other AI companies, including the “neoclouds” like Coreweave who have been some of its biggest customers. So far, Nvidia and Jensen Huang have said that they have “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised,” but that hasn’t settled things as the investigation continues.
- What could China get from Jensen Huang? It’s difficult to overstate Nvidia’s power in today’s AI landscape. The company’s chips are the bedrock upon which advanced AI technology in the US is being built, and demand has consistently outpaced supply for years. Nvidia has also been an influential investor in a wide range of up-and-coming AI companies in recent years, with about $99 billion worth of equity investments in frontier AI labs, neoclouds, infrastructure companies, and more. Its chief executive has even become close with President Donald Trump. This is why, as both cofounder and longtime CEO of Nvidia, Jensen Huang would be a valuable target for a foreign adversary with sights on the American AI industry. Read Article >

- The future of AI hinges on… Jensen Huang’s sex life? I would prefer that these people’s sex lives were none of my business but I guess we have to talk about Jensen Huang and the National Security Incident. Who could have guessed that the guy who was out here signing titties might not have great judgment about how to behave around women? Alice Huang — no relation to Jensen — is a former TV reporter. That was before she became “an executive” at Megaspeed, which bought $4.8 billion of hard-to-get Nvidia chips, starting around the time she was being photographed with Jensen in a Taipei bar in 2024. “To many in the industry, the well-funded push by Megaspeed into A.I. appeared to come out of nowhere,” The New York Times wrote, tactfully. Our girl Alice is also an alleged honeypot who was recruited by the Chinese Ministry of State Security. (China is denying all this, btw.) Read Article >

In addition to the Board of Directors announcing the investigation, Huang sent a memo to Nvidia employees acknowledging the affair. You can read the full text below. Read Article >

The New York Times reported last month that Huang had developed a “close relationship” with the Megaspeed executive, which he later admitted was romantic in nature in a memo to the company. US officials believe she was feeding information directly back to Beijing. Read Article >

articles.title: Commerce Dept. Chip Inquiry Was Halted After Nvidia Intervention
articles.body:
Commerce Dept. Chip Inquiry Was Halted After Nvidia Intervention (nytimes.com) 46
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from The New York Times: Investigators at the Commerce Department were deep into a monthslong investigation of a Singaporean company that they suspected of smuggling Nvidia's artificial intelligence chips into China when their work came to a sudden halt late last year. The investigation centered on Megaspeed, a data center company led by an executive who U.S. officials now believe to be a Chinese spy who had a relationship with Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang. But the case was abruptly transferred to the Justice Department last year. The shift came after Commerce Department investigators working on the case received an email from Nvidia's general counsel seeking information about the inquiry into Megaspeed.
It is not necessarily unusual for Commerce Department agents working on a case to speak with a company's representatives about issues involving their firm. But what was unusual was the content of the message. Tim Teter, Nvidia's general counsel, said that Jeff Kessler, a top official at the department, had given Nvidia permission to reach out about the case. The agents were alarmed that Nvidia had invoked the name of Mr. Kessler, their superior, who was nominated to his role by President Trump. Some viewed Mr. Kessler's interaction with Nvidia as violating government procedure and potentially tainting the case, according to current and former government officials and others familiar with the incident.
It is not clear what led to Mr. Teter's outreach to the department, but the recent revelations about Mr. Huang's acknowledged affair with a Megaspeed executive have only intensified scrutiny of Nvidia's role in influencing policy on chip sales to China. [...] The incident raised questions about what Mr. Kessler, who reports directly to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, had discussed with Nvidia. It also raised the possibility that those discussions could become their own subject of inquiry. Perhaps inadvertently, some officials said, Mr. Kessler had opened himself to accusations of undue influence and potentially jeopardized his department's work on Megaspeed. The case was quickly transferred to the Justice Department in an effort to avoid any potential compromise of the government's investigation of Megaspeed, these people said. The Justice Department is conducting a criminal inquiry into Megaspeed, according to people familiar with the matter.

articles.title: The race is on to sue Nvidia
articles.body:
Nvidia’s stock slid more than 4% on Monday, the first trading day after its board said it would investigate CEO Jensen Huang over his relationship with Alice Huang, an executive U.S. intelligence believes was spying for China.
Securities lawyers were already moving. At least four firms, including Schall, Brown & Schwartz and Levi & Korsinsky, announced investigations Monday into whether Nvidia misled investors. Robert Bartlett, a Stanford Law professor and securities law expert, expects them to have plenty of company.
“I would definitely wager that there’ll be a filing,” Bartlett said in an interview Monday morning, adding that he wouldn’t be surprised if a case had been filed by the end of the day. Plaintiffs’ lawyers have good reasons to be first in line; under federal securities law, the first complaint triggers a public notice, and investors then have 60 days to ask the court to be named lead plaintiff. A firm that files early gets a head start on signing up investors with large losses, as well as on shaping the story of the case. Bartlett was right, in fact. A case surfaced Monday afternoon in the Northern District of California, where Nvidia is headquartered.
Rosen Law Firm, a New York-based plaintiffs’ firm that specializes in securities class actions, filed it on behalf of Mark Kistenmacher, a retail investor who made seven purchases totaling roughly $20,500 this year, according to a schedule attached to the complaint. (Rosen was lead counsel in a $250 million settlement with Alibaba and ranks among the most active filers of such cases.) The proposed class covers anyone who bought Nvidia securities between Oct. 9, 2025, and Nov. 8, 2026, and the suit names both Nvidia and Huang.
The complaint accuses them of misleading investors about Huang’s ties to Megaspeed, the Singapore-based data center outfit where Alice Huang was considered a top exec, and it points to three statements as proof: Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo’s late-October claim that Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang were “not unusual or unexpected,” the company’s even earlier claim that it found “no evidence of diversion” of its chips, and Jensen Huang’s Oct. 30 comment to Bloomberg that Nvidia’s dealings with Megaspeed were “normal and not unusual.”
All three were false or misleading, the suit says, because Huang was having an affair with Alice Huang. Kistenmacher is asking for unspecified damages, interest and attorneys’ fees, and he wants a jury trial.
While much remains unknown, the legal theory here doesn’t depend on anything the board’s investigation may turn up about Huang’s private life. When The New York Times first reported on Huang’s ties to Alice Huang last month, Rizzo really did tell the Times that the relationship was “not unusual or unexpected.” Rizzo separately told another outlet, The Hill, that “Megaspeed has been no different than many other regional cloud customers. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.”
Of course, the world now knows that was not true. Worse, the Times reports that U.S. intelligence had been monitoring Alice Huang for more than a year.
From a securities perspective, Bartlett said, the company’s earlier statement was “clearly a misleading statement.” And because Huang is CEO, Bartlett said, “his knowledge gets imputed to the company.” In other words, Nvidia is treated as having known what its chief executive knew.
The Kistenmacher complaint makes the same argument.
Bartlett predicted a “classic fraud on the market” claim, in which investors argue they paid prices that reflected false or incomplete public information, and lost money when the truth emerged. This early lawsuit relies on that theory, and Monday’s drop of $7.97 per share, or 4.27%, gives the attorneys involved a lot to work with. Damages in such cases are tied to the stock’s decline, and Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies in the world, so you can imagine a settlement could prove exceedingly expensive.
That means a large payment from the company and its directors-and-officers insurers, but typically no personal consequences for the CEO or the board. It is also a civil matter, so Huang isn’t facing prison over it. The irony, as Bartlett noted, is that the suit is brought in the name of Nvidia’s shareholders, and shareholders ultimately pay for the settlement, directly or through insurance premiums.
Bartlett sorted Nvidia’s wider exposure into buckets. The first is the securities fraud claim, which is the clearest immediate problem for the company and potentially for Huang. The second is governance: what the board knew and when. It’s possible directors were kept in the dark, but the board also has oversight duties, and once the Times began reporting on the Megaspeed connection, the company should have had reporting lines to bring a critical risk like this to directors. If it didn’t, or if directors didn’t act, board-level liability is possible.
A third category, one that would change everything, would arise only if the board’s investigation finds Huang knew about the intelligence connection. That would be “a whole other ball game,” as Bartlett said. (The board said in a statement to the public Sunday that it has no reason to believe national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.)
There’s also the question of government action. The SEC can seek an officer-and-director bar for intentional securities-fraud violations, which Bartlett said is technically on the table. But he doubts the current SEC under Chairman Paul Atkins would have the appetite, given President Trump’s support for Huang. A roughly two-year clock after discovery of the facts would leave room for a future administration to act, but the window would be tight, and Bartlett posited that’s pretty unlikely when asked about it.
It’s worth underscoring that neither law firm announcements nor this newly filed complaint is a sign of a strong case. Plaintiffs’ firms are quick to publish these notices when they see an opportunity. Which firm winds up leading the case is decided later by the court, and that decision usually depends on which investor has suffered the biggest loss. Kistenmacher said in his filing that he’s willing to serve as lead plaintiff, but the court will ultimately choose among the competing investors. No doubt they’ll materialize soon.

articles.title: ClickHouse Acquires Xata
articles.body:
Xata is joining ClickHouse
By:
Monica Sarbu
Published:
Reading time:
6 min read
Today, we're excited to announce that Xata is joining ClickHouse to bring agentic capabilities to ClickHouse Managed Postgres.
Together with ClickHouse, we're building a Postgres platform designed for modern applications and AI agents, combining high-performance production workloads on local NVMe storage with Xata’s technology for instant database provisioning, instant copy-on-write branching, and scale-to-zero compute.
Nothing changes for Xata customers in the short term and we continue to accept new sign-ups. In parallel, we're working on bringing branching and an agentic tier to ClickHouse Managed Postgres. We will eventually migrate Xata customers to ClickHouse Managed Postgres. You can also read ClickHouse's announcement.
What is Xata
It’s undeniable that this year software development has changed forever, with agents and software factories now doing the grunt work. However, the increase in coding output has uncovered new bottlenecks. For many companies the database workflows are now the bottleneck: every pull request and every agent run needs a safe, isolated database with production-like data.
Traditionally, creating a copy of a production database is a slow and expensive process, especially when dealing with terabytes of data. Creating a database for every pull request or agent run simply doesn't scale with traditional cloning. With copy-on-write branching, however, there's no need to copy the data, making it possible to create a new branch with production data in seconds.
This is exactly what we’ve built at Xata. Even if a database has multiple terabytes of data, creating a branch takes only around 3 seconds. This means the schema and the data appear as if they were instantly copied to the child branch. At the same time, the child branch is fully independent: it has its own compute, running on a different physical node, and nothing that happens on the child branch impacts the parent database.
The key capabilities are:
- Instant database provisioning: Create a new, fully functional Postgres database instantly.
- Instant copy-on-write branching: Create database branches in seconds, without duplicating the underlying data. You only pay for the diff: create 50 branches of a 1TB database and you’re billed for something much closer to 1TB than 50TB.
- Scale-to-zero compute: Automatically suspend idle databases and wake them on the next connection, in about one second, minimizing costs.
- Anonymized production data: Remove sensitive information before data leaves production, so developers and agents can safely work with database branches.
Together, these capabilities make it remarkably cheap to run a branch per PR, per agent run, or even per SQL session. AI-native customers like Sapien, Enginy, David AI, Runner AI, and LoopAI each create thousands of database branches every week.
You might also know Xata from our open-source projects in the Postgres ecosystem, including pgstream, for logical replication with anonymization and DDL support, and pgroll, for zero-downtime, reversible schema changes.
Why ClickHouse
Earlier this year, ClickHouse launched ClickHouse Managed Postgres, which became generally available today. Built on local NVMe storage, it's currently the fastest Postgres service out there, and not by a small margin.
When we started talking with the ClickHouse Managed Postgres team, it quickly became clear just how complementary the two services are: ClickHouse Managed Postgres is optimized for high-throughput, long-lived production workloads, while Xata is designed to provision large numbers of small, short-lived databases in seconds, with production-like data and capabilities like instant branching and scale-to-zero that are particularly well suited for agentic workloads.
Both platforms run unmodified vanilla Postgres and share a strong focus on reliability and stability. The common foundation puts us in a great position to move quickly on integrating the two platforms. In fact, David AI is an example of a customer that already uses ClickHouse Managed Postgres and Xata together and they shared the following with us:
As an AI company working with large volumes of data, we need reliable infrastructure that help us move fast. We moved from Neon to ClickHouse Managed Postgres for better reliability and performance, and our users immediately noticed how much faster everything felt. Xata’s branching has been a great fit for our devs (and AI coding agents!), making it easy to build and test in parallel. Bringing both together means high-performance Postgres and instant branching in a single platform, simplifying our infrastructure and giving our team more time to build.
Best-in-class OLTP and OLAP
By almost any measure, Postgres is the most popular OLTP database and ClickHouse is the most popular OLAP database. Combining the two is something teams have been stitching together themselves for years. The Postgres team at ClickHouse has been making that integration first-class: very fast replication from Postgres into ClickHouse and a unified query layer to build applications.
An integrated transactional and analytical data platform is something we've wanted to build since Xata's early days, when our first product paired Postgres with a search and analytics engine.
On a personal level, we've long admired ClickHouse and already knew the founders and many of the engineers, which gives us confidence that together we can take this vision much further.
What Xata enables
A database branch for every pull request and agent run
The GitHub integration enables automatically creating an isolated database branch for every pull request. These branches can be integrated into CI/CD pipelines, allowing code changes to be safely tested before merging into production. Since they are only needed for testing, branches are often scaling to zero after only a few minutes, minimizing costs.
The same approach applies to coding agents, where every agent run can have its own isolated database to develop and test changes without affecting production.
For details on the branch-per-PR use case and the cost savings it provides, see this blog post.
Powering AI platforms
AI platforms that embed Postgres are seeing an explosion in demand: first thousands, then hundreds of thousands, and eventually millions of databases per week. There are two main use cases: instant database provisioning for every new application, and a database branch for every deployment preview, allowing code changes to be tested safely against production data.
Because unused databases scale to zero, platforms can run very large fleets of small, mostly idle databases at a fraction of the cost, while keeping full compatibility, since it's simply vanilla Postgres.
How it works
Two key technologies enable fast branching and short wake-up times: our Xatastor storage engine and warm pools for compute instances.
Xatastor is our storage engine, which provides separation of storage and compute, high multi-tenancy, copy-on-write branching, compression, thin provisioning, and more. It exposes ZFS zvols over the network using the NVMe/TCP protocol. Because it works at the block-device level, we can run unmodified vanilla PostgreSQL. For a deep-dive into the Xatastor architecture, see this dedicated blog post.
We use warm pools of compute instances to obtain super fast provisioning, wake-up after scale-to-zero, and branching times. This removes the actual node and pod provisioning from the hot path of making a new database or branch available. You can find more information about how this works in this blog post.
What's next
Building Xata has been an incredible journey over the last five years. We're extremely proud of the technology we've built, and even more proud of the team behind it, which is now joining ClickHouse.
We've tackled some really difficult engineering challenges, and it's been incredibly rewarding to see developers and customers embrace these capabilities, creating exponentially more branches as they expand their usage.
What excites us most about this next chapter is that the vision behind Xata is more relevant than ever, and as part of ClickHouse, we're in the best possible position to bring it to fruition.
What this means for you:
- If you're a Xata customer: you can continue using it as usual. We'll integrate Xata's features into ClickHouse Managed Postgres, and once there's feature parity, we'll migrate customers as smoothly as possible, ideally with no impact on the service.
- If you're a ClickHouse Managed Postgres customer: branching, scale-to-zero and an agentic tier are coming to ClickHouse Managed Postgres
- If you're new to both: you can get started with ClickHouse Managed Postgres or sign up for Xata today.
We're excited about what we can build together with ClickHouse, and this is just the beginning.
Give every agentic workload its own Postgres branch
Create instant database clones with production-like data for every agent, workflow, and CI/CD pipeline.
Related Posts
A thousand Postgres branches for $1
See how we reduced branching times from 20+ seconds to around a second and what use-cases these speed improvements enable.
Inside Xatastor: ZFS + NVMe-oF for millions of Postgres databases
Read the technical details of our new distributed storage system, which is the key to scaling to a huge number of Postgres instances.
