articles.title: AI hardware startup Nominal triples valuation to $3B in 8 months
articles.body:
Nominal, a four-year-old, Austin-based startup that offers an AI platform purpose-built for engineering and testing complex hardware, like aircraft, nuclear reactors, and smart factories, has raised another big round of financing that triples its valuation. On Monday, it announced a $240 million Series C at a $3 billion valuation led by Lightspeed Venture Partners and co-led by Insight Partners.
This follows the company’s announcement in March of a $155 million Series B extension at a $1 billion valuation, led by Trae Stephens at Founders Fund. That round was a “preemptive” deal — meaning an offer initiated by the investor, not the startup. Other investors in the company include Sequoia, General Catalyst, and Lux Capital.
Nominal says that it has 80 commercial and government organizations as customers. One of its key customers is Anduril, the defense company co-founded by Stephens. Nominal also won a government contract in October when the Air Force selected it for a $71.2 million Strategic Funding Increase (STRATFI) investment, which is a program that requires matching funds from outside the Air Force.
Nominal CEO and co-founder Cameron McCord (pictured) is a former U.S. Navy submarine officer and an Anduril alum.

articles.title: Show HN: STE80 Humanizer – de-AI text by writing 80% of the way to ASD-STE100
articles.body:
STE80 Humanizer makes AI-written text read like a careful person wrote it, without changing what it says. It combines two methods:
- The humanizer method. Remove the 26 tells from Wikipedia's Signs of AI writing, in the catalog of blader/humanizer.
- Karpathy's STE80 method. Rebuild the sentences "80% of the way to ASD-STE100", the controlled English of aircraft maintenance manuals.
Before:
Great question! Kubernetes liveness probes are a powerful mechanism that enables the kubelet to determine whether a container is healthy — and it's not just a health check, it's your first line of defense. When a probe fails, the container will be automatically restarted by the kubelet, ensuring that your application remains available. However, it's important to note that misconfigured probes could potentially cause cascading restarts, so parameters like initialDelaySeconds and failureThreshold should be carefully tuned.
Get this right, and your cluster heals itself.
After:
A liveness probe tells the kubelet if a container is healthy. If the probe fails, the kubelet restarts the container. This keeps the application available.
A bad probe can also cause many restarts. For example, a timeout that is too short makes healthy containers fail the probe. To prevent this, set initialDelaySeconds and failureThreshold to values that fit your application.
The goal is text that people read easily. Getting past AI detectors is not a goal.
Most humanizers only remove phrases. The text loses "Great question!" and "seamless", but it keeps long sentences that carry three ideas, hide the actor and stack hedges. It still reads like AI. You can see it in the worked example in SKILL.md:
On 2 October 2026, Andrej Karpathy posted tips for one problem: as LLMs do more of the work, people spend more time reading and understanding what the models produce. His first tip:
Ask your LLM to explain something in ASD-STE100, it's a controlled language specification originally developed for aerospace maintenance documentation. LLMs well-versed in this language and it comes with heavy constraints on clean writing style that I often find a lot more readable. Sometimes I've tried to soften it a bit e.g. ask for "80% of the way to ASD-STE100" because the spec is quite stringent.
The post then goes up a ladder: diagrams, then HTML pages, then explainer videos. His conclusion is that our work moves "up the abstractions into oversight and understanding". Clear output is the bottleneck, and writing is the first step.
The STE overview graphic from Karpathy's post. Click to enlarge. Note: a later fact check found errors in the dictionary panel (D). In ASD-STE100 Issue 9, "approximately" is approved, "TEST" is approved only as a noun (not as a verb), and there is no entry for "in order to". This skill follows Issue 9.
ASD-STE100 (Simplified Technical English) is from the 1980s aerospace industry. It was made for mechanics whose first language is not English, because a misread step on an aircraft can kill. Its rules:
- 20 words per instruction and 25 per description
- one instruction per sentence
- active voice and simple tenses
- one meaning per word, with about 900 approved words
- one topic per paragraph, and six sentences at most
Why "80%"? At 100%, "check" and "test" are nouns only, "may" and "should" are banned and many common words are not allowed. Normal prose sounds stiff. At 80%, you keep the full structure and only as much vocabulary as still sounds natural:
Karpathy's tip is about readability. It does not remove chatbot phrases, so Pass 1 does that first.
SKILL.md has two numbered lists:
- §1 to §26: the AI tells (Pass 1).
- S1 to S15: the STE80 structure rules (Pass 2).
Both lists are compact tables with a short example. Pass 2 says what changes between 80% and Strict. The full entries, with Watch for, Problem, Before and After, are in references/ai-tells.md and references/ste80-rules.md. Weak alone means: act only if other tells are near. The skill reports its edits by number, for example "§1, §8, S2", so you can look each one up.
Once installed, the skill answers to /ste80-humanizer. It also starts by itself when you ask to humanize, simplify or de-AI a text, or ask for STE.
npx skills add Dodaios/ste80-humanizer
Global install for one agent, or for all of them:
npx skills add Dodaios/ste80-humanizer --global --agent claude-code
npx skills add Dodaios/ste80-humanizer --global --agent codex
npx skills add Dodaios/ste80-humanizer --global --agent cursor
npx skills add Dodaios/ste80-humanizer --global --agent '*'
Without --global, the skill goes into the current project only. The skills CLI from Vercel works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode and many more agents.
/plugin marketplace add Dodaios/ste80-humanizer
/plugin install ste80-humanizer@ste80-humanizer
Download this repo as a ZIP (Code → Download ZIP). Upload it in Settings → Capabilities → Skills.
/ste80-humanizer
<paste text>
Or just ask:
This sounds like ChatGPT wrote it. Make it sound like a person.
Rewrite this README 80% of the way to ASD-STE100.
Explain how TLS handshakes work in STE.
Light touch: just remove the AI stuff from docs/intro.md.
Convert docs/runbook.md to strict STE.
Does this email sound like AI? Just tell me, don't rewrite it.
Match your voice. Add a sample of your own writing. The skill then matches your sentence length, words and punctuation.
Fidelity first. The skill keeps every fact, keeps "may" as "may", keeps "40+" as "40+", adds nothing and flags contradictions in the source. In our tests, this was the clearest difference from a plain prompt (see Tests).
More examples: references/ste80-rules.md. Full strict rules and a checklist: references/strict-mode.md. More than 100 plain-word swaps: references/word-swaps.md.
scripts/ste_check.py is a small Python linter with no dependencies. It flags many Pass 1 tells, such as not-X-but-Y, chatbot phrases, run-ups, fake depth, stacked hedges, vague authority and association, "-ing" riders, inflated claims, AI words, hyphen pairs and curly quotes. It also flags the measurable Pass 2 rules: sentence and paragraph length, semicolons, dashes, passive voice, perfect and progressive tenses, "-ing" forms and phrasal verbs.
python scripts/ste_check.py README.md
python scripts/ste_check.py --strict docs/runbook.md
cat draft.txt | python scripts/ste_check.py -
It is a heuristic, not an AI detector and not a compliance checker.
evals/ has four cases in the claude plugin eval format: a README rewrite, an explanation from scratch, a strict runbook and a casual LinkedIn post that does not mention STE. Run them with claude plugin eval . --allow-tools Write,Edit,Bash.
What we saw: when the prompt names ASD-STE100, the base model already gets the style mostly right. The skill made the difference in fidelity. In the LinkedIn rewrite, the run without the skill invented a quote and changed "40+ customers" to "40-odd". The run with the skill kept every fact. In the README rewrite, it kept "you may need to" and flagged a contradiction in the source. These are small tests, so treat them as a hint, not proof.
- STE is for clear explanatory text. For fiction, speeches and brand copy, the skill does Pass 1 only.
- STE is an English standard. For other languages, the skill applies the tells and the structure rules, but not the English word lists.
- "STE style" is not "STE compliant." Compliance needs the official dictionary, trained writers and review.
- Andrej Karpathy on X, 2 October 2026: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2105819303471976479
- ASD-STE100 Issue 9 (2025): https://www.asd-ste100.org
- Wikipedia, Signs of AI writing (WikiProject AI Cleanup)
- blader/humanizer by Siqi Chen (MIT). Pass 1 follows its 26-pattern catalog and order, with new examples. Its license notice is in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md.
- Hacker News discussion of STE skills (July 2026): https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49114639
This skill does not contain the ASD-STE100 specification or its dictionary. The STE rules are paraphrased and simplified. ASD-STE100 and Simplified Technical English are trademarks of ASD (AeroSpace, Security and Defence Industries Association of Europe). This project is not affiliated with or endorsed by ASD.

Once installed, the skill answers to /ste80-humanizer. It also starts by itself when you ask to humanize, simplify or de-AI a text, or ask for STE.
npx skills add Dodaios/ste80-humanizer
Global install for one agent, or for all of them:
npx skills add Dodaios/ste80-humanizer --global --agent claude-code
npx skills add Dodaios/ste80-humanizer --global --agent codex
npx skills add Dodaios/ste80-humanizer --global --agent cursor
npx skills add Dodaios/ste80-humanizer --global --agent '*'
Without --global, the skill goes into the current project only. The skills CLI from Vercel works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode and many more agents.
/plugin marketplace add Dodaios/ste80-humanizer
/plugin install ste80-humanizer@ste80-humanizer
Download this repo as a ZIP (Code → Download ZIP). Upload it in Settings → Capabilities → Skills.
/ste80-humanizer
<paste text>
Or just ask:
This sounds like ChatGPT wrote it. Make it sound like a person.
Rewrite this README 80% of the way to ASD-STE100.
Explain how TLS handshakes work in STE.
Light touch: just remove the AI stuff from docs/intro.md.
Convert docs/runbook.md to strict STE.
Does this email sound like AI? Just tell me, don't rewrite it.
Match your voice. Add a sample of your own writing. The skill then matches your sentence length, words and punctuation.
Fidelity first. The skill keeps every fact, keeps "may" as "may", keeps "40+" as "40+", adds nothing and flags contradictions in the source. In our tests, this was the clearest difference from a plain prompt (see Tests).
More examples: references/ste80-rules.md. Full strict rules and a checklist: references/strict-mode.md. More than 100 plain-word swaps: references/word-swaps.md.
scripts/ste_check.py is a small Python linter with no dependencies. It flags many Pass 1 tells, such as not-X-but-Y, chatbot phrases, run-ups, fake depth, stacked hedges, vague authority and association, "-ing" riders, inflated claims, AI words, hyphen pairs and curly quotes. It also flags the measurable Pass 2 rules: sentence and paragraph length, semicolons, dashes, passive voice, perfect and progressive tenses, "-ing" forms and phrasal verbs.
python scripts/ste_check.py README.md
python scripts/ste_check.py --strict docs/runbook.md
cat draft.txt | python scripts/ste_check.py -
It is a heuristic, not an AI detector and not a compliance checker.
evals/ has four cases in the claude plugin eval format: a README rewrite, an explanation from scratch, a strict runbook and a casual LinkedIn post that does not mention STE. Run them with claude plugin eval . --allow-tools Write,Edit,Bash.
What we saw: when the prompt names ASD-STE100, the base model already gets the style mostly right. The skill made the difference in fidelity. In the LinkedIn rewrite, the run without the skill invented a quote and changed "40+ customers" to "40-odd". The run with the skill kept every fact. In the README rewrite, it kept "you may need to" and flagged a contradiction in the source. These are small tests, so treat them as a hint, not proof.
- STE is for clear explanatory text. For fiction, speeches and brand copy, the skill does Pass 1 only.
- STE is an English standard. For other languages, the skill applies the tells and the structure rules, but not the English word lists.
- "STE style" is not "STE compliant." Compliance needs the official dictionary, trained writers and review.
- Andrej Karpathy on X, 2 October 2026: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2105819303471976479
- ASD-STE100 Issue 9 (2025): https://www.asd-ste100.org
- Wikipedia, Signs of AI writing (WikiProject AI Cleanup)
- blader/humanizer by Siqi Chen (MIT). Pass 1 follows its 26-pattern catalog and order, with new examples. Its license notice is in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md.
- Hacker News discussion of STE skills (July 2026): https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49114639
This skill does not contain the ASD-STE100 specification or its dictionary. The STE rules are paraphrased and simplified. ASD-STE100 and Simplified Technical English are trademarks of ASD (AeroSpace, Security and Defence Industries Association of Europe). This project is not affiliated with or endorsed by ASD.

articles.title: France Accuses Iran of Supermarket Fridge Hacking
articles.body:
France Accuses Iran of Supermarket Fridge Hacking (bbc.com) 133
			
		 	
				France has accused Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of being behind last month's cyberattacks on fridges and freezers across the country. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said the attack was "unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression," adding those who were responsible would be hit with sanctions "at the European level." The BBC reports:  The cyber-attack last month saw fridges and freezers in hundreds of supermarkets across France heated up, which spoilt fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros. Then last week, dozens of supermarkets across several other European countries were also impacted by a cyber-attack that targeted fridges and freezers. It is not known if the instances are linked.
Barrot said the attack on France's supermarkets "marks the first large-scale cyber-attack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation's interests and the security of the French people." He said the government had summoned the Iranian ambassador to Paris to "lodge a very strong protest against this extremely grave act." France will take "any other necessary and proportionate measures" to respond to the incident and "deter anyone who might seek to repeat it," Barrot added.
Separately on Monday, the Paris prosecutor said an investigation had been opened into the head of an offensive cyber unit associated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as well as his two deputies. Laure Beccuau named the unit as Shahid Kaveh, which she said had an affiliation with the electronic and cyber centre of the IRGC. Shahid Kaveh is the name given to a cluster of hackers thought to be directly employed by the Iranian regime. [...] The French government has not said how it reached the conclusion that Iran was responsible, and attribution of cyber attacks is extremely hard as hackers are able to hide their locations.

articles.title: The future of AI hinges on… Jensen Huang’s sex life?
articles.body:
I would prefer that these people’s sex lives were none of my business but I guess we have to talk about Jensen Huang and the National Security Incident. Who could have guessed that the guy who was out here signing titties might not have great judgment about how to behave around women?
The future of AI hinges on… Jensen Huang’s sex life?
NVIDIOT.
NVIDIOT.
Alice Huang — no relation to Jensen — is a former TV reporter. That was before she became “an executive” at Megaspeed, which bought $4.8 billion of hard-to-get Nvidia chips, starting around the time she was being photographed with Jensen in a Taipei bar in 2024. “To many in the industry, the well-funded push by Megaspeed into A.I. appeared to come out of nowhere,” The New York Times wrote, tactfully. Our girl Alice is also an alleged honeypot who was recruited by the Chinese Ministry of State Security. (China is denying all this, btw.)
You know shit is going good when your corporate spokesperson has to tell the Times that of course your company does not disclose classified information to your customers
What is Megaspeed? Well. The company has ties to the Chinese military and builds data centers in “Southeast Asia” (it has offices in Singapore and Indonesia) to sell compute to Alibaba. The chips it is using to do that are banned from being imported to China. Incidentally, Nvidia has been lobbying very intensely to get rid of import controls on its chips so it can sell them in China.
This is all public knowledge in part because Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly “oversaw” a memo detailing Alice’s recruitment and relationship with Jensen, and then someone leaked it. (Powerful memo game, Marco, getting credit for one you didn’t even write!) Rubio passed his little note around in May, ahead of a trip to China taken by President Donald Trump. Jensen initially didn’t make the list of invitees on the trip — at least, not until Trump saw media coverage of the perceived snub. Trump and Jensen? They’re close. Which makes it even more interesting that Trump was personally briefed on the findings and did nothing, according to the Times.
You know shit is going good when your corporate spokesperson has to tell the Times that of course your company does not disclose classified information to your customers. John Rizzo, the spokesman, also told the Times that Nvidia’s customers don’t ask Nvidia to lobby for changes to the chip restriction. Bit of a hat on a hat, John. First of all, they don’t have to — Nvidia’s financial incentives do it for them. Second, imagine this is a regular company. The business model of Megaspeed is that the chips are restricted, and that Megaspeed gets ahold of them. Megaspeed has no incentive to upend this situation! Unless, you know, it’s acting against its financial interest because it’s a front for Chinese spies… in which case, that statement is going to be embarrassing.
Speaking of embarrassing, Rizzo told the Times “that Mr. Huang’s interactions with Ms. Huang were ‘not unusual’ and consistent with the kinds of meetings he has with any of Nvidia’s many customers.” Oh, okay. Who else was Jensen fucking?
Nvidia has an extraordinary structure
Because two days after that statement, Jensen sent the most incredible email addressed “To my colleagues at Nvidia” in which he admitted he had been “unfaithful.” Then, he wrote, “To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust.” Are… your wife and family on the Nvidia employee email list?
Well, yes! His son is a director of product management; his daughter is a senior marketing director. He even gave a job to his son-in-law!
Also, Nvidia has an extraordinary structure. Jensen has 60 direct reports. Leave aside that there is no possible way to manage that many people well. I would like to direct your attention to something else entirely: If he is in trouble, there is no part of the company that is untouched. The usual problems attain, of course — he was in a position to have gotten any information she might have requested! He could have left company laptops available for infiltration! But because of the structure, he also could have issued commands to his many direct reports that benefited the CCP. Neat! I sure hope someone who knows a lot about cybersecurity is going through Nvidia with a fine-toothed comb.
Is he in trouble? Well, Nvidia is opening an investigation into Jensen, who is also its largest individual shareholder. (At least there’s no dual-class stock!) Nvidia shares are, as of this writing, down almost five percent, which seems like an underreaction.
I don’t know where Jensen’s actual wife, Lori, is in all this
Perhaps more consequentially, the Democratic Party just swept back into power and Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) seems mad. Also, the voters hate the data centers that house Nvidia chips, and I notice a lot of ambitious politicians thinking about the next presidential elections. For instance, there’s Rubio’s name attached to the memo. I also notice Trump’s popularity is at an all-time nadir. Besides any Democrats positioning themselves for a run, a Republican looking to create some daylight between himself and Trump could easily do so by going to town on Jensen, who is Trump’s buddy. I do not think Rubio is the only ambition monster to worry about.
I don’t know where Jensen’s actual wife, Lori, is in all this. They got married in 1985. She gave up her job as a microchip designer to raise their kids. I would be very surprised if there is a prenup. I would be somewhat surprised if there was a postnup. Jensen doesn’t own as much of Nvidia as Jeff Bezos did of Amazon when he cheated on and divorced his wife, but it’s something to keep an eye on, if Lori decides she’s out.
We’ve talked once or twice about Nvidia’s central role in the AI ecosystem — and specifically, that it is heavily involved in financing AI neoclouds. It has investments in SpaceX, CoreWeave (where it was, as of the time of the IPO, the company’s second-biggest customer), and OpenAI, among others. Jensen has been promoting “compute as an asset class.”
Nvidia is, effectively, the central bank of AI
One of the reasons I have been uncertain about when and how the AI bubble will pop is that it seems to me that Nvidia can bail out any or all of these companies anytime it needs to, just like it did for CoreWeave when its IPO was threatened. Neoclouds exist because Nvidia wanted to create competition for its chips, so its biggest customers — Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Oracle — couldn’t exert too much pricing pressure. Certainly I am not the only person who has noticed that Nvidia is, effectively, the central bank of AI. If Nvidia is in a particularly bad way, it kind of seems like, at minimum, the neoclouds get fucked too. Oddly, CoreWeave is up about 6 percent as of this writing; the stock market moves in mysterious ways.
Maybe that is why our nation’s foremost thought leaders on X are posting things like “Whomst among us hasn’t accidentally fucked a Chinese spy? That’s how it is on this bitch of an earth.” I’m kidding, here’s investor/loudmouth Bill Ackman: “We should all support him and his family. Onward.” Shaun Maguire, partner at VC firm Sequoia: “I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership.” (Elon Musk took a quick break from complaining about Dave Chappelle’s comedy to type “I agree” to Maguire’s note.)
So Jensen can’t go down, as there’s no one who can replace him, and Nvidia can’t go down, as nothing can replace it. The AI industry better hope there isn’t some further revelation coming that would make one of these things unavoidable, such as the investigation finding proof that Alice directly accessed Nvidia’s systems while Jensen was showering or something. Might also be bad if, say, a US Commerce Department inquiry into Megaspeed was halted after Nvidia intervened. Didn’t we just hear somewhere that Jensen had been influencing the Trump administration’s policy on export controls?
Anyway, as of this note, Jensen isn’t planning to step down as CEO. Might as well settle in for the most fun we’ll have until we find out that Musk did IVF with a family member of Chinese President Xi Jinping.

articles.title: Merz: Google Cloud is sovereign enough for intelligence agencies
articles.body:
Merz: Google Cloud is sovereign enough for intelligence agencies
At the Digital Summit in Berlin, the chancellor touted AI’s potential — and gave U.S. cloud services a blank check.
Can Germany — and Europe — still catch up in digital technology? The prospects look promising if you ask the chancellor. As political tensions rise, Germany wants to make and enforce decisions independently, “in line with our values and security interests”, Merz said in his speech at the Digital Summit.
That, he told the business, trade association and government officials in attendance, is “the essence of digital sovereignty”. Above all, it requires a determined, strategic effort to build up domestic capabilities. Germany must be able to produce and control everything from hardware to software on its own terms. Merz laid out ambitious goals with passion — then added a caveat: “This cannot mean that we strive for autarky.”
AI as an existential question
Merz said he is seeking deep, reliable cooperation with “like-minded partners”, addressing in particular Canadian AI and Digital Minister Evan Solomon, who was in attendance. “It is our strategic responsibility to ensure that Europe plays a leading role in shaping technological change.” The chancellor became increasingly emphatic about the importance of laying the right foundations for the future. Digital sovereignty, he said, is becoming an “existential question” in the context of AI.
The changes will be dramatic, a shift of historic proportions. “We are not standing on the threshold of such a change today. We are in the middle of it”, Merz said. “The central question in the economic order is no longer: make or buy. It is: who sets the rules.” Dealing with the expected developments is not only a political or economic challenge, but a challenge for society as a whole.
And suddenly Google is sovereign enough
Just one robot handshake and a tour later, the ambitious Friedrich Merz — who had just called for a push toward digital independence — had become someone else. Asked about his ambitions and plans by Germany’s intelligence agencies, which apparently want to develop their new offline cloud solution with Google as a project partner, Merz emphasized “that Google also invests in Germany and Europe, and that we can enable European sovereignty here with an American provider.” For years, German and European providers have tried to compete with U.S. hyperscalers. One of their key demands has been that German and European institutions act as anchor customers to make those investments worthwhile. Germany’s Federal Office for Information Security and the European Commission are working on comprehensive sets of criteria specifying the security level a cloud provider must offer for different uses.
“European infrastructure”
But Friedrich Merz, whose Chancellery also coordinates the intelligence agencies, is undeterred: “This is not a fully integrated infrastructure; it is a European infrastructure.” Experts have been arguing over precisely these issues for years. U.S. companies have set up complicated structures to address, at least to some extent, security concerns about structural dependence or a “kill switch” scenario, in which government orders could lead to the cloud being deliberately shut down.
One thing is clear: No cloud service from a U.S. hyperscaler can go for long without provider updates — not even an “air-gapped” cloud, like the one Germany’s intelligence agencies want to use. Within a few months, they would have to find somewhere to migrate before the system became unreliable. For Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who had just been so enthusiastic about sovereignty, there is no doubt: “I have a high level of trust in our agencies that the data we have there is safe and protected, even if, for example, an American provider builds a large cloud infrastructure, but it is secure for us.”
(mki)

So exciting!! Can’t wait to learn more about @ultorg
        
      
        
        Justin Duke@jmduke
          This presentation by @eirikbakke on a generic UI abstraction to navigate a relational database is the most exciting bit of interaction design I've seen in a long, long time.
vimeo.com/372006027
        
      
        
        Petri Aukia@aukia
          The future never came: I expected dynamic multi-dimensional spreadsheet to sooner or later become the norm ever since I saw Lotus Improv.
With @ultorg you get to wonder – perhaps the multidimensional UI is to a set of database tables, not to a spreadsheet.
        
“Harmonic is building mathematical superintelligence. Deep, detailed analysis of our system's outputs is crucial for rapid advancement of our research agenda. Ultorg provides, by far, the best tool for visualizing and investigating our data. It is an invaluable tool for our research.”
Tables of Data
Whether in finance, engineering, operations, or the life sciences, you are likely working with tables of data in spreadsheets, CSV files, or an external database. Spreadsheets are excellent tools for managing a single table of data. They are a poor fit for database tasks, however, where data must be combined and queried in many different ways.
Ultorg is a general-purpose, graphical user interface for relational databases. That means any data that's organized into tables with rows and named columns. Behind the scenes, Ultorg generates SQL queries that execute either remotely or on your local computer.
Connect to:
- PostgreSQL
- Microsoft SQL Server
- MySQL/MariaDB
- DuckDB and Parquet
- Google BigQuery
- Microsoft Access Files (.mdb/.accdb)
- Microsoft Excel Files (.xls/.xlsx)
- Google Sheets
- CSV/TSV Files
- Other JDBC-based data sources
- In beta: Oracle, Snowflake, SQLite, Athena, Exasol
Visual Joins
A join is a fundamental database operation that combines data from two different tables, based on a common identifier such as “Room Number” or “Customer ID”. Joins are frequently needed when working with multi-table datasets.
In Ultorg, you can quickly join data from multiple tables or data sources, and interact with the result through a single, spreadsheet-like data manipulation surface.
For SQL-based data sources, Ultorg will recognize existing foreign key relationships, and suggest relevant joins. Or you can join on arbitrary fields, e.g., to combine data from a spreadsheet and a CSV file.
One-to-Many Relationships
A join between two tables will often involve a one-to-many relationship, where each row in the first table can match multiple rows in the second table.
Ultorg will visualize any combination of one-to-many relationships, in a compact but readable way, using a specially developed system of visual data layouts. Sorting, filters, and formulas can be applied at any level, and joins can be chained or included side-by-side without losing or duplicating rows.
Among visual database tools, Ultorg is unique in its ability to handle one-to-many relationships in a general way.
One-to-many relationships also occur inside database queries, when grouping on fields to calculate sums or averages, or when nesting one query within another. Ultorg will visualize each stage of such data flows.
For example, you can see the individual values that contribute to a group-wise sum. This lets you audit the query visually. You can tweak filters and calculations in the input, while gaining confidence in the aggregated totals.
SQL Without SQL
At first glance, Ultorg's direct manipulation interface resembles a spreadsheet. The tabular layout you see on the screen, however, represents a real database query, which can be refreshed and modified without risking changes to the underlying raw data.
A visual query lets you see exactly the data you need for a particular business task, without descending into a code editor, form designer, or flow chart. Even for database experts, Ultorg will serve as a rapid alternative to hand-typed SQL.
Most SELECT queries that can be written in the core SQL language have a visual equivalent in Ultorg. For example, you can express arbitrary combinations of joins, filters, calculations, and subqueries.
Dynamic Autolayout
In business or engineering data, or in the social sciences, you may be dealing with hundreds of fields of various data types—text, numbers, and dates—spread across dozens of tables, each with thousands (or millions) of rows.
To retain sanity, it is essential not to have to spend time tweaking formatting settings for each individual field, or for every new database query.
Ultorg eliminates such hard, manual labor, by analyzing your data on the fly and deriving carefully tuned defaults. For example, label placements, table column widths, text field dimensions, decimal precision, and pagination are all handled automatically. You can see all your data with fewer keystrokes.
Ultorg's typographical engine can visualize records and one-to-many relationships using a combination of general-purpose strategies, such as nested tables, forms, and crosstabs.
Ultorg's visual data layouts are analogous to the hand-designed user interface screens you might see in traditional, tailored database applications. But in Ultorg, they are available immediately, for any data, without custom programming.
Create, Read, Update, Delete
From Ultorg, you can also edit data, stored in a relational database, in a Microsoft Excel workbook, or in Google Sheets.
You can edit values in individual cells, pick values from a dropdown, insert rows, or fill down, like in a spreadsheet.
You can review changes before committing to the database. Multiple users can edit at the same time.
For internal business operations, Ultorg can serve as an alternative to custom CRUD interfaces, or as a way to supercharge your spreadsheet-based recordkeeping.
Connect to Your Data, Right Now
Start Ultorg and connect immediately to your data source. No “cloud” required; all data stays private on your computer or corporate network.

just connected @ultorg to the @MusicBrainz database and WOW this thing is cool hytradboi.com/2022/ultorg-a-…
      
        
        Valery Sibikovsky@combdn
          Wow! 
It is so refreshing to see such a revelation — a work of art in user interfaces!
(Warning: no micro-interactions, no gradients.)
          
        
      
        
        Tom Larkworthy@tomlarkworthy
This thing blew my mind for how good a SQL admin interface can be. I was pretty happy with metabase until this talk. Wow! Really wow!
      
        
        Pedro Paulo@pedrovc
This is outstanding work! The trick is how to integrate it with users' workflows. If people can leverage Ultorg without leaving Excel/Salesforce/any CRM/ERP this is massive.

articles.title: Locating the source of a mysterious beep
articles.body:
Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude
9th November 2026
Our house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven’t unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room started intermittently beeping. The beeps were far enough apart that standing in the room and trying to determine the source of the noise was frustrating, and I really didn’t want to dig through every one of those boxes. So I had Claude Code build Beep Locator, a software system for triangulating the source of a mysterious beep using multiple devices scattered around the room.
Here’s what Beep Locator looks like after it has been running for a while:
You run Python web server to show the primary UI, and then use the QR code or URL to connect as many devices as you can spare to act as listeners—I was using two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro and a Surface Ultra.
The devices then play noises to each other to help estimate their locations. This didn’t work particularly well, so I added a “Rough mode” where you can drag their icons around in the space to provide rough locations which are then adjusted based on those sounds.
Once that’s set up, the devices all listen for the beep!
I added a clapping mode too so I could test it by clapping my hands in different locations around the room—displayed as diamonds on the map. This helped me gain confidence that it was capable of locating a sound.
Beeps show up on the map as an X, plus a line in the “Sounds located” log. You can replay these sounds (from each device in turn) to confirm they are the mysterious beep you are looking for, then click “This is the mystery beep” to mark them as such.
Once you’ve confirmed the mysterious beep frequency the system will listen out for it, measure the interval between beeps, and use the triangulated locations to lock down the most likely location on the map.
The system worked as intended. It gave me the position of the beep to within about 40cm, then I dug through that specific pile of boxes and found an ancient carbon monoxide detector that desperately wanted its batteries replaced.
How it works
When I started working through this problem with Claude it quickly dug up BeepBeep: A High-Accuracy Acoustic-Based System for Ranging and Localization Using COTS Devices, a 2007 paper by Chunyi Peng, Guobin Shen, Yongguang Zhang, Yanlin Li, and Kun Tan. Here’s that paper’s abstract:
We present the design, implementation, and evaluation of BeepBeep, a high-accuracy acoustic-based ranging system. It operates in a spontaneous, ad-hoc, and device-to-device context without leveraging any pre-planned infrastructure. It is a pure software-based solution and uses only the most basic set of commodity hardware – a speaker, a microphone, and some form of device-to-device communication – so that it is readily applicable to many low-cost sensor platforms and to most commercial-off-the-shelf mobile devices like cell phones and PDAs. It achieves high accuracy through a combination of three techniques: two-way sensing, self-recording, and sample counting.
That sounded exactly like what we needed to build!
Beep Locator runs a Python web application server that does most of the work. The listening devices then connect to that server via WebSockets and present a UI which requests browser microphone access. The listeners mainly work by recording a 60 second buffer of recent audio. They also run a simple beep detection algorithm (see detector.js), which uses Fast Fourier Transform and a high-pass filter to identify potential beeps. It sends these events to the main server.
When a beep is reported, the server has a device play a short chirp (the device with the lowest round-trip time to the server), then asks every listener upload a clip from about 0.6s before the beep to 0.8s after that chirp. This chirp allows the clips to be aligned with each other, a crucial step in locating the beep.
How I built it
I started this project using Claude Code Cloud via my iPhone, with Opus 5.5 running in Extra thinking effort mode. Here’s that shared starter session, which began with this prompt against a newly created empty GitHub repository:
Write out a problem.md file describing the problem we want to solve
There is a device beeping in a room and I cannot find it
I want to set up several devices - laptops, phones, iPads - around the room all listening at the same time and have them help triangulate where the beep comes from
There needs to be a Python web app which coordinates it all - one device shows a web page for the app, other devices join a URL which turns them into listeners - all via browser WebAudio and WebSockets back to the Python server app
Ideally I wouldn't need to manually input the relative locations of the devices - it would be amazing if they could play sounds to each other in order to locate each other in 2D space - is that even possible though?
That got me this problem.md file. As part of writing that up Claude found and read the BeepBeep paper, which is described in that file.
The research looked good, so I told it:
Ok try and build it, add a mechanism so you can send new code to the listeners which they will then run automatically - that way I can set everything up in the room and then leave you alone to continue hacking and experiment while I do something else
That got me to this point—most of the system was built, but nothing had actually tried running it yet.
I cloned the new repository to my laptop and fired up Claude Code... and then Fable 5.2 was released, and this project seemed like an excellent opportunity to put that through its paces.
I had Claude Code on my laptop start the server running, then made sure it could both see what was happening and make live changes to the software as it ran.
This was already baked into the software: Opus 5.5 had built an installModule() method on the listeners that could be triggered over the WebSocket connection, meaning the admin server could execute arbitrary new code on any of its clients.
On some devices, web pages that listen on the microphone request user permission any time the page reloads. The hot-swap module mechanism meant that we could deploy new code without having to manually interact with each of the listening devices in turn.
From that point on my involvement was mainly to sit by the laptop chatting with Fable 5.2 about what was going on, and occasionally requesting new features. Here are some of the feature prompts I ran:
I think we need to make it so I can drag things around on the map in “rough mode”, where my job is just to put them roughly where they are, then switch out of rough mode and it attempts to get them accurate
This gave me the ability to drag listeners around the map.
what’s a good way for me to test this I wonder? Can we have it listen for claps, then I could clap and it could identify the location of the clap? [...]
Claps should use a different symbol on the map than beeps
That added the thing where any time I clapped it would show on the map as a different symbol from the beeps.
each symbol on the map should include a HH:MM:SS timestamp
That made it easier to spot which symbol likely reflected which real-world sound.
The log should show beeps and claps with their timestamps AND have a little play button which, when clicked, replays the recorded noise from each of the listeners in sequence (with clear text on screen showing which listener recorded which snippet) while temporarily turning off microphone recording while that replay plays
Now I could replay sounds, making it much easier to identify which recorded clip was the mysterious beep I was looking for.
There should be a button next to a recording for “This is the mystery beep” - then I can hit replay to see and then confirm it was the mystery beep if that’s the one I am looking for
Then the system can categorize noises in the future to see if they are likely that same mysterious beep and use that information to build a more accurate idea of where it is
At this point I was getting close—I had a solid idea of where the beep was coming from, but wouldn’t it be neat if I could reposition the listeners around that point to get an even finer location?
I want a feature for this, I don’t want to have to restart each listening device etc, I want to be able to click a “Reposition the devices” button which lets me switch into repositioning, then I click “Repositioned” and it puts me into Rough mode and asks me to roughly locate them, then I do that and click, then it starts up again. The previous session can be read-only viewed through the app.
And since I had one spare device, I then said:
add a feature where the map includes a spot that is a suggestion for a location that it would be useful to add a listener at - based on data collected so far
Giving Claude Code ears
I think the most interesting part of this project is that I demonstrated it’s possible to give Claude Code ears.
Claude doesn’t have native audio input (yet), but it can run JavaScript and Python code that can analyze audio captured by a microphone.
I told it to run a web server with WebSocket connections to multiple listening devices, then had it both run a WebAudio microphone on those devices and hook them up so they could be sent fresh JavaScript code to execute via that WebSocket.
Then I could pretty much leave Claude alone, hacking away at the problem, querying the audio logs, and reconfiguring its ears to help it solve the problem.
I’m reminded of a similar hack I heard about at GitHub Universe a few weeks ago, where Martin Woodward told me he had been debugging the GitHub Universe Badge computers by plugging them into a computer via USB-C and then pointing a webcam at their screen, so his coding agent could tell if updates were working correctly or not.
Figuring out ways to let coding agents perceive the world around them is a whole lot of fun.
More recent articles

- Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too - 3rd November 2026
- The U.S. Census Bureau and “Super Intelligence” - 2nd November 2026
- The October inflection point for vibe game development - 28th October 2026

I’m reminded of a similar hack I heard about at GitHub Universe a few weeks ago, where Martin Woodward told me he had been debugging the GitHub Universe Badge computers by plugging them into a computer via USB-C and then pointing a webcam at their screen, so his coding agent could tell if updates were working correctly or not.
Figuring out ways to let coding agents perceive the world around them is a whole lot of fun.
