articles.title: Trump Backs Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Amid Chinese Spy Affair Investigation
articles.body:
Trump Backs Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Amid Chinese Spy Affair Investigation (apnews.com) 69
			
		 	
				President Donald Trump says the FBI is investigating Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a woman alleged by U.S. intelligence to have gathered information for Beijing. "I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he'll be in good shape," Trump said at a White House briefing. The Associated Press reports:  Trump suggested the extraordinary step of directly involving himself in a counterintelligence investigation, a sign of his friendly relationship with Huang and the possible geopolitical stakes. "I did speak to him today just to see if he's feeling all right, how you're doing," Trump said. "He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy."
Trump is slated to meet next week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, but he was noncommittal about bringing up the situation with Xi. "No, I don't think so," Trump said. "I mean, maybe. I'm sure President XI will ask me about it. I just know Jensen very well. I just think he's a very honorable man."
  Nvidia has launched its own independent investigation into whether Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. Meanwhile, China has denied the allegations. "The so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said during a regular news briefing Monday.
Further reading: Commerce Dept. Chip Inquiry Was Halted After Nvidia Intervention

articles.title: A short seller flagged Nvidia CEO’s ties to a suspected Chinese spy six months before the scandal
articles.body:
Six months before the Nvidia spy scandal emerged, the New York-based short seller firm Culper Research had already raised questions about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s unusually close relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that buys Nvidia chips. She is now suspected to be a Chinese spy.
The Nvidia CEO admitted to an extramarital affair over the weekend, and the company has now opened a formal investigation into his relationship with Alice Huang (who shares his last name but is not related). U.S. intelligence officials believe she was recruited by the Chinese government to collect intelligence on Jensen Huang and influence his position regarding U.S. export controls on advanced AI chips.
Culper’s May 13 report is resurfacing because it picked up on the connection between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang while investigating Megaspeed’s ties to Nvidia.
In particular, the report called the relationship between the two executives “uncomfortably close,” noting that the Nvidia CEO was spotted partying and socializing with Alice Huang on multiple occasions. The report even claimed that some Nvidia employees wondered whether they had a “special relationship.”
Culper Research also theorized the China business that Nvidia lost to export controls had been rerouted through Southeast Asia, and that Megaspeed, a major chip buyer in the region, was secretly financed by Chinese tech giant Alibaba through shell companies. It pointed to financial records that showed Megaspeed’s total liabilities and equity had grown from $33 million at the end of 2023 to around $3 billion by the end of 2024, much of it in the form of refundable deposits from an unidentified source.
Financial Times reported Monday that documents show Alibaba lent money to Megaspeed through subsidiaries.
Culper is a short seller, so it stood to financially benefit from making these allegations, and those about possible illegal chip diversion have not been independently verified. Its report is available on the web and was posted to X back in May.

articles.title: I did a meditation and it sort of changed my personality?
articles.body:
In March 2025, I went on a Jhourney meditation retreat that was one of the most profound experiences of my life, and deeply reshaped how I related to myself.
If you had told my pre-retreat self that this was going to happen, I wouldn’t have believed you. I’d done some meditation before—including a 10-day vipassana retreat—and while it didn’t do nothing, I was underwhelmed. I felt pretty resistant to spending that much time staring at the inside of my head: it seemed really hard to actually trust anything I learned that way, because it was such a complicated system. And besides, my brain seemed to work fine the way it was.
I’d read some writing by serious meditators who seemed to be having a different experience, filled with insights and bliss, but it wasn’t one that I felt particularly drawn to. That much navel-gazing and wireheading felt self-indulgent, and anyway they seemed weird enough that whatever they were doing probably wouldn’t work for me.
Then, in a moment of life imitating Bay Area House Party, we got Jhourney, a meditation retreat startup promising to speedrun you to the bliss part (tagline at the time: “Life-changing meditative bliss used to take thousands of hours to learn. We teach it in a week.”) When I heard them strongly recommended not only by the serious meditators I’d been reading, but also by a couple more hard-nosed coworkers, I decided to see what the hype was about.
Jhourney teaches a style of meditation nominally focused on altered states called jhanas. Jhanas are blissful-feeling states that you can “relax into” if you release enough of what you might call tension or clenching or tanha, and then focus on an enjoyable open-hearted sensation like smiling, a joyful memory, or feeling care for a loved one. If done right, you can start a feedback loop of enjoying the enjoyment, and end up in a state of deeply absorbed euphoria.
I say Jhourney is nominally focused on that because the jhanas are actually kind of a Trojan horse for improving your life and relationships, which somehow doesn’t sell as well as wireheading. Jhourney’s unofficial motto is “come for the bliss, stay for the personal growth.” The growth happens because a lot of the tension you’re trying to release in jhana meditation is downstream of repressed or “stuck” feelings, either small ones (“I don’t want to be hearing that sound over there” leading to micro-clenching the head and neck) or big ones (“I can’t let myself feel this sadness or I’ll cry and that would be shameful” leading to tensing the various face and chest muscles that would otherwise be helping you cry). In order to get into jhana states, a lot of people (like me!) end up having to work on untangling knots of emotional clenching, and this usually leads to a lot of growth.
My first experience of my Jhourney retreat was showing up and being handed an 80-page handbook of meditation instructions.
This already blew my mind a little, because I had never read anything about spirituality or emotions that I considered good. The “best” stuff I’d read about the mind was vapid pop-psychology, padding out truisms with engaging fluff until the result somehow became a marketable book. The rest was indistinguishable from astrology—it was never clear enough that I could tell whether it applied to me, which meant it didn’t seem to make falsifiable predictions. As for spiritual writing, it mostly felt like word-association mumbo-jumbo, with authors throwing around words that had the right vibes but that I wasn’t sure they themselves even really understood. Heck, the previous meditation retreat I’d been on had included watching an hour-long recording of the now-dead founder talking about how he could sense quantum vibrations.
The Jhourney handbook didn’t have these problems, because it was written by software engineers. It was epistemically conservative and shockingly lucid, completely mumbo- and jumbo-free. To help with the inherently fuzzy language, they explained everything from multiple angles. They gave clear gears-level explanations of why they thought things worked the way they did. They even took a detour to explain their teaching philosophy so that students were oriented about why they were doing what they were doing. It was masterful pedagogy.
Between the written instructions and the teachings from live meditation sessions, pretty soon I could get to a point that felt like the “on-ramp” to a jhana. But every time I got there, I would get stressed and “grabby” about what to do next, and “fall off” the ramp.
By the time I got to day 4 of the retreat, I was feeling really frustrated about this, in a way that was starting to loop on itself. I was frustrated that I couldn’t reach jhana, and frustrated that the frustration was making things harder. I tried Jhourney’s recommended way of working with negative emotions, which was a self-compassion meditation. But no matter how much I tried, it didn’t really resonate; I couldn’t cultivate any emotional experience of self-compassion.
In fact, I realized I couldn’t remember ever having had a real emotional experience of receiving compassion, and that that was probably kind of fucked up.
A bunch of my friends were on the same retreat. Since I had no access to self-compassion, of course I used this realization to start worrying that they would judge me for having a hard time meditating because I was fucked up, adding even more layers to the feedback loop of doom.
Days 4–6 were pretty bad. Every day Jhourney gave us a survey of “how was your day on a scale of 1-10 with 5 as a normal day?” I rated day 6 a 1.5. (To their credit, Jhourney knew this meant I needed extra help and offered lots of 1:1 time with different facilitators, although none of it made that much difference.)
At this point, in one of my desperate attempts to think myself out of my feelings pickle, I started thinking a lot about the metaphor of the elephant and the rider. The idea is that people usually identify with everything that happens in their mind, but this is actually a confusion; it’s more accurate to think of “you,” the conscious part, as a small human rider perched atop a large lumbering elephant that often does its own thing. The only things that are actually in the rider’s action space are things like “say words to the elephant,” “visualize mental images to the elephant,” “direct attention to a particular aspect of experience,” etc. Everything else—including all emotions and many thoughts—is the elephant’s job.
In this frame, the fact that the self-compassion meditation wasn’t working for me wasn’t really “my” fault. Whether the emotional experience of self-compassion happened was up to the elephant, and the only thing “I” (the rider) could do was to keep gently saying the words or doing the technique or whatever, and wait for the elephant to steer, at its own pace.
Around that point I decided to give up on the Jhourney curriculum and just do whatever seemed like it would feel nice.✻ Ironically, Jhourney more or less recommends doing this in various parts of the handbook, but I was too into following rules to follow the part of the rules where they told me to stop following the rules. I broke the rule of silence to ask for some reassurance from a close friend who was also on the retreat. When I got back to meditating, I made up a technique for myself where I imagined sending love and compassion to the elephant instead of to “myself.” This turned out to be a cheat code: I immediately felt an outpouring of warmth, and the reassuring things I was telling myself started to emotionally resonate.
I really wish I could describe better what happened after that, but unfortunately it was a while ago and involved a lot of subtle mental movements, plus it’s hard to track what’s happening while a chunk of your psyche is liquefying. I remember a sort of sense of “going inside” the feeling of compassion and love for the elephant, having it take up more and more of my attention, and feel more and more deep, rich and meaningful. Then some kind of rush of energy and a full-body frisson that I’ve learned often happens when my brain has rearranged itself.† I don’t think this strictly qualifies as a jhana by Jhourney’s rubric, because it wasn’t stable and self-sustaining, but it otherwise felt close to how they describe first jhana.
When I got up and walked outside, I gradually noticed that the world felt pretty different. I realized that I’d always carried a “refrigerator hum” of subtle body tension that was now gone. Walking around the retreat center looking at the views felt amazing, like I could have spent days just melting into the landscape. The Lipton peppermint tea at the hot drink station tasted unreasonably good. I would sometimes tear up with joy or gratitude for no reason. I felt much deeper care and connection with my friends.
Maybe that makes it sound a little gooey and impersonal, like I took a drug that replaced my normal self with a puddle of love or something. The actual experience was the opposite; somehow it felt like this was all happening because it was easier to be myself. The care and connection wasn’t coming from some foreign love puddle; it came out because a bunch of psychic gunk had sloughed off and made it easier for the real essence of Ben-ness to shine through.
And then I used my newfound mastery of emotions and self-compassion to live happily ever after flailed around trying to integrate everything back into normal life.
One of the big changes I noticed after the retreat was that my emotions got 2–3× more intense. I think this was net positive in the end, but it made coming back to work hard—I had a stressful role managing a large team, and I also needed to catch up from a week of being incommunicado, which was extra stressful. And it wasn’t exactly helpful that suddenly, if someone was annoying on Slack, it would sometimes make me want to shoot flames out my ears.
Over the next couple weeks, the intensity settled back down and the changes in my moment-to-moment experience went maybe 80% of the way back to normal (e.g., I stopped spontaneously tearing up in normal circumstances). Some of them stayed, though:
- A lot of my shame/cringe reflex turned into a self-compassion reflex. I used to get super embarrassed by minor mistakes (things like, I don’t know, forgetting to lock a public bathroom door and having someone walk in). Now those things come with a very clear sense of “gosh, what a normal-person type of mistake that millions of other people have also made, it probably didn’t even register for the other person.”
- I became much more easily moved by art. I went from being moved to tears by a poem or piece of music maybe once a year to once a week.
- I stayed much more aware of my more subtle emotional responses. I remember listening to some instrumental folk music I’d probably listened to 100 times before, suddenly noticing that the melody felt deeply nostalgic and then realizing that was two levels further out on the feelings wheel than I’d ever felt for music.
- I still felt much less of a need to be distracted or stimulated than before. I used to listen to podcasts at 2× speed whenever I wasn’t fully focused on a task (e.g. if I was doing chores or walking). Now I have no desire to do this, and when I do listen to podcasts, 2× speed feels unpleasant. Similarly, I started to dislike a lot of restaurant food, and to really enjoy very simple home-cooked meals that I would have considered too bland before.
- Friends continued to mention that my body language was different. One noted: “more upright posture, more open shoulders, more fluid and gentle.” Another described me as “‘leaving less,’ as in, spending less time ‘out of the room’ in interactions.”
These were great changes, but even better, a bunch of mindset and relational shifts also stuck around.
Mindset-wise, I guess I’d just say I got feelings-pilled.
If you’d asked me what the deal with emotions was before the retreat, I probably would have said something like:
Positive emotions are nice, although you shouldn’t let them distract you too much from your long-term goals. Painful emotions are responses to stimuli that are part of our evolutionary inheritance, but are largely maladaptive today because we’re in an environment so different from where they arose. Assuming you have good enough self-control not to act out on them, their main effect is to make you dumber, which you should mitigate by not engaging with whatever makes you emotional until you’ve chilled out.
My new view is more like the following (this is still an oversimplified strawman and reality is a lot messier):
All emotions are important and beautiful components of unconscious/intuitive cognition.‡ I do mean all, even ones that our culture really doesn’t like—for example, anger is a sign that something you care about is threatened and needs protecting, and fully welcoming it can help bring clarity about what exactly needs protecting and how. If you’re curious to learn more about the beautiful and constructive aspects of negative emotions, I recommend the book The Language of Emotions, Joe Hudson’s podcast (search for the emotion you’re interested in), or here are some specific articles summarizing his views on anger, fear, and shame. However, they sometimes create impulses to do things that aren’t actually good ideas. In the process of socializing ourselves not to follow those impulses, we’ve been trained to try to make the emotions themselves go away in painful ways, by repressing them or clenching up around them. Unintuitively, repression and clenching actually cause the emotions to “stick around” in some sort of partially metabolized state, which has negative side-effects, like anxiety, thought-looping, numbness, blind spots, impaired reasoning, bringing up secondary emotions as defenses, etc. A different way of working with these emotions, that’s better for you in the long term, is to figure out how to welcome and accept them. This eventually leads to them feeling less bad, and giving you more impulses that are good ideas and fewer bad ones. But it’s not as simple as “just stop repressing.” Welcoming emotions requires fully feeling them; if they’re strong, that can be too overwhelming to work unless you have a deep felt sense of safety. That safety can be provided in many different ways, e.g. a therapist, friends, some kinds of meditation, etc. If you don’t have access to enough safety, repressing or clenching temporarily might be your best option.
The main thing that changed my view here was spending days at the retreat paying close attention to my own emotional experience. For example, near the beginning of the retreat, one of the facilitators claimed that thought-looping was usually a sign of a stuck or repressed emotion. I was really skeptical, but then I had several very clear experiences of thought-looping around something, going off to a private place to cry about it, and immediately stopping the thought spiral and relating to it differently.§ It was a lot easier to see this clearly on the retreat than in normal life: doing lots of meditation both made it easier to notice my own thought processes, and also faster to “unstick” or welcome the underlying emotions.
Similarly, I’d ended a long-term relationship right before the retreat, which I’d felt a lot of internal conflict and self-doubt about. My therapist had often told me things like “if you felt enough of your feelings you’d feel clear about this decision,” which sounded crazy to me at the time (uh, it’s a really hard call and there are a lot of tradeoffs that I don’t know how to weigh!). But on the last day of the retreat I noticed that I felt much clearer that a lot of the things I didn’t like about that relationship were real and important, and felt much more confident in my choice to end it.
Of course, I’d already heard plenty of people say things like “you can’t make this kind of decision logically, you have to listen to your heart,” but I never really understood what they were talking about. In retrospect, I just didn’t have the ability to do the “listen to your heart” internal move, because the pipes were clogged by too much repressed gunk. I wish those soundbites had included a second sentence like “of course listening to your heart can be much easier said than done, so if it feels hard or unclear for you, here are some first steps to get started with, and be prepared for it to take you many hours (or years) to figure out what your heart is trying to say.”
This new mindset really shifted the way I related to my emotions. While I still often experience them as painful, it’s much less than I used to, and now I start from the assumption that they’re not “actually” painful or bad, and that the best thing to do with them is to figure out how to accept them, welcome them, and find the wisdom or beauty in them. Overall this feels a lot better—when I run into something stressful or hard, instead of just flailing around not knowing what to do about it, it feels more like I have some kind of sense of direction or overall orientation, which is really comforting and grounding.
I also noticed that a lot of these ways of thinking about emotional difficulty within myself were also useful metaphors for thinking about emotional dynamics between people. Just like resisting your own emotions is a common coping strategy but ultimately doesn’t work very well, resisting other people’s emotions is also a really common but damaging pattern, which I would guess is very involved in a lot of (most?) relational damage. For example, I realized that a big part of the root problem of the relationship that I had just ended was that both of us were missing the capacity to accept a bunch of each other’s emotions, which was something I hadn’t been able to articulate clearly at the time. I now think practices explicitly focused on welcoming each other’s emotions are a really valuable tool for nurturing relationships over time.
In fact, I started to notice that a lot of sticky problems—both in my personal life, but also the type that I ran into as a manager—were partly downstream of people resisting emotions of one type or another. Alice is hard to communicate with, because she frequently monologues about unimportant details, because she wants to prove she understands everything, because she has a bunch of stuck fear/resentment about not being taken seriously. Bob and Clara have a persistent disagreement about strategy, because Clara doesn’t care enough about Bob’s opinion to engage, because Bob was cruel to her once; Clara never complained because she’s avoiding the feeling of having been hurt by it. Dave’s team is underperforming but Erin, the exec sponsor, doesn’t want to manage him out, because she’s scared of the conflict and of making Dave’s reports, who like him, angry.
Of course, just because a problem is caused by stuck emotions doesn’t mean that unsticking them is the best way to solve it; but it was still a really useful lens to view what was going on.
The other shift that stuck around was in my relationships. I made a huge improvement in my friendships, which a few different things contributed to:
- I felt a lot clearer about what I wanted from close friendships—mainly, a strong felt sense of safety and care—and that this felt like a big missing piece in my life.
- I also started getting better at feeling those. With a lot of my shame reflex dissolved, I felt generally safer with people overall—my intuitive predictions about how they’d respond to things I did felt more positive. I also got a lot better at noticing and appreciating the different ways people expressed care for me.
- Because I felt generally safer, I also got more willing to take risks or be vulnerable, which helped build closeness faster. A friend reflected that I seemed more courageous.
This also meant that my “friend type” changed—I cared more about emotional connection and less about intellectual connection. Luckily, even though I live in a really heady milieu, I was still able to find a lot of big-hearted people and gradually build up a set of close friends who are wonderful at both. So far, this is the change I’m the happiest about.
My dating life changed a bunch as well:
- I started being able to feel much more strongly attracted to people. For example, later that year, I got a crush on someone that was stronger than any crush I’d had in high school.
- I had a run of anxious-attachment-ish experiences, which I’d never had before, although they got way milder over time.‖ I’m not totally sure what was up with this; I think it partly had to do with calibrating to the new level of attraction I could feel.
- The extra safety and courage I mentioned above were helpful in dating too: I got much more comfortable with communicating tricky things or being in weird situations (e.g. ones outside the standard script of “meet someone on an app, go on some dates, become exclusive”). A friend commented that it seemed like I had more degrees of freedom.
These changes have been really wonderful overall, but also kind of intense. Becoming much more emotionally aware solved a bunch of my problems, like wanting deeper friendships or not understanding why my relationship was unsatisfying. But it turns out winning that boss fight just made all the enemies level up. My old problems got replaced with horrible new problems, like that sometimes my newly deep friends and I would have conflicts, or that I would be more into the person I was dating than they were into me.
The part of my life where I feel the most mixed about the impact is work. About six months after my retreat, I got a pretty bad case of burnout and left my role managing a big team for a significantly less ambitious IC role. I don’t think the retreat was the main cause of my burnout—the main cause was that I didn’t have enough background in the area I was managing to have the type of impact that I wanted to, with a side helping of some difficult working relationships. But it turns out my new psyche had also gotten worse at repressing or avoiding emotion, and that made everything harder.
I think of repression as the emotional equivalent of technical debt or deferred maintenance: a way of avoiding an immediate cost, in this case feeling uncomfortable feelings, in exchange for paying a higher cost later to clean it up.¶ Like tech debt or deferred maintenance, sometimes repression or avoidance can be the right strategy, if you’ll have more resources to deal with the problem later! My role exposed me to a constant stream of low-grade painful things, like people being disappointed or annoyed at me, me being disappointed or annoyed at other people, projects not going well, office snacks being replaced with worse snacks, and so on. With less ability to avoid or repress, I had to feel more of them fully as they came up, and that was really draining. It also required enough time and attention that I had to defer a bunch of maintenance on my personal life.
Even now that I feel like my energy levels have mostly recovered, I’m still not sure whether I want to go back to the center of the vortex. It’s not just that I would have to start deferring maintenance again; I’m also much more aware of a lot of maintenance I’d already deferred and really want to clean up—things like investing in friendships, like I mentioned above.
If I were only working toward my personal growth and happiness, I’d say this change was clearly good. My life feels much richer and more whole, and taking a less ambitious role forced me to release some layers of ego attachment to having a “shiny” job or career, which was deeply freeing. But… I also care a lot about my impact on the world, and I think the next few years will probably be a critical period where my work could be especially high-leverage. From that perspective, it’s sad to feel resistant to maxing out on work right now.
I feel pretty unsure about what to take away from all this. Here are some disconnected reflections.
- I would never have said that I had a problem with self-compassion or self-esteem before doing this retreat, because I was able to say the right self-compassionate words when I directly asked myself things. But from my point of view afterwards, it’s clear that I did have a big self-compassion problem; even though I could say the words, I wasn’t really feeling them or acting like they were true. Having the actual embodied experience and habits of self-compassion is the closest I’ve come in real life to The Vitamin.✻✻ “My deepest darkest fantasy is that I collapse on the street and I am rushed to the hospital. They perform a bunch of tests and find out I am severely deficient in some kind of vitamin. Then I start taking the vitamin and I become the happiest cleverest person alive because all my problems were caused by this one deficiency."
- Jhourney is doing something really cool and is way better than most/all other meditation retreats on several axes (amount of support available, pedagogical excellence). That said, you probably shouldn’t expect to have this life-changing of an experience; I would guess I had something like a 95th-percentile-plus outcome in terms of long-term effects. I still think it’s awesome as an introduction to both meditation and embodied emotional awareness.
- I feel like I got really lucky on timing: if the retreat had ended one day earlier, I don’t think I would have gotten to the life-changing part. That freaks me out a lot.
- At first I concluded from this that I should get super into meditation. Then I did two more retreats (another Jhourney retreat and a Dustin DiPerna introduction to mahamudra retreat) and neither one of them had nearly as large of an effect. The second Jhourney retreat was really helpful in reinforcing my daily practice, and I do think a daily meditation practice was helpful in stabilizing the changes that became permanent, but I’m not even totally sure about that.
- Jhanas are definitely real. Also, it was kind of wild hearing somebody tell me something that sounded totally fake (“achieve bliss on demand using nothing but your brain”) and then back it up with an 80-page engineering manual and meticulous data on success rates. Overall this made me much more likely to believe that various other types of “woo” phenomena are real, at least in the sense that people are accurately describing their experiences. (I still believe the universe runs on physics, but a lot of woo things have physics-compatible explanations, especially if you buy that people’s intuitions can sometimes do spooky things.)
- I described this as “chang[ing] my personality” in the title, but I don’t want to oversell the magnitude. I do have a lot of conversations where someone asks me “so how come you’re so <like X>” and I tell them “I did this weird meditation retreat a couple years ago.” But also, there are a lot of different aspects of personality, and even though a bunch of those completely changed for me, most of them are still the same, so I’m still very similar to my past self in an absolute sense.
- What flags should tip you off that you should maybe be staring into your emotions more? Here are some things that I think might be clues (a lot of which described me, in retrospect):
  - You often get stressed and stuck in thought loops
  - You’re easily annoyed or frustrated
  - You have too much scarcity mindset—you often worry this is the best job or relationship or whatever that you’ll ever have, in a way that’s not justified by the fundamentals
  - You seek out a lot of distraction or stimulation; it’s not very enjoyable to just exist in the present
  - You feel a lot of internal conflict or uncertainty about what you want
  - There are parts of yourself that you really don’t like or wish were different
  - You feel some missing depth, richness, or meaning in your life but can’t put your finger exactly on what
I’m also just left with a lot of questions:
- Was this set of experiences… good?
  - I’m really confident that it will be good for my own long-term life happiness. But the timing meant that I feel less willing to sign up for intense work during what might be one of the most critical periods for humanity, which feels bad even if the change was positive. I feel kind of unsure how to balance these.
  - My shoulder Jeremy Bentham says I should have just kept playing push-pin. My shoulder, uh… deva? says if I follow my heart my impact on the world will be higher, even if it’s less predictable or legible. I don’t really feel like I buy either of these.
- It seemed like before this I was in a personality attractor basin with a lot of numbing and repression. How exactly did this happen, and more importantly, how can I/we avoid having it happen to as many people in the future?
  - I have some sort of fuzzy leads on this (e.g. when I was young it was really easy to make me cry so I got picked on a lot in school), but not a particularly complete picture (e.g.: does this happen to everyone who has that experience? If not, what makes the difference?)
- Mechanistically, what did the elephant meditation do? Why did it work so suddenly and create such a lasting shift? (Was that in fact what was responsible for most of the lasting shift? How much of it was instead about what I learned at a cognitive level?)
- Is the glowy, “easier to be the essence of Ben” state that I ended up in right afterwards something that can be stabilized (or have aspects stabilized)? If so, how?
- More generally—where do I go from here? I’m convinced that doing the right type of introspection or meditation type thing for a week can unlock amazing things, and it feels like there are more amazing things out there to unlock, but I wish I had a better way of navigating towards them than semi-randomly trying things.
A draft reader asked what I would tell my past self, or someone like me, about this arc. Ultimately, I’d boil it down to:
- There are probably a bunch of feelings that you’re refusing to welcome into your experience, and this is probably involved in a bunch of the things that are unsatisfying about your life and relationships.
- You can improve this by gradually, in a safe context, paying loving attention to the uncomfortable parts, from a place of wanting to know and care for yourself rather than to fix yourself.
- When that’s hard, remember that it’s not your fault. You’re just the rider; elephants gonna elephant. Let it go where it needs to and keep loving it as best you can.
Thanks to Alex Allain, Catherine Olsson, Elena Lake, Jess Ocean, Rahul Dalal, and Sasha Chapin for feedback on a draft of this post.

articles.title: Google Unveils Two New Specialized AI Chips to Widen Its Challenge to Nvidia
articles.body:
Google Unveils Two New Specialized AI Chips to Widen Its Challenge to Nvidia 16
			
		 	
				Google is expanding its AI chip lineup with two specialized TPUs arriving next year: the TPU 8tx, which encrypts sensitive data at the chip level for confidential computing, and the TPU 8i Max, which combines two TPU chips to provide more processing power and memory for long-context workloads. The move broadens Google's challenge to Nvidia as demand outstrips supply, with Google saying every TPU it currently has is already committed to customers. Quartz reports:  The 8tx is designed for sensitive, privacy-focused jobs run by clients including public-sector bodies and businesses in heavily regulated sectors, according to Bloomberg. It pairs with a central processing unit from Advanced Micro Devices and encrypts data at the chip level. Normally, data must be decrypted in memory as the machine works on it, [said Amin Vahdat, Chief Technologist for AI & Infrastructure at Google].
The 8i Max is meant for AI applications that need long context windows, meaning the volume of information a model can take into account within one request. Vahdat said that matters for drug discovery, math and coding. The chip packs two TPU chips together, giving it extra processing muscle and memory.
Both variations are reconfigured versions of existing silicon rather than new designs, Vahdat said. Google changed them to handle tasks customers have requested. They follow two TPU models Google released this year, according to Bloomberg, which said the chip unit used to release one new processor every two years. "We could build a single chip that tries to address the whole market, or by building specialized versions of the chips, we actually can deliver much more value," Vahdat said, according to Bloomberg.

articles.title: Son Lux’s Music Video for ‘Out Into Us’ Is an Atmospheric Foray Between Past and Present
articles.body:
Son Lux’s Music Video for ‘Out Into Us’ Is an Atmospheric Foray Between Past and Present
Son Lux’s newest music video is an atmospheric mini-epic. Last month, the video premiered at MASS MoCA—the piece is a joint commission by the museum and Pioneer Works and made in collaboration with Alex Cook—as an immersive, 17-minute installation titled “Out Into Us (Slow Down),” complementing the release of the band’s ninth studio album.
“In the last decade, social media has created a reality in which music is often eclipsed by visuals, served up in an endless buffet of bite-sized and contextless flavors,” says a statement. For this multimedia work, the artists leaned instead toward deeply felt human experiences, like how long it can take to do or understand something. Portraying a multigenerational family seated around a table and passing the time in one another’s company, the video transports us back at least a century as scenes of a giant dust cloud evoke the Dust Bowl.
Cook conjures tension, atmosphere, and moments of disrupted reality in a slippage of past and present. The Dust Bowl itself was inherently linked to an intense period when homesteaders, dreaming of prosperous lives for themselves, plowed vast swaths of prairie for their farms. In the process, they uprooted native grasses that held the topsoil in place. Then, exacerbated by drought, millions of acres of topsoil eroded completely from the Great Plains’ persistent and powerful winds, sending farms and habitats into ruin.
Taking surprisingly meta turns, the the sound and visuals provoke curiosity, togetherness, hope, and grief. The family passes delicious dishes around the table and works on a puzzle depicting an idealized landscape in the tradition of the Hudson River School—a far cry from their depicted reality, yet a type of historical propaganda that helped entice homesteaders to the plains. These bucolic tableaux and their romantic ideals could even be said to have functioned something like social media does today, as a way to spread information. Instead, Cook and Son Lux confront us—watch to the end—with quite another definition of a screen.
“Sound can create a sanctuary—a space in which we can remember what it feels like to be present in our bodies and lost in our thoughts,” says the band’s guitarist, Rafiq Bhatia. “When you decrease the playback speed of a piece of music, you can really linger in its hidden corners and shadows: passing tensions and moments of release become whole rooms you can step into and stay for a while.”
See more on Cook’s Vimeo.

articles.title: Show HN: A 15 MB self-hosted Netflix and Spotify for your media server
articles.body:
English · 简体中文 · हिन्दी · Español · Français · العربية · Português · Русский · 日本語 · Deutsch · 한국어 · Italiano · Polski · Nederlands · Türkçe · Українська
HolyArrs is one self-hosted app for your shows, movies and music.
Browse like a streaming app, ask for what you want, and it handles the rest.
About 15 MB to download · about 140 MB of RAM idle with 10,000 titles · amd64, arm64, armv7
The six apps it replaces download 718.2 MB together.
Quick start · Why · What it does · Moving from other apps · The manual · Help
Save this as docker-compose.yml in a new folder on a local disk:
name: HolyArrs
services:
  holyarrs:
    image: holyarrs/holyarrs:latest
    container_name: holyarrs
    environment:
      - PUID=1000
      - PGID=1000
      - TZ=America/New_York
    volumes:
      - /your/local/path:/config
      - /path/to/movies:/movies #optional
      - /path/to/tv:/tv #optional
      - /path/to/music:/music #optional
      - /path/to/downloads:/downloads #optional
    ports:
      - 6262:6262
    restart: unless-stoppeddocker compose up -d
Open http://your-server:6262 and make the owner account. A short setup walks you through folders, a downloader and a Source.
No API keys to hunt down. No second container. Every setting is explained in the manual further down.
A normal media server runs six apps: Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr, Bazarr, Prowlarr and Seerr.
That's six logins, six ports, six update cycles and six API keys to copy between them. When a show doesn't land, you check six places to find out why.
I wanted one app. One login, one port, one place to look.
So I built it.
About 48 times smaller. Compressed registry download, linuxserver.io images, amd64, measured 2026-11-08. Idle RAM measured with 10,000 titles and 55,000 movies and episodes.
Someone asks for a title. HolyArrs searches your Sources, picks the best release with your Pick rules, sends it to your downloader and files it in your library. Your media server hears about it when it lands.
See every page in motion
- Downloaders: qBittorrent, Transmission, Deluge, SABnzbd, NZBGet
- Media servers: Plex, Jellyfin, Emby
- Sources: any Torznab or Newznab indexer, or Prowlarr or Jackett
- Moves your setup from: Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr, Prowlarr, Bazarr, Seerr, Overseerr, qBittorrent, SABnzbd
Open Settings > Move from other apps, add each old app's address and API key (or a backup zip), pick what comes over, run Try it, then Move. You can undo a move later.
HolyArrs only reads your old apps and changes nothing in them, so you can run both side by side until you trust it.
Keys and passwords stay behind; you type them in again or import them from a file. Custom formats, tags and history don't come over. Media files never move. Step by step: Move from other apps.
- Downloading by itself. HolyArrs connects to qBittorrent, SABnzbd and the others. It doesn't replace them.
- AI or MCP features. Not in 1.0.
- Phone and TV apps. Not built. The web app works on a phone.
- Music in Explore is still being built.
What's next is on the roadmap. You vote, I build. Post ideas on r/HolyArrs.
Do I keep qBittorrent or SABnzbd? Yes, for now. HolyArrs connects to the downloader you already run. A built-in downloader is planned for a later release.
Can Sonarr and Radarr keep running while I try it? Yes. HolyArrs reads them once and never changes them.
Is it free? Yes. It's free and open source.
Everything below is reference. The full guides live at docs.HolyArrs.com.
Pulling holyarrs/holyarrs:latest gets the right image for your machine.
On a NAS? See Unraid, Synology and other NAS boxes.
Images live on Docker Hub as holyarrs/holyarrs.
name: HolyArrs
services:
  holyarrs:
    image: holyarrs/holyarrs:latest
    container_name: holyarrs
    environment:
      - PUID=1000
      - PGID=1000
      - TZ=America/New_York
    volumes:
      - /your/local/path:/config
      - /path/to/movies:/movies #optional
      - /path/to/tv:/tv #optional
      - /path/to/music:/music #optional
      - /path/to/downloads:/downloads #optional
    ports:
      - 6262:6262
    restart: unless-stoppeddocker run -d \
  --name=holyarrs \
  -e PUID=1000 \
  -e PGID=1000 \
  -e TZ=America/New_York \
  -p 6262:6262 \
  -v /your/local/path:/config \
  -v /path/to/movies:/movies `#optional` \
  -v /path/to/tv:/tv `#optional` \
  -v /path/to/music:/music `#optional` \
  -v /path/to/downloads:/downloads `#optional` \
  --restart unless-stopped \
  holyarrs/holyarrs:latest
Container settings go in compose. Everything else is set in the app.
Each one is written <outside>:<inside>. Change the left side only.
More variables (reverse proxy, URL base, save path): Environment variables.
Put FILE__ in front of any variable to read its value from a file, such as a Docker secret:
environment:
  - FILE__HOLYARRS_ALLOWED_HOSTS=/run/secrets/holyarrs_hosts
PUID and PGID must match the user that owns your media folders. Find them with:
id youruser
# uid=1000(youruser) gid=1000(youruser)
HolyArrs never changes the owner of your media or download folders. Give that user write access to them, because HolyArrs makes folders and moves files.
Open http://your-server:6262 and make the owner account right away. There is no default password. Until you make it, whoever opens HolyArrs first becomes the owner.
The setup that opens next asks for your folders, a downloader and a Source. Guide: First run.
The four optional mounts are the easy way to start. The cost: each mount is its own filesystem inside the container, so every import is a full copy.
Want instant moves that take no extra space? Mount one parent folder with downloads and Library folders inside it, and give your downloader the same mount at the same path. Guide: Folders.
Use a named volume for /config. Media folders can stay host folders. Guide: Install.
holyarrs.key in your config folder is what opens your stored passwords and keys. Backups don't include it, so keep a copy somewhere else. As the owner, open Settings > Backups and choose Download key kit. See Backups.
docker compose pull
docker compose up -d
If the new version changes how data is stored, HolyArrs makes a backup first. To go back to it: docker exec holyarrs /holyarrs restore --pre-update, then docker restart holyarrs. Never remove /config during an update. See Updates.
- The owner account is made at first visit. There is no default password.
- Stored passwords and keys are encrypted with holyarrs.key.
- The image has no shell inside it.
- Don't forward port 6262 on your router. Use a VPN such as Tailscale, or a reverse proxy with HTTPS.
- Report security problems privately: SECURITY.
The image has no shell, so docker exec -it holyarrs /bin/bash won't work. HolyArrs' own commands do:
- Follow the log: docker logs -f holyarrs
- Check your setup. Every line says OK, WARN or FAIL, and each WARN or FAIL says how to fix it:
docker exec holyarrs /holyarrs doctor
- Locked out of the owner account: docker exec -i holyarrs /holyarrs reset-owner
- Version number: docker inspect --format '{{ index .Config.Labels "org.opencontainers.image.version" }}' holyarrs
More: Troubleshooting.
Read CONTRIBUTING, then Architecture and Setup. Open an issue before a big change.
On your first pull request a bot asks you to accept a short licence agreement (CLA.md). One click, once.
HolyArrs is free and open source under the GNU AGPL-3.0.
Want to build it into a closed product? Email support@HolyArrs.com for a commercial licence.
HolyArrs is free, but it isn't free to run. Every install talks to a metadata server I pay for every month. Sponsors cover that, and buy more hours for the things you vote for.
Built by CoderLuii.
If HolyArrs saves you from running six apps, a star helps other people find it.

articles.title: M John Harrison becomes first science fiction author to win the Booker prize
articles.body:
Eighty-one-year-old M John Harrison has won the Booker prize for The End of Everything, a postapocalyptic novel set on a near-future Kent coast, becoming the oldest winner in the award’s history.
Gaby Wood, chief executive of the Booker Prize Foundation, said that while plenty of previous winners had dabbled in science fiction, Harrison’s was “the first Booker winner to have emerged from the bona fide SF world”. She called it “a historic win, for a writer whose decades of work are lightly worn on every page”.
Harrison, who has been publishing for six decades, overtakes Margaret Atwood, who was 79 when she shared the prize in 2019 for The Testaments. He received the £50,000 award and trophy at a ceremony in London on Monday evening.
The End of Everything, Harrison’s first Booker nomination, is set a few decades from now, years after a disaster nobody can properly account for. Set on the Kent coast, the novel sees Phillip Tennent and his ageing aunt Marnie attempting to survive alongside the looming threat of the mysterious iGhetti: vast, shape-changing beings whose origins and intentions are never explained. At 198 pages, it was the shortest book on the shortlist.
Mary Beard, chair of the judges, said the decision was unanimous, reached after a full day of discussion. “It’s a book that turns you upside down, raises a wry smile – and surprisingly, given the subject matter, leaves you with a twinge of optimism,” she said. “One main point of the book is that if, or when, such an apocalypse comes it will be incomprehensible. And the old rules won’t matter either … This is the politics of now seen through the lens of the future.”
Harrison, born in Rugby, Warwickshire, in 1945, sold his first story in 1965 and spent most of the 1970s running the books pages of the speculative fiction magazine New Worlds. Alongside his novels he has written five short-story collections and the “anti-memoir” Wish I Was Here (2023). Climbers took the Boardman Tasker prize for mountain literature in 1989, Nova Swing the Arthur C Clarke award in 2007, and The Sunken Land Begins to Rise Again the Goldsmiths prize in 2020. Once a keen climber and fell runner, he sat on the Booker judging panel in 2022.
This year’s shortlist included two former winners: Marlon James, the bookmakers’ favourite, for The Disappearers, and Douglas Stuart for John of John. Elizabeth Strout’s The Things We Never Say, Luke Kennard’s Black Bag and Rebecca Perry’s debut May We Feed the King completed the list. Each shortlisted author receives £2,500.
Writing in the Guardian on his inspiration last week, Harrison described The End of Everything as “a disaster story in which the disaster is the failure to comprehend”, with aliens who arrive “as incomers from another dimension, paralleling the gentrification of places like the UK’s south-east coast”. He admitted to passing on to the reader “some of the puzzlement and confusion of the characters”, but said he hoped the issues were transparent – among them “the collapse of rationality that comes with Trumpism and the internet”.
His win marks a rare moment of mainstream recognition for a writer long revered by his peers but at the margins of literary fiction. On BBC Radio 4’s Front Row last month, Harrison said he had been “working for 40 to 50 years to shift the balance, both as a novelist and as a critic”, adding: “Why shouldn’t a well written [work of] SF be considered to be literary fiction?”
Even admirers concede the book is not an easy read. In a rave review for the Guardian, Michel Faber said it “exposes the terrifying insecurity of life right now”, but warned that “it won’t be for everyone”.
The win is timely in the age of AI. Beard noted that the “i” in iGhetti hints “at something digital, but you can’t be sure”, while Wood described the book’s post-apocalyptic landscape as “Large Language Model-dotted”.
The judging panel also included Pulp frontman Jarvis Cocker, authors Patricia Lockwood and Raymond Antrobus and Guardian journalist Rebecca Liu. They considered 163 books published in the UK or Ireland between 1 October 2025 and 30 September 2026.
It is the first Booker win for Serpent’s Tail, an imprint of the independent publisher Profile Books, and its fifth nomination. Hungarian-British author David Szalay won last year with Flesh; other recent winners include Samantha Harvey’s Orbital, Paul Lynch’s Prophet Song and Shehan Karunatilaka’s The Seven Moons of Maali Almeida.
- The End of Everything by M. John Harrison (Profile, £16.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

Hungarian-British author David Szalay won last year with Flesh; other recent winners include Samantha Harvey’s Orbital, Paul Lynch’s Prophet Song and Shehan Karunatilaka’s The Seven Moons of Maali Almeida.
- The End of Everything by M. John Harrison (Profile, £16.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

Per-session fees in places where the fee is published, by the company that runs the app. Sources are listed at the bottom of the page.

Every place in the data, by state. The source column names where each fee comes from and when that page was last updated or checked. A city name links to its Park Graph parking page when there is one.

For parking lot owners
The fee in this report is paid by the driver, on top of your rate. Park Graph charges a per-transaction software fee on the operator side and does not add a separate convenience fee on the driver. Parking app fees FAQ
- How much does ParkMobile charge per parking session?
- Per ParkMobile's own help pages, its per-session fee runs from $0 to $0.75 depending on the city, with a median of $0.35 across 289 U.S. places, as of Nov 5, 2026. The fee is set place by place, so check the zone you park in.

- From the app companies' own help pages and from city parking pages, checked on Nov 5, 2026. 296 rows come from ParkMobile's help center, one article per city or zone. Each row's exact page is in the source_url column of the CSV.

articles.title: Queens Public library under ransomware attack e-borrowing suspended
articles.body:
We are open as scheduled but experiencing a significant network outage affecting all locations.
This disruption, the result of a ransomware attack, impacts the following services:
- Queens Public Library website
- QPL Mobile App
- Public Computers at most open locations
- Digital Media Services
The following services have been restored:
- Free Wi-Fi access at all open locations
- Check-out and return machines
- Public Computers at seven locations: Central Library, Far Rockaway, Flushing, Glen Oaks, Hunters Point, Jackson Heights, and Kew Gardens Hills
All QPL locations remain open as scheduled. However, certain virtual and in-person programs may be impacted. Please check with your local branch.
You can continue to borrow and return books and other materials at all locations. During this outage, however, renewals are unavailable. As a reminder, customers are not charged late fines on borrowed materials.
Check this page for updates. You can also check our social media channels:
You may call (718) 990-0728 for assistance.
We apologize for any inconvenience and ask for your patience and understanding as we manage this challenge. Our team is working diligently to restore full access. Please note it will take some time before the Library’s network and systems are restored.

articles.title: Real Motors’ Project Ares is a cyberpunk fantasy made real
articles.body:
Electrification has done wonderful things for motorcycle design. By getting rid of the engine and the fuel tank that supports it, designers have the freedom to do whatever they want, and the results have been occasionally brilliant. I’m a big fan of the vaguely retrofuturistic stylings of the Maeving RM2 and the quirky minimalism of BMW’s CE 02, but nothing yet has quite left me so awestruck as Project Ares.
Real Motors’ Project Ares is a cyberpunk fantasy made real
Real Motors’ debut machine brings Night City vibes to the street, but it’s not the sportbike you might be expecting.
Real Motors’ Project Ares is a cyberpunk fantasy made real
Real Motors’ debut machine brings Night City vibes to the street, but it’s not the sportbike you might be expecting.
This all-electric machine is the first offering from South Carolina-based Real Motors, and it bears a shape that would not look out of place on the streets of Night City, the main setting in Cyberpunk 2077. There’s a little bit of Star Wars in there and maybe even some Wipeout, too, but it’s never derivative. Most importantly, it’s real. Project Ares starts at $20,000 and ships next year in limited volumes, but don’t let its future cafe racer vibe fool you. This doesn’t quite feel like you might expect.
Origins
CEO and cofounder Trent Dingman tells me that Real Motors started as a challenge between him and Michael Feng (design engineer and the other cofounder) to “build the coolest possible thing, the best design, and show people what we can do.”
Project Ares is the first coolest possible thing: an all-electric motorcycle designed and built in Greenville, right in the heart of the battery belt, not far from already-big and still-developing EV players like BMW, Scout Motors, Volvo, and Redwood Materials.
The white bike is an early prototype that’s substantially smaller than the bike I rode, Prototype 04, evocatively called “Ghost” thanks to its distinctive fairing. From a distance, it just looks like glossy black, nothing too special. Come closer, though, and you see the translucence. From in the saddle, you can spot the charger’s cooling vanes, situated inside where the tank would normally be. You can follow the bright orange high-voltage lines as they snake through and around the bike’s battery pack.
Things aren’t finalized yet, but that pack will be roughly 15 kilowatt-hours, charging at up to 3.3 kilowatts over a standard SAE J1772 charging port on the very top of its “tank.”
The pack powers an electric motor officially rated at 101 horsepower and an insane 738 pound-feet of torque. However, that latter figure requires some context. The number Real Motor quotes is the torque measured at the wheel, after being multiplied by the bike’s gearing. Most motorcycles quote actual torque at the engine or motor output shaft. Measured in the same way, the actual output of the Ares’ motor is probably somewhere closer to 200 pound-feet, still putting it among the strongest twisting motorcycles on the planet.
Those are substantial numbers, but then the Ares is carrying some substantial weight.
Ergonomics
While the Ares may look like it was sent from the future, it’s built in a present where we’re still stubbornly waiting for mass-produced solid-state batteries to fully enter reality. That means big batteries like this one weigh a lot.
Project Ares has a total weight of 485 pounds. That puts it right in line with Zero Motorcycles’ SR/F, which has similar power output and battery size. However, the Ares is nearly an inch and a half longer than the Zero.
From a more traditional sportbike perspective, the Ares weighs nearly 100 pounds more than a Ducati Panigale V4 and has a wheelbase roughly three-quarters of an inch longer.
Having only seen it in photos, I didn’t expect that volume. I had in my mind a diminutive cafe racer, the classic style of machine typified by British riders who like to splay themselves over their motorcycle’s tanks as they buzz from one cuppa to another.
And that’s definitely the way the Ares is set up. The bars are set low, putting your chest and head down close to that translucent tank. The pegs are likewise up high, delivering maximum clearance for cornering and putting you into that classic posture.
But whereas most cafe racers are skinny and svelte, the Ares has a wide saddle hinting at the mass of the machine beneath you. That aggressive geometry plus its weight made for a somewhat wobbly start as I got a feel for things, but I was quickly up to speed.
In the saddle
Riding “Ghost” was a refreshingly distraction-free experience. This prototype lacked mirrors, a choice prioritizing aesthetics over safety. But it did free me from worrying about anything behind. With only a minimalist LCD in front, I could focus exclusively on the ride.
Project Ares has three speed settings. Dingman warned me before I got in the saddle that the bike had neither traction control nor antilock braking. With that torque figure, theoretically enough to liquefy the rear tire, I started in mode 1, the lightest, to be safe.
I didn’t need to worry. While I’ve found some preproduction EVs to be a real handful, with overly aggressive throttles leading to bikes that want to buck you off the back, I immediately felt at home on the Ares. There’s no abrupt lurching forward as you twist the grip, just a smooth application of increasing power.
It wasn’t long before I was up to mode 2, then mode 3, then grinning like a fool with the throttle pegged wide open and my chest flat on the tank. Even in its most aggressive, the Ares is easy to manage, with plenty of power to entertain but such a smooth delivery that it never does anything unexpected.
What was unexpected was how it turns. Again, I had a vision of a razor-sharp racing machine, but the Ares takes a bit of muscle. Unlike the aforementioned Panigale, which drops onto its side with just a hint of pressure on the handlebars, the Ghost required a strong, sustained push to turn.
I wouldn’t call it reluctant as such, but the feeling is more of a cruiser than a sportbike. A cruiser with extremely sporty components, though. The unmarked suspension on my prototype felt plenty good, but buyers can spec top-shelf Öhlins dampers if they like. Brembo brakes are also on offer, meaning that while this bike comes at a premium price, you at least get premium components befitting something named after the son of Zeus.
Practicalities
So it’s a heavier, more intentional ride than its cafe racer style and ergos may imply, but the blame for much of that lies in today’s battery technology.
Which leads us to perhaps the biggest question of all: range. The Ares spec sheet lists 120 miles in the city on a charge. Frankly, I didn’t come close to that efficiency during my day in the saddle, but don’t hold that against it. It’s still pre-production, after all, and lots could change in the next few months.
Also, I spent a good portion of that day with the throttle pinned open, which is not ideal for maximizing longevity.
That said, I’ve yet to meet an electric motorcycle that can live up to its range estimates when ridden hard and at speed. I doubt this one will shatter that paradigm. Even so, Project Ares is already fast, fun, and astonishingly good looking. While the world of motorcycling may be evolving, style still counts for a lot.
Photography by Tim Stevens / The Verge

articles.title: Meet the Sad Wives of AI
articles.body:
If i had to listen to another minute of my husband talking about Claude Code, I might have actually died. It was 11 pm in Berkeley, California, where I was home alone with our 10-month-old daughter, and 2 am in Cambridge, Massachusetts, where he was visiting for his newish job in AI. “JUST LOOK AT THIS!” he shouted. The FaceTime camera zoomed toward a laptop sitting on a hotel bed. “SEE?!”
See what, I thought. I wanted to shower. I still had to take the dog out.
“ARE YOU LOOKING?” he shouted again. I wasn’t. I was looking at our real baby. But that’s the thing. There are two babies in this household now: the small human one and the large language model. Both demand constant attention. Both keep us up at 2 am.
Is this a Sophie’s choice kind of situation? Please. I’d kill the AI baby in an instant.
There’s a strange and under-discussed side effect of the AI boom: what it’s doing to family dynamics. By which I mean: how it’s potentially destroying family dynamics. I’m sure this applies to all kinds of families, gay or straight, rich or poor, with any AI-pilled members. The technology is coming, has come, for us all. But for the purposes of this story, I mostly spoke to white-collar heteros in the Bay Area, because that’s where a certain psychological crisis seems most acute. Often it goes like this: He works in AI, and she does everything and anything else. Other times, it’s bleaker: He desperately wants to work in AI—or feels he must work in AI—and she wants him to do literally anything else.
Either way, the men go in and the women want out. How many? It depends on how you define “working in AI.” About 71 percent of “AI-skilled workers,” according to one report, are men, and there are roughly 35,000 open AI roles in the US at any given moment. Broaden that to include investors and you’re adding thousands more. Broaden it further to include every man who has mentioned to his wife that he is “looking at some opportunities in the space”—and we’re in the millions. Conservatively, that means hundreds of thousands of spouses, partners, and girlfriends, holding down the fort while someone mansplains the singularity to them. There are, in other words, a lot of us, and more of us are surfacing—gasping for air and a single conversation that doesn’t involve LLMs—by the day.
There’s a name for our ranks. I call us the sad wives of AI.
First of all, I’m sorry. AI is already the only thing most people talk about here, and it’s even worse for the sad wives.
One of them moved from New York for her husband’s career. He cofounded an AI company; now he’s head of design at another. “He’s so passionate about it,” she says. “I go along to get along.” That is, when she can remember what it is he does, exactly. “My eyes glaze over a bit. I tend to check out. I forget.” She does say his company is at the forefront of … something. Mostly, she’s tired. “I did not expect how homogenous it would be,” she says. “In New York, I had a friend who’s a teacher, a friend who’s a nurse, a friend in fashion, a friend in finance—and none of us talked about our jobs when we went out. Every time I go out in San Francisco, it feels like I’m at a work happy hour. I don’t get it.”
In a way, it can’t be helped. Most days it feels like every billboard in the city is about AI. Every. Single. One. “I’m on the edge,” another AI wife tells me, “while my husband drives by and is like, ‘Oh wow, that’s my company’s billboard.’ Cool. Great.” She, like almost every sad AI wife I talk to, doesn’t want me to include the specifics of her situation. Marriages, social standings, and finances—anything to protect the equity!—are on the line.
Some of the sad wives are obscenely rich; others are struggling. But the more I talk to them, the more I hear the same lines, the same complaints, the same clichés. The hours. The obsession. The sense that missing this moment would mean, for their AI-pilled spouses, missing the most important technological shift of a lifetime. “They really want to ride the wave,” one AI wife says. Another: “He’s always depressed about something.”
Yana van der Meulen Rodgers, the chair of labor studies and employment relations at Rutgers University, has a blunt take: What’s happening in Bay Area households isn’t just a lifestyle story. It’s a labor market story. The AI boom, Rodgers says, is creating a “perfect storm” of forces reshaping household dynamics, playing out along predictably gendered lines.
The story is older than Silicon Valley, of course. Every major technological boom has produced the same figure, the person who gives everything to the wave. During the industrial revolution, it was the factory worker. During the Gold Rush, it was the men who left their families and headed west. During the dotcom boom, it was the founders sleeping under their desks in SoMa. Now, it is the person who is building, building, always building—vibe coding at midnight, constantly upgrading their models—convinced that stopping for five minutes means missing everything. Economists call this the “ideal worker.” Rodgers calls it a trap. “Someone who works many hours, giving all of themselves to this new force,” she says. “That means less time at home for the partner, less time for care work.”
Though things keep changing, some analyses suggest that women are about 20 percent less likely than men to use generative AI. “It’s a function not of gender per se,” Rodgers suggests, “but of the occupations that women hold.” Women are disproportionately represented in jobs—education, health care, social services—that right now use AI less. The result could be a compounding disadvantage. Over time, it means less access to the boom’s financial rewards, more responsibility for the domestic labor it generates.
And what happens when it doesn’t work out for the men? Many, if not most, won’t make it in AI, a lucrative but volatile business. “With job loss comes some depression,” Rodgers says. “Within the household, if one person is going through adverse mental health effects around job loss or uncertainty, the other naturally becomes the support person.” The cruel irony, for some sad wives, is that the moment their husband does leave AI, whether by choice or by force, there’s no relief. Now he’s home. Spiraling. Now she’s managing that too.
It was nearing the end of my therapy session. I had been rambling for 50 minutes about the mental load, the changing hormones, whether my postpartum depression could really just be traced to the fact that it took longer than anticipated to fit back into my jeans. Then my therapist interrupted and asked what exactly my partner did for work again. “Oh,” I said. “Well, he’s head of AI at his company.”
What she said next, I had to write down. Her client base, she allowed, is almost entirely women—women whose husbands, more often than not, are in some way professionally adjacent to AI. And it’s affecting their relationships. The pressure to keep up means zero boundaries at home. The very masculine energy of it all. And the constant fighting, which is about something bigger than them. He’s off in another world, a world of prompts and benchmarks and epiphanies, while she’s firmly in this one.
The resentment builds quietly. Several of these sad wives, my therapist added, have turned down job opportunities in AI themselves. Not because they weren’t qualified, but because it’s hard to raise kids and disrupt civilization at the same time.
Princess Diana famously said there were three people in her marriage. For the sad wives of AI, the third is a chatbot. I spoke to a few other family therapists, and they agreed with mine: The phenomenon is getting worse. “It’s a lot of tech wives,” one said, sighing. “A lot of tech wives.”
A tiktok meme has been making the rounds recently: young women at their laptops or doing their makeup, captioned something like, “Working so hard so my man can work on his AI startup that loses $30K a month.” The comments section stands in solidarity: “I’m ded.” “Yas queen.” “Just so he can have ‘founder’ in his bio.” I tried to reach out to some of these women. None bit.
I should also say I didn’t bother speaking to any of the actual husbands for this story. I’m sick of hearing from the men of AI. So many of us are. They have podcasts and Senate hearings and magazine profiles and probably a group chat with the president. They’ve been talked to—and I can’t stress this enough—enough.
On an unseasonably warm evening, I met up with two friends at a wine bar. Both are partnered with men somewhere on the AI spectrum—tangibly building it, wildly chasing it, or simply unable to shut up about it. We ordered something orange and natural, the kind of wine that signals you have opinions.
We were in Oakland, which has always prided itself on being the anti–San Francisco—more diversity, less venture-funded cold brew. It has never been home to a single major tech company. It didn’t matter. Within four minutes, we were talking about AI.
It’s so existential. I think about it and then I get depressed.
Yeah. Don’t think about it!
We thought about it for the next two hours.
Every night, it’s just existential dread.
And then, the men. Neither of my friends’ husbands actually makes money from AI. Not yet.
There is this sense, I offered, among people in AI—and people adjacent to it, and people who are pretty sure it’s coming for them—that this is their last chance. They’ve tried everything else, these men, from writing screenplays to investing in crypto. It’s AI or bust. Their partners, meanwhile, have quietly taken on a second job: emotional support. Chief Existential Officer, uncompensated. No one asked us if we wanted the gig.
So what happens now?
Maybe we’ll just go back to the Stone Age.
One friend has started lobbying for her family to become Outdoor People. The kind who go into the wilderness and disconnect. For a whole week, no access. Just don’t tell Claude.
A pause.
Do we want dessert?
Here’s how Bridget Balajadia, a clinician at Lupine Counseling in San Jose, characterizes the AI husband’s situation: “If you don’t respond to an email at midnight, you could wake up and not have a job.” It’s relentless. “In this industry, you’re reachable all the time. You’re thinking about it in the shower, when you’re having sex, it never leaves.” And when it never leaves, the relationship buckles. “It turns into this around-the-clock thing where neither partner is getting what they need. They’re both building walls of resentment.”
Which—we know already. But then Balajadia tells me two surprising things. The first is that some sad wives of AI don’t want to talk to her about their husbands. Why? “I’ve already worked through this with my chat,” they say. By which they mean … ChatGPT. Yes. Not only is AI driving a wedge between couples. It’s also become a primary tool for attempting to salvage their marriage.
Balajadia isn’t impressed. “They’re not having great outcomes,” she says. “It’s not going to challenge you. You end up being validated. Then both of you don’t move the needle in conflict.”
It gets worse. ChatGPT subsequently, in some situations, helps these sad wives explore the possibility of cheating. Some of them, Balajadia says, get “validating messages,” such as: “Yes, it makes sense that you’re seeking attraction elsewhere because your partner’s not giving it to you. He’s emotionally unavailable.” She pauses. “That’s probably not a great idea. You probably should address the stuff that’s coming up in your marriage, not go have sex with someone else.”
Some wives, it must be said, have uncomplicated relationships with AI. One tells me it has “supercharged” her life—wedding planning, caring for aging parents, housekeeping, veterinary advice. While her husband is focused on how AI will change the economy, she’s interested in how it will change her. Optimize her, really. “There’s just not enough hours in the day if I don’t try to gain efficiencies in some things.” In fact, she’s just vibe coded something or other. Maybe one day he’ll be a sad AI husband.
Or robots will fix everything. Another wife tells me that her husband, who founded an AI startup, is convinced they will have a household robot within the decade. “Maybe after we have kids, I’ll be like, ‘Bring a robot in,’” she says. “Right now, I can’t wrap my mind around it, though maybe people felt that way about washing machines.” This in response to the question I ask everyone: Has any part of the AI boom made things better at home? Could it ever?
The responses are generally uninspiring. Most of the time, the closest thing to a silver lining any sad wife can offer is that AI has given them something new to talk about at dinner.
Each time it’s the same pattern: a generation (of men) convinced this is their moment, and everyone else trying to figure out where they fit. A bubble. And bubbles, as anyone who was here in 2001 can tell you, tend to burst. One AI wife—the one who drives past billboards for companies her husband has backed—puts it simply: “Half of our income is dependent on AI doing well.”
Mine too. More than half, to be frank.
Flying home from that same trip to Massachusetts, my husband found himself watching the screen of the passenger next to him. It was playing Train Dreams, a movie about a man who leaves his family for logging and railroad work in the American West, a century ago. Even without sound, he got a little emotional. “Is that what I’m doing right now?” he asked me later.
The man in the film ultimately loses his wife and young daughter. He’s filled with regret for much of his life.
“But I’m doing it for our daughter,” my husband assured me. And: “I’ve always wanted the things I’ve worked on to be necessary.”
I thought about that for a while. Then I asked him to take the dog out.
What Say You?
