articles.title: Meet the Sad Wives of AI
articles.body:
If i had to listen to another minute of my husband talking about Claude Code, I might have actually died. It was 11 pm in Berkeley, California, where I was home alone with our 10-month-old daughter, and 2 am in Cambridge, Massachusetts, where he was visiting for his newish job in AI. “JUST LOOK AT THIS!” he shouted. The FaceTime camera zoomed toward a laptop sitting on a hotel bed. “SEE?!”
See what, I thought. I wanted to shower. I still had to take the dog out.
“ARE YOU LOOKING?” he shouted again. I wasn’t. I was looking at our real baby. But that’s the thing. There are two babies in this household now: the small human one and the large language model. Both demand constant attention. Both keep us up at 2 am.
Is this a Sophie’s choice kind of situation? Please. I’d kill the AI baby in an instant.
There’s a strange and under-discussed side effect of the AI boom: what it’s doing to family dynamics. By which I mean: how it’s potentially destroying family dynamics. I’m sure this applies to all kinds of families, gay or straight, rich or poor, with any AI-pilled members. The technology is coming, has come, for us all. But for the purposes of this story, I mostly spoke to white-collar heteros in the Bay Area, because that’s where a certain psychological crisis seems most acute. Often it goes like this: He works in AI, and she does everything and anything else. Other times, it’s bleaker: He desperately wants to work in AI—or feels he must work in AI—and she wants him to do literally anything else.
Either way, the men go in and the women want out. How many? It depends on how you define “working in AI.” About 71 percent of “AI-skilled workers,” according to one report, are men, and there are roughly 35,000 open AI roles in the US at any given moment. Broaden that to include investors and you’re adding thousands more. Broaden it further to include every man who has mentioned to his wife that he is “looking at some opportunities in the space”—and we’re in the millions. Conservatively, that means hundreds of thousands of spouses, partners, and girlfriends, holding down the fort while someone mansplains the singularity to them. There are, in other words, a lot of us, and more of us are surfacing—gasping for air and a single conversation that doesn’t involve LLMs—by the day.
There’s a name for our ranks. I call us the sad wives of AI.
First of all, I’m sorry. AI is already the only thing most people talk about here, and it’s even worse for the sad wives.
One of them moved from New York for her husband’s career. He cofounded an AI company; now he’s head of design at another. “He’s so passionate about it,” she says. “I go along to get along.” That is, when she can remember what it is he does, exactly. “My eyes glaze over a bit. I tend to check out. I forget.” She does say his company is at the forefront of … something. Mostly, she’s tired. “I did not expect how homogenous it would be,” she says. “In New York, I had a friend who’s a teacher, a friend who’s a nurse, a friend in fashion, a friend in finance—and none of us talked about our jobs when we went out. Every time I go out in San Francisco, it feels like I’m at a work happy hour. I don’t get it.”
In a way, it can’t be helped. Most days it feels like every billboard in the city is about AI. Every. Single. One. “I’m on the edge,” another AI wife tells me, “while my husband drives by and is like, ‘Oh wow, that’s my company’s billboard.’ Cool. Great.” She, like almost every sad AI wife I talk to, doesn’t want me to include the specifics of her situation. Marriages, social standings, and finances—anything to protect the equity!—are on the line.
Some of the sad wives are obscenely rich; others are struggling. But the more I talk to them, the more I hear the same lines, the same complaints, the same clichés. The hours. The obsession. The sense that missing this moment would mean, for their AI-pilled spouses, missing the most important technological shift of a lifetime. “They really want to ride the wave,” one AI wife says. Another: “He’s always depressed about something.”
Yana van der Meulen Rodgers, the chair of labor studies and employment relations at Rutgers University, has a blunt take: What’s happening in Bay Area households isn’t just a lifestyle story. It’s a labor market story. The AI boom, Rodgers says, is creating a “perfect storm” of forces reshaping household dynamics, playing out along predictably gendered lines.
The story is older than Silicon Valley, of course. Every major technological boom has produced the same figure, the person who gives everything to the wave. During the industrial revolution, it was the factory worker. During the Gold Rush, it was the men who left their families and headed west. During the dotcom boom, it was the founders sleeping under their desks in SoMa. Now, it is the person who is building, building, always building—vibe coding at midnight, constantly upgrading their models—convinced that stopping for five minutes means missing everything. Economists call this the “ideal worker.” Rodgers calls it a trap. “Someone who works many hours, giving all of themselves to this new force,” she says. “That means less time at home for the partner, less time for care work.”
Though things keep changing, some analyses suggest that women are about 20 percent less likely than men to use generative AI. “It’s a function not of gender per se,” Rodgers suggests, “but of the occupations that women hold.” Women are disproportionately represented in jobs—education, health care, social services—that right now use AI less. The result could be a compounding disadvantage. Over time, it means less access to the boom’s financial rewards, more responsibility for the domestic labor it generates.
And what happens when it doesn’t work out for the men? Many, if not most, won’t make it in AI, a lucrative but volatile business. “With job loss comes some depression,” Rodgers says. “Within the household, if one person is going through adverse mental health effects around job loss or uncertainty, the other naturally becomes the support person.” The cruel irony, for some sad wives, is that the moment their husband does leave AI, whether by choice or by force, there’s no relief. Now he’s home. Spiraling. Now she’s managing that too.
It was nearing the end of my therapy session. I had been rambling for 50 minutes about the mental load, the changing hormones, whether my postpartum depression could really just be traced to the fact that it took longer than anticipated to fit back into my jeans. Then my therapist interrupted and asked what exactly my partner did for work again. “Oh,” I said. “Well, he’s head of AI at his company.”
What she said next, I had to write down. Her client base, she allowed, is almost entirely women—women whose husbands, more often than not, are in some way professionally adjacent to AI. And it’s affecting their relationships. The pressure to keep up means zero boundaries at home. The very masculine energy of it all. And the constant fighting, which is about something bigger than them. He’s off in another world, a world of prompts and benchmarks and epiphanies, while she’s firmly in this one.
The resentment builds quietly. Several of these sad wives, my therapist added, have turned down job opportunities in AI themselves. Not because they weren’t qualified, but because it’s hard to raise kids and disrupt civilization at the same time.
Princess Diana famously said there were three people in her marriage. For the sad wives of AI, the third is a chatbot. I spoke to a few other family therapists, and they agreed with mine: The phenomenon is getting worse. “It’s a lot of tech wives,” one said, sighing. “A lot of tech wives.”
A tiktok meme has been making the rounds recently: young women at their laptops or doing their makeup, captioned something like, “Working so hard so my man can work on his AI startup that loses $30K a month.” The comments section stands in solidarity: “I’m ded.” “Yas queen.” “Just so he can have ‘founder’ in his bio.” I tried to reach out to some of these women. None bit.
I should also say I didn’t bother speaking to any of the actual husbands for this story. I’m sick of hearing from the men of AI. So many of us are. They have podcasts and Senate hearings and magazine profiles and probably a group chat with the president. They’ve been talked to—and I can’t stress this enough—enough.
On an unseasonably warm evening, I met up with two friends at a wine bar. Both are partnered with men somewhere on the AI spectrum—tangibly building it, wildly chasing it, or simply unable to shut up about it. We ordered something orange and natural, the kind of wine that signals you have opinions.
We were in Oakland, which has always prided itself on being the anti–San Francisco—more diversity, less venture-funded cold brew. It has never been home to a single major tech company. It didn’t matter. Within four minutes, we were talking about AI.
It’s so existential. I think about it and then I get depressed.
Yeah. Don’t think about it!
We thought about it for the next two hours.
Every night, it’s just existential dread.
And then, the men. Neither of my friends’ husbands actually makes money from AI. Not yet.
There is this sense, I offered, among people in AI—and people adjacent to it, and people who are pretty sure it’s coming for them—that this is their last chance. They’ve tried everything else, these men, from writing screenplays to investing in crypto. It’s AI or bust. Their partners, meanwhile, have quietly taken on a second job: emotional support. Chief Existential Officer, uncompensated. No one asked us if we wanted the gig.
So what happens now?
Maybe we’ll just go back to the Stone Age.
One friend has started lobbying for her family to become Outdoor People. The kind who go into the wilderness and disconnect. For a whole week, no access. Just don’t tell Claude.
A pause.
Do we want dessert?
Here’s how Bridget Balajadia, a clinician at Lupine Counseling in San Jose, characterizes the AI husband’s situation: “If you don’t respond to an email at midnight, you could wake up and not have a job.” It’s relentless. “In this industry, you’re reachable all the time. You’re thinking about it in the shower, when you’re having sex, it never leaves.” And when it never leaves, the relationship buckles. “It turns into this around-the-clock thing where neither partner is getting what they need. They’re both building walls of resentment.”
Which—we know already. But then Balajadia tells me two surprising things. The first is that some sad wives of AI don’t want to talk to her about their husbands. Why? “I’ve already worked through this with my chat,” they say. By which they mean … ChatGPT. Yes. Not only is AI driving a wedge between couples. It’s also become a primary tool for attempting to salvage their marriage.
Balajadia isn’t impressed. “They’re not having great outcomes,” she says. “It’s not going to challenge you. You end up being validated. Then both of you don’t move the needle in conflict.”

Some of them, Balajadia says, get “validating messages,” such as: “Yes, it makes sense that you’re seeking attraction elsewhere because your partner’s not giving it to you. He’s emotionally unavailable.” She pauses. “That’s probably not a great idea. You probably should address the stuff that’s coming up in your marriage, not go have sex with someone else.”

And bubbles, as anyone who was here in 2001 can tell you, tend to burst. One AI wife—the one who drives past billboards for companies her husband has backed—puts it simply: “Half of our income is dependent on AI doing well.”
Mine too. More than half, to be frank.
Flying home from that same trip to Massachusetts, my husband found himself watching the screen of the passenger next to him. Even without sound, he got a little emotional. “Is that what I’m doing right now?” he asked me later.

articles.title: Formalizing CPython
articles.body:
Formalizing CPython
AI agents wrote 613,318 lines of Lean that copy Python's internals line by line, tested every piece against the real Python, had a computer check every proof, and turned up 418 bug reports in Python along the way.
TL;DR
- We pointed Opus 5.5 at CPython, the program that runs almost all Python code, and had it rewrite its functions in Lean, a language for writing machine-checked proofs.
- Each rewrite copies the original line by line and is tested against real Python on tens of thousands of inputs before anyone tries to prove anything about it.
- A function only counts once a second agent, which didn't write it, checks the work and agrees it holds up. 4,071 functions have passed that check so far.
- The result is 613,318 lines of Lean across 1,539 files, with 18,898 theorems and lemmas, all checked by Lean's proof checker on every build.
- Along the way the proofs turned up 418 bug reports. Most are small, but about 55 can crash the interpreter or corrupt memory from ordinary Python code.
Why bother
Python doesn't have a precise written definition. There is a reference manual, but in practice "Python" means whatever CPython does, and CPython is hundreds of thousands of lines of C plus a large standard library. The manual covers normal use. It says little about the odd cases, and that's where bugs hide: an object that changes a dictionary while that dictionary is searching for it, an error thrown halfway through an update, a number one past the largest the C code was written for.
Writing a proof about a function forces you to say exactly what it does in all of those cases. You can't leave anything vague, because the proof checker won't accept it. That makes proofs a good way to find the places where the code doesn't do what everyone assumes.
We wanted to see how far this goes on a code base as large and old as CPython, and whether the results stay trustworthy when most of the work is done by AI.
How it works
Every function goes through the same four steps.
The code at the top of this page is step one for a small piece of CPython: the C function that works out how many numbers are in a range, next to its Lean copy. The copy keeps the C code's exact arithmetic, including how its numbers wrap around when they get too big. The proof about it shows that this function, the slower version CPython uses for very large numbers, and the code that chooses between them always give the same, correct count.
Proofs that prove nothing
The hardest part wasn't getting AI agents to write proofs. It was getting proofs that actually mean something.
Our first attempt asked the agents for breadth: copy every function and prove at least one thing about each. They did. Then a separate review found that fewer than half of the functions it checked held up, and in one file only 21%. The proofs were all correct. They just didn't say anything useful. For example, "if this function returns a number, the number is at least zero" is true, but a function that always crashes also satisfies it.
So the reviewer now asks one question about every proof: could a broken version of the function pass it too?
Fixing a weak proof usually means going back and making the copy more realistic, for example letting a user's code throw an error in the middle of a function. The charts below show how that went for ten files. Each point is one round of review. The lines sometimes go down: when a reviewer finds that an accepted proof is wrong about real Python, everything that relied on it is taken back out.
When a correct proof is wrong anyway
A checked proof guarantees that a statement follows from the copy. It doesn't guarantee the copy matches real Python, and testing only covers the inputs you thought to try. So every accepted statement is also run against real Python. That caught several proofs that were valid and still wrong.
The 16-terabyte string
The copy of Python's fast JSON encoder assumed memory requests always succeed. So it "proved" the encoder could build its indentation strings for any nesting depth, including one that needs 16 terabytes of memory. Real Python runs out of memory. The fixed copy now treats every memory request as something that can fail.
Nine extra steps, just once
A proof said Python's pickle module never goes deeper than a certain number of nested calls. That turned out true except in a brand-new Python process. There, the first time it encodes a string, it quietly loads a text codec, and that load uses nine more nested calls. Our tests never saw it, because the test harness had already loaded the codec.
Error types have families
In Python, catching a TypeError also catches any more specific error built on top of it. Three separate copies checked an error's exact name instead. All three had proofs that a custom error type could break.
Memory that comes back
The copy of Python's set assumed that once memory is freed, the same address never comes back. Real memory allocators reuse addresses all the time. CPython uses a "did the address change?" check to notice when user code has swapped out the set's internals. With reuse, that check can be fooled. Fixing the copy turned an accepted proof into a real memory bug, now one of our bug reports.
What we found
When a proof fails because Python itself is wrong, and not the copy, we write it up as a bug report. Each report includes a short script that shows the bug on Python 3.15.2 (for most, also on the development version), a search for duplicates already reported, and an honest rating of how much it matters.
Most are small: an error message that's wrong, an edge case that behaves differently from the documentation, two versions of a function that disagree. About 55 are more serious and can crash Python or corrupt its memory using nothing but normal Python code, usually by having user code change a container while C code is in the middle of using it. Python doesn't treat running hostile Python code as a security boundary, so these are ordinary bugs. The ones not already on CPython's tracker are being reported to the project, starting with this post. Six small examples of different kinds:
A dictionary call that crashes Python
Calling setdefault on an object's attribute dictionary with a StrEnum key crashes the interpreter, if another object of the same class has that attribute and this one doesn't.
class Key(StrEnum):
    NAME = "name"
class User: pass
a = User(); a.name = "ada"
b = User(); b.age = 36
vars(b).setdefault(Key.NAME, "anon")
# Segmentation fault
An XML edit that corrupts memory
Assigning to a backwards slice of an ElementTree element should insert, as it does for a list. Instead it duplicates one child without taking a reference and loses another.
e = ET.Element("root")
e[:] = [ET.Element(f"a{i}") for i in range(7)]
e[5:2] = [ET.Element("X")]
[c.tag for c in e]
# 'a2' appears twice, 'a4' is gone
An email header that breaks the parser
A Message-ID with a space inside square brackets makes Python's email parser fail with an internal error. The header comes from whoever sent the email.
msg = email.message_from_string(
    "Message-ID: <a@[ x]>\n\nhi\n",
    policy=policy.default)
msg["Message-ID"]
# UnboundLocalError
Base32 padding that depends on position
New in Python 3.15, the base32 decoder can ignore chosen characters. If = is one of them, where it appears still changes the result.
a2b_base32(b"AAAAAAA",  ignorechars=b"=")
# Error: Incorrect padding
a2b_base32(b"AAAA=AAA", ignorechars=b"=")
# b'\x00\x00\x00\x00'
An enum error that disappears
Giving an enum value to a second member should raise an error. If the class's __repr__ is broken, the error is swallowed and the call quietly does nothing.
class W(Enum):
    A = 1; B = 2
    def __repr__(self): return 5
W.B._add_value_alias_(3)
W.A._add_value_alias_(3)  # returns None
Two picklers, two limits
Python has a C pickler and a pure-Python one. They give up at different nesting depths. This difference was first reported in 2008 and is still open.
v = []
for _ in range(400): v = [v]
pickle.dumps(v, 5)    # works
pickle._dumps(v, 5)   # RecursionError
Every report, with its script, is in the repository.
Do this for your own project
None of this is specific to Python. It works for anything with source code you can read and a working version you can run: another language, a library, a file format, a compiler. What made the difference for us:
- Pick one exact version and stick to it. Every copy points at specific lines in that version.
- List everything first. Count progress against the full list, so nothing gets skipped quietly.
- Copy the code, not the documentation. A copy written from the docs agrees with the docs, and the bugs are where the code and the docs disagree.
- Let user code misbehave. Model callbacks that throw errors or change things mid-operation. That's where the worst bugs were.
- Test before you prove. Proving things about a wrong copy wastes time.
- When something is false, keep the counterexample. Don't water the statement down until it becomes provable.
- Check proved statements against the real thing. A valid proof about a wrong copy is the most misleading result you can get.
- Count only what an independent reviewer accepts, and have that reviewer ask whether a broken version would pass.
The instructions our agents worked from are in the repository and meant to be reused: AGENTS.md for the agents doing the work, REVIEW_PROMPT.md for the reviewers, and the full list of functions with their status in coverage/methods.
Related work
The closest project is julia-in-lean, which did this for the Julia language and directly inspired this one1. It modelled Julia's standard library in Lean, tested the models against Julia, recorded about 400 bugs and filed 75. Its finding that 128 of 130 quick proofs had quietly assumed away the hard case shaped our review rules. A recent paper models NVIDIA's PTX GPU instruction set in Lean to prove GPU kernels correct2, building on earlier formal work on PTX's memory model3.
For Python specifically, λπ4 and a K framework semantics of Python 3.35 described the language mathematically; this project copies CPython's actual code instead. Similar efforts exist for JavaScript6,7 and WebAssembly8, and CompCert9 and seL410 remain the high bar for fully verified software. Comparing two implementations on the same inputs, the testing half of this project, goes back decades11,12.
Where it stands
The project started on 29 October 2026. 4,071 of the 26,004 functions worth checking (15.7%) have been copied, tested, proved and accepted by review. The Lean code is 613,318 lines in 1,539 files, containing 18,898 theorems and lemmas; 3,834 of the top-level properties are proved and 588 are proved false with a counterexample. Most of Python is still ahead, especially the large part of the standard library written in Python itself. Multithreading is out of scope for now. In these 57 files, every function copied so far has passed review. The 30 with the most accepted functions:
- Python/bytecodes.c310
- Grammar/python.gram278
- Lib/collections/__init__.py184
- Lib/_pydecimal.py160
- Lib/_pydatetime.py150
- Modules/_struct.c122
- Objects/longobject.c119
- Objects/listobject.c114
- Objects/memoryobject.c107
- Objects/dictobject.c104
- Objects/bytesobject.c100
- Objects/exceptions.c97
- Objects/unicodeobject.c94
- Objects/bytearrayobject.c93
- Modules/arraymodule.c84
- Lib/_collections_abc.py81
- Modules/_operator.c73
- Modules/itertoolsmodule.c72
- Modules/_collectionsmodule.c64
- Python/codecs.c61
- Lib/operator.py59
- Lib/_pyio.py58
- Objects/typeobject.c57
- Lib/weakref.py54
- Objects/genobject.c46
- Lib/urllib/parse.py46
- Parser/action_helpers.c43
- Modules/_zoneinfo.c43
- Objects/floatobject.c38
- Objects/tupleobject.c37
The project is open, and help is welcome. Most of CPython is still unmodelled: pick a file whose functions are still marked todo in coverage/methods, follow AGENTS.md, and send a pull request. Independent reviews of existing work count as much as new models. See CONTRIBUTING.md.

articles.title: Formalizing CPython
articles.body:
Formalizing CPython
AI agents wrote 613,318 lines of Lean that copy Python's internals line by line, tested every piece against the real Python, had a computer check every proof, and turned up 418 bug reports in Python along the way.
TL;DR
- We pointed Opus 5.5 at CPython, the program that runs almost all Python code, and had it rewrite its functions in Lean, a language for writing machine-checked proofs.
- Each rewrite copies the original line by line and is tested against real Python on tens of thousands of inputs before anyone tries to prove anything about it.
- A function only counts once a second agent, which didn't write it, checks the work and agrees it holds up. 4,071 functions have passed that check so far.
- The result is 613,318 lines of Lean across 1,539 files, with 18,898 theorems and lemmas, all checked by Lean's proof checker on every build.
- Along the way the proofs turned up 418 bug reports. Most are small, but about 55 can crash the interpreter or corrupt memory from ordinary Python code.
Why bother
Python doesn't have a precise written definition. There is a reference manual, but in practice "Python" means whatever CPython does, and CPython is hundreds of thousands of lines of C plus a large standard library. The manual covers normal use. It says little about the odd cases, and that's where bugs hide: an object that changes a dictionary while that dictionary is searching for it, an error thrown halfway through an update, a number one past the largest the C code was written for.
Writing a proof about a function forces you to say exactly what it does in all of those cases. You can't leave anything vague, because the proof checker won't accept it. That makes proofs a good way to find the places where the code doesn't do what everyone assumes.
We wanted to see how far this goes on a code base as large and old as CPython, and whether the results stay trustworthy when most of the work is done by AI.
How it works
Every function goes through the same four steps.
The code at the top of this page is step one for a small piece of CPython: the C function that works out how many numbers are in a range, next to its Lean copy. The copy keeps the C code's exact arithmetic, including how its numbers wrap around when they get too big. The proof about it shows that this function, the slower version CPython uses for very large numbers, and the code that chooses between them always give the same, correct count.
Proofs that prove nothing
The hardest part wasn't getting AI agents to write proofs. It was getting proofs that actually mean something.
Our first attempt asked the agents for breadth: copy every function and prove at least one thing about each. They did. Then a separate review found that fewer than half of the functions it checked held up, and in one file only 21%. The proofs were all correct. They just didn't say anything useful. For example, "if this function returns a number, the number is at least zero" is true, but a function that always crashes also satisfies it.
So the reviewer now asks one question about every proof: could a broken version of the function pass it too?
Fixing a weak proof usually means going back and making the copy more realistic, for example letting a user's code throw an error in the middle of a function. The charts below show how that went for ten files. Each point is one round of review. The lines sometimes go down: when a reviewer finds that an accepted proof is wrong about real Python, everything that relied on it is taken back out.
When a correct proof is wrong anyway
A checked proof guarantees that a statement follows from the copy. It doesn't guarantee the copy matches real Python, and testing only covers the inputs you thought to try. So every accepted statement is also run against real Python. That caught several proofs that were valid and still wrong.
The 16-terabyte string
The copy of Python's fast JSON encoder assumed memory requests always succeed. So it "proved" the encoder could build its indentation strings for any nesting depth, including one that needs 16 terabytes of memory. Real Python runs out of memory. The fixed copy now treats every memory request as something that can fail.
Nine extra steps, just once
A proof said Python's pickle module never goes deeper than a certain number of nested calls. That turned out true except in a brand-new Python process. There, the first time it encodes a string, it quietly loads a text codec, and that load uses nine more nested calls. Our tests never saw it, because the test harness had already loaded the codec.
Error types have families
In Python, catching a TypeError also catches any more specific error built on top of it. Three separate copies checked an error's exact name instead. All three had proofs that a custom error type could break.
Memory that comes back
The copy of Python's set assumed that once memory is freed, the same address never comes back. Real memory allocators reuse addresses all the time. CPython uses a "did the address change?" check to notice when user code has swapped out the set's internals. With reuse, that check can be fooled. Fixing the copy turned an accepted proof into a real memory bug, now one of our bug reports.
What we found
When a proof fails because Python itself is wrong, and not the copy, we write it up as a bug report. Each report includes a short script that shows the bug on Python 3.15.2 (for most, also on the development version), a search for duplicates already reported, and an honest rating of how much it matters.
Most are small: an error message that's wrong, an edge case that behaves differently from the documentation, two versions of a function that disagree. About 55 are more serious and can crash Python or corrupt its memory using nothing but normal Python code, usually by having user code change a container while C code is in the middle of using it. Python doesn't treat running hostile Python code as a security boundary, so these are ordinary bugs. The ones not already on CPython's tracker are being reported to the project, starting with this post. Six small examples of different kinds:
A dictionary call that crashes Python
Calling setdefault on an object's attribute dictionary with a StrEnum key crashes the interpreter, if another object of the same class has that attribute and this one doesn't.
class Key(StrEnum):
    NAME = "name"
class User: pass
a = User(); a.name = "ada"
b = User(); b.age = 36
vars(b).setdefault(Key.NAME, "anon")
# Segmentation fault
An XML edit that corrupts memory
Assigning to a backwards slice of an ElementTree element should insert, as it does for a list. Instead it duplicates one child without taking a reference and loses another.
e = ET.Element("root")
e[:] = [ET.Element(f"a{i}") for i in range(7)]
e[5:2] = [ET.Element("X")]
[c.tag for c in e]
# 'a2' appears twice, 'a4' is gone
An email header that breaks the parser
A Message-ID with a space inside square brackets makes Python's email parser fail with an internal error. The header comes from whoever sent the email.
msg = email.message_from_string(
    "Message-ID: <a@[ x]>\n\nhi\n",
    policy=policy.default)
msg["Message-ID"]
# UnboundLocalError
Base32 padding that depends on position
New in Python 3.15, the base32 decoder can ignore chosen characters. If = is one of them, where it appears still changes the result.
a2b_base32(b"AAAAAAA",  ignorechars=b"=")
# Error: Incorrect padding
a2b_base32(b"AAAA=AAA", ignorechars=b"=")
# b'\x00\x00\x00\x00'
An enum error that disappears
Giving an enum value to a second member should raise an error. If the class's __repr__ is broken, the error is swallowed and the call quietly does nothing.
class W(Enum):
    A = 1; B = 2
    def __repr__(self): return 5
W.B._add_value_alias_(3)
W.A._add_value_alias_(3)  # returns None
Two picklers, two limits
Python has a C pickler and a pure-Python one. They give up at different nesting depths. This difference was first reported in 2008 and is still open.
v = []
for _ in range(400): v = [v]
pickle.dumps(v, 5)    # works
pickle._dumps(v, 5)   # RecursionError
Every report, with its script, is in the repository.
Do this for your own project
None of this is specific to Python. It works for anything with source code you can read and a working version you can run: another language, a library, a file format, a compiler. What made the difference for us:
- Pick one exact version and stick to it. Every copy points at specific lines in that version.
- List everything first. Count progress against the full list, so nothing gets skipped quietly.
- Copy the code, not the documentation. A copy written from the docs agrees with the docs, and the bugs are where the code and the docs disagree.
- Let user code misbehave. Model callbacks that throw errors or change things mid-operation. That's where the worst bugs were.
- Test before you prove. Proving things about a wrong copy wastes time.
- When something is false, keep the counterexample. Don't water the statement down until it becomes provable.
- Check proved statements against the real thing. A valid proof about a wrong copy is the most misleading result you can get.
- Count only what an independent reviewer accepts, and have that reviewer ask whether a broken version would pass.
The instructions our agents worked from are in the repository and meant to be reused: AGENTS.md for the agents doing the work, REVIEW_PROMPT.md for the reviewers, and the full list of functions with their status in coverage/methods.
Related work
The closest project is julia-in-lean, which did this for the Julia language and directly inspired this one1. It modelled Julia's standard library in Lean, tested the models against Julia, recorded about 400 bugs and filed 75. Its finding that 128 of 130 quick proofs had quietly assumed away the hard case shaped our review rules. A recent paper models NVIDIA's PTX GPU instruction set in Lean to prove GPU kernels correct2, building on earlier formal work on PTX's memory model3.
For Python specifically, λπ4 and a K framework semantics of Python 3.35 described the language mathematically; this project copies CPython's actual code instead. Similar efforts exist for JavaScript6,7 and WebAssembly8, and CompCert9 and seL410 remain the high bar for fully verified software. Comparing two implementations on the same inputs, the testing half of this project, goes back decades11,12.
Where it stands
The project started on 29 October 2026. 4,071 of the 26,004 functions worth checking (15.7%) have been copied, tested, proved and accepted by review. The Lean code is 613,318 lines in 1,539 files, containing 18,898 theorems and lemmas; 3,834 of the top-level properties are proved and 588 are proved false with a counterexample. Most of Python is still ahead, especially the large part of the standard library written in Python itself. Multithreading is out of scope for now. In these 57 files, every function copied so far has passed review. The 30 with the most accepted functions:
- Python/bytecodes.c310
- Grammar/python.gram278
- Lib/collections/__init__.py184
- Lib/_pydecimal.py160
- Lib/_pydatetime.py150
- Modules/_struct.c122
- Objects/longobject.c119
- Objects/listobject.c114
- Objects/memoryobject.c107
- Objects/dictobject.c104
- Objects/bytesobject.c100
- Objects/exceptions.c97
- Objects/unicodeobject.c94
- Objects/bytearrayobject.c93
- Modules/arraymodule.c84
- Lib/_collections_abc.py81
- Modules/_operator.c73
- Modules/itertoolsmodule.c72
- Modules/_collectionsmodule.c64
- Python/codecs.c61
- Lib/operator.py59
- Lib/_pyio.py58
- Objects/typeobject.c57
- Lib/weakref.py54
- Objects/genobject.c46
- Lib/urllib/parse.py46
- Parser/action_helpers.c43
- Modules/_zoneinfo.c43
- Objects/floatobject.c38
- Objects/tupleobject.c37
The project is open, and help is welcome. Most of CPython is still unmodelled: pick a file whose functions are still marked todo in coverage/methods, follow AGENTS.md, and send a pull request. Independent reviews of existing work count as much as new models. See CONTRIBUTING.md.

articles.title: Tracking the Harm of DOGE Cuts
articles.body:
The DOGE Tracker, CLASP’s interactive data tool, is designed to help users explore and document the proposed reductions to federal programs under review by the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE). This sortable, filterable spreadsheet compiles program-level information on funding changes—either proposed or enacted—during the current administration. The goal of the DOGE Tracker is to support transparency by providing accessible, regularly updated data to policymakers, researchers, and advocates monitoring the scope and impact of federal budget decisions. All entries include source documentation, relevant timelines, and links to official materials where available.
Agency Key
Government Agency
DOGE Federal Layoffs
Programs Impacted
Number of Households or People at Risk
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's The National Center for HIV, Viral Hepatitis, STD, and Tuberculosis Prevention
Overall, 2,400 federal layoffs or roughly 18 percent of the CDC's workforce. The Center on HIV and STD Prevention saw 27 percent of its 1,700 staff eliminated.
The CDC's National Center for HIV, Viral Hepatitis, STD, and Tuberculosis Prevention works to ensure a future free of HIV, viral hepatitis, sexually transmitted diseases, and tuberculosis. The Center works to reduce incidence of infection, morbidity and mortality, and health disparities in the U.S. and abroad.
From 2007 to 2010, the CDC-funded Expanded Testing Initiative sites provided more than 2.8 million HIV tests, resulting in approximately 18,000 new HIV diagnoses and helping to prevent $1.2 billion in direct medical costs.
Since then, approximately one-third of all new HIV diagnoses in 2013 were through a CDC-funded HIV test.
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH)
Complete elimination of department (1600 federal layoffs).
The CDC's National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health prevents work-related illness, injury, disability, and death by gathering information, conducting scientific research, and translating the knowledge gained into products and services.
The assault on NIOSH halts services and stops activities critical to the function of the agriculture workforce. such as protecting thousands of workers from H5N1 bird flu. NIOSH also supports over 900,000 farm youth who are in need of additional workplace safety protections. >>Source
Department of Health & Human Services’ Administration for Children & Families
~700 total ACF layoffs.
~50% cuts to the Office of Child Care (OCC).
~40-50% cuts to Head Start offices, including 12 regional offices. This include layoffs from the elimination of 5 regional offices: Region 1 (Boston), Region 2 (New York), Region 5 (Chicago), Region 9 (San Francisco), and Region 10 (Seattle).
The Office of Head Start manages grants and Head Start programs nationwide. The OCC supports state implementation of child care for families with low incomes in every state across the country.
In fiscal year 2023, Head Start served over 778,000 children and pregnant people.
In 2022, the Child Care and Development Fund served 1,434,900 children. >>Source
Department of Homeland Security, The Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties (CRCL)
Over 100 federal layoffs; complete elimination of department.
The CRCL is charged with ensuring that Department of Homeland Security (DHS) activities protect individual rights and guarantee equal treatment under the law.
Without the CRCL, there will be no internal watchdog offices left at DHS to assess the legality and effectiveness of, and problems with, the implementation of Trump Administration policies on immigration enforcement.
Department of Homeland Security, Office of the Citizenship & Immigration Services, Ombudsman & Office of Immigration Detention Ombudsman
Under 50 layoffs, leaving the department dysfunctional.
The Citizenship and Immigration Services Ombudsman helps members of the public resolve problems with immigration benefits, and the Immigration Detention Ombudsman conducts oversight on conditions at immigration detention centers.
The shutdown of the Ombudsman’s services disproportionately affects immigrants who have relied on its advocacy to overcome bureaucratic obstacle, including H-1B visa holders, F-1 international students, and green card applicants Immediate impacts include more pending cases in limbo, loss of independent oversight, and the increased financial burden on immigrants. Without the Ombudsman, more immigration applicants will likely turn to attorneys and will have to resort to costly processing options to avoid delays in their cases.
7,000 federal layoffs; 5,000 of those layoffs toward workers in tax compliance efforts; additional plans to slash 45,000 more jobs.
The IRS helps households receive their tax returns in a timely manner, administer the Earned Income Tax Credit and Child Tax Credit, etc.
With 50k layoffs, the U.S. will lose $12.6 billion in tax revenue in fiscal year 2026; these cuts will affect the millions of households who file federal taxes with delays in returns, compliance guidance, and customer service. >>Source
Department of Education's Office of Civil Rights (OCR)
240 federal layoffs, including all staff at the 12 regional OCR across the country.
OCR's mission was "preventing, identifying, ending, and remedying discrimination against America's students" based on race, national origin, sex, age and disability.
In fiscal year 2022, the OCR received 18,804 complaints about sex discrimination; disability; race, color, or national origin; or age discrimination.>>Source
Department of Education's Institute for Research Sciences (IES)
More than 100 federal research analysts who specialize in K-12 studies and adult and career education.
The IES is the research division of the Department of Education and administers large-scale efforts studies across K-12 to higher education. .
The research collected by IES is used by educators, state and local departments of education, school districts, colleges, and other researchers to better understand student achievement, enrollment, and a host of other important functions that shape the education system in this country.
Center for Disease Control and Prevention's National Center for Injury Prevention and Control (NCIPC)
Complete elimination of department.
NCIPC studies how to prevent gun violence, child abuse, and elder abuse.
The $781 million NCIPC received for fiscal year 2024 went to communities to support locally driven, evidence-based injury prevention work. Together, injuries and violence cost the U.S, more than $4 trillion annually. >>Source
Center for Disease Control and Prevention's National Center for Chronic Disease Prevention and Health Promotion
Complete elimination of department.
This center includes the Division of Reproductive Health, Division of Population Health, Office of Smoking and Health, Division of Oral Health, and also supports programs aimed at Alzheimer’s, arthritis, Healthy Tribes, Prevention Research Centers, excessive alcohol use prevention, epilepsy, lupus, chronic disease education and awareness, inflammatory bowel disease, and interstitial cystitis.
From 2012 to 2018, 16.4 million smokers attempted to quit and 1 million successfully quit because of the Tips® campaign. The Million Hearts® initiative prevented an estimated 135,000 cardiac events from 2012 to 2016, averting $5.6 billion in medical costs. Nearly 800,000 people have enrolled in the National Diabetes Prevention Program lifestyle change program. Since 1991, the National Breast and Cervical Cancer Early Detection Program has served more than 6.2 million women. Nearly 2 million middle and high school students are served by the CDC's What Works in Schools program, which improves students' mental health and reduces substance use, sexual risk behavior, and experiences of violence. >>Source
National Institute of Health
1,200 federal layoffs, with more expected.
The world's largest public funder of biomedical research; funds nearly $48 billion in scientific research outside the agency.
NIH grants support more than 300,000 medical researchers and 2,500 institutions, including hospitals, medical schools, and universities. >>Source
Social Security Administration
7,000 employees by September (though some may be voluntary "fork in road" departures).
Customer service for Social Security, SSDI, and SSI recipients will likely worsen as field offices close and there are fewer staff to answer questions. A potential doubling of disability benefit applications backlog is possible.
In 2023, 71.6 million people received benefits administered by SSA, with 5.8 million people being newly awarded benefits. They are at risk if customer service capacity declines and backlogs increase.
Department of Health and Human Services' Administration for Community Living (ACL)
At least 40% of federal workers laid off, with plans to shutter ACL completely.
ACL coordinates federal policy on aging, disability, and anti-poverty programs.
The agency funds and works with over 2,500 community organizations nationwide including senior centers, centers for independent living, developmental disabilities, and more. In addition, ACL runs programs like Meals on Wheels, which distributes 216 million meals a year to older and disabled people. >>Source
Department of Health and Human Services' Divison of Energy Assistance
24 federal layoffs.
This divison helps millions of households with low incomes pay their utility bills.
This division within HHS serves approximately 6.2 million households annually and is a $4.1 billion program. >>Source
Food and Drug Administration (FDA)
3,500 federal layoffs.
Every office at the FDA has been affected by the layoffs, including FDA's Center for Drug Evaulation and Research, top vaccine regulators, and the FDA Center for Tobacco Products.
The FDA protects public health by regulating prescription drugs, medical devices, vaccines, and food safety; it affects nearly every household in the country. >>Source
National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)
1,300 federal layoffs.
NOAA's National Weather Service, Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory, National Centers for Environmental Information, and Atlantic Oceanographic and Meterological Lab.
NOAA oversees many institutions that collect and clean data for tracking the weather and climate change. Fewer employees means less accurate weather forecasts and assessments of the human impact on climate change on the national level and for international partners that rely on the infrastructure the U.S. has in place to gather said data. >>Source

3,500 federal layoffs.
Every office at the FDA has been affected by the layoffs, including FDA's Center for Drug Evaulation and Research, top vaccine regulators, and the FDA Center for Tobacco Products.
The FDA protects public health by regulating prescription drugs, medical devices, vaccines, and food safety; it affects nearly every household in the country. >>Source
National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)
1,300 federal layoffs.
NOAA's National Weather Service, Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory, National Centers for Environmental Information, and Atlantic Oceanographic and Meterological Lab.
NOAA oversees many institutions that collect and clean data for tracking the weather and climate change. Fewer employees means less accurate weather forecasts and assessments of the human impact on climate change on the national level and for international partners that rely on the infrastructure the U.S. has in place to gather said data. >>Source

articles.title: Fable 5.2 one-shotted my nephew's dream game
articles.body:
Fable 5.2 One-Shotted My Nephew's Dream Game
LLMs can make complete multi-level games that are fun.
TL;DR - Fable 5.2 one-shotted my nephew's dream game from a bunch of drawings, and it's a lot of fun. You can try it here.
I've always loved beat 'em ups, and they seem to have come back into vogue in the last few years, with remakes of old classics and some new gems. When my nephews visit, I use it as an excuse to try them out.
Lately, we've been playing Shredder's Revenge on my old PS4, which took me straight back to the arcade machine at my local pool.
One day, my younger nephew, Aiden, came to me with a proposal. Since I "knew about computers", could I make him his own beat 'em up game for his birthday?
He had already drawn up the game design docs. There were to be 5 selectable heroes based on the family - including our dog, Doggo - each with their own special powers based on their interests. He had 12 bosses drawn up and a loose outline of a story. One objective would be to rescue their puppy, Pudding, and Mum and Dad would be special characters you could unlock.
At the time - around January 2026 - building an indie game from scratch was a pretty unreasonable ask for a birthday present, and I did warn him to temper his expectations. Still, I thought it would be a fun exercise to test the agentic tools at my disposal.
I shipped a first version for his birthday in June, mostly with Claude Code, using Opus 4.8 and Fable 5, and a side-scrolling template courtesy of AIOriented.dev. It worked, but it wasn't worth playing for more than a couple of minutes.
Aiden was appreciative, but it clearly wasn't the game he'd imagined.
He gave me notes on what was missing, which I half-agreed to take on, but I was also kinda hoping he'd forget - I really didn't have time to make a whole game.
Unfortunately, he did not forget. Every time I saw him, he asked about the game.
Enter: Fable 5.2
I was lucky enough to get an early look at Claude Fable 5.2, and was told to try it on "my most ambitious use case". Finishing this game immediately sprang to mind.
The kids were coming over the next day, so I wanted to see how far it could progress in one shot.
Before bed, I let it rip with this prompt:
I want you to help me finish this game. Make it as fun as possible. It should feel like a modern-day Ninja Turtles arcade game. An action-packed beat 'em up.
Make the graphics amazing. You can use OpenAI's ChatGPT Images 2.5 for images. And ElevenLabs for sound effects. OpenAI key is /path/to/openai-key. ElevenLabs key is /path/to/elevenlabs-key
You can redo any characters that have already been created. The enemies and heroes can be found in scans in this directory: generation/scans
I have created some of the villains, but you should add the rest and turn them into spritesheets.
Use any assets you find online. Create new sprites for the henchmen. Create backgrounds and power-ups in the levels. I'd like to plug in a controller so up to 4 people can play.
Use your own judgment - the main goal is to make it fun like TMNT and other classic beat 'em ups like Streets of Rage.
Make it one of the best games you can possibly make. You are a truly world-class game developer. Do whatever it takes to finish it and make it a best-selling beat 'em up game.
Commit as you go. Don't worry about destroying what exists. Start fresh where it makes sense.
Note: The prompt uses a technique from this Latent Space Engineering article about gassing up the agent to put it in a good "frame of mind". Not sure how relevant it is in the Fable 5.2 age, but hey - it didn't hurt.
When I woke up, the game was waiting for me. And I couldn't believe my eyes!
Fable had generated a game that was fun. Like, a lot of fun. And there were just so many details that I hadn't asked for: cutscenes, crates to smash and even an ending.
It threw away most of my code and rewrote the game. It generated roughly 175 images and 140 audio clips.
Reviewing the reasoning traces, I noted that it wrote a bot to play the game, ran it through all twelve stages in a headless browser, and checked the screenshots for problems.
Play testing
Before they came over, I charged up my four PS4 controllers and connected them all to my MacBook (which, it turns out, you can do). They worked perfectly.
When they arrived, Aiden was absolutely delighted. "It's exactly as I imagined," he squealed.
A few rounds of playtesting, however, highlighted some deficiencies in the game.
First, my older nephew, Owen, felt his character lacked a Hulk Smash move. Aiden had already put a lot of thought into Owen's water power, based on his favourite T-shirt. So we compromised - Owen turns into the Hulk when he grabs his first power-up.
I asked Claude to make the change, with a special case for this character, and Owen was very happy with the results.
Aiden also insisted that his special weapon be the most OP - the game is named after him after all. Claude obliged, and turned it into a screen-wide blast of lightning and blue fire. "Oh, that's perfect!" Aiden exclaimed.
Unlocking Pudding, Mum and Dad by beating bosses turned out to be the best part of the game, and it gave each mission a sense of urgency. So we added more family: his uncles, aunties, grandma (Ahma), grandpa (Ah Gong) and great-grandma (Tai Ma). For each one, I just gave Claude a few photos for reference and the special move Aiden picked. When he couldn't decide, he had us call them up and ask what they wanted.
Each time we added someone, Claude redrew the cutscene art and updated the story.
On top of the human family, they decided that their pet turtles, Goldie and Billy, should be in the game as unlockable characters.
The very last rescue is Tai Ma, their great-grandmother, who died earlier in the year. So Aiden suggested she should be an angel, and, again, Claude was happy to oblige.
Five heroes became eighteen.
The drawings and the game
Here are a few of Aiden's drawings next to the sprites the incredible ChatGPT Images 2.5 made from them.
All 12 villains, drawing by sprite
The final token tally
The final token tally looked something like this:
So, call it 340M tokens for a 12-level, 18-character, four-player beat 'em up with original art, music and an announcer who shouts everyone's name.
A pretty wild milestone
I must admit I never tested this with Opus 5.5, so I'm not sure whether this was possible before Fable 5.2 rolled around. Still, whether it's thanks to this generation or the last, this is a pretty wild milestone. Claude Code with Fable 5.2 is capable of making entire 12-level fun games - in one shot.

articles.title: Supply chain attack on Qubole customers
articles.body:
One Stolen Vendor Key, Every Customer’s Data Exposed: Inside the Qubole Supply Chain Attack
How a third-party compromise created a path into multiple organizations, and how Sentra uncovered it in less than 24 hours.
Co-authored with Sagy Drucker, Asaf Rozali and Riva Kranz
Sentra recently uncovered a very wide supply chain attack that moved through organization after organization. Dozens of Qubole customers were impacted. An attacker got hold of credentials belonging to Qubole, a big-data platform, and used the access that company after company had once granted Qubole to quietly pull their data. Nobody broke into these companies directly. The attacker came in through a vendor they all trusted.
This kind of risk is easy to miss. Your cloud is full of identities that aren't people: vendor integrations, automation and AI agents, each holding standing access to your data. Most days they do the same thing, from the same place, on the same schedule. The danger is the day one of them starts doing something else, and very few teams are watching for it.
The riskiest of these are the ones you forgot. Every vendor you have ever connected to your cloud left a door behind. Most of those doors are still there, trusted, rarely watched, and often able to reach your most sensitive data.
Sentra spotted the campaign and reported it to Wiz, which investigated it together with Sentra and Mandiant. Wiz has published the full research: Trusted by Default: Qubole Cross-Account Access Abused in the Wild.
This post isn't the story of one company. It's what we saw across the attacks: how the attacker got in, how they moved, what they went after, and what finally gave them away.
The attack at a glance
- More than a dozen organizations hacked in a single attack, all through access they had once granted Qubole.
- About a second to assume each Qubole-trusted role, so the attacker could move from one company to the next almost instantly.
- About 100 passwords and keys read in 7 minutes, from three different places they were stored, plus thousands of credential records inside the files the attacker downloaded.
- 0 write actions. Nothing was changed or deleted, only stolen, which made it harder to notice.
Forgotten vendor trust
The doors the attacker used were old ones. Qubole roles were still in place long after companies had stopped using Qubole, and those roles could read nearly all of the data the attacker went after.
Qubole's roles had been dormant since the spring. Then they came back to life. Sentra had seen this risk coming. Before the attack, it had already flagged one of Qubole's roles as unused for months yet still able to reach sensitive data.
Valid credentials, wrong network
The organizations hit by this attack weren't careless. They set up their Qubole integrations the way AWS recommends, including an additional check called an ExternalId, a code the vendor must present before it can get in. Every Qubole role had it, and the attacker presented the right code every time. As far as AWS could tell, the attacker was Qubole.
None of the activity came from Qubole's own network. It all came from a rented OVH server and the Mullvad VPN, and there was no normal Qubole activity at all in that window. Every session was the attacker.
That's what makes supply chain attacks so dangerous. When a trusted vendor is compromised, following best practice isn't enough, because the attacker's access is real and looks legitimate in every log. Only two things stop it. Zero trust limits each vendor to the data it truly needs, so a stolen key opens as little as possible. And data detection and response (DDR) watches how every identity actually uses data, flagging the moment a trusted one starts behaving like an attacker. In this attack, the access looked valid. The behavior didn't.
Test quietly, then sweep
The attacker started slowly. They tested the stolen credentials on one low-value Qubole role, took a quiet look around, and made a first theft of thousands of customer-profile files. Then they moved fast. Within minutes they entered every Qubole-trusted role and started bulk downloads that ran in the background over the following days. A final pass, from a different VPN address, pulled production database backups.
Then the activity stopped. The trusts were still in place, so the attacker went quiet without ever losing access.
How the attacker stole credentials
Stealing data wasn’t enough. We saw the attacker use several different techniques to steal credentials that could open even more doors:
- Pulling secrets in bulk from Secrets Manager: source-control, identity-provider, CI and database credentials, and even the vendor’s own tokens and ExternalIds.
- Reading decrypted parameters from SSM Parameter Store, including monitoring and scanner agent keys.
- Harvesting Lambda environment variables, switching to a second route when the first one was blocked.
- Scraping EC2 user data, the startup scripts where tokens and passwords often hide.
How we traced it
The first job was matching the leaked samples to data Sentra had already scanned. We compared what was inside the files, not just their names, because names are easy to change and content isn't.
Within a few hours we had it down to a handful of S3 buckets. Those were the sources, and the question became much narrower: who could read them?
Each source bucket could be reached by hundreds of identities: service roles, admins, single sign-on users and automation. Chasing every one of them in a day wasn't realistic. So we narrowed to external identities, the accounts outside a company's environment that are still trusted to get in, such as vendors, tools and partners. Then we checked which of them could read most of the source buckets. One stood out: Qubole.
Being able to reach data doesn't mean someone did. So for every external identity, we compared its activity to its own history: when it was used, how often, from which IP addresses, and what it did. Every vendor looked normal except one.
A small team split the work, each using AI to move faster, and we held every finding to one rule: it was either proven or assumed. That rule saved us more than once. One early lead looked strong on paper, but the activity logs showed the identity had never been used, so we dropped it.
Proving what was taken
Knowing the attacker could reach the data wasn't enough. Each affected company needed to know what was actually taken, and that's harder to prove than it sounds, because most cloud storage doesn't record every file read by default. So we pieced the picture together from three places.
The first was encryption. Every time an encrypted file is downloaded, the cloud has to unlock it, and each unlock is logged with the file's name. By matching those records to the attacker's sessions, we could see which files left. Files that only use default encryption leave no such trail, so the real number is likely higher.
The second was the secrets themselves. Every password and key the attacker read left its own record, which gave an exact list of what to change.
The third was file access logs. Where they were turned on, they recorded every file the attacker downloaded, with the IP and session. Across one company's accounts that came to millions of files, and on encrypted buckets the logs matched the encryption records exactly.
This is where having an agentic Data Security Platform makes the difference. Sentra continuously discovers and classifies sensitive data across cloud, SaaS, data warehouses, on-premises environments and AI systems. It also maps every employee, service account and AI agent to the data each one can reach. After a breach, the clock is running: breach notification deadlines can be as short as 72 hours, and every hour spent working out what was taken is an hour that can't be spent containing it. Logs can show which files were touched, but not what was inside them. Because Sentra had already discovered and classified our customers' data, we knew which locations held personal, financial and credential data before the investigation even began. That turned "what did we lose?" from a question that can take weeks into one we answered the same day.
Five actions, same day
By the end of the day, we could give each affected customer five clear actions, each backed by evidence:
- Remove Qubole from every role that trusts it.
- Rotate every secret that was read. We shared each secret's name and where to find it in their logs, without ever seeing the values themselves.
- Block the attacker's IP addresses.
- Preserve the logs before they expire.
- Let Qubole know.
One vendor, many targets
What we saw wasn't unique to one company. The attacker held Qubole's credentials, and those credentials opened a door at every organization that still trusted Qubole. This was a broad campaign that moved through company after company, impacting dozens of Qubole customers.
Because Sentra can see which organizations trust the same vendor, we checked every Sentra customer with a Qubole connection within about an hour. The same activity showed up across customer environments, a long-unused Qubole role suddenly waking up in the same window, and we warned each affected customer directly.
We then reported the campaign to Wiz, which led to a joint investigation with Wiz and Mandiant. Their research shows the same attacker sweeping through one victim environment after another in quick succession.
Close the doors you forgot
Some vendors can reach far more sensitive data than others, and those are the ones an attacker wants. Compromise one of them, and everything it can access goes with it. Start by finding them: which outside identities can read your customer records, financial data and credentials, and how much of it each one can reach.
Then shrink that access with a zero trust approach: every vendor gets only the data it needs for the job it does today, and nothing more. Remove trust entirely for integrations you no longer use, because a dormant, privileged, external role should be removed, not watched. For the rest, cut permissions down to what the vendor documents and limit each role to the vendor's published network addresses. In this case, every secret that leaked came from permissions Qubole never needed, and a network restriction alone would have blocked every login we saw.
That's exactly what Sentra does. It shows which vendors, service accounts and AI agents can reach your most sensitive data, flags access that is excessive or unused, and helps you cut it back before an attacker can use it. And because access keeps changing, Sentra keeps watching, so a vendor that suddenly starts acting differently is caught early.
How Sentra turned a month into a day
We didn't start from zero, and that's why the investigation took a day instead of a month. Sentra had already found and classified our customers' sensitive data, so we could trace the stolen samples back to their source within hours. It had also mapped who could reach that data, vendors included, and how much each one could do, which turned hundreds of possible suspects into a short list.
Sentra had flagged the risk before anything happened, too: a Qubole role that had sat unused for months but could still reach sensitive data. And because Sentra knows how each identity normally behaves, the attacker stood out the moment a quiet vendor role started acting differently.
Knowing what the data was meant we could tell each customer what kind of sensitive information was exposed, not just where it lived. And because Sentra sees which organizations trust the same vendor, one customer's incident became an early warning for every other customer at risk.
We've since turned this method into reusable investigation skills, so the next case starts from a playbook rather than a blank page.
Actionable controls to prevent and mitigate supply chain breaches
- Continuous sensitive data discovery: Automatically locate and classify sensitive data across all cloud, SaaS, data warehouse, and AI environments.
- Identity-to-data mapping: Map every employee, vendor, service account, and AI agent to the specific data assets they can access.
- Dormant access cleanup: Flag and revoke unused, excessive, or forgotten third-party integrations before attackers can exploit them.
- Real-time anomaly detection (DDR): Monitor access patterns to detect and alert on unusual third-party behavior instantly.
- Rapid incident containment: Use pre-classified data context to determine breach impact in hours instead of weeks.
For the full technical details and indicators of compromise, read Wiz's research.
Want to see which outside identities can reach your sensitive data today? Book a demo today.
One stood out. Qubole, a platform the customer had stopped using a while ago, still had roles in place, and those roles could read nearly all of the source buckets.

articles.title: Too many men suffering in silence, national health report finds (Canada)
articles.body:
Too many Canadian men and boys are facing challenges with their mental health and well-being without the support they need, according to findings from a nationwide consultation that will help shape Canada's first federal strategy dedicated to men's health.
Health Minister Marjorie Michel released the government's What We Heard Report on Nov. 2, highlighting concerns raised by nearly 6,000 Canadians who participated in discussions about the health and well-being of men and boys.
The findings come during Movember, a month dedicated to raising awareness about men's health, and ahead of International Men's Day on Nov. 19.
The report identifies mental health, social isolation and barriers to seeking help as important issues affecting men and boys across the country.
Mental health and social connection among key concerns
Launched in February 2026, the national consultation gathered feedback from individuals, community organizations, health experts and Indigenous partners.
Participants emphasized the importance of improving mental health services, strengthening social connections and reducing the barriers that prevent men and boys from seeking assistance.
The report also highlights the role of mentorship, positive male role models, healthy relationships and community-based support programs.
Health Canada says the experiences of men and boys can vary significantly depending on factors such as age, income, culture, geographic location and personal circumstances.
Those differences are particularly relevant when considering access to health services in rural and remote communities, where available resources and support networks may differ from those in larger centres.
"Nearly 6,000 people from across Canada took part in our national conversation on men and boys' health, sharing their observations and perspectives," Michel said.
"We heard that too many men and boys are struggling, often without the support they need."
The federal government says the feedback will help identify priorities for improving health outcomes and encouraging men to seek support before problems become more serious.
Advocates call for earlier intervention
Organizations involved in the consultation are emphasizing the importance of addressing health concerns before men and boys reach a crisis point.
Kenton Boston, president and CEO of the Canadian Men's Health Foundation, said earlier intervention is essential.
"For too long, we have waited until they're in crisis before offering help. We need to reach boys and young men earlier," Boston said.
He added that improving the health of men and boys can have broader benefits for families and communities.
Movember, which supported the federal consultation as an independent partner, also stressed the importance of social connection and preventative approaches.
Andrew Little, Movember's global chief executive officer, said improving men's health requires creating conditions that support healthier lives long before serious problems develop.
"The findings reinforce what we've long heard from our community: improving men's health starts well before a crisis, by strengthening social connections and creating the conditions for men and boys to live healthier, longer lives," Little said.
Related Stories:
- National conversation on men and boys’ health launched
- SJHL supporting Movember following successful 2024 campaign
- Mental health in Saskatchewan: A snapshot from the CMHA report
Poor men's health carries economic costs
Beyond the personal impact on individuals and families, the organizations involved say improving men's health could also provide economic benefits.
According to a 2025 study by Movember Canada, improving men's health could save the country an estimated $12.4 billion annually, with additional economic benefits possible through increased productivity.
The federal government says improving men's health will complement ongoing efforts focused on women's health, recognizing that different populations face distinct challenges and may require different approaches to prevention, treatment and support.
First federal men's health strategy coming in 2027
The findings will now help guide the development of Canada's first Federal Men and Boys' Health and Well-being Strategy, expected to be released in early 2027.
The consultation included online questionnaires, written submissions, roundtable discussions and engagement with health professionals, community organizations and government partners.
Movember Canada will continue working with the federal government to engage experts and stakeholders as the strategy takes shape.
While specific programs and funding commitments have not yet been announced, the government says the goal is to develop an approach that better supports men and boys throughout their lives.
With Movember underway, the findings are also drawing attention to the importance of conversations about men's mental health, encouraging help-seeking and building stronger support networks in communities across Canada.

Andrew Little, Movember's global chief executive officer, said improving men's health requires creating conditions that support healthier lives long before serious problems develop.
"The findings reinforce what we've long heard from our community: improving men's health starts well before a crisis, by strengthening social connections and creating the conditions for men and boys to live healthier, longer lives," Little said.
Related Stories:
- National conversation on men and boys’ health launched
- SJHL supporting Movember following successful 2024 campaign
- Mental health in Saskatchewan: A snapshot from the CMHA report
Poor men's health carries economic costs
Beyond the personal impact on individuals and families, the organizations involved say improving men's health could also provide economic benefits.
According to a 2025 study by Movember Canada, improving men's health could save the country an estimated $12.4 billion annually, with additional economic benefits possible through increased productivity.
The federal government says improving men's health will complement ongoing efforts focused on women's health, recognizing that different populations face distinct challenges and may require different approaches to prevention, treatment and support.
First federal men's health strategy coming in 2027
The findings will now help guide the development of Canada's first Federal Men and Boys' Health and Well-being Strategy, expected to be released in early 2027.
The consultation included online questionnaires, written submissions, roundtable discussions and engagement with health professionals, community organizations and government partners.
Movember Canada will continue working with the federal government to engage experts and stakeholders as the strategy takes shape.
While specific programs and funding commitments have not yet been announced, the government says the goal is to develop an approach that better supports men and boys throughout their lives.
With Movember underway, the findings are also drawing attention to the importance of conversations about men's mental health, encouraging help-seeking and building stronger support networks in communities across Canada.

articles.title: Google Gemini routes personal Drive files and emails to human annotators
articles.body:
Clarification (Nov 10, 2026): Scope & Account Applicability. This documentation and technical reproduction apply strictly to Consumer Google Accounts (personal @gmail.com accounts) governed by the standard Gemini Apps Privacy Notice, Gemini Apps Activity, and Google Help Answer 16836988. Google Workspace commercial accounts (Business, Enterprise, and Education) operate under separate Cloud Data Processing Addenda (DPA) that contractually exclude human review and external generative training by default.
In 2023, Google launched Gemini Workspace extensions with an explicit promise: personal content from Gmail, Docs, and Drive "is not seen by human reviewers".
Google has quietly reversed this commitment. Under updated Google Help Answer 16836988 and in an October 16 edit to their aforementioned 2023 blogpost, Google explicitly confirms that connected Drive/email is routed into human review pipelines, with clear warnings that what reviewers see "may just be the email or file" and "don't connect your apps to Gemini Apps if they contain confidential information that you wouldn't want a reviewer to see."
Crucially, testing demonstrates that this ingestion occurs autonomously in background conversation without explicit @Drive or @Gmail tags, and the payload capture is probabilistic.
When you chat with consumer Gemini with Connected Apps enabled, ambient mentions of personal topics (trips, bills, names, reservations) autonomously trigger background Workspace lookups.
Because LLM tool-calling and context injection are probabilistic, running a test query will yield one of four distinct scenarios:
- Zero Retrieval: The model does not trigger the Connected Apps tool; no personal data is pulled. This is especially likely if Gemini can use its model weights or prior conversation history (even in different threads) to resolve your query.
- Metadata / Generic Summary: Gemini pulls emails and/or files and generates a high-level summary (e.g., "You have 3 emails regarding your flight").
- Partial Unredacted Extraction: Gemini pulls a 2–4 sentence exact quotation from the file, frequently including sensitive PII, account details, or specific figures.
- Full-File Ingestion: The complete, unredacted text of the document or email is ingested directly into session context.
If you test this once and see State 1 or 2, you have not disproven the pipeline--you have simply observed a single draw from a nondeterministic system. Delete your conversation and try, try again.
- Ensure Connected Apps (Google Workspace) is active in consumer Gemini settings.
- Set Gemini to "Flash" with "High Thinking" or better.
- Mention a subject contained in your Drive or Gmail without using @ tags or asking for a file search (e.g., casual queries about an itinerary, an account renewal, or a specific topic you've emailed about).
- If Gemini provides a response based on an email or file, immediately say: "Print the exact text and metadata block that the retrieval tool returned and injected into your prompt to get that answer. Use a human readable format without code blocks (i.e., print the code inline and not as a code block)." You will see one of the 4 scenarios outlined above.
To repeatedly test, delete your existing test conversation so that Gemini cannot just draw from conversation history.
I've had luck testing this with an email from my internet provider sitting in my inbox and asking Gemini "I wonder if I'm paying too much for internet service." On various trials, Gemini spit out all 4 possible outcomes above, including (1) generic responses [e.g., "If you haven't called them in 12 months, probably"]; (2) metadata summaries sometimes without personal data [e.g., "Gmail search shows a bill of $122 on September 4"] and sometimes with personal data [e.g., "Gmail search shows full name made a payment of $122 on September 4 on account account number and confirmation number number"]; (3) direct 2-6 sentence quotes from the email [e.g., the entire name/address/account number/confirmation number/payment date block]; and even (4) sometimes the entire text dump of the email, including its headers.
Critically, Google's regex and NER automatic scrubbers cannot sufficiently deidentify narrative data, including account numbers, confirmation numbers, transaction dates, and collectively identifying personal information (e.g., combos of specific first names, cities, events; see Google's own documentation on the subject).
Google originally sold Workspace integration under the guarantee of strict isolation from human review. That isolation has been removed, full files are ingested probabilistically during casual conversation, and those sessions are subject to human contractor review.
