articles.title: Mathematicians Are Like Luddites
articles.body:
Stretching an analogy real far
Mathematicians are like Luddites. Yes, the actual weavers, not just the slur against people who are against technology. They were weavers in general: weavers, knitters, and cloth finishers defending the value of their skill and lifestyle.
Etymology
Maybe astrology for men, but just as fun.
The Proto-Indo European root tek-/tekō/*tek/: to plait/to weave.
Text: words and letters woven together.
Context: that which is woven together (con-*).
Textile. Subtle: the underlying (sub) thread.
Subtext. not etymologically a duplicate of “subtle” but sure feels like one.
Technology: from the word tekne, which means “craft”. Weaving is an old craft, about 20,000 years old. Flint knapping and fire making are older, and damned hard, but weaving has a combination of freedom and skill.
We talk about ideas as though we were handling fabric because, for a very long time, making fabric was one of our most sophisticated skills .
History of Weavers
Master weavers in the Tudor era had to work crazy fast. I don’t recall the exact number, but it’s a combination of speed and skill that isn’t really matched today. Especially in the speed aspect, done by hand.
The raw material, (the text) of weaving, has always been really really time consuming to make. And producing it was necessary to do anything further with it.
Until the Jacquard loom and its cousins, ironically maybe the first true programs. So the computer came for weavers before computers even existed, and Jacquard inspired Babbage.
The Luddites were skilled weavers. The automated looms suddenly collapsed one aspect of their skill, previously inextricably tied to the production of the raw material.
They did not react well to that disappearing, and sought to destroy the machines. But their position in society now ran against economics and therefore the wheel of progress, and their interests became less and less relevant.
When they started destroying, the response was brutal. Troops came in and shot many of them, as did factory owners.
Later, the whole industry sublated. Because the literal raw material of weaving, the cloth, became so cheap, made to measure and prefabricated (off the rack) clothing became possible and soon common. The design aspect of the art was still valuable. This is basically the province of a fashion designer now. But fashion design scales (that’s what a fashion line is), and most of the jobs disappeared. The few that remained are maybe even more prestigious and better paying, but much fewer.
History of Mathematicians
For most of history, mathematics was a hobby of the rich. Later, when basic arithmetic became more widespread, it gained a lower skilled class: “human computers” and scribes (long) before that. Ordinary computation was relegated to them. Abacuses and the like help diffuse this. But abstract math has always had a big cliff blocking further progress and learning into it.
Mathematicians have always had to do computation, but it was not their self conception of their main job after a point. Especially in the 1900s, the research center of math unmoored itself from most other sciences. Leaving a more and more insular group, essentially high priests and sometimes hierophants.
Until the machines have really taken off recently.
Mechanization in both fields
Leibniz worked on a mechanical calculator in the 1670s. He wanted to automate work so “excellent minds” wouldn’t really need to argue, but just “calculate”. Later, de Prony’s large table-making project divided labor into a few people choosing methods, a supervisor group turning the methods into instructions, and god knows how many performing arithmetic. Babbage described this organization in 1832, explicitly comparing it to a cotton mill.
Mechanization has changed both fields, in similar ways. The raw material of math is the proof, and the raw material of weaving is the cloth. Now both are cheap to make. Definitions are harder to launder, but I expect AI will succeed at that too within a year.
While machines are not generally intelligent, the few that are at the frontier of both industries (esp math because ai is a lot better at the virtual than the physical world right now) have greater position than ever. Certainly they can do way more than before by using these tools.
In any case, both math and weaving have changed.
Weaving underwent its own reorganizations. Patterned cloth required skill long before Jacquard, and there was still a high skill ceiling even as tools improved. His mechanism, demonstrated in 1801 and developed commercially around 1804–05, used punched cards to determine which warp threads rose. btw this is where the gpu warp term comes from. A design could be encoded and repeatedly executed aka mechanized.
The British Luddites did not simply rise against the Jacquard loom. Different textile workers opposed different machines and employment practices. In 1808, before the named Luddite disturbances, a Royton handbill protested Parliament’s rejection of a minimum-wage bill. In Arnold in 1811, framework knitters destroyed 63 frames belonging to unpopular hosiers. Yorkshire croppers were skilled cloth finishers threatened by shearing machinery; Lancashire weavers faced power looms. These people already used machines. The dispute was about which machines, under whose control, on what terms, and with what effect on the value of their work.
Mathematicians have tried to stem the tide in some ways, saying that they didn’t want the machines to do their work. Recently they had some declaration (I’m not gonna look it up) about “human mathematics” but economics is against this desire too. And so progress’s wheel rolls (and crushes). Math, against common mathematician belief, is valuable. Really, really valuable. It was just too damn hard to use usefully (until now). The AI galaxy brain is redeeming math’s commercial value, which is why normal people would care. Normal people interact with math through its fruits, and if you took a math paper and turned it upside down and had them read it, it wouldn’t be any less confusing.
The analogy to fashion designers is that the machine can synthesize or spin up new “cloth” so quickly now, leaving people at least for a while at a higher level.
This loops back to the idea of technology and tekne, the Greek conception of arts, or skills that can be improved. Craft is mechanistic and teleological. The machines can grind through the mechanistic aspect, but its teleology is still up for grabs. For now.
The analogies collapse as AI advances because of its meta-aspect, inserting itself into the workflow at every level. I think the order of what AI masters is the human tech tree, turned backwards. So I expect weaving and fashion design to fall after math, but I very much believe they will. AI will supply its own teleology.
Some people at the very highest end still have a position because they can simply use the tools, especially for math, in a way that others can’t because they can just read the outputs. And hardly anyone can do that. And while the AI might produce stuff that outstrips them, they’re still a lot less outstripped than other people, giving an even smaller group of this already small group an exalted position. But I expect it to pop like a bubble in the end, and for the end to be a very finite amount of time away.
The craft itself is greater than ever, for both. Or more like for 1.5. One of my old obsessions was tailoring, and watching the old tailors die is pretty depressing. Ready-made clothing transformed the mass market, though bespoke tailoring survives, but only for the best.
So, yeah you should be mad as a mathematician. You have (had) a meaningful position with respect to status and salary, at least among people you cared about. The scarcity behind that is dissolving. And that sucks.
More literal and metaphorical cloth will be produced than ever, but it’s rly different.
It’s not likely to ratchet backwards, leaving math in this new state.

articles.title: David Ellison says AI could be the ‘biggest creative unlock in modern history’
articles.body:
During Paramount Skydance’s latest earnings call, CEO David Ellison said “it’s hard to imagine” AI won’t have a bigger impact on the film industry than CGI. In response to a question about the company’s outlook for AI, Ellison said:
David Ellison says AI could be the ‘biggest creative unlock in modern history’
Paramount Skydance’s CEO compared AI to CGI, but said it ‘will never be a replacement’ for artists.
“I think when you zoom out and look at production, AI really has the potential to be the biggest creative unlock in modern history. The last time we saw anything close to this was really the, you know, advent of CGI and digital composites in the early 90s. That technology gave birth to amazing stories like Jurassic Park and Terminator 2, and it’s hard to imagine that AI is not going to have a more significant impact than that. And I personally believe that’s going to be an incredible unlock on creativity.”
Ellison gave Terminator as an example, describing how it cost $4 million to make, but “if you wanted to make that picture today, shot for shot, it’s $60 to 70 million.” He went on to suggest AI might be able to help with that: “We think these tools will help unlock more original storytelling by being able to make the budgets more digestible to be able to take that amount of risk.”
Ellison said AI will “significantly” reshape Paramount Skydance’s business, saying the company has been developing its own AI tools. As a result of those tools, Ellison claims, “content will be easier to produce, projects across the organization will speed up, and how we work will transform.” He emphasized that “all of this makes the value of premium IP and live events more valuable, not less.”
Ellison also noted that “in a world of AI slop, we think there will always be a premium for truly hand-crafted storytelling.” He added, “We also continue to believe that artificial intelligence is a tool for artists and will never be a replacement for them.”

articles.title: Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember
articles.body:
Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember
·4 minute read
Today, we're introducing Muse Ember, our smallest and most efficient model designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing.
Muse Ember delivers more intelligence per dollar than Claude Haiku 5.5 or GPT-6 Luna at any reasoning setting: it matches Haiku's best score at about a third of the cost and beats every Luna setting. It also sits on the efficiency frontier of the full Artificial Analysis leaderboard: no model scores higher for less per task.
For more details about our evaluations, see our report.
Muse Ember is available today on the Meta Model API, at $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens.
In early testing, our partners put Muse Ember to work on the kinds of tasks agents repeat all day, from reviewing contracts to writing code.
Agents
Agents spend most of their tokens on many small, structured steps, and Muse Ember is built for exactly that. It can carry a business workflow end to end, pulling records, calling tools in sequence, and updating systems across apps.
With a 1M-token context window and up to 512K output tokens, it can take in a full codebase or document set in a single call.
Coding
Muse Ember is built for the coding subtasks an agent sends off hundreds of times a session: reading files, running tests, making targeted fixes.
For the hardest problems, pair it with Muse Wonder: Muse Wonder plans, Muse Ember handles the volume.
Multimodal
Muse Ember natively understands text, images, audio, and video, so agents can read screenshots, charts, and scanned documents, or work from voice memos, meeting recordings, and video without a separate model. It can work through long real-world documents, operate a computer directly from screenshots, and pick out fine visual detail.
Safety
Before release, we evaluated Muse Ember under our Meta Superintelligence Scaling Framework, including chemical and biological, cybersecurity, and loss-of-control risks. Across the categories assessed, our evaluations found that Muse Ember remained below the framework’s high-risk thresholds. Though it’s a small model, it received the same core safety training and testing. We also evaluated how Muse Ember behaves when acting on users' behalf. That covers whether it respects user intent, handles sensitive information appropriately, resists instructions hidden in web pages, documents, or tool outputs that try to redirect it, and seeks human input before high-impact actions.
Availability
Muse Ember is available today on Muse Code and Meta Model API as muse-ember-1.0. It costs $0.10 per million input tokens, $0.004 per million cached input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, with a 1M-token context window and up to 512K output tokens. Muse Ember supports the Responses API.
When we introduced Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, we said we would use them to develop specialized models we can bring to everyone. Muse Ember is the first trained using Muse Wonder Full. It rounds out our portfolio of models: Muse Wonder for the hardest problems, Muse Spark for coding and agentic workflows, and Muse Ember for repeatable coding and agentic tasks at scale at about $0.14 per Artificial Analysis task, a cost low enough to run in every product, for everyone.
Our goal is personal superintelligence: models that help you pursue your goals, create what you imagine, deepen your relationships, and take action on what you value most. Bringing it to everyone takes more than frontier capability. It takes frontier capability at a price that scales. We have even more efficient models in training and look forward to sharing what's next. Muse Ember, Muse Spark and Muse Wonder are now available on Google Cloud and Oracle Cloud.

articles.title: Amazon saves millions by replacing Sonnet 4.6 with Strands Decider
articles.body:
For a while, Amazon and AWS teams relied on Claude Sonnet 4.6 to label tickets in an internal system without breaking the bank.
Sonnet 4.6 fit the goldilocks choice of balancing intelligence with cost. Considering it dealt with one of the world’s largest internal ticketing systems, the nine month old model did well. However, two Amazon engineers recently swapped out Sonnet 4.6 for Strands Decider, a decision model we launched a month ago, that performed just as well at 98% less cost. This change will save millions of dollars of token costs in a year.
Carr and Mehul, who work on the internal ticketing system, walk through how this happened below.
Replacing an LLM’s job with a decision model
We had Sonnet 4.6 labeling tickets at enormous scale. The tickets could be customer escalations, capacity requests, automated alarms, security findings, or anything else across the company that needed to fit within 20 category types. The agent ran with a long system prompt on every ticket, generating JSON and reasoning against a fixed set of labels.
A decision model can’t generate text. It’s first given some state and a question with a set of options, then the decision model returns a probability for each option plus a confidence score. We saw this method fit perfectly with ticket labeling: the state is the ticket, the options are the label catalog.
We started with the original Strands Decider 2B. On a test set of tickets, the E4B Gemma 4 build got clearly better results, so we switched to it. Afterwards, we tuned how confident the model needed to be before applying a label. The results showed E4B beating production Sonnet on a separate set of our tickets.
We ran E4B on SageMaker ml.g5.xlarge instances (one A10G, 24 GB each). The model used about 19 GiB,
and one request took about 640 ms on one instance. The endpoint autoscales with traffic, but its network
was isolated, preventing outbound access to the container. SageMaker copies the model weights in from
S3 before start-up.
Customers can do this too! Apart from our ticketing APIs, everything in the path is a standard AWS service. Ticket events land in an SQS queue that then triggers a Lambda function. It reads the ticket data and calls the model, a SageMaker AI Endpoint with Strands Decider. AppConfig holds the switch (described below), and CloudWatch carries the logs, metrics and alarms. The stack is defined in CDK with deployment stages for Beta, Gamma, and Prod.
Running Sonnet 4.6 and Strands Decider on the same tickets
We didn’t want to flip a switch and hope. The labeling Lambda reads a three-way setting from AWS AppConfig on every message:
- BEDROCK: Sonnet labels every ticket, but Strands Decider isn’t called.
- DUAL: Both the Sonnet and Strands Decider models are called in parallel. The results from the
Sonnet model are applied to the ticket and compared with Strands Decider results.
- DECIDER: Strands Decider labels every ticket and Bedrock isn’t called.
What we measured
The token drop had two sources. Strands Decider produced one output, the choice, instead of a JSON answer. Its prompt was also much shorter than Sonnet 4.6’s. Production’s label descriptions alone are longer than Strands Decider’s 4,096-token window, so we rewrote each of the 20 labels as a one- or two-sentence criterion and sent them as the options of a single choice question, plus a “none” option. The ticket data is the same as what Sonnet gets, except that on long tickets Strands Decider drops the oldest comments to fit.
Below is a graph of our Lambda durations on the day we turned off the Sonnet usage, showing the average Lambda execution duration dropping 74%.
What it costs
At published us-east-1 on-demand prices:
Sonnet’s cost per ticket comes straight from the token counts above. Strands Decider’s depends on how busy each instance is. At about 640 ms per request, one instance can handle about 5,600 tickets an hour, which would be $250 per million tickets at full use. We keep headroom for bursts, and in practice it comes to about $500 per million. That is about 44 times cheaper than Sonnet, a 98% reduction.
These are published list prices. They leave out the Lambda, which also runs for less time per ticket now.
One thing that surprised us was that JSON key order changed the answer. Sending the same content with keys in a different order moved the output probabilities by up to 0.19. We now send every request with sorted keys, so if you serve a decision model behind an API, check this before you compare runs.
Our lessons
This worked because the task is a closed choice from a known catalog, the volume is high, and the latency of the old path mattered. If your labels need explanation text, if the catalog changes weekly, or if you can’t fit the useful context into a few thousand tokens, a decision model probably can’t replace the LLM’s job.
The part we’d copy regardless of model is the three-way switch. Running both on real traffic, then judging every disagreement, told us more than any offline eval would have. It also meant going back was a 45-second config change.
The world of agents gets a lot more exciting (and less costly) with decision models. If you’re running a classification agent, try the Strands Decider repo and its serving notes.
