articles.title: Exact – a new cross platform UI framework by the Expo team
articles.body:
Write an app once. It runs natively on the web, macOS, iOS, and Linux, and an AI agent can build it, run it, see it, and test it on every one of them. Tip Try it with a coding agent. On a Mac with Xcode, Rust, Bun, and Chrome installed, give Claude Code this prompt: Clone https://github.com/expo/exact and follow its README to make a new Exact app with `exact new`. Run `bun scripts/exact.mjs setup` once first. Make a todo list where I can add items, check them off, delete them, and see how many are left. Put the view in Contract and keep the list in `app.ts`. Write an `app.test.contract`, pass it on web, macOS, and the iOS Simulator with `scripts/agent.mjs`, then open the app for me on all three. A fresh agent given the earlier version of this prompt on a clean clone (2026-10-04, Hermes already in the machine cache, Cargo's cache warm) finished in about 57 minutes, and its tests passed on all three platforms. About 25 of those minutes were the first macOS and iOS builds, roughly 13 minutes each; later builds take a minute or two. On a machine that has lacked Hermes, its source build came first and added time. Current setup downloads and verifies the pinned host/iOS bundles once instead; ordinary builds stay offline. One app.contract, the same screen on three hosts, captured by the agent driver. Softwear is a demonstration store you can generate from exact-templates: it shows Alternative Apparel's catalog, is not affiliated with that brand, and takes no real orders or payments. Exact is a cross-platform application runtime. You describe your interface in Contract, a small declarative language, and you write your data logic in TypeScript or Rust. The Contract compiler turns the interface into a compact plan. On the web, that plan becomes one ES module over a ~20 KB runtime that drives the real DOM. On macOS, iOS, and Linux, a Rust runner executes the same plan, a Rust layout kernel computes every box with CSS rules, and each platform draws with its own tools: AppKit, UIKit, or a GPU painter. There is no webview and no JavaScript bridge in the UI, and no app JavaScript runs before the first pixel. Note Exact is pre-1.0 and changes daily. There is no API stability, no backwards compatibility, and no migration guide, by design (rules/DEFERRED.md). This repository, exact2, is a rebuild of an earlier one ("exact1"). Its design documents are imported under llp/research/ as research, never as authority. Upgrade note (2026-10-16): Snapback mutation replies with ok: false now throw refused(why) and expose failure(slot); see the before/after and inherited-app commands. Exact assumes much of the code will be written by AI agents. An agent can make an app, run it, look at it, operate it, and prove it works without a person in the loop. - Ten operations, the same on every host. tree · screenshot · tap · type · state · layout · logs · clock · prefer · perf drive the web, macOS, iOS (Simulator or a real iPhone), and Linux through one script, scripts/agent.mjs. There are ten on purpose: the predecessor's agent API grew to eighty wire names, one reasonable addition at a time. - The clock belongs to the agent. Between two operations nothing moves. Instead of sleeping until an animation finishes, the agent says clock +60000 or clock settle and reads the result. No timing flakes, no waits. - Tests are scripts of those operations. An app.test.contract file runs unchanged on any host, with no second evaluator. - Every tool speaks to machines. contract build --json gives diagnostics with stable ids and source ranges. contract symbols gives navigation. A development source map leads from any node on screen back to the line that declared it. The driver refuses to drive a build older than its sources and names the rebuild. - Contract is small on purpose. A whole app fits in a context window. Every write is declared, every list is keyed, every value is typed. Mistakes are refusals that say what to do, not quiet misbehavior. bun scripts/agent.mjs web tree "tap change-station" "type station-search Palo" \ "clock +60000" state "screenshot out.png" Speed of the app and speed of the loop. Each budget in rules/RULES.md is tracked on every commit, and a regression is a P0 with a name on it. How the design keeps those numbers: - The boot path executes and compiles nothing. TypeScript is compiled to Hermes bytecode at build time and loads after the first pixel. The first frame comes from data baked into the plan. - Pay only for what you use. GPU rendering, the Markdown editor, text flow, and browser SQLite are separate artifacts, loaded on demand. Nothing is a feature flag on a core crate. - The web gets its own small runtime. On the RealWorld ("Conduit") benchmark, Exact's runtime was up about 300 ms before the React SSR build had hydrated. It used 26 KB of code against React's 81 KB (LLP 1071). - Edits land in about a tenth of a second. On a fresh app made by exact new, a saved Contract or TypeScript edit was rebuilt and in the page in 99 ms. What you write is CSS: the vocabulary, the layout model, the development loop. What you leave unsaid is the platform's: controls, colour, type, motion, gestures, the keyboard and accessibility come out as an app built by hand with UIKit or AppKit would have them, and on the web as a carefully built web app would. What you write wins. The order is author, then platform, then CSS's default, and one test settles a dispute: would someone who knows the platform notice? (LLP 1115) - Layout is CSS's, because a person can't see a layout default, only its result. A bare node is display: block, box-sizing: content-box, flex-direction: row, flex-shrink: 1, the same as a bare
. - Names are CSS's, because names are what you write: font-size, object-fit, text-overflow, line-clamp, light-dark(), env(safe-area-inset-top). The compiler refuses an alias and names the web's spelling. - Unsaid presentation is the platform's. Text is the system's label colour and size (17 points on an iPhone, 13 on a Mac, the reader's setting in a browser), a button is the system's button, a pushed screen has the system's Back. An app that says less looks more at home. - The browser is the parity oracle for layout and for what you wrote. Native layout given the same inputs, Canvas 2D, SVG, gradients, and authored motion are checked against what Chrome draws. - The web is also the development loop. You work on the seconds-long web loop, and the native hosts are swept behind you. - Any unavoidable deviation in layout is declared, with its reason, in llp/1001-kernel-v1.spec.md. For example, Taffy has no position: static. Writing the web doesn't mean the lowest common denominator. Where a platform can do more (real HTML in an SVG foreignObject on the web, MapKit through a native module on Apple), Exact lets it. flowchart LR subgraph author["You write"] C["app.contract
view · state · actions"] D["app.ts or a Rust crate
data sources"] end C --> K["Contract compiler"] --> P["plan
tables + bytecode"] P --> W["Web
one ES module, ~20 KB runtime,
the browser's DOM and CSS"] P --> R["Rust runner
+ layout kernel (Taffy)"] R --> M["macOS
AppKit + CoreText"] R --> I["iOS
UIKit + CoreText"] R --> L["Linux
vello GPU / tiny-skia CPU"] D -.->|answers, checked against declared shapes| W D -.-> R - Contract (contract/) is compiled in four passes: syntax, types, analysis, and lowering. At build time the plan is baked: constant data is evaluated into it, so the first frame needs nothing else. - The runner (runner/) is the plan's virtual machine. It handles keyed component instances, events, timers on a seekable clock, and the data seam. - The kernel (kernel/) is a columnar node arena with CSS layout through a patched Taffy. The host measures text: CoreText on Apple, cosmic-text on Linux. On the web, the browser lays out the same CSS itself, so the web build carries no layout engine. - Hosts (host/) present the tree. The web host writes DOM nodes, and the browser runs CSS transitions. The Apple host is a static library with a C ABI under AppKit and UIKit presenters. The Linux host paints the tree itself, onto DRM/KMS with evdev input, or into an offscreen buffer. - Data sources sit below one seam. TypeScript runs on Hermes on native hosts and in the browser's own engine on the web. Rust runs natively, and can be replaced live (as a shared library, or as Wasm on iOS and the web). Every answer is checked against the shape Contract declared. Grants control network, files, SQLite, and secrets. - Optional pieces are separate artifacts: a wgpu GPU module (Metal on Apple, WebGPU in the browser), native modules (a hyphenated tag backed by a platform widget, like MapKit), and a game engine add-on. These steps were run on macOS on Apple Silicon. Linux works for the web loop and the Linux host. - Rust through rustup. The pinned stable toolchain in rust-toolchain.toml installs itself the first time Cargo runs. - Bun 1.4.2, the version package.json pins. Node and npm are not needed. - Google Chrome. The agent drives the web through headless Chrome. Set CHROME to use another Chromium. - Xcode, for the macOS and iOS hosts. - Hermes, only for TypeScript apps on native hosts. Exact consumes Ibex's pinned, attested 260318099.0.4 release bundle; ordinary Cargo builds are offline and never download or compile an engine. Install it once for each target before building (for this Mac, use aarch64-apple-darwin): cargo run --manifest-path vendor/ibex/crates/hermes-lean-sys-installer/Cargo.toml -- --target The installer verifies the bundle and publishes it under ~/.cargo/hermes-lean-sys/. The v4 set supports macOS, Linux, Windows, iOS devices and the universal iOS Simulator, plus tvOS devices and arm64 tvOS Simulators. Linux and Windows select Ibex's English intl tier; Apple keeps Hermes's OS-backed Intl. HERMES_LEAN_SYS_DIR is only an explicit development override, not normal setup. To install the pinned Bun beside any existing installation: curl -fsSL https://bun.sh/install | BUN_INSTALL=~/.bun-1.4.2 bash -s bun-v1.4.2. Use ~/.bun-1.4.2/bin/bun for the commands below if it is not on your PATH. bun scripts/exact.mjs setup installs the declared stable and web nightly Rust toolchains, their components/targets (the nightly's clippy lints a game's web bake), matching wasm-bindgen, pinned Binaryen and Bun dependencies, installs the pinned Hermes host bundle and the iOS/tvOS bundles this Mac builds, and fetches the crates of exact2's lock and the game SDK's (game/app/shells.lock), since every bake resolves offline. It keeps Binaryen in ~/.cache/exact/binaryen; builds find it automatically. setup --check invokes Ibex's installer in its offline check mode for that same target set. The resolver authenticates the canonical receipts, archives, compiler and host/target HBC pairing without installing anything; its exit status and diagnostic are the check's result. git clone https://github.com/expo/exact.git cd exact bun scripts/exact.mjs setup bun host/web/dev.mjs # Caltrain, at http://127.0.0.1:8765/ The first run compiles the toolchain, which takes a few minutes. After that, open apps/caltrain/app.contract, change some text, and save. The page rebuilds and reloads in about a tenth of a second. Add --lan to open the same page from a phone on your network. The server answers only to the names it prints (a DNS-rebinding guard; any other Host gets 421); to share it through a tunnel such as tuft host, name the tunnel's host with --allow-host (repeatable; name:port pins a port). An allowed name reaches the page and its reload stream, never the local installer's token. bun host/apple/build.mjs --run # macOS bun host/apple/build.mjs --ios --run # an iOS Simulator (--device --run for a connected iPhone) cargo build --profile host-dev -p caltrain-linux # Linux: a DRM/KMS console, or headless anywhere (--release to ship) A first native build takes ten to fifteen minutes on a laptop; later builds reuse it and take a minute or two. Watch its output rather than waiting blind. iOS commands use an iPhone simulator that's already booted, or boot the newest iPhone Pro. To choose one, set EXACT_SIM to its name or UDID (or pass --sim to build.mjs), and keep the same setting for agent.mjs ios. On Linux, a development build can serve its screen with EXACT_VNC=1 and EXACT_VNC_PASSWORD set to 1–8 bytes. It listens on 127.0.0.1:5900; an explicit EXACT_VNC=host:port selects another address. Production bakes ignore both variables. bun host/web/build.mjs caltrain-web # the build the agent's web host serves bun scripts/agent.mjs web tree "tap change-station" "type station-search Palo" state "screenshot out.png" bun scripts/agent.mjs web --test apps/caltrain/app.test.contract Swap web for macos, ios, or linux once that host is built. Caltrain's three tests take about two seconds on the web host. Each operation is one shell argument, so quote it: "type new-todo Buy milk" types Buy milk (everything after the target is the text). "screenshot film.png over 600 every 50" films motion as a contact sheet; use an .apng name to get an animation. bun scripts/exact.mjs new ../hello # or run `bun link` once, then `exact new ../hello` cd ../hello bun exact.mjs contract types app.contract -o app.contract.d.ts # first run builds the compiler bun exact.mjs web # the dev loop, at http://127.0.0.1:8765/ bun exact.mjs test web tests/*.test.contract # the app's *.test.contract, or the files named bun exact.mjs mac --run # this Mac bun exact.mjs ios --run # an iOS Simulator exact new creates a standalone app: app.contract (the view), app.ts (its data), app.json (the manifest: name, bundle id, hosts, deploy policy), and small web/ and apple/ host crates. Its AGENTS.md (and CLAUDE.md) points a coding agent at docs/start-here.md, the one guide it must read, and at bun exact.mjs help for the commands, including bun exact.mjs contract … for the compiler and contract vocab for the card of what an app writes (--all: every tag and property Contract accepts). Before any of it, run bun scripts/exact.mjs setup once; setup --check names everything this machine is missing without changing it. It has its own Cargo workspace, which uses your exact2 checkout by path. To drive it from exact2, point EXACT_APP_DIR at it: EXACT_APP_DIR=../hello bun host/web/build.mjs hello-web EXACT_APP_DIR=../hello bun scripts/agent.mjs web --app hello tree "screenshot hello.png" Look at every screenshot, not just the test result: a test passes on a layout that spills off the screen. bun exact.mjs agent "screenshot out.png" shows the app on each host in its own session; for a copy you launched yourself, use xcrun simctl io screenshot out.png on iOS. bun scripts/exact.mjs also runs apps from this repository as real Mac apps: exact run markdown README.md, or exact install markdown to put mdview on your PATH. exact list shows what's here. An app's AGENTS.md asks its agent to record friction in one line, bun exact.mjs feedback note "". A failed or slow drive, build or verify, and a passing test or verify, end with one line naming it, at most once a day per project. A note stays in the app's .exact/ with exact2's commit, the last command's verb, exit code and duration, and the OS; never any command output, or the app's code or files. It goes to Expo (https://exact-diaries.ccheever-0f6.workers.dev) only when the project's answer allows: always, or a yes to ask, the default, after bun exact.mjs feedback shows exactly what would go. bun exact.mjs feedback never stops it for a project; EXACT_FEEDBACK=0 silences the nudges and refuses every send on the machine. docs/diary.md has the details. An agent building an app starts at start-here.md, the only required reading, then looks up the recipe for each question. For more, read the complete guide for humans, or look things up in the guide for agents or the grammar and vocabulary reference. Contract describes what an app shows and how its state changes. It doesn't fetch, read files, or run arbitrary code. That's what data sources are for. Here is a complete todo app: a Contract file, a TypeScript file, and a test. This exact app was built for web, macOS, and the iOS Simulator, and its test passed on all three. To try it in an app created with exact new, replace app.contract and app.test.contract with the examples below. In app.ts, keep the generated export const appId = … line and replace the rest with the TypeScript below. // app.contract: the view, its state, and what each action changes. It names no colour, // font or control size: each host draws its own heading, field, button, checkbox and list. shape Todo id: string title: string done: bool shape Change count: number component Todos state draft = "" mutation changed as shape Change refreshes todos resource todos = todos() as shape Todo[] derive left = todos.filter(t => not t.done).length action edit(value: string) draft = value action add if draft.trim() != "" send changed = addTodo(draft.trim()) draft = "" action toggle(id: string, done: bool) send changed = setDone(id, done) action remove(id: string) send changed = removeTodo(id) view list appearance="auto" height="100%" section header text `${left} left` role="heading" testId="count" row input value=draft input=edit submit=add placeholder="What needs doing?" aria-label="New todo" testId="new-todo" flex=1 min-width=0 button press=add buttonStyle="filled" testId="add" text "Add" section for t in todos key=t.id row testId=`todo-${t.id}` input type="checkbox" checked=t.done change=toggle(t.id) aria-label=t.title testId=`toggle-${t.id}` text t.title flex=1 button press=remove(t.id) destructive=true testId=`remove-${t.id}` text "Delete" // app.ts: keeps the list, and answers what app.contract asks for import type { Answer, Sources } from './app.contract.d.ts'; export const grants = ''; // e.g. 'net.fetch https://api.example.com' type Todo = { id: string; title: string; done: boolean }; let todos: Todo[] = []; let next = 1; const sources: Sources = { todos: () => todos, addTodo: ([title]) => { todos = [...todos, { id: String(next++), title, done: false }]; return { count: todos.length }; }, setDone: ([id, done]) => { todos = todos.map((t) => (t.id === id ? { ...t, done } : t)); return { count: todos.length }; }, removeTodo: ([id]) => { todos = todos.filter((t) => t.id !== id); return { count: todos.length }; }, }; export const answer: Answer = (source, args, store, storage, native) => sources[source](args, store, storage, native);// app.test.contract: runs on any host with `scripts/agent.mjs --test` test "add, finish and delete" expect text "count" == "0 left" type "new-todo" "Buy milk" tap "add" type "new-todo" "Walk the dog" type "new-todo" key "Enter" expect text "count" == "2 left" tap "toggle-1" expect text "count" == "1 left" tap "remove-1" expect tree missing "todo-1" expect tree has "todo-2" The view never edits the list itself. An action sends a mutation to a source, app.ts changes its data and answers, and refreshes todos asks for the list again. Data lives in one place, and every change to it is a named, typed call an agent can see. This list lives in memory. To keep it across launches, give app.ts a grant like sqlite.open app:/data/todos.db and use storage.sqlite, as Fieldnotes does. - No JavaScript in the view, and no I/O. Expressions have no effects. Effects happen only in actions, as assignments, send, refresh, or commands like focus(…) and share(…). Data crosses one seam: a source answers, and the runner checks the answer. - No loops in actions, no await. A list is a view's keyed for, a computation is a derive or a fn (an action may name a value with let), and anything slower lives in a source. A list that changes changes where its data lives, through a mutation, as in the example above. That's what lets the plan be baked, diffed, inspected, and executed the same way on four hosts. - No escape hatch; access hatches. Nothing steps outside the plan. Where an app needs a platform widget, it uses a native module: a hyphenated tag like exact-map, backed by Swift, Kotlin or Rust, laid out by the kernel like any other box. Where it needs the platform object Exact itself built (a UIView, a navigation controller, a DOM element), it marks the node hatch="word" and its native code is handed that object: an access hatch, the panel a machine is built with so its insides can be reached. It configures what Exact made and changes Contract state only by acting on authored nodes, as a person would. These limits serve the principles. An agent can't wire up a data race it can't write. A plan with no JavaScript in it starts fast. A view written in CSS's own words lays out the same on every host and looks at home on each. $ cargo run -q -p contract -- build app.contract app.contract:4:5 [type-assign] `count` is `number`, cannot assign `string` app.contract:7:23 [lower-unknown-attr] `text` has no attribute `size`; `size` is spelled `font-size` here, the web's name (LLP 1017 §8.1) One run reports up to twenty independent errors, not just the first. Other subcommands: --json for tools, symbols (definitions and references as JSON), fmt (source-preserving), types (generates app.contract.d.ts for TypeScript sources), and rust (shapes for a Rust data crate). The full language is specified in LLP 1006, LLP 1017.000 (v1.1), and LLP 1017.003. Data sources are covered in LLP 1027. Each app lives in apps//. Run one on the web with bun host/web/dev.mjs --app , on macOS with bun host/apple/build.mjs -apple --run, and on iOS by adding --ios. All of these screenshots come from the web host, taken by scripts/agent.mjs. To learn from, start with Shelf, the recipe app. It names no colour and no font size, and scripts/no-tells.mjs holds it to that, so it shows what an app that leaves presentation to the platform looks like on each host. Then read these four for what each teaches. They were written before LLP 1115 and paint their own colours and sizes, so take their structure, not their style: The v1 bar, from rules/DEFERRED.md: one real application, not a demo, runs from a single Contract source on web, macOS, iOS, and Linux, within the time budgets in rules/RULES.md. Caltrain is that application, and it runs on all four. Everything else here was admitted because a real app needed it. - Four hosts. Web, macOS (AppKit, no SwiftUI), iOS (UIKit, on the Simulator and on devices), and Linux (GPU or CPU painting, DRM/KMS or headless). Existing Swift apps can embed Exact sessions through ExactKit (LLP 1031). - Layout and text. CSS block, flex, and grid; position: static and containing blocks; aspect-ratio; declared fonts; text around shapes (LLP 1043.000). - Paint. Gradients, shadows, backdrop-filter, glass materials, complete SVG (LLP 1055), Canvas 2D on every host (LLP 1056), and a wgpu GPU canvas loaded after first pixel. - Motion. CSS transitions, springs, @keyframes, follow-and-release gestures (pan, swipe, pinch) with release velocity, layout transitions, exit animations, and scroll- or drag-linked timelines (LLP 1002, LLP 1063). - Lists. Virtualized lists, vertical or horizontal, one level deep (LLP 1070). The rows of a vertical list are its platform's: UIKit's separators and highlight, a table on the Mac, one line between rows on the web, with nothing drawn by the app (LLP 1115.000, D16). - Controls and media. Inputs, select, a WYSIWYG Markdown editor on the web, macOS, and iOS (LLP 1045), images including animated ones, video (LLP 1042), pickers for an app's declared file types, and share. - Data. TypeScript or Rust sources, optionally on a worker. Grant-checked fetch and streams, files and SQLite (native and in the browser), Keychain secrets, and OAuth sign-in. A router keeps a stack per tab (LLP 1038). - Native modules. Platform widgets as hyphenated tags (LLP 1024). - The web, server side. Pages pre-rendered at build time or per request by a Rust renderer, then adopted in place instead of hydrated (LLP 1048). - Delivery. scripts/deploy.mjs publishes the web root and signed update bundles, which installed apps fetch after first pixel. Apple apps check every fifteen minutes while active under every activation policy; deploy.check.interval overrides the interval in seconds. Checks stage a candidate; deploy.activate controls when it applies. TypeScript and Rust logic can be replaced live in development. Every web build gets an install page, and exact release signs and notarizes a Mac app (LLP 1030). - Agents and tests. The ten operations on every host, including a physical iPhone; Contract tests; source maps; filmed screenshots. - Windows. Apps default to ink on a DirectX 11 composition swap chain, or CPU when the manifest declares game. host.windows.painter: "ink" or "cpu" selects either painter, and EXACT_PAINTER overrides both. Skirmish is a standalone game built with Exact's optional game engine; the CPU default preserves its module-owned window presentation. See LLP 1149 D12. Windows Desk demonstrates native controls over Contract and the kernel with an app-local Win32 presenter; general Windows control parity and delivery remain unfinished. - Android. Admitted (2026-10-07) and early. An app builds for Android and runs on an emulator or a phone: bun exact.mjs android builds it, bun exact.mjs test android runs its tests, and bun exact.mjs agent android … drives it (LLP 1107). It needs the Android SDK, the Rust target aarch64-linux-android, and the Hermes Android bundle, which exact setup installs with the target. Delivery and store packaging don't exist yet. - No JSX or React tier. Nothing runs JavaScript above the data seam. The door stays open, but no one is building it. - TypeScript can't import npm packages' code yet. app.ts imports its own local files; from a package it imports only types (import type), which the build checks and never runs. - Code updates in production. Signed delivery covers plans and assets. Signed delivery of TypeScript or Rust modules isn't implemented, and app-store rules limit it anyway. - Linux editing. The web and Apple hosts edit; Linux reads. Linux also has no word segmenter, so flowed Thai, Lao, Khmer, and Myanmar text breaks only at spaces. - Out on purpose for v1. Camera access, a gesture arena, general layout animation, grid or masonry virtualization, a general webview beyond iframe, and a devtools UI. - No packaged CLI. You work from a source checkout. exact new apps refer to it by path. QUEUE.md lists what would make sense to do next, and llp/current/ holds the design documents in play. Start with rules/RULES.md, one page on how work happens here, and rules/DEFERRED.md, what v1 deliberately leaves out. Agents should also read AGENTS.md. In short: - Six blocking checks, 65 seconds in total. Anything slower runs asynchronously, per commit. cargo build --all-targets --keep-going cargo test --tests --no-fail-fast cargo clippy --all-targets --keep-going -- -D warnings && cargo fmt --all -- --check bun scripts/caps.mjs # budgets: 1,500 lines per source file, document caps bun scripts/boot.mjs # counts the module graph before first pixel cargo check --workspace --all-targets --keep-going # every crate compiles The first three build and test Cargo's default-members. The last compiles every other crate too, so a host or an app outside them cannot stop compiling unseen. It needs the pinned Bun (package.json) first on PATH: app crates' build scripts run it. - Verify by running, not by reading. Build the app a change touches and drive it: bun scripts/smoke.mjs drives the whole app on that host. - Delete; don't deprecate. Before 1.0 there are no compatibility shims. Generated files are built, never committed. - Agents remove apparatus freely and add none (checks, scripts, registries, design documents) without a person saying so. - Design happens in LLPs. These are numbered documents in llp/. A spec gets written only when it has an implementer and a date. Detailed operational notes cover toolchains, the Contract CLI's JSON formats, source maps, TypeScript and Rust data modules, storage, live replacement, delivery trust, the install page, and the stress harnesses. They're in docs/reference.md. Open issues are files under issues/ (how that works). The workspace is MIT-licensed (Cargo.toml). Exact’s Snapback4 adapter uses published 0.4.33 with the matching immutable Rust source revision 3653cae823145170df3e720f5e321bd1b5b4d79d. See the adapter guide for wiring and device rebuilds.

articles.title: Exact – a new cross platform UI framework
articles.body:
Write an app once. It runs natively on the web, macOS, iOS, and Linux, and an AI agent can build it, run it, see it, and test it on every one of them. Tip Try it with a coding agent. On a Mac with Xcode, Rust, Bun, and Chrome installed, give Claude Code this prompt: Clone https://github.com/expo/exact and follow its README to make a new Exact app with `exact new`. Run `bun scripts/exact.mjs setup` once first. Make a todo list where I can add items, check them off, delete them, and see how many are left. Put the view in Contract and keep the list in `app.ts`. Write an `app.test.contract`, pass it on web, macOS, and the iOS Simulator with `scripts/agent.mjs`, then open the app for me on all three. A fresh agent given the earlier version of this prompt on a clean clone (2026-10-04, Hermes already in the machine cache, Cargo's cache warm) finished in about 57 minutes, and its tests passed on all three platforms. About 25 of those minutes were the first macOS and iOS builds, roughly 13 minutes each; later builds take a minute or two. On a machine that has lacked Hermes, its source build came first and added time. Current setup downloads and verifies the pinned host/iOS bundles once instead; ordinary builds stay offline. One app.contract, the same screen on three hosts, captured by the agent driver. Softwear is a demonstration store you can generate from exact-templates: it shows Alternative Apparel's catalog, is not affiliated with that brand, and takes no real orders or payments. Exact is a cross-platform application runtime. You describe your interface in Contract, a small declarative language, and you write your data logic in TypeScript or Rust. The Contract compiler turns the interface into a compact plan. On the web, that plan becomes one ES module over a ~20 KB runtime that drives the real DOM. On macOS, iOS, and Linux, a Rust runner executes the same plan, a Rust layout kernel computes every box with CSS rules, and each platform draws with its own tools: AppKit, UIKit, or a GPU painter. There is no webview and no JavaScript bridge in the UI, and no app JavaScript runs before the first pixel. Note Exact is pre-1.0 and changes daily. There is no API stability, no backwards compatibility, and no migration guide, by design (rules/DEFERRED.md). This repository, exact2, is a rebuild of an earlier one ("exact1"). Its design documents are imported under llp/research/ as research, never as authority. Upgrade note (2026-10-16): Snapback mutation replies with ok: false now throw refused(why) and expose failure(slot); see the before/after and inherited-app commands. Exact assumes much of the code will be written by AI agents. An agent can make an app, run it, look at it, operate it, and prove it works without a person in the loop. - Ten operations, the same on every host. tree · screenshot · tap · type · state · layout · logs · clock · prefer · perf drive the web, macOS, iOS (Simulator or a real iPhone), and Linux through one script, scripts/agent.mjs. There are ten on purpose: the predecessor's agent API grew to eighty wire names, one reasonable addition at a time. - The clock belongs to the agent. Between two operations nothing moves. Instead of sleeping until an animation finishes, the agent says clock +60000 or clock settle and reads the result. No timing flakes, no waits. - Tests are scripts of those operations. An app.test.contract file runs unchanged on any host, with no second evaluator. - Every tool speaks to machines. contract build --json gives diagnostics with stable ids and source ranges. contract symbols gives navigation. A development source map leads from any node on screen back to the line that declared it. The driver refuses to drive a build older than its sources and names the rebuild. - Contract is small on purpose. A whole app fits in a context window. Every write is declared, every list is keyed, every value is typed. Mistakes are refusals that say what to do, not quiet misbehavior. bun scripts/agent.mjs web tree "tap change-station" "type station-search Palo" \ "clock +60000" state "screenshot out.png" Speed of the app and speed of the loop. Each budget in rules/RULES.md is tracked on every commit, and a regression is a P0 with a name on it. How the design keeps those numbers: - The boot path executes and compiles nothing. TypeScript is compiled to Hermes bytecode at build time and loads after the first pixel. The first frame comes from data baked into the plan. - Pay only for what you use. GPU rendering, the Markdown editor, text flow, and browser SQLite are separate artifacts, loaded on demand. Nothing is a feature flag on a core crate. - The web gets its own small runtime. On the RealWorld ("Conduit") benchmark, Exact's runtime was up about 300 ms before the React SSR build had hydrated. It used 26 KB of code against React's 81 KB (LLP 1071). - Edits land in about a tenth of a second. On a fresh app made by exact new, a saved Contract or TypeScript edit was rebuilt and in the page in 99 ms. What you write is CSS: the vocabulary, the layout model, the development loop. What you leave unsaid is the platform's: controls, colour, type, motion, gestures, the keyboard and accessibility come out as an app built by hand with UIKit or AppKit would have them, and on the web as a carefully built web app would. What you write wins. The order is author, then platform, then CSS's default, and one test settles a dispute: would someone who knows the platform notice? (LLP 1115) - Layout is CSS's, because a person can't see a layout default, only its result. A bare node is display: block, box-sizing: content-box, flex-direction: row, flex-shrink: 1, the same as a bare
. - Names are CSS's, because names are what you write: font-size, object-fit, text-overflow, line-clamp, light-dark(), env(safe-area-inset-top). The compiler refuses an alias and names the web's spelling. - Unsaid presentation is the platform's. Text is the system's label colour and size (17 points on an iPhone, 13 on a Mac, the reader's setting in a browser), a button is the system's button, a pushed screen has the system's Back. An app that says less looks more at home. - The browser is the parity oracle for layout and for what you wrote. Native layout given the same inputs, Canvas 2D, SVG, gradients, and authored motion are checked against what Chrome draws. - The web is also the development loop. You work on the seconds-long web loop, and the native hosts are swept behind you. - Any unavoidable deviation in layout is declared, with its reason, in llp/1001-kernel-v1.spec.md. For example, Taffy has no position: static. Writing the web doesn't mean the lowest common denominator. Where a platform can do more (real HTML in an SVG foreignObject on the web, MapKit through a native module on Apple), Exact lets it. flowchart LR subgraph author["You write"] C["app.contract
view · state · actions"] D["app.ts or a Rust crate
data sources"] end C --> K["Contract compiler"] --> P["plan
tables + bytecode"] P --> W["Web
one ES module, ~20 KB runtime,
the browser's DOM and CSS"] P --> R["Rust runner
+ layout kernel (Taffy)"] R --> M["macOS
AppKit + CoreText"] R --> I["iOS
UIKit + CoreText"] R --> L["Linux
vello GPU / tiny-skia CPU"] D -.->|answers, checked against declared shapes| W D -.-> R - Contract (contract/) is compiled in four passes: syntax, types, analysis, and lowering. At build time the plan is baked: constant data is evaluated into it, so the first frame needs nothing else. - The runner (runner/) is the plan's virtual machine. It handles keyed component instances, events, timers on a seekable clock, and the data seam. - The kernel (kernel/) is a columnar node arena with CSS layout through a patched Taffy. The host measures text: CoreText on Apple, cosmic-text on Linux. On the web, the browser lays out the same CSS itself, so the web build carries no layout engine. - Hosts (host/) present the tree. The web host writes DOM nodes, and the browser runs CSS transitions. The Apple host is a static library with a C ABI under AppKit and UIKit presenters. The Linux host paints the tree itself, onto DRM/KMS with evdev input, or into an offscreen buffer. - Data sources sit below one seam. TypeScript runs on Hermes on native hosts and in the browser's own engine on the web. Rust runs natively, and can be replaced live (as a shared library, or as Wasm on iOS and the web). Every answer is checked against the shape Contract declared. Grants control network, files, SQLite, and secrets. - Optional pieces are separate artifacts: a wgpu GPU module (Metal on Apple, WebGPU in the browser), native modules (a hyphenated tag backed by a platform widget, like MapKit), and a game engine add-on. These steps were run on macOS on Apple Silicon. Linux works for the web loop and the Linux host. - Rust through rustup. The pinned stable toolchain in rust-toolchain.toml installs itself the first time Cargo runs. - Bun 1.4.2, the version package.json pins. Node and npm are not needed. - Google Chrome. The agent drives the web through headless Chrome. Set CHROME to use another Chromium. - Xcode, for the macOS and iOS hosts. - Hermes, only for TypeScript apps on native hosts. Exact consumes Ibex's pinned, attested 260318099.0.4 release bundle; ordinary Cargo builds are offline and never download or compile an engine. Install it once for each target before building (for this Mac, use aarch64-apple-darwin): cargo run --manifest-path vendor/ibex/crates/hermes-lean-sys-installer/Cargo.toml -- --target The installer verifies the bundle and publishes it under ~/.cargo/hermes-lean-sys/. The v4 set supports macOS, Linux, Windows, iOS devices and the universal iOS Simulator, plus tvOS devices and arm64 tvOS Simulators. Linux and Windows select Ibex's English intl tier; Apple keeps Hermes's OS-backed Intl. HERMES_LEAN_SYS_DIR is only an explicit development override, not normal setup. To install the pinned Bun beside any existing installation: curl -fsSL https://bun.sh/install | BUN_INSTALL=~/.bun-1.4.2 bash -s bun-v1.4.2. Use ~/.bun-1.4.2/bin/bun for the commands below if it is not on your PATH. bun scripts/exact.mjs setup installs the declared stable and web nightly Rust toolchains, their components/targets (the nightly's clippy lints a game's web bake), matching wasm-bindgen, pinned Binaryen and Bun dependencies, installs the pinned Hermes host bundle and the iOS/tvOS bundles this Mac builds, and fetches the crates of exact2's lock and the game SDK's (game/app/shells.lock), since every bake resolves offline. It keeps Binaryen in ~/.cache/exact/binaryen; builds find it automatically. setup --check invokes Ibex's installer in its offline check mode for that same target set. The resolver authenticates the canonical receipts, archives, compiler and host/target HBC pairing without installing anything; its exit status and diagnostic are the check's result. git clone https://github.com/expo/exact.git cd exact bun scripts/exact.mjs setup bun host/web/dev.mjs # Caltrain, at http://127.0.0.1:8765/ The first run compiles the toolchain, which takes a few minutes. After that, open apps/caltrain/app.contract, change some text, and save. The page rebuilds and reloads in about a tenth of a second. Add --lan to open the same page from a phone on your network. The server answers only to the names it prints (a DNS-rebinding guard; any other Host gets 421); to share it through a tunnel such as tuft host, name the tunnel's host with --allow-host (repeatable; name:port pins a port). An allowed name reaches the page and its reload stream, never the local installer's token. bun host/apple/build.mjs --run # macOS bun host/apple/build.mjs --ios --run # an iOS Simulator (--device --run for a connected iPhone) cargo build --profile host-dev -p caltrain-linux # Linux: a DRM/KMS console, or headless anywhere (--release to ship) A first native build takes ten to fifteen minutes on a laptop; later builds reuse it and take a minute or two. Watch its output rather than waiting blind. iOS commands use an iPhone simulator that's already booted, or boot the newest iPhone Pro. To choose one, set EXACT_SIM to its name or UDID (or pass --sim to build.mjs), and keep the same setting for agent.mjs ios. On Linux, a development build can serve its screen with EXACT_VNC=1 and EXACT_VNC_PASSWORD set to 1–8 bytes. It listens on 127.0.0.1:5900; an explicit EXACT_VNC=host:port selects another address. Production bakes ignore both variables. bun host/web/build.mjs caltrain-web # the build the agent's web host serves bun scripts/agent.mjs web tree "tap change-station" "type station-search Palo" state "screenshot out.png" bun scripts/agent.mjs web --test apps/caltrain/app.test.contract Swap web for macos, ios, or linux once that host is built. Caltrain's three tests take about two seconds on the web host. Each operation is one shell argument, so quote it: "type new-todo Buy milk" types Buy milk (everything after the target is the text). "screenshot film.png over 600 every 50" films motion as a contact sheet; use an .apng name to get an animation. bun scripts/exact.mjs new ../hello # or run `bun link` once, then `exact new ../hello` cd ../hello bun exact.mjs contract types app.contract -o app.contract.d.ts # first run builds the compiler bun exact.mjs web # the dev loop, at http://127.0.0.1:8765/ bun exact.mjs test web tests/*.test.contract # the app's *.test.contract, or the files named bun exact.mjs mac --run # this Mac bun exact.mjs ios --run # an iOS Simulator exact new creates a standalone app: app.contract (the view), app.ts (its data), app.json (the manifest: name, bundle id, hosts, deploy policy), and small web/ and apple/ host crates. Its AGENTS.md (and CLAUDE.md) points a coding agent at docs/start-here.md, the one guide it must read, and at bun exact.mjs help for the commands, including bun exact.mjs contract … for the compiler and contract vocab for the card of what an app writes (--all: every tag and property Contract accepts). Before any of it, run bun scripts/exact.mjs setup once; setup --check names everything this machine is missing without changing it. It has its own Cargo workspace, which uses your exact2 checkout by path. To drive it from exact2, point EXACT_APP_DIR at it: EXACT_APP_DIR=../hello bun host/web/build.mjs hello-web EXACT_APP_DIR=../hello bun scripts/agent.mjs web --app hello tree "screenshot hello.png" Look at every screenshot, not just the test result: a test passes on a layout that spills off the screen. bun exact.mjs agent "screenshot out.png" shows the app on each host in its own session; for a copy you launched yourself, use xcrun simctl io screenshot out.png on iOS. bun scripts/exact.mjs also runs apps from this repository as real Mac apps: exact run markdown README.md, or exact install markdown to put mdview on your PATH. exact list shows what's here. An app's AGENTS.md asks its agent to record friction in one line, bun exact.mjs feedback note "". A failed or slow drive, build or verify, and a passing test or verify, end with one line naming it, at most once a day per project. A note stays in the app's .exact/ with exact2's commit, the last command's verb, exit code and duration, and the OS; never any command output, or the app's code or files. It goes to Expo (https://exact-diaries.ccheever-0f6.workers.dev) only when the project's answer allows: always, or a yes to ask, the default, after bun exact.mjs feedback shows exactly what would go. bun exact.mjs feedback never stops it for a project; EXACT_FEEDBACK=0 silences the nudges and refuses every send on the machine. docs/diary.md has the details. An agent building an app starts at start-here.md, the only required reading, then looks up the recipe for each question. For more, read the complete guide for humans, or look things up in the guide for agents or the grammar and vocabulary reference. Contract describes what an app shows and how its state changes. It doesn't fetch, read files, or run arbitrary code. That's what data sources are for. Here is a complete todo app: a Contract file, a TypeScript file, and a test. This exact app was built for web, macOS, and the iOS Simulator, and its test passed on all three. To try it in an app created with exact new, replace app.contract and app.test.contract with the examples below. In app.ts, keep the generated export const appId = … line and replace the rest with the TypeScript below. // app.contract: the view, its state, and what each action changes. It names no colour, // font or control size: each host draws its own heading, field, button, checkbox and list. shape Todo id: string title: string done: bool shape Change count: number component Todos state draft = "" mutation changed as shape Change refreshes todos resource todos = todos() as shape Todo[] derive left = todos.filter(t => not t.done).length action edit(value: string) draft = value action add if draft.trim() != "" send changed = addTodo(draft.trim()) draft = "" action toggle(id: string, done: bool) send changed = setDone(id, done) action remove(id: string) send changed = removeTodo(id) view list appearance="auto" height="100%" section header text `${left} left` role="heading" testId="count" row input value=draft input=edit submit=add placeholder="What needs doing?" aria-label="New todo" testId="new-todo" flex=1 min-width=0 button press=add buttonStyle="filled" testId="add" text "Add" section for t in todos key=t.id row testId=`todo-${t.id}` input type="checkbox" checked=t.done change=toggle(t.id) aria-label=t.title testId=`toggle-${t.id}` text t.title flex=1 button press=remove(t.id) destructive=true testId=`remove-${t.id}` text "Delete" // app.ts: keeps the list, and answers what app.contract asks for import type { Answer, Sources } from './app.contract.d.ts'; export const grants = ''; // e.g. 'net.fetch https://api.example.com' type Todo = { id: string; title: string; done: boolean }; let todos: Todo[] = []; let next = 1; const sources: Sources = { todos: () => todos, addTodo: ([title]) => { todos = [...todos, { id: String(next++), title, done: false }]; return { count: todos.length }; }, setDone: ([id, done]) => { todos = todos.map((t) => (t.id === id ? { ...t, done } : t)); return { count: todos.length }; }, removeTodo: ([id]) => { todos = todos.filter((t) => t.id !== id); return { count: todos.length }; }, }; export const answer: Answer = (source, args, store, storage, native) => sources[source](args, store, storage, native);// app.test.contract: runs on any host with `scripts/agent.mjs --test` test "add, finish and delete" expect text "count" == "0 left" type "new-todo" "Buy milk" tap "add" type "new-todo" "Walk the dog" type "new-todo" key "Enter" expect text "count" == "2 left" tap "toggle-1" expect text "count" == "1 left" tap "remove-1" expect tree missing "todo-1" expect tree has "todo-2" The view never edits the list itself. An action sends a mutation to a source, app.ts changes its data and answers, and refreshes todos asks for the list again. Data lives in one place, and every change to it is a named, typed call an agent can see. This list lives in memory. To keep it across launches, give app.ts a grant like sqlite.open app:/data/todos.db and use storage.sqlite, as Fieldnotes does. - No JavaScript in the view, and no I/O. Expressions have no effects. Effects happen only in actions, as assignments, send, refresh, or commands like focus(…) and share(…). Data crosses one seam: a source answers, and the runner checks the answer. - No loops in actions, no await. A list is a view's keyed for, a computation is a derive or a fn (an action may name a value with let), and anything slower lives in a source. A list that changes changes where its data lives, through a mutation, as in the example above. That's what lets the plan be baked, diffed, inspected, and executed the same way on four hosts. - No escape hatch; access hatches. Nothing steps outside the plan. Where an app needs a platform widget, it uses a native module: a hyphenated tag like exact-map, backed by Swift, Kotlin or Rust, laid out by the kernel like any other box. Where it needs the platform object Exact itself built (a UIView, a navigation controller, a DOM element), it marks the node hatch="word" and its native code is handed that object: an access hatch, the panel a machine is built with so its insides can be reached. It configures what Exact made and changes Contract state only by acting on authored nodes, as a person would. These limits serve the principles. An agent can't wire up a data race it can't write. A plan with no JavaScript in it starts fast. A view written in CSS's own words lays out the same on every host and looks at home on each. $ cargo run -q -p contract -- build app.contract app.contract:4:5 [type-assign] `count` is `number`, cannot assign `string` app.contract:7:23 [lower-unknown-attr] `text` has no attribute `size`; `size` is spelled `font-size` here, the web's name (LLP 1017 §8.1) One run reports up to twenty independent errors, not just the first. Other subcommands: --json for tools, symbols (definitions and references as JSON), fmt (source-preserving), types (generates app.contract.d.ts for TypeScript sources), and rust (shapes for a Rust data crate). The full language is specified in LLP 1006, LLP 1017.000 (v1.1), and LLP 1017.003. Data sources are covered in LLP 1027. Each app lives in apps//. Run one on the web with bun host/web/dev.mjs --app , on macOS with bun host/apple/build.mjs -apple --run, and on iOS by adding --ios. All of these screenshots come from the web host, taken by scripts/agent.mjs. To learn from, start with Shelf, the recipe app. It names no colour and no font size, and scripts/no-tells.mjs holds it to that, so it shows what an app that leaves presentation to the platform looks like on each host. Then read these four for what each teaches. They were written before LLP 1115 and paint their own colours and sizes, so take their structure, not their style: The v1 bar, from rules/DEFERRED.md: one real application, not a demo, runs from a single Contract source on web, macOS, iOS, and Linux, within the time budgets in rules/RULES.md. Caltrain is that application, and it runs on all four. Everything else here was admitted because a real app needed it. - Four hosts. Web, macOS (AppKit, no SwiftUI), iOS (UIKit, on the Simulator and on devices), and Linux (GPU or CPU painting, DRM/KMS or headless). Existing Swift apps can embed Exact sessions through ExactKit (LLP 1031). - Layout and text. CSS block, flex, and grid; position: static and containing blocks; aspect-ratio; declared fonts; text around shapes (LLP 1043.000). - Paint. Gradients, shadows, backdrop-filter, glass materials, complete SVG (LLP 1055), Canvas 2D on every host (LLP 1056), and a wgpu GPU canvas loaded after first pixel. - Motion. CSS transitions, springs, @keyframes, follow-and-release gestures (pan, swipe, pinch) with release velocity, layout transitions, exit animations, and scroll- or drag-linked timelines (LLP 1002, LLP 1063). - Lists. Virtualized lists, vertical or horizontal, one level deep (LLP 1070). The rows of a vertical list are its platform's: UIKit's separators and highlight, a table on the Mac, one line between rows on the web, with nothing drawn by the app (LLP 1115.000, D16). - Controls and media. Inputs, select, a WYSIWYG Markdown editor on the web, macOS, and iOS (LLP 1045), images including animated ones, video (LLP 1042), pickers for an app's declared file types, and share. - Data. TypeScript or Rust sources, optionally on a worker. Grant-checked fetch and streams, files and SQLite (native and in the browser), Keychain secrets, and OAuth sign-in. A router keeps a stack per tab (LLP 1038). - Native modules. Platform widgets as hyphenated tags (LLP 1024). - The web, server side. Pages pre-rendered at build time or per request by a Rust renderer, then adopted in place instead of hydrated (LLP 1048). - Delivery. scripts/deploy.mjs publishes the web root and signed update bundles, which installed apps fetch after first pixel. Apple apps check every fifteen minutes while active under every activation policy; deploy.check.interval overrides the interval in seconds. Checks stage a candidate; deploy.activate controls when it applies. TypeScript and Rust logic can be replaced live in development. Every web build gets an install page, and exact release signs and notarizes a Mac app (LLP 1030). - Agents and tests. The ten operations on every host, including a physical iPhone; Contract tests; source maps; filmed screenshots. - Windows. Apps default to ink on a DirectX 11 composition swap chain, or CPU when the manifest declares game. host.windows.painter: "ink" or "cpu" selects either painter, and EXACT_PAINTER overrides both. Skirmish is a standalone game built with Exact's optional game engine; the CPU default preserves its module-owned window presentation. See LLP 1149 D12. Windows Desk demonstrates native controls over Contract and the kernel with an app-local Win32 presenter; general Windows control parity and delivery remain unfinished. - Android. Admitted (2026-10-07) and early. An app builds for Android and runs on an emulator or a phone: bun exact.mjs android builds it, bun exact.mjs test android runs its tests, and bun exact.mjs agent android … drives it (LLP 1107). It needs the Android SDK, the Rust target aarch64-linux-android, and the Hermes Android bundle, which exact setup installs with the target. Delivery and store packaging don't exist yet. - No JSX or React tier. Nothing runs JavaScript above the data seam. The door stays open, but no one is building it. - TypeScript can't import npm packages' code yet. app.ts imports its own local files; from a package it imports only types (import type), which the build checks and never runs. - Code updates in production. Signed delivery covers plans and assets. Signed delivery of TypeScript or Rust modules isn't implemented, and app-store rules limit it anyway. - Linux editing. The web and Apple hosts edit; Linux reads. Linux also has no word segmenter, so flowed Thai, Lao, Khmer, and Myanmar text breaks only at spaces. - Out on purpose for v1. Camera access, a gesture arena, general layout animation, grid or masonry virtualization, a general webview beyond iframe, and a devtools UI. - No packaged CLI. You work from a source checkout. exact new apps refer to it by path. QUEUE.md lists what would make sense to do next, and llp/current/ holds the design documents in play. Start with rules/RULES.md, one page on how work happens here, and rules/DEFERRED.md, what v1 deliberately leaves out. Agents should also read AGENTS.md. In short: - Six blocking checks, 65 seconds in total. Anything slower runs asynchronously, per commit. cargo build --all-targets --keep-going cargo test --tests --no-fail-fast cargo clippy --all-targets --keep-going -- -D warnings && cargo fmt --all -- --check bun scripts/caps.mjs # budgets: 1,500 lines per source file, document caps bun scripts/boot.mjs # counts the module graph before first pixel cargo check --workspace --all-targets --keep-going # every crate compiles The first three build and test Cargo's default-members. The last compiles every other crate too, so a host or an app outside them cannot stop compiling unseen. It needs the pinned Bun (package.json) first on PATH: app crates' build scripts run it. - Verify by running, not by reading. Build the app a change touches and drive it: bun scripts/smoke.mjs drives the whole app on that host. - Delete; don't deprecate. Before 1.0 there are no compatibility shims. Generated files are built, never committed. - Agents remove apparatus freely and add none (checks, scripts, registries, design documents) without a person saying so. - Design happens in LLPs. These are numbered documents in llp/. A spec gets written only when it has an implementer and a date. Detailed operational notes cover toolchains, the Contract CLI's JSON formats, source maps, TypeScript and Rust data modules, storage, live replacement, delivery trust, the install page, and the stress harnesses. They're in docs/reference.md. Open issues are files under issues/ (how that works). The workspace is MIT-licensed (Cargo.toml). Exact’s Snapback4 adapter uses published 0.4.33 with the matching immutable Rust source revision 3653cae823145170df3e720f5e321bd1b5b4d79d. See the adapter guide for wiring and device rebuilds.

articles.title: Show HN: DBDelve – Open-Source DB Client Made with Rust and GPUI
articles.body:
Hi HN, I’m Shayan and a few months ago I started building a DB Client DBDelve with a focus on performance and just making something that feels good to use (in the spirit of Zed, Ghostty, and other tools that just feel pleasant to use).
For my workflow I’ve always looked for performance, especially since some time ago I had a really outdated machine and any kind of bloat was really noticeable, I remember using DBeaver and it just crashing on me multiple times, I also had to use postGIS which just made it worse. I migrated all my essential dev tools to use the ones with performance in mind (Zed, Ghostty etc) but the only thing that was missing was DB Client. The main choices everyone has are DBeaver which is a memory hog and an overkill for most of the tasks imo. The other options like Datagrid, Beekeeper, TablePlus are either electron based so bloated and memory hogs or paid and closed-source.
DBDelve 0.3.6 against DBeaver 25.3.1 on the same Postgres table, median of 5 runs each (2026-10-11, M1 Pro, 32 GB). Times are from the action to the rows rendered.
                            DBDelve   DBeaver
  Launch                    1.1 s     5.2 s
  Idle memory               133 MB    606 MB
  1,000-row query           0.21 s    1.96 s
  1M rows, time             56 s      208 s
  1M rows, memory [1]       4.9 GB    17 GB
[1] The whole 1M-row, 100-column table pulled into memory on purpose, with the row limit off. Not a normal use case; DBeaver's heap limit had to be raised manually for the benchmark.
Scrolling perf with 1 million rows loaded with 100 columns each: https://youtu.be/V2MOhJYFqIE
It has most of the features most devs would need for 90% of their workflow plus some more I thought would be a nice touch:
Readonly, read-write and Full Access modes
Glass themes (If you’re into them, I am)
Keyboard focused with every keybinding customizable
Organization of connections into projects
Me and some other folks have been daily driving it for more than a month now and most good feedback comes on it having a really simple UI to navigate, very stable for its age and the performance of course. I’m also sharing here because those people tell me this has potential to grow so I’m trying my hand at distributing it.
Just want to give a huge shoutout here to the Zed team for GPUI, it's a breeze to work with if you just get through them not updating the crate officially on crates.io but the community has found the solutions for it, you just have to dig deep for it. It performs extremely well and just the HTML-like structure of it, makes it easy to understand for someone from a web dev background and agents are very good at writing it too. GPUI component also solves a lot of problems with having a good component library we can use. I think for anyone starting a GPUI project now, GPUI-kit makes a lot of sense, it just bundles GPUI, GPUI-component together and has some optimizations adding retained mode which is experimental but could provide a lot of benefit, so think all things considered it should be the default way.
The major optimization I did was just lowering the memory overhead by using packed rows which reduced the memory usage by 40% on large datasets (8.1GB to 4.9GB on a 4GB table loaded in app), everything else came bundled in with Rust and GPUI mostly or they just made it very easy.
Limitations:
It's not signed and notarized, identity verification from apple's side has been a nightmare but it should be signed soon.
Don’t expect feature parity with more mature clients for now, the general direction of this right now is the zed way of adding features in but after making sure the core workflows are done with a high quality.
Do give it a try, you can import your connections from dbeaver and tableplus.
https://github.com/ShayanAbbas1/dbdelve

articles.title: AlphaProof Code
articles.body:
Introducing AlphaProof Code: a breakthrough in verifying complex software at depth
How Google DeepMind researchers built a new agentic framework that formally verified the code of Signal’s cryptographic protocol — long considered to be a grand security challenge
Today, we’re sharing a milestone in software security long considered to be a grand challenge: Google DeepMind researchers guided AI agents to mathematically prove key security properties of the actual code underlying the Signal protocol, the technology that protects billions of private conversations in apps like Signal and Google Messages.
This breakthrough discovery was made using AlphaProof Code, a novel agentic framework for formal verification at unprecedented depth that combines human expertise with AI agents. Formal verification—mathematically proving code runs correctly without flaws—is the highest standard of security assurance; however, it is difficult and often labor-intensive.
Our work marks the first time AI has been used to formally verify a widely deployed cryptographic protocol at this depth. It's also the first time the implementation of a widely deployed protocol like this has been formally verified by any method, with or without AI.
How we verified Signal
AlphaProof Code is a multi-LLM agentic framework that splits the work of formal verification the way a research team would: human experts work with AI to decide what to prove, and a group of AI agents does it.
First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signal’s security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every one. From there, agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language that mathematically proves the accuracy of code.
Next, the agents audited the proof and highlighted areas that needed a second look by a human – just one percent of the codebase, a massive time savings. Because Lean automatically checks the rest, our experts could focus their review where human judgment matters most.
Cryptographic protocols underpin nearly all digital communication, from online banking to web browsing, and a single flaw can expose millions of people at once. That's why experts have spent decades formally analyzing them.
But most protocol verification stops at the design level. Our agents went further, proving that the compiled code fulfills the key security properties – such as keeping messages protected before and after a device is temporarily compromised – down to the exact code running on devices. Because real-world vulnerabilities often hide in the gap between design and implementation, bridging this gap makes these proofs vastly more complex.
Even at this complexity, our verification process took just four weeks – a task that historically takes expert teams years – proving that Signal's core cryptographic code delivers the security protections our experts specified.
To confirm that AlphaProof Code can tell correct code from buggy code, we reintroduced two real, previously fixed bugs into an isolated version of Signal's code. In both cases, the system produced a machine-checked proof that the buggy version was insecure.
While prior formal verification work has necessarily focused on smaller scopes, this new approach enables a significant expansion. Traditionally, verifying that production code strictly matches its cryptographic design required extensive manual effort, making the use of AI agents to automatically translate live code into valid Lean theorems a great breakthrough. As AI-driven security threats grow, having the core Signal protocol rigorously verified with automated theorem proving gives us even greater confidence that our code delivers on its privacy guarantees.
The future of security
Achieving this long-standing challenge demonstrates how AI can bring elite security assurance to businesses, governments, and critical infrastructure, helping defend against agent-driven cyber threats.
Verifying Signal's core cryptography lays the groundwork to secure other vital systems, from medical device firmware to power grid software.
Scaling these techniques requires continued research. Paired with automated defense agents like CodeMender, formal verification can help counter the speed and scale of modern cyber threats to create software with mathematical proof that its protections work.
We are open-sourcing our formal verification artifacts for community use. Read the technical paper below.
Acknowledgements
This research was developed by Swarat Chaudhuri, Andrew Ferraiuolo, Anton Kovsharov, Tej Chajed, Sam Schlesinger, Karn Seth, Jonathan Katz, Charles Sutton, and Pushmeet Kohli.
We thank Eric Wieser for help with open-sourcing our code, Owen Jones for program management support, and Martín Abadi, Christopher Henson, Katerina Hristova, Henryk Michalewski, Jonathan Protzenko and George Tsoukalas for helpful discussions. We thank Signal's Rolfe Schmidt, Michael Rosenberg, and Ehren Kret for their feedback on our methodology. We also thank Tulsee Doshi, Four Flynn, Kate Olszewska, Alicia Huang, Andy Liu, Benoit Schillings, Raluca Ada Popa, Melvin Johnson, Koray Kavukcuoglu, Demis Hassabis, and Sundar Pichai for their support of the project.

Verifying Signal's core cryptography lays the groundwork to secure other vital systems, from medical device firmware to power grid software.
Scaling these techniques requires continued research. Paired with automated defense agents like CodeMender, formal verification can help counter the speed and scale of modern cyber threats to create software with mathematical proof that its protections work.
We are open-sourcing our formal verification artifacts for community use. Read the technical paper below.

articles.title: Fireworks AI security breach impacts Notion and their customers
articles.body:
Notice about the Fireworks AI incident that may impact some Notion workspaces
This notice is about the security incident at one of our vendors, Fireworks AI, that may impact some Notion workspaces. For the latest on the Fireworks AI incident, see their official security updates here.
Following an investigation by the Notion security team, we have determined that <1% of Notion workspaces may have been affected by the Fireworks security incident. Some unattributable chat sessions with Notion AI may have been exposed in this incident. “Unattributable” means the chats weren't labeled with who wrote them or which workspace they came from, and the transcripts did not contain tool call results. Beyond what’s in the chat transcript itself, there’s no information tying the chat back to a workspace, user, or company. No other data from within the workspace is affected.
What is Fireworks AI and how we used them
Fireworks is one of the most-used global AI infrastructure platforms powering tens of thousands of customers, and used by hundreds of thousands of developers. We used Fireworks for classification jobs to help customers understand their own AI usage through a feature in Notion called Insights, and we used them as a general inference provider to serve open-weight models inside our product. The Insights feature has been disabled as we investigate this incident, and we are no longer serving open-weight models through Fireworks.
What happened and how we addressed it
We learned from Fireworks about potential incidents earlier this month, and we shut down all connections to their systems out of an abundance of caution.
On November 6, Fireworks notified us that malicious actors may have accessed potential customer data. Our team immediately began another internal investigation. On November 8, Fireworks confirmed this new dataset for us.
Upon analysis of the new data, we discovered that it included unattributable Notion AI chat transcripts used for the Insights feature. Chats weren't labeled with who wrote them or which workspace they came from, and the transcripts did not contain any tool call results. Beyond the words in the chat transcripts themselves, the data contained no information that could specifically identify the workspace, user, or company.
No other Notion data from your workspace is affected, and we continue to monitor this incident.
If neither you nor your workspace owner has heard from us, that means your workspace is not affected, and no action is needed right now.
For the workspaces impacted by the Fireworks AI incident (<1% of the Notion workspaces), we have contacted the workspace owners. Affected customers will be able to retrieve and review the affected data securely inside their workspace.
For the workspaces affected by the Fireworks AI incident, workspace owners can view the affected data by going to their workspace sidebar → ?  → Security incident review. 
To review and download your affected data, open this link in a desktop browser and make sure you’re using the latest version of Notion. This data is not accessible on mobile.
Workspace owners on Enterprise plans can access:
- A CSV of your workspace’s data affected by the incident. Only workspace owners can see this data.
- An annotated CSV of the same affected workspace data with additional metadata, such as the user associated with each chat transcript, to help you understand and run your own analysis of the impact. These added annotations and metadata were not exposed as part of the incident. Additional annotated fields are marked with __metadata or __analysis respectively. Only workspace owners can see this data.
- Note: These resources are only available if you have managed members for your workspace. Reach out to your account team if you have questions.
Workspace owners on all other plan types can access:
- A page that includes a link they can share with affected members to review their own data.
For other workspace roles:
- Workspace owners can provide a link to members so members can see their own affected data.
- Once shared, the link will provide members with a CSV of only the member's own data affected by the incident.
We recommend that you treat this data as if it were exposed. If you or anyone on your team pasted sensitive information like passwords, API keys, or other credentials into Notion AI during this timeframe, we recommend rotating them right away.
FAQs
What is Fireworks and how did Notion use them?
Fireworks AI is one of the most used global AI infrastructure platforms powering tens of thousands of customers and used by hundreds of thousands of developers.
As of November 3rd, we have disconnected our systems from Fireworks, deleted all data in the Fireworks system, and stopped sending all data and traffic to Fireworks. We have also halted all training runs.
We previously used Fireworks for classification jobs to help customers understand their own AI usage through a feature in Notion called Insights and as a general inference provider to serve open-weight models inside our product.
What does “unattributable” mean? Could the conversations still contain sensitive information?
Following an investigation by the Notion security team, we have determined that <1% of Notion workspaces may have been affected by the Fireworks security incident. Some unattributable chat sessions with Notion AI may have been exposed.
"Unattributable" means the chats weren't labeled with who wrote them or which workspace they came from. The transcripts also did not contain tool call results (e.g., Notion page content, or external data pulled in by Notion AI.) Beyond what’s in the chat transcript itself, there’s no information tying the chat back to specific workspaces, users, or companies. No other data from within your workspace is affected.
As a precaution, we recommend that you treat this unattributable data as if it were exposed. If anyone on your team pasted sensitive information like passwords, API keys, or other credentials into Notion AI during this timeframe, we recommend rotating them right away.
How did Notion use Fireworks with the Learning and Early Access Program (LEAP)? 
Customers in the Learning and Early Access Program (LEAP) volunteer their data to help Notion test new AI technology. In the past, we used this volunteered data to experiment with training task-specific models on Fireworks.
Where can I learn more about Notion’s security practices?
Visit our Security page for an overview of Notion’s security and privacy practices. For more information on security policies, security audit reports, penetration test results, and additional resources, visit the Notion Trust Center.
