articles.title: E-means: 10x faster k-means at equal loss
articles.body:
I’m excited to open-source e-means: a modern, robust k-means algorithm developed at Meta FAIR. A replacement of Lloyd's algorithm, e-means delivers a ~10× speedup in both epochs and wall-clock time while achieving lower loss.
100,000 datapoints in 200 clusters, two wide Gaussians and three small ones, cut off at a box, on a light uniform background. Lloyd has 1 update against 97 per epoch for e-means.
Across a large range of scales and datasets, e-means reaches a test loss below Lloyd's at 25 epochs, in 1.2 to 3 epochs. Measured end to end, that is a 10–45× wall-clock reduction on GPU against the state-of-the-art Lloyd implementation (Flash-KMeans[2]), and 8–15× on CPU against Faiss[1]. Speed and quality usually trade against each other in k-means, while e-means achieves both better speed and loss.
Given a fixed dataset of n points X = {x1, ..., xn} ⊂ Rd and an integer k, the k-means problem is to find k centroids C = (c1, ..., ck) minimizing the mean squared distance between each point and its nearest centroid:
It's a static dataset, unlike codebook learning inside VQ-VAEs, where the distribution to cluster is constantly moving.
The goal of e-means is to provide a modern optimization rule for the k-means problem. We started this project from the following observations:
For e-means, we chose to do mini-batch updates with exponential moving averages[6], which we found to be most efficient for the k-means problem. Contrary to previous mini-batch approaches, e-means requires no hyperparameter tuning because it automatically sets the batch size and step size with scaling laws (see Automatic hyperparameter tuning with scaling laws). In addition, e-means improves the initialization and the dead-cluster revival strategy, adds a cosine-scheduled decay rate, and introduces a finalization stage that reduces the training loss for a negligible runtime penalty at the end of training. e-means is highly parallelizable, and comes with specialized kernels that translate its algorithmic advantage into wall-clock speedups.
The centroid update rule is the central component of e-means. This section aims to provide an overview of update rules for k-means clustering. All methods maintain, for each cluster j, a sum Sj and a count Nj of the points assigned to it, and take the centroid as their ratio:
They differ only in how Sj and Nj are updated. Below, sj and nj denote the sum and the count of the points in the current batch that are assigned to cluster j (both zero if none are).
Lloyd’s algorithm[7] assigns every point to its nearest centroid and recomputes the statistics from scratch, using the full dataset as the batch:
so cj is the exact mean of the points currently assigned to it. Each update costs one full pass over the data, and the procedure is repeated a fixed number of times (typically 20 to 50 iterations).
MacQueen’s update[3] accumulates the statistics without ever discarding them:
so cj is the uniform mean of every point assigned to cluster j since the start of training, including points assigned under earlier, possibly poor, centroid positions. This was later partially addressed by Staleness-Reduction Mini-Batch K-Means[8], a hybrid method between k-means and MacQueen. They obtained important speedups, but only on very low numbers of clusters.
e-means works on mini-batches and replaces this sum with an exponential moving average:
so older assignments are forgotten at rate α, and the centroid tracks recent assignments rather than the whole history. This update rule is typically used for moving distributions, hence their adoption for training VQ-VAEs[6]. What we found is that it’s also extremely efficient for static datasets if it’s combined with e-means’ other components, and hyperparameters are properly tuned.
The e-means project started from previous work at Meta FAIR by Hugo Touvron and Hervé Jégou, who had found that mini-batch k-means by gradient descent could beat Lloyd’s algorithm. While I could reproduce these results, I found that the performance of gradient-descent based centroid updates is unstable at large learning rates, unlike exponential moving average updates. I suspect that is because EMA updates guarantee that the centroid is always in the convex hull of points assigned to it, while gradient descent updates may overshoot past that hull.
In order to achieve the lowest loss at a fixed number of epochs, we chose exponential moving average updates, hence the name e-means for our method.
If you set the batch to the full dataset, B = n, and α = 1, then Nj and Sj become exactly the count and sum of the whole cluster, so one e-means iteration becomes exactly one Lloyd iteration. Lloyd is an extreme case of e-means without cosine scheduling on the learning rate. However, our hyperparameter search found that this extreme setting is highly suboptimal, which explains why e-means largely outperforms Lloyd. Below, the loss is measured for every batch size B and step α: Lloyd lands in a corner, well outside the region where the loss is lowest.
This hyperparameter study motivated us to derive scaling laws that automatically pick the optimal batch size B and step size α.
To better understand why e-means reaches better losses than Lloyd at convergence, we plotted a few trainings on toy datasets to evaluate their ability to escape local minima. Repeating trainings over 200 seeds, we found that e-means is much less likely to fall in pathological configurations compared to Lloyd.
Our explanation for that is that mini-batches provide more noisy updates that are more likely to explore the optimization landscape and escape local minima. Lloyd, with its always decreasing loss, is more likely to exploit found local minima and never escape them.
An essential property of e-means is that practitioners don't need to set any additional hyperparameter compared to Lloyd's algorithm. We fitted two scaling laws to set the batch size B and step size α0 from any problem's characteristics (n, k, T), and found them to exhibit strong generalization on unseen datasets and problem scales.
Regret = (MSE with the law − best MSE over the grid) / best MSE, median over configurations. Held-out datasets: SIFT, SPACEV, and the VIBE[9] datasets arXiv and AG-News. Held-out size: one value of n left out of the fit and predicted.
We propose two equations to choose the batch, the default law and the quality law. The “quality law” trades off throughput for better clustering quality against the “default” law. Below we plot the training data for our scaling laws: validation MSE against step size α0 (left) and batch size B (right).
Toy example showing the importance of dead-cluster revival.
The main issue with mini-batch k-means is that it is prone to “dead” clusters, centroids that end up with zero assigned points during optimization. This reduces the effective size of the codebook, which is especially problematic for the large codebooks increasingly used today.
A common mitigation is to reinitialize clusters that fall below a certain size threshold, as done in EnCodec[10], where dead centroids are simply replaced by random samples drawn from the incoming batch. While this helps, it does not fully resolve the issue. Instead of sampling arbitrary points from the batch, we revive dead clusters by splitting large, existing ones: we sample an active cluster with probability proportional to its size and split it into two. We found this approach, adapted from Faiss k-means, to be significantly more effective at eliminating dead clusters and preserving codebook capacity.
1 million vectors, k = 16,384, 5 epochs, mean over 5 seeds; only the revival policy varies. A cluster counts as dead when fewer than ten vectors are assigned to it at the end, a thousandth of an average cluster. Imbalance: how uneven the cluster sizes are (1 = all equal). From the paper’s revival ablation table.
We validated e-means on 24 different embedding and synthetic datasets and configurations (see paper). For the video we ran 234 configurations of e-means against k-means (16 datasets, 100k to 100M points): explore every curve in the results map.
Repo: faiss/contrib/e_means.
If you use e-means, please cite the paper (arXiv:2611.09501):

articles.title: N-able takes its remote access service offline after researcher publishes dozens of zero-day bugs
articles.body:
Remote access company N-able has confirmed it took down its cloud-hosted offering to fix a slew of security vulnerabilities that were published online this week, giving the company no advance notice to fix them.
In a status update on its website, the company said its hosted N-Central offering for customers is now offline “while we take the necessary actions to secure the environments and implement appropriate remediation.” The company also urged customers to take down their own self-hosted deployments of N-Central, fearing that attackers could use the publicly disclosed exploits to hack into customer networks.
N-able said during this time customers will not be able to use their N-Central service, which allows corporate customers to remotely access and manage other devices and systems on the same network. Remote access technologies are a frequent target of hackers, as these systems can grant vast access to a company’s network and internal data.
Security researcher Ben Bales released the “zero-day” bugs on GitHub on Sunday. In a post on X, Bales dubbed the bugs Able2Shell, describing them as a mix of vulnerabilities capable of stealing credentials, creating new administrative accounts, and gaining root access to affected N-able systems.
Bales told Bleeping Computer that he publicly released the bugs as the company allegedly failed to patch the flaws reported in a different product.
N-able said that it has no evidence of successful exploitation against any of its customer environments. A spokesperson for the company did not respond to a request for comment about whether it has the ability to check, such as server logs, or if it has no way to check.

articles.title: The global pledge to use AI for climate good is a cruel joke
articles.body:
At this point, reading through the latest splashy pledge to use AI for the good of the environment feels like downing a nonalcoholic beer. Admittedly, I’m suspicious from the onset. How can this be good? But I love beer and our planet enough to give it a whirl — and hey, why not try a little harm reduction?
The global pledge to use AI for climate good is a cruel joke
A pledge to make AI less of an environmental disaster is floating around United Nations climate negotiations this month, but it’s just lip service.
Negotiators from more than 190 countries around the world are in Antalya, Turkey, this month for the annual United Nations climate summit, called COP31 (the 31st “Conference of the Parties” that ratified the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change). Turkey previewed its Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge ahead of the convening, inviting delegates from other countries to endorse the pledge before its official launch on November 16th.
Like that nonalcoholic beer, it’s deeply unsatisfying
The pledge actually includes some common sense measures that could curb planet-heating pollution from energy-hungry AI data centers. Unfortunately, like that nonalcoholic beer, it’s deeply unsatisfying.
At first glance, many of the ingredients you’d expect from a real commitment on AI’s environmental impact are here. It sets out to ensure that data centers are increasingly powered by clean energy, calling for internationally recognized standards for responsible AI development. Similarly, it pushes for reporting requirements so that there’s greater transparency into the impact data centers — which run primarily on fossil fuels — already have on the environment. It even acknowledges the need to manage the tons of e-waste created by the generative AI boom.
And yet, there is no there there because, as the text states clearly, “these objectives of the pledge are voluntary and non-prescriptive, create no new obligations, and are to be implemented in accordance with national circumstances.” In other words, these are voluntary commitments that countries can choose to follow or not follow based on their whims.
There’s also no way this pledge will garner the support of the most influential player in this game (at least for now). The US has way more data centers than any other country, but Donald Trump has pulled the nation out of the global climate accord and has no official delegates at the summit in Turkey.
The last point in the pledge is to ensure that advances in generative AI can be used to create more renewable energy and reduce greenhouse gas emissions, particularly in economically developing countries. To that end, research published in a Nature journal in August found that AI causes more carbon emissions by boosting fossil fuel production than it would help avoid through gains in renewable energy.
When it comes down to it, this pledge offers a placebo effect at best. In the face of data centers demanding tremendous amounts of electricity and spurring the development of more fossil fuel infrastructure, negotiators can’t be seen as doing nothing about the issue. And with global average temperatures still on the rise, we could all use an emotional support beverage.

articles.title: Ember’s latest self-heating 14-ounce mug is $50 off
articles.body:
If you were cool on the $149.95 original price of the 14-ounce Ember Mug 3, you might warm up to the current discount happening at Amazon, Ember, and Best Buy for several colors of the (top rack) dishwasher-safe mug. It’s 33 percent off, dropping to $99.99 — still not cheap, but cheaper, and notably just $10 more than the 10-ounce version.
Ember’s latest self-heating 14-ounce mug is $50 off
A great deal on a dishwasher-safe mug that stays hot. We also found discounts on Blu-rays and self-coiling USB-C cables.
The Mug 3 affords you a couple of ways to control your drink’s temperature. A power button on the bottom of the mug can cycle between five temperature presets (125 to 145 degrees Fahrenheit), or you can use the app. It includes a sipping lid, and Ember claims that the Mug 3’s battery can keep drinks hot for up to three hours with the lid on. Without it, drinks stay hot for 80 minutes, the same battery claim as the Mug 2.
As we inch closer to the gift-getting season, the Ember Mug 3 seems like a solid product to snag for a coffee or tea lover who works from home, or for parents who have their hands full with kids and could always use a cuppa.
Some more great Verge-approved deals
- Criterion Collection DVDs and Blu-rays are half off through December 6th at Amazon and Barnes and Noble, meaning you have plenty of time to assemble a wishlist of movies you want to buy ahead of the holiday season. The company’s catalog of films is vast, and it’s the best place to get limited edition releases of cherished films, old and new. Some of Criterion’s recent physical releases have been a hit, especially because they’ve quickly sank in price. KPop Demon Hunters on 4K Blu-ray is just $24.99 at Amazon and Barnes and Noble. Also, The Complete Kubrick boxset (currently the only way to get 4K Blu-ray versions of every one of the director’s legendary films) is half off, too, down to $299.99.
- I’ve been wanting a USB-C cable that coils itself magnetically since my colleague Sean Hollister wrote about his favorites last year. That said, they tend to be a little pricey even if their tech specs are similar to cheaper cables, mostly due to the party trick. However, Werewolf (the company that makes the clever VFLEX for powering older gadgets via a USB-C power bank or wall charger) makes its own six-foot magnetic USB-C cable that’s just $12 right now (originally $27.50). It’s braided and supports up to 240W power passthrough, so it meets my criteria.
- Google’s Pixel Watch 5 smartwatch is $100 off in both the Wi-Fi and LTE configurations at Amazon, though not all colors are included in the discount. The most affordable (and smallest) option is the 41mm Wi-Fi Pixel Watch 5, which costs $299.99. The larger 45mm watch face adds $30 to the price tag compared to the smaller version, whether you want Wi-Fi or LTE. One of the biggest improvements made to this generation is its GPS tracking. Google claims that it can outperform the Apple Watch Ultra 3 and Garmin Fenix 8 Pro — both of which cost a lot more — and we were impressed during our hands-on testing. Victoria Song tested it in the signal-congested West Village in Manhattan, walking in zigzags in an attempt to throw off the tracking. It wasn’t perfect, but it more accurately tracked turn-by-turn movement better than the Ultra 3. Read our review.

articles.title: Anthropic targets $1.4 trillion IPO
articles.body:
Anthropic confirmed on Tuesday that its IPO could be one of the biggest ever, even while falling short of previous expectations. Its IPO price is expected to be between $70.00 and $78.00 per share, which would put its valuation as high as $1.4 trillion, according to the New York Times. The Wall Street Journal reports that according to its sources, Anthropic is “aiming for its shares to start trading Thursday or Friday next week.”
Anthropic targets $1.4 trillion IPO
Anthropic’s public offering is expected to make it one of the world’s most valuable publicly traded companies as soon as next week.
As Reuters notes, the Anthropic IPO was previously expected to be valued at as much as $2 trillion. As of last week, Anthropic’s rival OpenAI was valued at $1.25 trillion.
Those lower expectations follow months of debate around AI safety, and what that means, while midterm election results showed souring public opinion toward AI companies and data center projects they’re heavily investing in. And that doesn’t even include this weekend’s revelations about an alleged Chinese spy’s involvement with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
Anthropic:
The initial public offering price is expected to be between $70.00 and $78.00 per share. Anthropic has applied to list its Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol “ANT.”

articles.title: FDA Warns GLP-1s May Increase Risk of Sudden Blindness
articles.body:
FDA Warns GLP-1s May Increase Risk of Sudden Blindness 63
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from NBC News: The Food and Drug Administration said Monday that GLP-1 drugmakers must add a warning label about a rare eye condition that can cause sudden blindness. The condition, called nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, or NAION, affects the optic nerve, which carries signals from the eye to the brain. When blood flow to the nerve is reduced or blocked, it can cause sudden vision loss. The condition is permanent with no known treatment. The FDA said "there is a potential increased risk of rare NAION" in people taking GLP-1 drugs. The agency's requirement applies to all GLP-1s, including Novo Nordisk's Ozempic and Wegovy and Eli Lilly's Mounjaro and Zepbound, as well as several older GLP-1 diabetes medications. [...] Previous research has found that GLP-1 use may increase the risk of NAION, and Lilly has said it was aware of studies on the potential link.
The FDA said it began looking into a possible link after a 2024 study published in JAMA Ophthalmology that found diabetes patients prescribed semaglutide were four times as likely to develop NAION as those not prescribed the drug. The agency said it reviewed reports of side effects submitted to its adverse event monitoring system and analyzed data from multiple clinical trials. Cases of NAION have been reported for all currently marketed GLP-1 drugs, the FDA found. However, FDA scientists were not able to identify a mechanism for how the drugs could increase the risk of the eye condition. Risk factors for NAION can overlap with conditions seen in people taking GLP-1 drugs, including Type 2 diabetes, obesity, sleep apnea and hypertension. "Patients and caregivers should be aware of a potential increased risk of NAION, a rare condition that can result in acute, painless, decreased vision in one eye, including permanent vision loss," with GLP-1 use, the FDA said in the release.

articles.title: Jensen Huang’s alleged honeypot scandal has inspired some top-notch memes
articles.body:
Jensen Huang, the CEO and co-founder of the world’s most prominent chip company, has allegedly been honey-trapped by a suspected Chinese spy, and the news has struck the internet like a match to gasoline.
Huang has long been seen as a wife guy (or so everyone assumed). He and his wife, Lori, have been together since the 1980s, and both of their children work at Nvidia. Huang has been the closest thing the tech world has to a rock star, with fans lining up for selfies and autographs. Of all the AI overlords, the leather-jacket wearing Huang has seemed like the most level-headed and least erratic, which is why this plot twist has hit so hard.
The potential fallout is mind-boggling. Nvidia looms so large over the U.S. stock market that even the company’s domestic drama is a market risk. Countless AI startups depend on Nvidia chips, so any shake-up at the top would ripple far beyond the company. And Nvidia has no publicly disclosed succession plan, so if Huang leaves, it’s unclear who’d take over.
Is this how the AI bubble bursts? It’s a question that will be answered in time, but in the meantime, a more pressing matter demands our attention: ranking the funniest memes about the scandal, with bonus points for AI images presumably generated using Nvidia chips.
There’s admittedly a lot to choose from, ranging from “500 Days of Summer” jokes to jokes about divorce lawyers to an AI-adaptation of the music video for Usher‘s song “Confessions Pt. II,” a track about cheating. Another person created a viral AI video that recreates the Coldplay concert where a startup CEO was caught on the Jumbotron hugging a colleague.
Huang publicly confessed to the affair just yesterday, so the internet has the rest of the week to get creative.
Yes, the internet is having a field day with this one.
As usual, AI-generated content is doing a lot of heavy lifting. Copyleaks, a software company that analyzes online content for signs of AI and digital manipulation, said Monday that it had seen “an explosion in AI-manipulated photos and videos of Huang and Alice Huang, ranging from memes to more subtle edits.” The tally includes at least 70 AI-related posts on X, which together drew around 8.42 million views and 64,362 engagements as of Monday morning. Those metrics have almost certainly climbed since.

articles.title: Peak Design’s Roller Lite Carry-On is bigger on the inside — and cheaper, too
articles.body:
When we sampled Peak Design’s Roller Pro last year, we loved almost everything about the camera gear powerhouse’s first attempt at a proper suitcase. Everything, that is, except for the price. Back then, during its crowdfunded launch, the Pro could be had for as little as $425. Today, you’re looking at $599.95 for the same roller bag.
Peak Design’s Roller Lite Carry-On is bigger on the inside — and cheaper, too
More efficient and more affordable, but less charming, too.
Peak Design has taken that feedback to heart in creating the Roller Lite Carry-On, part of a new series of suitcases that bring many of the Pro’s features and design concepts into a hard-sided clamshell design that’s more traditional and, crucially, more affordable, starting with the $449.95 Lite Carry-On.
It’s part of a new Lite family of suitcases. The slightly larger Lite Carry-On Plus costs $469.99 and measures 22.5 x 15 x 9 inches, while the $549.95 Lite Trunk is 30 x 16.1 x 13.8 inches. The former should still squeeze in most overhead compartments, while the latter is better off checked. Both, though, come in cheaper than the Pro.
That cost-cutting does result in bags with fewer features and less originality, but I still found the new Lite Carry-On to be a great travel companion, first for a two-day whirlwind journey to Rome, then for a week in Tucson, Arizona.
I travel a lot, spending far more time escorting my carry-on around airports than I do driving my car at home, so no surprise that I’m picky about what I drag through terminals and haul up into overhead compartments. I wouldn’t say that aesthetics are a primary concern, but everybody prefers a good-looking suitcase, and the Roller Lite passes that first test. It’s understated yet sophisticated in black, but the emerald green option called cypress might be even better. There’s also a hue called stone for those more into earth tones.
Regardless of color, I think the Lite Carry-On’s hard plastic shell looks better than the soft-sided Roller Pro, and I’d hazard a guess it’ll stand the test of time better, too. The second trip I took with the Lite started in a tiny puddle-jumper of a plane. The flight attendant gate-checked any bag with wheels, even though the Lite Carry-On (21.7 x 13.8 x 9 inches, slightly smaller than the Pro) would have easily fit in the overhead.
It came back to me from its trip to the belly of the aircraft with a few new scuffs and scratches, otherwise looking only a little worse for wear.
Specs
- Expandable from 38L to 45L.
- 21.7 x 13.8 x 9 inches (55 x 35 x 22.9cm) and 7 pounds (3.2kg).
- Spinner wheels designed for easy replacement when they wear out.
- Dual zipper and TSA-approved lock.
- The thin, space-saving carbon fiber handle helps to maximize interior space.
- Handle expands to lock at 90 or 100cm.
- Global carry-on compliant.
- Integrated grab handles on the top, bottom, and both sides.
- Backed by Peak Design’s lifetime warranty.
Durability was a big selling point on the Roller Pro, and that continues here. The Lite is even more repairable thanks to its easily replaced strap handles. They sit flush without taking up any room in the suitcase itself, yet are quite comfortable to use.
Both the Pro and Lite share the same carbon fiber handle, also easily replaceable. It’s my favorite feature, rising smoothly and dropping into place without a hitch. I especially love the dry carbon weave that’s exposed when it’s raised.
My only complaint is that the handle on top is too bulky, making it a clumsy fit through the luggage passthrough on my backpack. But otherwise, the carbon construction makes for a sturdier feel than the handle on my Tumi 19 Degree Aluminum roller, which costs three times as much.
While both share the same handle, the Lite’s design is a substantial departure from the Pro. The Pro offered a so-called “hybrid” layout, with the top opening up and swinging back into a single large compartment. The Lite is a more traditional clamshell with a zipper running the full circumference, splitting the case in two like a book.
When it comes to packing camera equipment and other gear, I think the Pro’s single main compartment is easier to live with, especially if you’re hauling some bulky telephoto glass.
But when I’m packing more items of clothing than camera gear, I actually prefer the Lite Carry-On’s two smaller compartments. I can separate clothes from everything else, which is useful when living out of a suitcase.
The Lite Carry-On lacks the Pro’s trick external pockets for laptops, passports, and the like. That doesn’t bother me, as that stuff always goes in my backpack, but if you’re looking for a single-bag travel experience, the Pro is better suited. The Lite is also missing the Cord Hook feature of the Pro, potentially useful for strapping a tripod or the like to the outside.
Inside, the right half of the Lite has a zippered flap cover with two large mesh pockets that don’t look or feel as good as the inner pockets on the Pro. You’ll still find a hidden pocket for tucking away an Apple AirTag tracker, though.
The other side has the same elastic-strap holding system as the Pro. You load it up with stuff, then stretch the two hooks across to latch on the other side. It’s a basic, flimsy-looking solution, but it works. When the agents at Leonardo da Vinci International Airport wanted to rummage around in my bag, those little bungee hooks kept everything from scattering over the floor in Fiumicino.
The Lite Carry-On has an integrated, TSA-approved lock, something missing on the Pro, and though it’s slightly smaller on the outside (21.7 x 13.8 vs. 21.8 x 14), removing that front pocket makes it substantially bigger on the inside: 38 liters vs. 34 on the Pro, expanding to 45 liters vs. 39.
The 2-inch expansion on the Lite is a great emergency solution if you picked up a few too many souvenirs in Seville, but the Lite feels loose and floppy when rolling around with its expansion zipper open. I don’t recommend it.
Otherwise, when fully zipped and packed, I really enjoyed wheeling the Roller Lite around. It was an easy glider over smooth terminal floors and didn’t rattle obnoxiously over rougher asphalt.
The Roller Lite Carry-On is undoubtedly a simpler suitcase than the Roller Pro that preceded it, and because of that, it doesn’t feel nearly as special to use or purpose-driven as Peak Design’s offerings typically are.
But then it’s $150 cheaper, roomier, is easier to pack, and, in my estimation, will prove even more durable. It may not be the ultimate roller bag for pro photogs, but it’s my new favorite suitcase for under $500. I’d even put it ahead of options from Tumi, Briggs & Riley, and others that cost many times more, aren’t as easily repaired, and don’t come with a lifetime warranty.
Photography by Tim Stevens / The Verge

articles.title: Let over Lambda–50 Years of Lisp (2008)
articles.body:
Let Over Lambda (ISBN 978-1-4357-1275-1, 376+iv pp.) is one of the most hardcore computer programming books out there. Starting with the fundamentals, it describes the most advanced features of the most advanced language: COMMON LISP. The point of this book is to expose you to ideas that you might otherwise never be exposed to.
This book is about macros, that is programs that write programs. Macros are what make lisp the greatest programming language in the world. When used properly, macros enable amazing feats of abstraction, programmer productivity, and code efficiency and security that are unheard of elsewhere. Macros let you do things you simply cannot do in other languages.
If you are looking for a dry coding manual that re-hashes common-sense techniques in whatever langue du jour, this book is not for you. This book is about pushing the boundaries of what we know about programming. While this book teaches useful macro skills that can help solve your programming problems today and now, it has also been designed to be entertaining and inspiring. If you have ever wondered what lisp or even programming itself is really about, this is the book you have been looking for.
2026 update: Let Over Lambda was published in 2008, to align with the 50th anniversary of Lisp's invention in 1958. A lot has changed since then, in both Lisp and programming practice in general. Although my thinking and opinions have evolved since, I still believe the book holds up well as a tutorial and explanation of why Lisp so special. Going forward, the entire book is free to read online (HTML, PDF). Happy lisping!

articles.title: AI usage generates a fragile codebase
articles.body:
AI usage generates a fragile codebase
I can only speculate as to the reasons why I was laid off from Meta in May, but I suspect that one of the reasons is that I was a little bit more resistant to adopting AI/LLMs as coding tools than some of my peers. Don't get me wrong, I generated at least 90% of my code using AI in my last few months there, which was the minimum for a decent rating. But AI didn't 10X the amount of code I was writing. It didn't even 2X it.
I was focused on code quality. I saw the code being pushed by some of my peers who were heavily reliant on AI, and I saw that it was brittle code. There were many subtle issues that would lead to tech debt in the long term, and even some glaring issues were ignored by very good programmers. For instance, I saw one of the best programmers on my team try to merge code that used javascript events for mouseover CSS effects rather than using the :hover selector, which is a totally unscalable way of writing mouseovers.
Now I'm employed at another large tech company and I've fully made the switch to generating 100% of my code using AI because that's the expectation today. Still, I can see lots of people becoming aware that this isn't a sustainable way to continue development of a large scale SaaS product. AI tends to solve the problems that can fit within its context window very well, but it's totally oblivious to the long term issues that can't be understood in that relatively small frame.
In this post I'm going to list four ways that AI usage results in a fragile codebase that isn't resilient to the demands of highly available and highly scalable SaaS applications.
By the way, every word of this article was written by a human. Even though the following image was generated by AI, this article isn't AI slop.
Four ways AI makes codebases fragile
Here are the four most common ways that I have seen AI generating a fragile codebase.
1. AI writes shallow tests
One of the most obvious failures of modern LLMs is that they tend to write simplistic automated test cases that don't cover the things that matter to humans. Frequently I see AI agents writing lots of tests of get/set methods which are trivial and don't typically require much testing. When AI writes e2e tests, they tend to only cover the cases which are already covered in the codebase. In other words, the AI writes tests only covering one type of user, or only covering surface level interactions. This creates massive gaps in the test coverage that are invisible to developers because they aren't captured by the line level coverage metric.
2. AI writes overly complex ccode
AI also tends to write overly complex code. It frequently uses two or three helper methods when a single one would suffice. It tries to follow coding guidelines, such as DRY, to a fault, without realizing that the added complexity of that rigidity makes the code more difficult for human developers to debug or understand.
3. Reliance on AI decreases human understanding
And that's the third issue with AI codebases: Humans don't understand them. The longer a company relies on AI agents to generate the code, the fewer developers are going to understand the codebase. This means that developers can't do the things that are necessary to build a resilient codebase. They don't understand the data structures and algorithms well enough to see when a pull request contains a new abstraction that doesn't work with the pre-existing structures.
4. AI moves too quickly to maintain a high quality bar
AI moves too quickly for human developers to maintain a high quality bar. Each pull request comes faster than the prior one and has to be reviewed in even less time. This leads to developers skimming the code and missing crucial details that result in long term tech debt. Small quality issues like testing gaps and poorly named variables accrue in the codebase until it becomes a morass of spaghetti code.
Four signs that you have a fragile codebase
If you're unsure whether coding agents are harming your codebase or not, then you might look for the following symptoms of a fragile, AI-generated codebase.
1. AI generated codebases have more incidents
When you switched the department over to agentic coding did the number of incidents slowly start rising? At first when we were all using agents to generate massive amounts of code, it didn't seem that different from traditional coding. The PRs came and were merged and everything seemed alright. But oh, there was that one p0 that came in at the end of the month, then there were two SEVs the following month. Then even more the next month. Now, after a year or two of agentic coding, it seems like there's an incident every weekend. AI coding agents are the reason why there are more incidents impacting customers.
2. Recovery from incidents takes longer in AI codebases
Not only are there more incidents, but the incidents take longer to be mitigated. The fact is that the human developers on your team now have a more shallow understanding of the codebase. If your coding agent can't find the issue that your customers are facing, then humans are going to have to dig through a codebase that is highly complex and poorly tested. They will essentially be entering unfamiliar territory, so it takes longer for them to figure out what is going wrong. Hence, companies lose more and more money to incidents that take longer to resolve.
3. AI generated codebases create errors that are only visible to users
When humans don't spend time in the code, they fail to see all of the use cases. They fail to understand how actual humans are using the code because they aren't ensuring that the AI is instrumenting analytics and catching all the errors properly. Hence, invisible errors start appearing in the codebase. Errors are uncaught and only visible to real world users, as opposed to the types of users that are being tested in automated tests or in developer manual testing.
4. AI results in a poor user experience
And that leads to the ultimate problem with AI codebases: they weren't made for humans. AI codebases are software made by AI for AI. They aren't being tailored to the way that human users use the product, and they aren't being tailored for the way human developers need to maintain the product. The experience degrades on both the user and the developer side, leading to a vicious cycle of enshittification.
Products made for humans require a human touch
The fact of the matter is that for a product to satisfy human customers, it has to be informed by a human perspective. Nobody likes ordering from machines at a restaurant. Shopping for clothes from a website always results in worse fits than shopping in person. The same is true of SaaS products. Any time you leave your SaaS product in the hands of a machine, you are losing the human touch that is valuable to your users and your developers. This may work for the cheapest products that only compete on price, but high quality software products will continue to have a human touch. The best, most expensive products will be tailored for human users by human developers. They will be charming and enjoyable to use. They won't be fragile because they won't be primarily developed by AI.

articles.title: CoreWeave bond yield tops 16% as AI credit stress rises
articles.body:
Debt markets are sending a message to AI data center builders: we're hiking the interest rate on your credit card and may put some new curbs on your credit limit.
That analogy comes courtesy of Jefferies global head of equity strategy, Christopher Wood, who put it in a note on Friday: "The most plausible way the AI capex arms race will end is that the credit card will be taken away."
That isn't happening yet, but credit markets have been spooked by the new political landscape — seeing more hurdles to data centers under Democratic governors in key states, along with a Democratic-controlled Congress.
The poster child for debt stress is neocloud Coreweave. The yield on its 2032 bond with a 9.625% coupon has climbed above 16%. Coreweave's five-year credit default swaps spiked above 1,289 basis points on Thursday, widening above their October peak, according to Deutsche Bank. The CDS eased 8% Friday to around 1,155.
"We've had plenty of warnings from the credit space," said Jim Reid, Deutsche Bank's global head of macro and thematic research, in a note on Friday. Debt and equities are now moving more in sync, he added, "so we'll have to see if credit goes any further."
Investors are demanding more compensation to insure against default among even companies with the strongest balance sheets and credit ratings, including Nvidia, Broadcom, and Amazon.com.
CDS on Nvidia debt is up 76% in the last month. Broadcom's CDS is up 49%, while Amazon's has gained 44%. Their CDS remain low on an absolute basis; Nvidia's spread stood at roughly 139 basis points, compared with about 298 bps for Oracle and roughly 1,100 for CoreWeave. A large increase from a low starting point does not imply the same credit risk.
Still, rising CDS are a sign that markets want more protection against default among even the largest and healthiest debt issuers. And rising CDS imply higher financing costs down the line.
The market is now grappling with the prospect that at least some data center spending will be delayed or scrapped under incoming Democratic governors in Ohio, Texas, and Georgia, the three states with much of the planned capacity.
Moratoriums could impact 45% of planned capacity in the U.S. with a large amount of that in Texas, according to Goldman Sachs. Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has said she's not opposed to data centers but wants a moratorium until the state legislature passes protections for communities.
None of these means AI debt financing is collapsing. Goldman tallies five AI bond deals totaling $67 billion since October 29, pushing total hyperscaler debt issuance this year to $296 billion. Goldman forecasts $440 billion of hyperscaler debt issuance next year, plus an additional $300 billion of project-level issuance across investment-grade and high-yield.
The Trump administration is vowing to support data centers. National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett told CNBC on Friday that he expects data center growth to continue as forecast, despite Democrats' big election wins.
What comes next
The big question now is how quickly AI spending will generate enough cash for hyperscalers to keep investors comfortable with future capex plans. For the neoclouds, any sign of consolidation or retrenchment in capex could result in fewer or shorter contracts for data center compute or delays in prepayments.
Goldman analysts said hyperscalers collectively reported negative free cash flow in the third quarter as capital spending exceeded operating cash flow.
"Delayed monetization and growth in purchase commitments—which we view as additional and sizable uses of cash, separate from Capex—are the key risks to more debt issuance, subject to market conditions," according to the bank.
Peak AI debt issuance may now be closer at hand. Bank of America analysts estimates that AI-related credit issuance will rise 31% from 2026 to 2027, hitting $685 billion, including public and private debt. They then see it falling 23% to $531 billion in 2028.
As for the risk? "Downside to these forecasts exists from a potential slowdown in AI infrastructure projects on the back of the Blue Wave, which will reduce capex needs and thus debt market funding," BofA said in a note.
-CNBC's Nick Wells and Michael Bloom contributed reporting

articles.title: Horible public key tricks
articles.body:
Horrible public key tricks:
—
So, I've always been somewhat annoyed at SSL/TLS. It requires everyone to go through a complex "ACME" dance just to put up a public website. Worse, certificates expire every few months, so it's not a one and done thing: even with automation, maintaining a certificate requires care to ensure the ACME client always has access to DNS records or the web server.
... and the whole system doesn't even work because certificates are issued over plaintext connections, and trusted certificate aurthorities use very secure keys like "4"
There is prior art of protest SSL implementations, but I do actually want to encrypt web traffic. Passive eavesdropping is a real risk... but preventing it doesn't require the whole certificate thing: therefore, the best choice is a protest certificate.
The only part of the certificate I directly control is the public key. Therefore, the simplest way to obtain a bad certificate is use a vanity private key such as 313333333337 (one of the most eleet primes). However, while the resulting public key would be weak, no one would know unless they try to break it.
A good protest should be obvious:
# openssl s_client -connectmaurycyz.com :443 < /dev/null 2>/dev/null \ |sed -n/BEGIN/,/END/p |grep -zE'////.?*////' --color=yes -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- MIIFAjCCA+qgAwIBAgISBkOkuuyaN1ypD3PAPrLMyT7tMA0GCSqGSIb3DQEBCwUA MDMxCzAJBgNVBAYTAlVTMRYwFAYDVQQKEw1MZXQncyBFbmNyeXB0MQwwCgYDVQQD EwNZUjIwHhcNMjYxMTA5MTcyOTQ2WhcNMjcwMjA3MTcyOTQ1WjAXMRUwEwYDVQQD EwxtYXVyeWN5ei5jb20wggEiMA0GCSqGSIb3DQEBAQUAA4IBDwAwggEKAoIBAQCg JyPf37Sj6PvU06m5 ////You+dont+actually+have+to+pick+random+privat e+keys//No+one+checks+these+things//A+certificate+authority+got+ away+with+the+number+4+for+a+year/////DSfCAfXcsJfBpnHekS0qnf5YLl c54VuUNRVINcDkEwJDwyB96+xE/uXhtiGdk8ty1PF6jciLEYCJBHcmqOa5pOyV8m 63yR3NE6hCQlaSLQQDo96Sb0/10aC5LqE7KwEskrP/qeCzT7vDN7fh+dXOGs+VMw eJvTAb0xHJpxhSK05i7DAgMBAAGjggIqMIICJjAOBgNVHQ8BAf8EBAMCBaAwEwYD VR0lBAwwCgYIKwYBBQUHAwEwDAYDVR0TAQH/BAIwADAdBgNVHQ4EFgQUBKBfDbwf dCnKeU83pMTWyFrJBwAwHwYDVR0jBBgwFoAUQBUtJnntMiCe35pyHdYyH4EMgQww MwYIKwYBBQUHAQEEJzAlMCMGCCsGAQUFBzAChhdodHRwOi8veXIyLmkubGVuY3Iu b3JnLzAnBgNVHREEIDAegg4qLm1hdXJ5Y3l6LmNvbYIMbWF1cnljeXouY29tMBMG A1UdIAQMMAowCAYGZ4EMAQIBMC8GA1UdHwQoMCYwJKAioCCGHmh0dHA6Ly95cjIu Yy5sZW5jci5vcmcvMTEwLmNybDCCAQsGCisGAQQB1nkCBAIEgfwEgfkA9wB1AExj 3JjlnB2riPYeij3ero+rRKM3e1+blMP7oZz8wb4mAAABocGRbw4AAAQDAEYwRAIg HShWaEI2nVJEizSI6sJ/jnLaABZ3aTKoUL3pLo1uOgsCIEn+XiT2WHhm9LGN6kug O9R7Z4q0HiFA4RZ7tIMJQH5XAH4AjspHC6zeavOiBrCkeoS3Rv4fxr+VPiXmm07k AkjzxugAAAGhwZFyfQAIAAAFAEE0hdwEAwBHMEUCIDSms4Vf0llcvcldJd2Ool8i AiUQQlS0Zzbej+7Y1aR7AiEA79Ll+t6inu1PkUIgzNTXkE0S20VHYEYel5fkdKSA VTQwDQYJKoZIhvcNAQELBQADggEBAFi3A4fcjj4UKa9MFz1a8DWc+Jya2gJng13m 2UFdWCaqsN7FJWQEjRiJ0npynmDnA3VMyjswUMHAMx4d8G3lHNPfZWGsCgpjVa/d IEoeZ6gTYjFa/Ovb64m4CcuQkm0GxcyAqMPs348e6Px32iU1R6MnV4UEUosnSPeK 4ocuI3SoR9LHxX/yHOKcYTKLpIMwMdaAmWt0N7l59GOb8o+dz3R7cxtVV/lrZReZ /YPEAYRiNi7f+jNI1JCp0i8wXUb9NN7WlbmcFDecDG/++cRpAkoIk4m/LJindsuu kErrVZ4yLqB0Hvm+uNvWxr9y/qKFTYw9POx1oaZJO/SwXZdDBeY= -----END CERTIFICATE----- 
First, let's look at mathematical framework of RSA. To generate a key, pick two large prime numbers (p and q) and multiply them to yeild the modulus (n). Pick a small number, e as public exponent.
The RSA public key is composed of the modulus (n) and the public exponent:
# Encryption requires knowing e (public) cyphertext = plaintext^e mod n
The private key contains the modulus and the private exponent (d) which is chosen to be the multiplicate inverse of e modulo n. Exactly how d is found is not relevent, but the process requires knowing p and q.
# Decryption requires knowing d (pivate) = cyphertext^d mod n = plaintext^e^d mod n = plaintext^(e*d) mod n = plaintext^1 mod n = plaintext
Ok, back to vanity keys. The standard value for e is 65537 (0x10001), because the small number of set bits makes encryption faster. In fact, the CA I used will refuse to sign keys with a non-standard public exponent, so I can't do anything funny there.
The modulus, n, is either 2,048 or 4,096 "user controlled" bits, so it's the ideal place to hide a message. However, to use the certificate, I'll need to find two large primes that multiply out to the vanity modulus.
My method starts by picking two random primes and calculating the resulting n value. Then, the bytes of n are modified to introduce message into the base64 encoding. Of course, the modified n is not the product of p and q, but this is fixable by setting q to n/p.
The resulting q value is very unlikely to be a prime (or integer), so I round it and find the next prime after the ideal q: which usually only requires changing the value of q by a few hundred. Since p and q are similar in size, a small change q only affects the least-sigifiant half of the product:
58174124 * 918491824 = 53432457262362176
(incrementing until the next prime...) 58174124 * 918491843 = 53432458367670532 
As long as the message is embedded into the upper half of n, it's likely to survive undamaged. The original p and newly selected q can now be used to construct a functional RSA private key in the usual manner.
From here, it's really just a matter of getting a certificate aurthority to sign the key:
# Single domain openssl req -new-key priv.pem -subj '/C=US/CN=example.com' >cert_request certbot certonly --manual--csr cert_request # Wildcard cat > config<<EOF [ req ] req_extensions = req_ext [ req_ext ] subjectAltName = @alt_names [ alt_names ] DNS.1 = *.example.com DNS.2 = example.com EOF openssl req -new-key priv.pem -config config -subj '/C=US/CN=example.com' >cert_request certbot certonly --manual--csr cert_request 
... although since base64 operates on groups of three byte, it is possible for the message to be misaligned and not readable. However, since the layout of the certificate is static, it is possible to adjust the message's placement until it works: this should take less than four attempts.
The result is a functional, trusted certificate with a longish message hidden in the public key. Renewal is done by resumbitting the CSR and repeating the ACME chalange, which can be automated.
Base64 is missing most punctuation, but it provides the full ASCII alphabet, and the ~150 (RSA-2048) or ~320 (RSA-4096) avalable charaters provides plenty of space for jokes. Another option would be to target the base16 displayed in most browser's certificate viewer: this would provide a lot more space (2 chars/byte instea of 0.75), but requires careful word choice.
As for security, this trick obviously reduces the entropy in the private key. However, it should still be secure: nearly identical methods have been considered as a form of compression. If the top-half of the modulus is fixed to a well known value, it doesn't have to be sent or stored as part of the key.
A reduction of around 1/2 can be achieved through division, but the state of the art can fix 2/3 of the key, reducing the size to 1/3 of standard RSA while retaining a similar level of security... although I should note that such tricks have largly been abandoned in favor of other crytosystems which can directly use small keys.
The manipulation of q may produce primes that are very close together, which makes it possible to factor n and recover the private key. A very small d value can also be a problem. Both of these are unlikely, but my script doesn't check for insecure values
However, regardless of the key's security, it should be perfectly fine for a public website: modern TLS provides forward secrecy, so eavesdropping requires a man-in-the-middle attack even if the private key is compromised.
Related:
- https://tom7.org/httpv/httpv.pdf: [⭐ World's worst TLS server ]
- /projects/badcert/gen.py: script to generate a vanity key
- https://rya.nc/cert-tricks.html: More vanity certs
- https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-540-79104-1_9: Actual cryptographer's opinions on fixing part of n

articles.title: Jensen Huang pulls out of ElevenLabs Summit amid Nvidia controversy
articles.body:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has pulled out of the ElevenLabs Summit scheduled for this Wednesday in New York, ElevenLabs, the voice AI company, confirmed Monday. He has also dropped out of other speaking engagements, including the Anthropic CEO Forum. Nvidia is an investor in ElevenLabs.
The withdrawals come after Huang admitted to an extramarital affair over the weekend, and Nvidia opened an investigation into his relationship with a possible Chinese spy.
“I owe my family and all of you an apology. I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” Huang said in a memo to the company.
The incident has rattled the AI industry, raising questions about Huang’s staying power as CEO and Nvidia’s own China ambitions.

articles.title: Here comes the sun[light]:An ambient Daylight Clock with time and space controls
articles.body:
Here comes the sun[light]: An ambient Daylight Clock with time and space controls
I built a Daylight Clock!
This analog clock has a 24-hour period, with midnight at the bottom and noon at the top. The lights around the circumference illuminate the current daylight span, based on the clock’s home latitude and longitude.
I also built a time-and-space control box:
What does this controller do?
- The knob at the bottom controls time, in increments of one week per click.1 The time knob in action: The sudden springs forward and falls back daylight shifts are when Daylight Savings Time begins and ends.
- The toggle on the side switches enables the control box’s time and space overrides; when this switch is off, the time knob controls the brightness of the edge lighting.2
- The vertical slider is a latitude selector, designed so that the world map—Equal Earth projection!—lines up with the length of the slider.3 The latitude slider in action:
- The three-way “relative longitude” toggle at the top sets position within the current time zone—i.e., whether the daylight computation is based on the west, central, or east edge of the given timezone.4 The longitude toggle in action:
Based on the relative longitude video, is it possible that this entire project was a way for me to illustrate the time zone grudge I’ve held for years? Not intentionally, but….
The grudge: I grew up in Michigan, on the west edge of the Eastern Time Zone (US); I later moved to the eastern side of that same zone, where the sun rises and sets a full hour earlier. This is distressing in the summer—by rights, the sun ought to set late in the summer!—and borders on criminal in the winter: the sun sets just after 4pm on the solstice. 😱
Envy-driven development (EDD):5 cceckman’s daylight-aware clock
My clock’s provenance is wholly attributable to my friend Charles and his very cool daylight-aware clock. In Charles’s words:
        I’ve always lived at middle latitudes of 35-40 degrees. I notice the change in daylight / nighttime hours across the course of a year; in the winter, ending work at a reasonable hour still feels like “working into the night”.
I wanted to have a little passive reminder about how much daylight I am / am not getting. Not one tied to my computer or phone – something more ambient. Naturally, a reminder of the passage of time is… a clock!
When Charles started building his clock I was covetous, and knew I had to build my own.
We made a few different design choices—his time display is digital, mine analog; his daylight illuminates outward from the circumference of the clock, mine inward6—but we both put noon at the top,7 and I used his daylight calculation code wholesale. Also his pair programming assistance to sleuth out a mysterious failure mode!8 9
My clock’s time-space control box was inspired by Charles’s nifty virtual interactive daylight visualization:
Physical design and construction: Clock body
The clock movement is an off-the-shelf 24-hour movement. You can just buy these!10
I designed the body of the clock and the body of the controller box in Cuttle.xyz, and cut the pieces on the laser-cutter at my local library’s free maker space(!).11 I designed the clock to have a circumference of exactly 48 neopixels on an Adafruit neopixel strip, so that the lights would subdivide nicely into the hours of the day.
Cuttle design here.
The outer decoration is from the astronomical face of the astronomical clock of the Zytglogge, in Bern, Switzerland. I digitized a photo of the Zytglogge, then cleaned it up and scaled it properly in Cuttle.
Painting was…an experience.
I used wood glue to make the press-fit connections permanent.
I painted the clock with acrylic paint, and attached the outer decorated ring with Blu Tack so that I can easily remove it and swap it for a different decoration.
Physical design and construction: Controller box
I designed the controller box in Cuttle, too.
Cuttle design here.
I used wood sealant on the front and acrylic paint on the sides.
I failed to make the box deep enough to fit the ensuing tangle of wires crammed inside, so it doesn’t sit completely flush against the wall. Ah well, can’t win ’em all.
Hardware design
The Daylight Clock runs off an Adafruit Feather RP2040 microcontroller. The rest of the components are:
- A strand of 48 neopixels,
- A real-time clock (RTC) component assembly, to maintain the current date and time even when the board isn’t powered, so that I don’t have to hand-set it every time I plug in the clock12
- A two-way toggle to enable/disable switch between “daylight based on current time” vs “daylight based on control box settings”
- A linear potentiometer, i.e., the slider to control latitude
- A rotary encoder, i.e., the knob to control date
- A three-way toggle to switch between the different longitude locations (west, middle, east), and
- Three LEDs to show that current longitude selection.
The microcontroller and all components live in the control box, except for the neopixels around the clock face, which are connected to the microcontroller via some hand-braided wires and a few connectors.The connectors are so that I can easily change the distance between clock and control box, without doing any additional soldering. The neopixels are powered through the board, which plugs in via standard wall wart.
The new-to-me aspects of this project were the RTC and—less glamorously!—the crimped wire connectors.
Software design
        I programmed the Adafruit Feather with CircuitPython, relying heavily on the
        asyncio library. asyncio allowed me to separate
        monitoring the state of the input controllers—“has the slider position changed? the toggle toggled? the knob turned?”—from re-computing each neopixel’s resultant color.
      
I ported the sunrise and sunset calculations from Charles’s Rust implementation of the NOAA solar calculator.
I’ve made the code available here—and standard houseplant programming caveats apply.
Retrospective
This project took a lot of calendar time, and a disproportionate amount of mental space.
Challenges:
- Deciding what I wanted the clock frame to look like
- Deciding how I wanted to decorate the clock face
- Deciding how I wanted to decorate the outer ring around the clock’s face
- Deciding that I was going to :just-flag: use a cardboard box for the controller…and then doing that, and discovering that I hated it and wanted to cut something out of wood
- Purchasing pre-painted wood to speed up the cut/paint processes
- Discovering that the library policies had changed so I couldn’t use their laser cutter on this wood
- Attempting to use a different maker space and/or hire a local shop to cut this wood for me
- Deciding to :just: use the default library wood and paint it myself afterwards
- A series of painting mishaps with the decorative face that resulted in an unusable mess after accidentally using an oil-based ink over some acrylic
- Recutting the face (…plus the wait time of signing up for a slot…)
- Discovering that I’d glued the clock sides upside down (luckily the sizing still fit backwards, and I didn’t have to go re-cut everything again…)
- Discovering that I’d installed the neopixel strip backwards (counterclockwise instead of clockwise)
Thankfully the result looks really cool, and works as intended, and I love having it on the wall.
I bet you want to make one of your own now, yeah?
Go for it!
To get you started:
Feel free to ask if you are building one and need more guidance at any step; I didn’t want to take the time (heh) to write a full tutorial, but I’m more than happy to assist retroactively.
Also, if you want to make one, but don’t want to deal with quite so many electronics:
- You could skip the control box: The majority of the technical challenges I encountered—both design and implementation—came from the addition of the controls. A Daylight Clock sans control box would still be pretty cool.
- You could use one of the Adafruit Feathers that is WiFi-enabled, and get the time via request, so you could skip setting up the RTC component.
- If using a WiFi-enabled microcontroller, you could create a webpage-based control panel instead of the physical one, which would also be pretty cool!
